Bundeswehr expands 'Schakal' fleet for NATO's eastern flank
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-29
09:33:23 UTC
18:33:23 KST

The Bundeswehr is pursuing a number of other major procurement programmes for main battle tanks, artillery systems, and air defences.
The Schakal is more than just a new armoured vehicle. It is a key component of the German army's so-called Medium Forces - a new category of troops designed to be rapidly deployable while also offering substantial firepower.
This capability is particularly important in the context of NATO's eastern flank.
Rapid forces for the eastern flank
The current security situation in Europe has fundamentally changed the demands placed on the Bundeswehr.
The central question once again is how German units can be quickly moved to an area of operations in the event of a threat, and how they can then hold their own there against a heavily armed opponent.
For NATO, the eastern flank is of particular importance.
Since Germany plays a key role within the alliance in reinforcing and defending this region, the Bundeswehr needs units that can cover large distances quickly.
This is precisely where the Medium Forces come in. They are intended to fill the gap between light, highly mobile units and heavy armoured troops.
The Schakal is the key combat vehicle for this task, with the Bundeswehr describing it as the "backbone" of the Medium Forces.
Germany had originally ordered 150 Schakal infantry fighting vehicles, but a further 35 are now being delivered. The contract not only covers the vehicles themselves, but also additional services for logistics, training and operations.
The timing is noteable. At the same time, the Bundeswehr is pursuing a number of other major procurement programmes. New main battle tanks, artillery systems, air defence systems and additional protected vehicles are being acquired in an effort to close capability gaps that have developed over the last few decades.
Why the Schakal?
Why is the Bundeswehr not relying solely on heavy tracked vehicles for this mission?
The answer lies in mobility.
The Schakal is based on the GTK Boxer, an eight-wheeled armoured vehicle, and unlike a heavy tracked tank, it can cover long distances on roads relatively quickly. It is precisely this combination of protection, firepower and mobility that is crucial for the Medium Forces.
The basic idea is simple: a unit should be able to move to a different theatre of operations at speed, and without having to depend on extensive transport capacity for every major redeployment.
With the new vehicle, the Bundeswehr is trying to close a gap between different vehicle classes.
On one side are heavily armoured tracked vehicles, such as the Puma infantry fighting vehicle, which offer high levels of protection and combat power but are less suited to rapid redeployment over long distances.
On the other are lighter vehicles, such as the Dingo, which are more mobile but do not have the same firepower as an infantry fighting vehicle.
The Schakal is intended to sit between these two - heavy enough for combat but mobile enough for rapid operations.
The Schakal uses the Boxer chassis and has an unmanned RCT-30 turret derived from the Puma infantry fighting vehicle. Its main weapon is a 30-millimetre automatic cannon.
This enables the vehicle, among other things, to engage lightly and moderately armoured targets. It also has capabilities for countering drones and aircraft, as well as the integrated MELLS guided missile system for engaging heavily armoured targets.
Ordering the vehicles is just the first step. It does not mean the new formations will be operational overnight.
Soldiers have to be trained, spare parts and ammunition provided, logistics structures set up and the new units fully established.
The first Schakals are scheduled to be delivered from the end of 2027, but it will be longer before the entire fleet and the supporting structures are fully in place.
The expansion of the Schakal fleet is therefore a long-term project, but it also highlights the direction in which the German army is heading - towards a force once again capable of deploying larger formations for a potential conventional conflict in Europe.

Forget Belgian roads, we need to talk about Dutch drivers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-29
09:32:01 UTC
18:32:01 KST

Forget Belgian roads, we need to talk about Dutch drivers
Molly Quell
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
Our regular columnist Molly Quell drove through Belgium and France on her holiday and has developed some strong feelings about road design.
I’ve just returned from the most sacred of Dutch annual traditions. No, not early Sinterklaas festivities or a kring party for my mother-in-law’s birthday.
The yearly pilgrimage to France.
Don’t tell the authorities, as they may well take my passport, but this was my first year making the summer trek south to soak up the sun, drink plenty of wine and contribute to the wear and tear on Belgian roads.
In fact, as a childless adult, I don’t often take a proper summer holiday. Who wants to pay three times more to have your vacation infested with irritable parents and their inevitably sticky children?
I usually have my vacation during the school year when the temperatures are better and teenagers are locked up in educational institutions rather than blasting an unending roll of TikToks at full volume at the table next to mine while their parents order more drinks and pretend everyone is enjoying the perfect summer getaway.
But due to a series of unfortunate events, (namely, being at the mercy of the schedules of people who do have children) I took part in the annual ritual of packing up a car and driving many, many hours to spend time complaining about the French in France.
As I rarely have the opportunity to drive around rural Belgium and France, my husband and I decided to make the most of it and tick off a series of “places we’d like to see but aren’t worth planning an entire weekend around.”
Dunkirk. Omaha Beach. Jules Verne’s grave (very cool). Jardins d’Étretat (also cool). Mont-Saint-Michel (less cool and more like the temperature of Satan’s sauna in August).
We saw a lot of things and thus we did a lot of driving. Therefore, I now consider myself an expert on the ins and outs of Western European roadway infrastructure.
It is classist and problematic to mock the Belgians for their accents. It is simply stating objective and true facts when you mock their roads. It isn’t merely the quality of the roads (which can have a sort of deep tissue massage effect) that is bad but how they are designed.
It is as though Belgian road engineers are required to sample every single variety of local Trappist beer before planning an interchange.
Belgian drivers are also unhinged, but in fairness if I had to commute over Mad Max-style infrastructure every day, I would also operate a motor vehicle like I had no regard for human life.
The French are much better drivers. There is plenty to disparage about the French as a nation and a people, but the overall quality of their driving is very good. They do have the tendency to drive a bit close to the bumper, which my Dutch husband suggests they could improve by “having more than six minutes of driving lessons.”
What is confusing about French roads is the liberal use of the term “round about” for any jumble of intersecting roads without a stop light. Roundabouts have a shape. It’s literally in the name. French roundabouts are what happens when the children of drunk Belgian road engineers scribble on the design plans.
At least the French are largely forgiving of cars with foreign plates driving through their convoluted roundabouts Mario Kart style.
Given these experiences, you would think returning back over the border at the end of the journey would be a welcome relief. It was certainly a relief for my jaw, which I no longer had to clench to keep my molars from bashing together, but the Dutch are not without their own problems.
South of the border, there was a general regard for the speed limit. The occasional outlier (nearly always in a BMW) would fly past you in Belgium or France, but mostly people minded the rules.
The second we crossed the border, yellow plates began zooming past us as though everyone had been informed there was only one plate of bitterballen for the party and it would be distributed on a first-come, first-serve basis.
Maybe it is the smoothness of the roads, but Dutch drivers react to the border marker like a cow does to seeing grass for the first time in the spring.
It was very obvious that these drivers had insider information about the country’s wealth of speed cameras as you would see a car zip past on the left, only to brake a few kilometers later to avoid racking up fines.
Hell isn’t a place where the chefs are British and the police are German. It’s where the intersections are French and the drivers are Dutch. And the Belgians waste hours lost on poorly marked roads instead of brewing beer.

Education minister: Parental and pedagogical responsibility off-balance in Western society
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-29
09:31:00 UTC
18:31:00 KST

Education minister: Parental and pedagogical responsibility off-balance in Western society
Education and Research Minister Kristina Kallas believes schools and teachers today are being saddled with an unrealistically heavy burden, while parents should take greater responsibility.
Speaking on Raadio 2's morning show, Kallas said all adults have a responsibility to support children and young people throughout their education. She said responsibility for raising a child is shared by parents, teachers and specialists from local governments, the Ministry of Education and Research and support services.
"There really is an imbalance, not only in Estonia but more broadly in Western society, between parental responsibility and teachers' responsibility," the minister said.
Kallas acknowledged that the responsibilities involved in supporting children currently fall primarily on teachers.
"Teachers today are expected to make sure children get enough sleep to be able to concentrate on their schoolwork, that they eat properly and have healthy habits. They also have to make sure children get enough exercise, are not addicted to social media and do not play too many computer games. Teachers have to check whether they have brought their notebooks and have their clothes for physical education," Kallas explained.
Kallas compared the current situation with her own school days when parents would be called to the school over such problems and expected to take responsibility.
"Today, all of this is the responsibility of the school and the teacher. Teachers are effectively expected to be both parents and teachers at the same time. In my view, that boundary is out of balance as well and parents' expectations of teachers are unrealistic," she said.
Kallas said that boundary needs to be shifted.
"A teacher's job is to teach children their subject and certain skills and competencies, but it is not their job to be responsible for raising a child 24/7," Kallas said.
There are currently around 1,600 students in Estonia who still do not know which school they will attend this fall. Kallas said around half of them have a school place but have not yet been entered into the system.
"Let's imagine that 800 of those children across Estonia are children whom no adult has ever taken an interest in. No one has wanted to deal with them — neither their parents nor the other adults around them," Kallas said.
"Today, they are in a situation where we are all tossing them around like a hot potato and looking for someone to blame: whether it is the City of Tallinn, the Ministry of Education and Research or the education minister personally," she added.
Kallas said looking for someone to blame would not resolve the situation.
"As a society, we have to acknowledge that we have been failing these children for quite some time. Now, they have finally come onto our radar, we are talking about them and trying to address their situation," she added.
Minister: Some children do not even know they have to attend school in the fall
Kallas stressed that it is the responsibility of local governments to identify and locate children who do not know where they will be studying this fall.
"Out of curiosity, I personally called 10 local governments yesterday and asked whether they had been looking for these children. Most of them had. They have called them and know where these children are," she said.
Kallas highlighted several issues affecting efforts to provide school places.
"For example, there are Ukrainian children whose names are on the list, but when they answer the phone, they say they are in Ukraine and are not sure whether they will return," she said.
At the same time, Kallas said there are children whom officials have been unable to reach at all, as well as those who answer the phone but are unaware that they are supposed to attend school this fall.
"For example, in one smaller town, the city government has said, 'Come and see us tomorrow and we'll discuss together what the child wants to do, what their grades are and how they can continue their education,'" Kallas said.
She said officials have encountered a wide range of circumstances involving these children and this is the first time their situations are actually being addressed.
"Perhaps the lesson for next year is that before we hand children their basic school graduation certificates and send them on their way, we should check whether they have actually applied anywhere to continue their education," Kallas said.
Kallas stressed that adults should pay closer attention to children's plans for the future, as many may be uncertain about what to do next. She said there are also children who have never even been asked what they want to do next.
"We should be providing career counseling and discussing children's futures with them while they are still in basic school, rather than waiting until they have walked out the school doors and then starting to look for them in the fall after summer vacation," Kallas said.
--
Editor: Marcus Turovski, Anna Gerda Nurmetalo
Source: "R2 Hommik!"

Rescuers push deeper into mudslide-hit areas at Xizang border port: emergency management official
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-29
17:26:31 CST
18:26:31 KST

GYIRONG, Xizang, Aug. 29 (Xinhua) -- Drones are flying ahead to scout conditions as rescue teams advance on foot toward key disaster-hit areas of Gyirong Port in southwest China's Xizang Autonomous Region, where blocked roads and the risk of secondary disasters are complicating the search for hundreds of people still missing.
As of 1 a.m. Saturday, seven people had been confirmed dead and 554 others remained missing at the port on the China-Nepal border, according to Xizang's emergency management department.
"We will race against time to search for every missing person and will not give up any hope," an official with a frontline working group of the Ministry of Emergency Management told Xinhua on Saturday.
The official said rescuers are pushing deeper into the disaster zone while authorities step up monitoring of secondary-disaster risks and work to keep emergency communications running.
To ensure efficient operations, the frontline working group has set up a temporary Party organization, while Party-member vanguard teams from fire and rescue forces have been deployed to key disaster-hit areas to carry out continuous search and rescue.
With road access cut off, fire and rescue teams are using drones to survey conditions deep inside the affected area. Two teams comprising 17 personnel have also been deployed to help set up monitoring posts.
Drones are sent ahead for reconnaissance before rescuers follow on foot into key affected areas, an approach aimed at ensuring rescue operations are precise, professional and safe, the official said.
The National Fire and Rescue Administration has dispatched 681 personnel from the national comprehensive fire and rescue force, along with 13 rescue dogs, 113 vehicles and 47 drones, as well as specialized rescue equipment.
Advance teams are pushing toward the core affected area via land and water routes and heavy-lift drone transport. Twenty-one rescuers have so far reached the border gate at Gyirong Port, according to the official.
The Ministry of Emergency Management (MEM) has also dispatched 60 personnel and 28 pieces of equipment from a natural disaster rescue center operated by China Anneng Group.
Road access is only one of the challenges facing rescuers. Experts said the mudslide was triggered by a high-altitude glacier collapse on the Nepalese side. Roads and communications were cut off in the aftermath, further complicating rescue operations.
Preventing secondary disasters and maintaining communications are therefore key parts of the emergency response, the official said.
The office of the National Commission for Disaster Prevention, Reduction and Relief and the MEM have organized rolling consultations with relevant departments to continuously monitor and assess secondary-disaster risks and guide rescue operations.
Two Wing Loong unmanned aerial vehicles have been deployed to provide uninterrupted emergency communications support. The working group has also coordinated with the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology on inspections of communications lines, emergency repairs and network optimization, with one base station restored to service and three new ones added.
Military, civilian and commercial satellite resources have also been mobilized for remote-sensing monitoring of the disaster site and surrounding areas, both upstream and downstream.
Meanwhile, the Ministry of Natural Resources, the Ministry of Water Resources, the China Earthquake Administration and relevant research institutions continue to monitor and issue early warnings for risks that include ice-rock avalanches, secondary mudslides and landslides.
China and Nepal are "having close communication and coordinating efforts for the search and rescue," according to China's foreign ministry, which has said that, for Chinese rescuers, "all lives are precious, regardless of their nationalities."
Looking ahead, the emergency management official said the frontline working group will focus on three priorities.
The first is to organize search and rescue operations in a scientific manner, making every minute count in the search for every missing person. Additional specialized rescue teams and equipment will be deployed as needed.
The second is to strengthen monitoring and prevention of secondary disasters. Slope-monitoring radar and other equipment are being deployed at search sites, while satellite remote sensing, drones and on-site monitoring will be used together to track secondary-disaster risks in real time and strengthen early warning and safety controls.
The third is to provide guidance on disaster relief and assistance for affected residents.
The working group, together with the National Food and Strategic Reserves Administration, has allocated 30,000 items of central government disaster-relief supplies, including tents, heating stoves, clothing, quilts, folding beds and moisture-proof mats.
It has also coordinated donations of more than 50,000 items of emergency supplies, including food and drinking water, and coordinated with the Red Cross Society of China to allocate another 2,500 items, including tents and quilts.
The working group will continue making every effort to ensure the basic living needs of people affected by the disaster are met, the official said. ■

China Focus: Rescuers conduct sweeping search at mudslide-stricken Gyirong Port
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-29
17:26:00 CST
18:26:00 KST

GYIRONG, Xizang, Aug. 29 (Xinhua) -- "Is anyone there?" Rescuers crouched down together and called out in unison every few meters, as they picked their way through mud, boulders and chunks of rock.
Since Saturday morning, the members of the Sichuan provincial fire and rescue corps of the China Search and Rescue team have been carrying out a sweeping search in key areas at the mudslide-stricken border port of Gyirong in southwest China's Xizang Autonomous Region.
The team has been searching the heart of the disaster zone, with torrents of muddy water still surging in the nearby waterway. They sifted through piles of rocks and picked through what appeared to be the wreckage of a vehicle, as seen in Xinhua video footage.
A fast-moving chain mudslide, triggered by a high-altitude glacier collapse on the Nepalese side, had left seven people dead and 554 others missing at Gyirong Port in Xizang on the China-Nepal border, as of 1 a.m. on Saturday.
China immediately sent professional rescuers, firefighters and military forces to search for those missing. A total of 2,141 rescue workers and 86 specialists have arrived at the disaster-hit area, according to the latest update by the region's emergency management department.
Rescuers at the site are also guarding against falling rocks and potential breaches of a barrier lake formed by the mudslide. Excavators were busy repairing a key road to facilitate entry into the port.
Earlier on Saturday, drones were seen delivering supplies to rescuers already stationed in the core disaster area, launched from a supply zone three kilometers away from the mudslide-hit port.
Huo Jianxin, a member of the advance group from the China Search and Rescue team, told Xinhua on Friday night that the team would deploy drones, search dogs and life-sign detectors in search operations. The team reached the core disaster zone on Friday afternoon.
"After we saw the situation here upon arrival, my team and I had just one hope: as long as there is even the slightest chance of finding survivors, we will never give up," Huo said.
Rescuers say operations remain challenging due to the harsh terrain, the risk of secondary disasters, damaged roads and disrupted communications.
The meteorological department is forecasting light to moderate rain or thunderstorms across most of Gyirong County until Sunday. The downpours could trigger flash floods, mudslides and landslides in vulnerable areas, potentially disrupting rescue work.
Local authorities have warned that a barrier lake, formed upstream of the port by the glacier collapse, sits in an unstable geological setting and could breach, endangering rescue operations downstream.
The mudslide has destroyed a section of the G216, a national highway leading to the port, seriously hampering emergency response and rescue efforts.
China Anneng, a state-owned engineering and rescue enterprise, deployed 60 technical and skilled personnel and mobilized 14 pieces of engineering rescue equipment, including excavators and loaders, to try to reopen the damaged section of G216.
Fire and rescue personnel have formed three specialized teams for search and rescue operations: one entering by rubber boats on waterways, another traveling on foot through mountainous terrain, and the third conducting aerial reconnaissance and supply drops via drones. ■

Temasek backs Singapore Airlines’ Air India investment amid growing scrutiny
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-29
09:20:52 UTC
18:20:52 KST

Temasek backs Singapore Airlines’ Air India investment amid growing scrutiny
News of the funding request prompted a lawmaker from Singapore’s opposition to urge that Temasek’s funds not be used
Air India’s request for about US$1.5 billion in fresh equity from owners Tata Sons and Singapore Airlines was first reported by Reuters this week. Singapore Airlines owns 25.1 per cent of India’s second-largest airline, with the rest owned by Tata.
News of the funding request prompted Kenneth Tiong, a lawmaker from Singapore’s opposition Workers’ Party, to urge that Temasek’s funds not be used to shore up the Indian carrier.
Singapore’s Business Times also ran a commentary arguing that Singapore Airlines could not realistically exit its Air India stake, with Tata the only plausible buyer. It questioned what its 25.1 per cent holding offered beyond a board seat and a share of the losses, while saying the strategic logic of the investment still held.
In a letter to the newspaper responding to that commentary, Juliet Teo, joint head of portfolio development at Temasek Singapore, said Temasek viewed Singapore Airlines’ decision to invest in Air India from a long-term perspective and was supportive of it.
The letter said the transformation of Air India involved complex, multi-year operational and integration challenges, with outcomes shaped by industry developments and external factors such as airspace disruptions, geopolitical developments and fuel price volatility.

Israeli attacks kill Palestinian farmer in Gaza, wound others in occupied West Bank
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-29
09:18:57 UTC
18:18:57 KST

Israeli forces have killed a Palestinian farmer in central Gaza and wounded another Palestinian in the south, while two others, including a child, were injured by Israeli fire in the occupied West Bank.
A medical source at Al-Aqsa Martyrs Hospital said on Saturday that the body of Mohammed Fayeq al-Attar was brought to the hospital after he was shot by Israeli forces east of Deir al-Balah in central Gaza.
Witnesses said an Israeli quadcopter drone opened fire on al-Attar while he was working on his farmland, killing him.
The attack came as Israeli military vehicles advanced beyond areas under Israeli control east of Al-Masdar village, as well as in Deir al-Balah and the Maghazi refugee camp, local sources said.
The incursions were accompanied by heavy Israeli gunfire towards Palestinian homes in the areas.
Targeting a displacement camp
In southern Gaza, a Palestinian was also wounded in an Israeli drone strike targeting a person inside a displacement camp in the Al-Mawasi area of Khan Younis, according to a medical source.
The attacks come amid continued Israeli violations of the ceasefire agreement in Gaza, which has been in effect since October 10, 2025.
Since the ceasefire took effect, Israeli attacks have killed 1,303 Palestinians and wounded 4,336 others, while rescue teams have recovered hundreds of bodies from beneath the rubble, according to Palestinian figures.
Live ammunition at civilians
Meanwhile, two Palestinians, including a 15-year-old child, were wounded by Israeli army fire in Al-Bireh in the central occupied West Bank, according to the Palestinian Red Crescent Society.
The group said its crews treated two people wounded by live ammunition in the Al-Amari refugee camp.
The child was among those injured, while a young Palestinian man was shot in the foot. Both were taken to hospital for treatment.
Israeli forces carry out near-daily raids across the occupied West Bank, frequently involving gunfire, home raids and arrests.
Israeli military operations and attacks by illegal settlers have intensified across the occupied territory since the start of Israel’s war on Gaza in October 2023, alongside the expansion of illegal settlements and increased restrictions on Palestinian movement.

U.S. Army officers defend armor’s role on modern battlefield
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-29
09:15:01 UTC
18:15:01 KST

- Army officers argue in a Modern War Institute essay that armored formations remain viable despite drone and precision-strike threats reshaping the battlefield.
- The Army's armor branch is testing new formation designs at units including the 1st Cavalry Division and 3rd Infantry Division under its transformation-in-contact initiative.
U.S. Army armor officers argue that armored formations remain viable on the modern battlefield despite the spread of drones and precision-guided weapons, according to an essay published by the Modern War Institute at West Point.
The piece, written by Lt. Col. Alan Hastings, Maj. James Casey and Capt. Elijah Leroux, responds to years of debate over whether tanks and mechanized formations still have a role given recent conflicts including the 2023 Ukrainian counteroffensive against Russia’s Surovikin Line and the 2020 Nagorno-Karabakh war, both cited as evidence that traditional maneuver warfare has grown harder to execute.
The authors identify two challenges limiting offensive maneuver today. The first is longstanding: peer adversaries can field armies large enough to man continuous, deep defensive lines, making penetration costly and raising the risk that an attacking force culminates before it can exploit a breakthrough. The second is newer, what the authors call a “reconnaissance-strike complex,” the fusion of pervasive sensors, drones and long-range precision fires that lets adversaries contest what the authors term the “air-ground littoral” even without traditional air power.
“There is no formation better suited to these tasks than US Army armored formations,” the authors write, arguing that armor operating within a combined arms team can survive dense reconnaissance-strike networks, break through prepared defenses and push into an enemy’s vulnerable rear.
The authors point to Ukraine’s counteroffensives in Kharkiv in 2022 and Kursk in 2024 as evidence that gaps in enemy sensor and strike coverage still create openings for offensive maneuver, arguing that modern battlefield conditions “encourage positional warfare, but do not dictate it.”
The essay outlines four conditions the authors say are necessary for successful maneuver: reconnaissance, masking, suppression and isolation. They describe an approach in which sensing drones and electronic warfare identify gaps in enemy defenses, loitering munitions and artillery blind enemy sensors to mask friendly movement, and layered fires suppress and isolate enemy formations before an armored breakthrough.
The authors cite ongoing experimentation within the Army’s armor branch under its “transformation in contact” initiative. In October 2025, 2nd Brigade, 1st Cavalry Division tested organizational changes that added a multifunctional reconnaissance-strike troop along with heavy cavalry and armored strike troops equipped with drones, loitering munitions and counterdrone and electronic warfare systems. In May 2026, 2nd Brigade, 3rd Infantry Division tested a different design intended to sense and strike targets out to 40 kilometers (25 miles).
Other units have been assigned specific roles in the broader effort. The 4th Infantry Division is leading work on formation survivability standards. The 1st Infantry Division is developing training standards for small unmanned aircraft systems. The 1st Armored Division is setting counterdrone training standards, and the 1st Cavalry Division is writing the armor strike platoon manual. The U.S. Army Armor School and III Corps have partnered on what the authors call the Armored Transformation and Standardization Initiative to coordinate the effort across the force.
The Armor School has also introduced new training programs, including a Robotics Master Trainer Course and a Robotics and Autonomous Systems Tactics Leader Course, intended to train soldiers and leaders in the Army’s 19-series armor specialties.
The authors acknowledge the transformation remains incomplete. They write that Army experimentation with unmanned aircraft has not yet reached the scale seen in recent conflicts, and that armored formations remain vulnerable to drones and loitering munitions until investments in short-range air defense and counterdrone units mature.
Hastings serves as squadron commander for 3rd Squadron, 16th Cavalry Regiment at Fort Benning, Georgia. Casey serves as executive officer for 1st Battalion, 635th Armored Regiment of the Kansas National Guard. Leroux is currently attending the Harding Fellowship Program at the University of Kansas. The authors note that the views expressed are their own and do not reflect the official position of the United States Military Academy, the Department of the Army or the Department of War.

Before Rosh Hashanah, Elul asks us to practice, persevere, and rise a little each day
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-29
09:13:28 UTC
18:13:28 KST

Elul is the Jew’s testing device ahead of the new year. For me, the lesson of Elul is made clear when I listen in our neighborhood to young and old practicing the sounding of the shofar.
Each day the notes get stronger. Then, on Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur, each ba’al tekiah (the congregation member who blows the shofar) climbs the peak before all assembled.
Hearing the actual sounding of the shofar makes me especially appreciative because a half-century ago there was another Elul when I could not even get a meager sound from my shofar. This is a tale that provided me with a lesson I will not forget.
Before making aliyah in 1977, I was a Conservative rabbi at the Beth Shalom congregation in Wilmington, Delaware. Our synagogue was most fortunate because our cantor was Andrew Salzer, a Holocaust survivor from Hungary.
When World War II ended, he and his wife and children could not obtain a visa to the United States. They had no one to sponsor them. Instead, they were permitted to enter Brazil. To earn a living, the family was given a house and a little store deep in an Amazon forest.
Salzers allowed into US
After a few years, the Salzers were finally allowed into the US. A relative heard about them and brought them to Wilmington, Delaware. They were given a delicatessen by the local federation, which was well located, and succeeded.
However, one day in Elul in the 1950s, Salzer went to the Beth Shalom synagogue to say kaddish. He was asked whether he could daven (pray), and gladly, he did. The congregation’s rabbi, Jacob Kraft, heard Salzer that morning and spoke with him. The rabbi urged the synagogue board to hire him, which they did.
His training in a synagogue choir in Budapest had poignantly brought Salzer’s beautiful voice to the synagogue.
A few years later, in 1970, Rabbi Kraft retired, and I became the rabbi of the synagogue. On a list in the United States for church and synagogue architecture, Beth Shalom is found there, noted for the bronze doors by Louise Kaisch enclosing the ark of the Torah scrolls. In Beth Shalom, we had daily minyanim (a minimum of 10 men needed to conduct prayers), which I know is still the case.
As I worked with the cantor, I learned that he had taught himself to sound the shofar. A friend had taught me, so during the month of Elul, Salzer and I alternated blowing the shofar.
One morning during Elul in 1973, when the synagogue was opened for the minyan, we discovered that it had been broken into – money collected for tzedakah (charity) had been stolen, and an attempt to take the air conditioner had failed because it was too heavy.
When we climbed the stairs to the second floor where my office was located, my door was ajar and the office – a mess. I had nothing there besides books, a portable typewriter, a few dollars, and my shofar. The typewriter was gone, and I realized the shofar had been moved from the shelf where I had left it.
Since it was my turn to blow the shofar, I took it down to the minyan chapel with me. Then the unexpected occurred. I tried to blow the shofar several times – no sound whatsoever. The minyan men and the cantor said, “Wait a few minutes, then try.” I put the shofar to my lips – nothing. I said aloud for all to hear: the thieves took the money, my typewriter, and stole the shofar notes.
This Elul, while we prepare for elections, we also pray for peace. Since October 7, we have been at war constantly. Can the powerful American President Donald Trump bring the war to an end?
As I think about my shofar, which would not sound but ultimately did, I recall one of Israel’s great athletes, tennis champion Shahar Pe’er.
Why remember her this Elul – you may ask?
At one point in her career, Pe’er, with a victory after a long drought, gave many people a boost. After being in the top 10 players in the world, slipping to somewhere down in the lower 100s must have been crushing for Pe’er.
However, she did not give up. “After the recent finals in Baku, where I lost,” she noted in the press, “I thought: ‘I’m not there, I cannot handle tennis anymore, I’m not strong enough for this.’”
This wasn’t the first time such doubts got the better of her, she said, adding that “in the past six months there were at least five or six times when I said: ‘All right, I’m done with tennis. I had a great career and reached amazing places, but enough is enough. There are more important things in life.’”
But Pe’er focused on what tennis meant to her, which is why she won that Suzhou tournament in China after losing in Baku. “All in all, I have something which I really love. I love being on the court,” Pe’er determined.
Then she informed her listeners why she had succeeded in the past and hopefully in the future. Her coach had told her: “If you have lost your love for tennis, quit, but not because of what your ranking is.”
So Pe’er, back then, made the court her personal crucible, in which she would remake herself, calling on inner strength. None of us can know how much she practiced, but the results were evident.
We all have our chance on the court of life. Maybe our serves have been ineffective, maybe our backhand has failed us, maybe a few lobs go over our head.
But we know down deep that we, too, can draw upon our inner strength. We can make that major pitch; we can help our children when it is not so easy; we can finally see our experiment work; we can tread forward in our lives.
I can even blow the shofar again.
Clearly, innovative steps we have feared to take need to be taken. We must all commit and move forward. Elul is the Jew’s testing ground before the new year. Though we intone them regularly, prayers can take on new meaning if we focus on what the words really mean and what the shofar sounds tell us.
My suggestion is to take Elul one day at a time; try to raise yourself just a little every day. When all the small elevations are stitched together, you are ready for the challenges of the High Holy Days, and then, of course, for the new year 5787. 
In memory of my beloved wife, Rita z’l, on her sixth yahrzeit.

Elul teaches us a Jewish lesson: The last siren has not sounded - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-29
09:12:38 UTC
18:12:38 KST

Last Sunday evening, I went with my son and grandsons to my first Australian Rules football match – the West Coast Eagles, the local side, against Hawthorn, the visitors from Melbourne. It rained most of the night, and 43,000 people appeared not to notice it.
I will not pretend to have understood it completely: 18 men a side on a field the size of a small village, no offside, and an oval ball that bounces as it wishes, with no attempt at consistency.
What I did understand immediately was the physicality. These men wear no helmets and no padding. They run at full pace into one another, are lifted and dropped onto wet turf, and get up.
Over the years, I have seen what trauma to a shoulder can look like. For 20 minutes I watched with a clinician’s flinch, quietly triaging the injuries in my mind. Then I stopped: the flinching was mine, and nobody out there had the slightest interest in it.
In the second quarter, my grandson mentioned that this was the final match of the season. At the final siren, the table freezes: the clubs above the line go through to the grand finals, everybody else goes home for six months.
I watched the field differently after that. It was late in the season, but not too late for one last push.
During the break, I checked my phone and saw the date. The 11th of Elul.
The last round
We are, right now, in the last round.
Rosh Hashanah begins on the evening of Friday, September 11. Between now and then sits Elul, and I think we misunderstand it almost entirely. We treat it as a corridor to a courtroom. The ledger is open, the pen already moving, only the sentencing is left. Dread, with a calendar attached.
That is not what Elul is meant to feel like. Elul is the last round of the season, and the entire point of a last round is that “it’s not over till it’s over.”
Everything about the month says so. The shofar sounds every weekday morning, not to frighten us, but to wake us while there is still time on the clock. The name of the month is read as an acronym for ani l’dodi v’dodi li – I am my beloved’s and my beloved is mine. This is not the language of a tribunal.
Rabbi Shneur Zalman of Liadi gave us the image I keep returning to: in Elul the King leaves the palace and walks out into the field, where any farmer, still dressed for work, may go up and speak with Him. No appointment, and no queue.
In a lifetime of working with people, those who worried me most were never those who had done the most damage. They were the ones who had privately decided the final siren had already gone. The brother not spoken to in 11 years, by a man who had stopped imagining he ever would, over something he can’t even remember any more.
The man in his late seventies who told me, with total conviction, that he was too old to become a different sort of husband. The woman who blamed nobody but herself for the harm she had done her family, and was certain that she was beyond forgiveness.
Not one of them was out of time. They believed they were, which is a different thing and far more dangerous, because a player who believes the season is over stops playing. A person who thinks he has nothing to live for, stops living.
The Jewish answer, in this month above all others, is that yes, it is late. But late is not all over.
Play the ball, not the man
Now the thing I had not expected.
Australian rules football is brutal. It was also, as far as I could see, entirely without malice.
The game’s most repeated instruction is play the ball, not the man. You may hit him, even hard, legally, repeatedly while contesting the ball. You may not hit him when he does not have the ball, just because he is him. In two and a half hours, I did not see a punch thrown, or a man standing over an opponent whom he had just flattened. They hit each other with everything they had, and when the ball moved on, they left it on the grass.
I have watched Jewish public life for a long time, and I am no longer confident we are playing the ball and not the man.
Contact was never our problem. Argument is our inheritance; the Talmud is a record of men going at one another for centuries, and the tradition calls it beautiful: machloket l’shem shamayim, dispute for the sake of Heaven.
Our problem is that we have stopped playing the ball.
Haredi and secular. Government and hostage families. Israel and the Diaspora. Right and Left, in Jerusalem, Melbourne and Manchester. Listen to almost any of it, and you will hear people not contesting the ball at all. They have gone for the man, and gone high.
The Talmud tells us that the Second Temple fell to baseless hatred; we sat on the floor last month on Tisha B’Av and said so out loud… and then went back to it before the fast was even out.
Elul does not ask us to stop arguing. It asks us to go back to the ball. Argue and disagree by all means but keep it focused on the topic, not the person.
As it happens, the local team was well beaten on the night, and the scoreboard made for uncomfortable viewing.
We spend Elul auditing the scoreboard: the tally, the year weighed and found wanting. Nobody in that stadium was applauding the scoreboard. They were applauding the effort made by every one of those 36 players – win or lose.
I suspect that is nearer to what is actually being asked of us.
There is work that can still change the outcome, even this late in the season: a phone call not yet made, a rival not yet forgiven, an apology 11 years overdue and still, today, entirely possible. All of this can change what sort of person walks out at the beginning of next season on Rosh Hashanah.
Last Sunday night, the rain kept falling. But the lights stayed on. The final siren sounded, and 43,000 people filed out into the night.
For us, though, the final siren is not until the shofar is blown on Yom Kippur. We still have time to score more points.
The writer is a rabbi and physician. He writes and teaches on Jewish ethics, leadership, and resilience. His work appears on rabbidrjonathanlieberman.substack.com and youtube.com. @rabbidrjonathanlieberman

How Trump’s illusion of short war against Iran collapsed
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-29
09:06:58 UTC
18:06:58 KST

A new Telegraph report shows that the gap between Washington’s initial calculations regarding the aggression against Iran and the reality on the ground has grown wider by the day. The Telegraph has reported that Donald Trump’s war with Iran, which according to the U.S. president was supposed to last only three weeks, has after six months turned into a war of attrition that is costly and drawn-out. According to the newspaper, Washington has not only failed to achieve its initial objectives, but the war has also created wide-ranging consequences for the region and the global economy. The Telegraph further emphasizes that Trump underestimated Iran’s ability to resist the world’s most powerful military force; to the extent that a war intended to bolster Trump’s political legacy could now become a lasting negative mark on his record.
The starting point of this war was a clear calculation in Washington: inflicting heavy military strikes on Iran would, within a short period, force Tehran to back down. This calculation rested on a fundamental assumption, that the enormous gap between U.S. and Iranian military capabilities would quickly translate into a political gap, and Tehran would be compelled to accept the cost of continued resistance.
But what unfolded on the ground diverged from this scenario. Iran was able, by drawing on its military and strategic capacities, to transform the war from a short, one-sided operation into a costly conflict. This does not mean that Iran is equal to the United States in terms of military power; rather, it means that Tehran succeeded in raising the costs of continuing the war for the United States and its allies.
In asymmetric wars, this very issue is of decisive importance. The weaker side does not necessarily seek to directly defeat the greater power; instead, it tries to raise the cost of victory so high that achieving political objectives becomes difficult. If Washington’s goal was to end the war quickly and impose its demands, the prolongation of the conflict for six months demonstrates that this initial calculation was not consistent with the reality on the ground.
The United States remains in a superior position in terms of air power, technology, intelligence, logistics, and strike capability. But war is not a purely military equation. The ultimate question is when military power can be converted into a political outcome.
Washington may be able to destroy targets and inflict heavy blows, but if it cannot—despite this superiority—end the war within its desired timeframe and compel the other side to accept its demands, it faces a strategic problem.
Indeed, six months of continued war is a significant indicator. A war that was supposed to end in three weeks has now become a prolonged crisis, which means the United States has been unable to manage the war within its expected political and temporal framework.
From this perspective, the main issue is not merely the damage inflicted on Iran; it is also the cost that the continuation of the war imposes on the United States itself. Military expenditures, force deployment, maintaining operational readiness, economic pressure, and political repercussions all increase over time. The longer the war drags on, the wider the gap between the cost paid and the expected political gain can become.
The most significant development of this war must be sought in the transformation of the “cost equation.” The United States entered the field assuming it could impose the costs of war on Iran, but Iran sought to demonstrate that continuing the war is not without cost for the United States either.
This is perhaps the most important aspect of the matter. Iran did not enter the war to alter the military balance with the United States; such a claim is fundamentally incompatible with the reality of the two sides’ power. The more effective objective is to prevent U.S. military superiority from being converted into a cheap political victory.
By resisting military pressure and maintaining its response capability, Iran has succeeded in raising the cost of Washington’s miscalculations. This same issue can also affect America’s future calculations. For if a great power knows that entering a war with Iran will not necessarily lead to a quick victory and may result in a prolonged and costly conflict, the decision to use military force again will become more difficult.
This matter is not limited to the United States. Other powers and Washington’s allies are also watching this war closely and drawing an important lesson from it: possessing military superiority does not necessarily mean having the ability to determine the political outcome of a war.
The most important issue in the six-month war between Iran and the United States is not merely the prolongation of the conflict; it is the collapse of a strategic calculation. Washington assumed it could use its military superiority to turn a short, controlled war into a political victory; but Iran managed to change this equation and raise the cost of continuing the war for the United States.
Therefore, America’s failure should not be sought solely in the sense of a military defeat. The more significant issue is the failure to rapidly achieve political objectives despite possessing overwhelming military superiority. A war that was supposed to last three weeks continues after six months. This fact alone shows that part of Washington’s initial calculations did not materialize.
Ultimately, perhaps the most important message of this war for the United States is that it cannot compel a country like Iran to submit quickly merely by relying on military power. Iran has shown that even against a far superior power, it is possible to constrain the opposing side’s decision-making space by raising the costs of war.
If this trajectory continues, the issue will no longer be confined to the war between Iran and the United States; Washington’s strategic credibility and the image constructed of America’s ability to impose its will in the international system will also enter a new phase.

GDLS delivers first XM30 Wolf vehicle to U.S. Army
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-29
09:03:48 UTC
18:03:48 KST

- General Dynamics Land Systems delivered its XM30 Wolf prototype to the U.S. Army at Aberdeen Proving Ground last Friday.
- Additional prototypes are planned for delivery to Fort Hood, Texas, ahead of testing that could lead to a full-rate production decision.
General Dynamics Land Systems delivered its XM30 Wolf infantry fighting vehicle to the U.S. Army at Aberdeen Proving Ground, Maryland, last Friday, according to a post by Geoffrey Norman, a retired Army brigadier general now working on the GDLS team.
Norman, who spent 30 years in the Army as a tanker and cavalryman, joined the Next Generation Combat Vehicle Cross Functional Team at Detroit Arsenal four years ago, where he worked with operational units and soldiers to help develop the requirements for both the XM30 and the M1E3 Abrams upgrade. He left the Army two years ago to join GDLS.
“This is huge event for me, professionally and personally,” Norman wrote. “I could not be happier to be part of the GDLS team that is delivering this incredible new capability on schedule to the Army, they need it now.”
XM30 is the Army’s program to replace the Bradley Infantry Fighting Vehicle, which has been in service for more than 40 years. General Dynamics Land Systems and American Rheinmetall Vehicles are the two finalists competing to build the vehicle, with both companies developing and testing prototypes in Michigan. The Army is expected to select a winning design in 2027.
“I want to say thank you to the incredible team of professionals at General Dynamics who make the XM30 Wolf program a success,” Norman wrote. “The dedicated program leaders, innovative engineers, resourceful supply chain professionals, and tireless manufacturing experts at Sterling Heights, Lima, Scranton, Tallahassee, Grand Rapids and London are absolutely committed to delivering the very best capability to our Army.”
Norman said the vehicle uses a Modular Open Systems Architecture intended to let GDLS add new software and technology through what he described as a “born-digital design purpose built for upgrades.”
“We will continue to improve the XM30 Wolf every single day, with new software drops, new technologies that easily integrate through our Modular Open Systems Architecture and an innovative born-digital design that is purpose built for upgrades,” Norman wrote.
Norman said the delivered vehicle is the first of several prototypes GDLS plans to complete and deliver to the Army.
“The work continues as this first vehicle gets into the Army’s hands,” Norman wrote. “Every day and night, GDLS is working to complete all our prototypes and deliver on time. That is our commitment and GDLS delivers on its commitments.”
According to Norman, additional XM30 Wolf vehicles will be sent to Fort Hood, Texas, where the Army will evaluate them as part of the process GDLS hopes will lead to a full-rate production decision.
“Soon those XM30 Wolf vehicles will be in a formation at Fort Hood, Texas, ready to get put through the crucible of their evaluation so GDLS can go into full rate production on the XM30 Wolf, the best Mechanized Infantry Combat Vehicle in the world,” Norman wrote.

Trump promised ‘regime change’: the hard-line core that has taken control of Iran
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-29
09:02:58 UTC
18:02:58 KST

U.S. President Donald Trump ordered the war against Iran six months ago, promising it would be short and decisive. But now, with the country under tightening sanctions, the Iranian leadership that was killed has been replaced by a hard-line core of generals and clerics with deep roots in the theocratic system. They repeatedly say they are prepared for a prolonged confrontation with the United States, while also showing they are willing to do whatever it takes to prevent any uprising at home.
All of this is far removed from Trump’s hopes at the outset of the campaign that the Islamic Republic would collapse, and from his later claims that “regime change” had brought more moderate and compromise-minded figures to the forefront.
Iran’s new leaders show little confidence that they can reach any agreement with Trump, after Iran was attacked twice while talks with the United States were underway. They also believe they could be attacked again once the Americans replenish their interceptor missile stocks.
Iranian officials have even threatened to escalate the war, while the continuing U.S. blockade and Trump’s plans to impose new sanctions threaten to choke an Iranian economy that is already deteriorating.
“If Trump wants to take action, we will retaliate in an earthquake-like manner,” Mohsen Rezaei, a former adviser to Iran’s supreme leader, Mojtaba Khamenei, said late last week. Rezaei was appointed earlier this month as secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council.
In a post on X, he wrote that “if the economic war continues, not a single drop of oil will be exported” from the Persian Gulf.
In a statement carried by Iranian state media Friday morning, the government vowed to stand firm against U.S. sanctions and what it called U.S.-Israeli “conspiracies.” It said diplomacy and defense were “complementary, coordinated and inseparable” tools for protecting the country’s national interests, security and territorial integrity.
The government said it would pursue both tracks simultaneously while focusing on curbing inflation, creating jobs, supporting domestic production and gradually reducing dependence on the U.S. dollar.
Determined to suppress domestic opposition
Rezaei’s appointment was part of a series of decrees recently signed by the supreme leader, who has not appeared in public since his father was killed. The decrees formally established Iran’s new senior leadership, including its top military posts, after their predecessors were killed at the start of the war.
Perhaps the most significant appointment was that of the commander of the Basij, the volunteer force affiliated with the Revolutionary Guard that maintains a feared presence in the streets and played a central role in suppressing the wave of protests that swept the country in January, during which tens of thousands were killed.
The post went to Hossein Taeb, a conservative cleric and former head of the Revolutionary Guard’s intelligence organization. Taeb led one of the first major crackdowns on protests in 2009, before being removed in June 2022 after the exposure of an Iranian plot to attack Israeli targets in Turkey.
His appointment is seen as a sign that the leadership is determined to prevent renewed unrest amid growing dissatisfaction over the state of the economy.
Khamenei, 56, has not appeared in public, in video or in audio recordings since his father, who served as Iran’s supreme leader for about 37 years, was killed in Israeli strikes. Mojtaba Khamenei is believed to have been wounded, and his absence from public view may reflect either the intense security surrounding him, given that he is likely an Israeli target, or the severity of his injuries.
In the meantime, he has surrounded himself with hard-line allies. In appointments announced Aug. 11 and 12, Khamenei elevated longtime associates with whom he had worked in the past.
“They are a clique of older senior officers who've served together over the last decades,” Sascha Bruchmann, an analyst at the International Institute for Strategic Studies’ Middle East office in Bahrain, told The Associated Press.
Rezaei, 71, led the Revolutionary Guard through its formative years, throughout the 1980-1988 Iran-Iraq War and until 1997. Since 2009, he has run for president several times as a hard-line candidate.
Ahmad Vahidi, 68, was appointed commander of the Revolutionary Guard after serving as acting commander since his predecessor was killed alongside the elder Khamenei.
In recent months, Gen. Ali Ozmaei was also appointed commander of the Revolutionary Guard navy and Ali Abdollahi was named chief of staff.
Bruchmann, who noted that Rezaei had been Vahidi’s commander for many years, said the appointments appear designed above all to ensure unity. “It looks like internal cohesion, as in hard core people are being pulled into the inner circle,” he said.
Moderates urge restraint
A senior oil analyst at Kpler, a company that provides data to international markets, said the appointments of Vahidi and Rezaei indicate “greater influence for officials associated with a tougher stance.”
Still, the analyst said escalation was not inevitable, and Iran could struggle to “escalate enough to restore deterrence without triggering retaliation that leaves it worse off.”
President Masoud Pezeshkian remains one of the most prominent voices calling for a negotiated solution. His allies argue that Iran risks pushing too far by continuing the war as its economy collapses.
“It is better to end the war today, when we are powerful and respected and the whole world acknowledges our victory,” Pezeshkian said last week.
He also defended a memorandum of understanding signed in June against criticism from hard-liners who argued that Iran had conceded too much.
Unlike ultra-hard-liners who reject any possibility of talks, Rezaei has left the door open to an agreement if the United States changes its position.
On Monday, he told Pakistani army chief Asim Munir, who is serving as a mediator, that the United States must “change its behavior and take practical steps to implement the terms” of a ceasefire agreement.
Ahmad Zeidabadi, a political analyst based in Tehran, wrote in a newspaper aligned with Pezeshkian that there are “serious differences over the future path of the country.” Hard-liners oppose normalization with the United States, he wrote, because “their survival depends on the existence of confrontation and hostility.”
A powerful figure atop the Basij
Despite hopes in the United States and Israel, there have so far been no signs of new protests, even as it becomes increasingly difficult for Iranians to afford basic goods.
Taeb’s appointment as Basij commander is a sign that the leadership wants to head off any possible uprising “before it even manifests,” Bruchmann told the AP. “Putting someone from an intelligence background in charge of the people that would do the crackdown makes sense,” he said.
Taeb, a 63-year-old cleric, headed the Basij when the force played a central role in suppressing the mass protests that erupted over Mahmoud Ahmadinejad’s reelection in 2009, when dozens were killed.
He developed a reputation for ruthlessness and was soon afterward appointed head of the Revolutionary Guard’s intelligence apparatus. He led the organization for nearly 13 years until he was removed in 2022, reportedly as part of an internal shake-up following a series of Israeli intelligence successes.
The Basij operates a nationwide network of volunteers who maintain a presence in streets, government offices and cultural institutions, with the aim of ensuring loyalty and ideological conformity to Iran’s theocratic system.
In the decree appointing Taeb, Khamenei ordered him to deepen the Basij’s presence in Iranian social life, use new technologies and “expand Basij activity worldwide against Zionist-American arrogance,” suggesting the organization could begin forging closer ties with Iranian proxies abroad.
The Basij has increased its presence during the war, while hard-liners have held nightly rallies in Tehran and other cities to mobilize support and deter anyone who might voice opposition.
It is not clear exactly how Taeb intends to strengthen the force, but in a recent speech he hinted that he plans to tighten control over society further. He warned that U.S. economic pressure is intended to create divisions inside Iran. “If the mosque becomes the center of the neighborhood, the nation will protect its unity, which will be a greater deterrent than any missile.”

We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
In recent months, the Kremlin has intensified recruitment for contract soldiers, stepped up data collection on reservists, and expanded the powers of the Russian National Guard.
At the same time, Russia’s Permanent Representative to the UN, Vasily Nebenzya, stated on August 20 that a new mobilization in the country is "not planned and not expected."

A state-run poll conducted by Russian Public Opinion Research Center (VTsIOM) in July 2026 revealed that 66% of Russian citizens believed "difficult times" lay ahead for the country, marking a 16 percentage point increase in public apprehension since the beginning of the year.
Driven by economic deterioration, long-range drone strikes on key infrastructure, and Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, public anxiety reached levels not seen since the collapse of the Soviet Union in 1991 and the hyperinflation crisis of 1992.

A rare Ukrainian Bulat tank turned up in a brigade that never had them
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-29
09:02:12 UTC
18:02:12 KST

- The rare T-64BM Bulat tank is now part of the Ukrainian army's 57th Motorized Brigade
- But the army never had very many T-64BMs, so where did the reassigned tanks come from?
- It's possible the Ukrainians are poaching training units in order to keep combat units in fighting shape
A rare armored vehicle has made a surprise appearance in the Ukrainian order of battle. A recent official photo depicts a three-person, 49-ton T-64BM alongside tankers from the Ukrainian army's 57th Motorized Brigade. The brigade holds the line in northern Ukraine around 30 km northwest of Kharkiv.
What's unusual is that the 57th Motorized Brigade was known to operate the lighter T-64BV tank, the standard tank in Ukrainian service. Moreover, the Ukrainian army doesn't have many T-64BMs. There were around 80 in the Ukrainian inventory on the eve of the wider Russian invasion in February 2022, and at the time all but a handful belonged to the 1st Tank Brigade and the 12th Independent Tank Battalion.
Both units had a single T-64BM battalion with around 31 tanks.
In 54 months of hard fighting, the 12th Independent Tank Battalion and 1st Tank Brigade—the latter now reorganized into the less tank-heavy 1st Heavy Mechanized Brigade—has lost around a quarter of their T-64BMs. Even if the units cannibalized a few T-64BMs from training grounds, today they'd both struggle to field a full battalion of T-64BMs.
Given the thin supply, where did the 57th Motorized Brigade's T-64BMs come from? It's a question that vexes French historian Stevius. And it may point to a growing shortage of the best tanks in the Ukrainian armed forces as losses deepen and years of combat take their toll on vehicles' material condition. "The use of a few specimens from training units to fill the gaps ... would tend to show that the Ukrainians have practically exhausted their stock of tanks that they can bring back to operational condition," Stevius noted.
Overall, the Ukrainians have lost no fewer than 1,400 tanks, according to a tally by the Oryx open-source intelligence collective. That's more tanks the the Ukrainian armed forces had in their inventory in 2022. The Ukrainians have largely made good their losses by restoring old stored T-64s and T-72s while also accepting donations of hundreds of surplus tanks from foreign allies.
But even with the restored and donated tanks, there's still a shortfall. It's fortunate, then, that tanks are growing less important by the day as tiny drones—which are lethal to tanks—fill the sky over the 1,200-km disputed gray zone in Ukraine.
Up-armored T-64
The $2.5-million T-64BM is a better-protected variant of the standard T-64, which the tank factory in Kharkiv produced first for Soviet forces and, later, for Ukrainian forces. To produce a T-64BM, the Kharkiv Tank Plant swapped in the 125-mm main gun from the newer T-80 tank, tweaked the fire controls and added slabs of Nozh modular armor on the front of the hull, the turret face and the roof.
The problem was, and still is, that the add-on armor weighs three tons. "The weight of the Nozh armor modules unbalances the tank toward the front and strains the shock absorbers," Stevius explained. Even replacing the T-64's 700-hp diesel engine with a more powerful 850-hp model didn't fully compensate for the added weight. That "results in the T-64BM Bulat suffering from underpowering, regularly causing engine overheating," Stevius pointed out.
Trending Now
Still, the type fought hard in the initial Russian invasion of eastern Ukraine starting in 2014. And eight years later, T-64BMs with the 1st Tank Brigade successfully defended the city of Chernihiv from invading Russian forces. "The faster autoloader on the T-64 allowed Ukrainian tank crews to achieve significant damage against surprised Russian units," Mykhaylo Zabrodskyi, Jack Watling, Oleksandr Danylyuk and Nick Reynolds wrote in a 2022 report for the Royal United Services Institute in London.
As the war ground on and drones replaced heavy vehicles as the main means of attack and defense for both sides, the T-64BMs lost some relevance. Yes, both sides still deploy tanks—but mostly as mobile artillery firing at targets located by drones many kilometers away.
The lighter usage of tanks belies the shortage of functional tanks owing to combat losses and wear and tear, however, especially on the Ukrainian side. A sweeping reorganization of Ukrainian force structure last year eliminated many tank battalions, but the tank shortage persisted even after the unit reduction.
Stevius is stumped. "The presence of a T-64BM Bulat in the 57th Motorized Brigade, which until now has only used T-64BV, is therefore a surprise because their number is insufficient to equip both two or even one tank battalion of the 1st [Heavy Mechanized Brigade] and the ranks of the 12th Independent Tank Battalion," Stevius mused.
The likeliest explanation is the most worrying. The Ukrainians stripped tanks away from training units while also compelling front-line battalions to go into battle with fewer tanks. All in order to make sure all the tank units have at least a few tanks.

Royal Navy Russian vessel monitoring rises 25%
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-29
10:00:51 BST
18:00:51 KST

Royal Navy activations to monitor Russian vessels around the UK increased by 25% during the first eight months of 2026 compared with the same period last year, with ships dispatched on four operations involving Russian vessels during August alone, the UK Defence Journal understands.
The increase has coincided with repeated movements of Russian warships, auxiliary vessels and sanctioned commercial ships through the North Sea and English Channel.
The latest activity saw HMS Duncan, HMS St Albans and HMS Severn conduct a concentrated 72-hour operation tracking Russian destroyer Admiral Levchenko and sanctioned cargo vessels General Skobelev and Sparta.
A Merlin helicopter from HMS St Albans also joined the surveillance operation, while HMS Mersey separately monitored the Russian replenishment vessel Akademik Pashin.
The Ministry of Defence said Royal Navy ships had been activated on four operations to intercept or monitor Russian vessels during August. HMS Severn alone was dispatched three times during the month.
Its earlier missions included tracking the Russian frigate Neustrashimy through the Channel and subsequently working with HMS Tyne to monitor frigate Admiral Gorshkov, hydrographic vessel Romuald Muklevich and Akademik Pashin.
The rise in monitoring activity follows the UK’s interdiction of sanctioned tanker Smyrtos in the English Channel in June.
First Sea Lord General Sir Gwyn Jenkins said: “The interception of the Smyrtos was a clear demonstration that the UK and Royal Navy will act against those who seek to evade sanctions to fund Russia’s egregious war on Ukraine.”
According to Jenkins, Russian-linked vessels have subsequently altered some of their routes, while Moscow has also used naval vessels to accompany sanctioned shipping.
He said: “Since that successful operation, we have seen Russian shadow fleet vessels increasingly forced to change their routes, imposing significant cost and delays to their journeys.”
Jenkins added: “Alongside our allies, this approach is forcing Moscow to divert Russian warships away from their core purpose. That is because Russia knows we stand ready to act again, should it be required.”
The UK has sanctioned more than 500 vessels associated with Russia’s so-called shadow fleet, a term commonly used for ships involved in transporting Russian oil and other cargoes while attempting to reduce their exposure to Western sanctions and regulatory controls. British authorities have increasingly linked maritime surveillance around the UK with enforcement of sanctions imposed following Russia’s invasion of Ukraine.
Jenkins said the Royal Navy would continue monitoring the activity. He said: “While this is a welcome development, we know there is no room for complacency. Shadow fleet vessels continue to pose an unacceptable risk to maritime security and the environment, wherever they sail.”
He added: “That is why we remain vigilant and will continue to work alongside allies to uphold and enforce international law.”
The most recent 72-hour operation involved a Type 45 destroyer, Type 23 frigate and River-class patrol vessel, with the Russian group tracked south through the North Sea and English Channel before responsibility was handed to a NATO ally near Ushant.
Commander Oli Ayers, Commanding Officer of HMS St Albans, said the frigate was operating as part of a wider NATO effort to monitor Russian naval and merchant movements.
He said: “As part of the UK’s response to increased Russian activity within UK waters, St Albans was part of a group of NATO warships and aircraft escorting Russian warships and merchant vessels through the North Sea and English Channel, monitoring their activity.”
The Ministry of Defence said the Royal Navy expects similar operations to continue over the coming months as Russian military and commercial vessels transit waters around the UK.

Tax promises, defence targets and Iran: Andy Burnham’s budget headaches
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-29
09:00:23 UTC
18:00:23 KST

1. Fiscal rulesThe biggest risk of Burnham as prime minister was always whether he would spook the bond markets and set in train a Liz Truss-style meltdown. Starmer’s allies often played up this fear but there is no doubt that Burnham had to ensure that markets knew he was a serious operator. Gilt yields rose after an interview last year in which he said the government was “in hock to the bond markets”. So, Burnham has committed to Rachel Reeves’s fiscal rules on debt and borrowing, though he has indicated he will “use, obviously, any flexibility within them” where he can borrow to fund further investment.
 2. Tax promisesBurnham has said he will “stick to the manifesto”, which promises no increases in income tax, national insurance or VAT, though he cautioned in an interview earlier this week that the public needed to be “realistic” about what needed to be funded and how difficult more spending would be. That decision to stick to no rises in personal taxation had left businesses fearing a tax raid – and Burnham has been urged by some leftwing and union leaders to consider further wealth taxes. But the prime minister told the FT this week he was loth to do more to increase the costs of doing business and did not want to target “wealth creators”. With each utterance, the possibilities of revenue raisers become ever narrower. Burnham hinted in the past that he hoped to unfreeze the personal allowance, which would amount to a tax cut, but has recently been more cautious about this because of the costs.
 3. Economic turmoilReeves left £23.6bn of “headroom” in her last budget, which gives Healey a buffer to meet the fiscal rule of balancing day-to-day spending with receipts. But the Iran war and subsequent rises in inflation and borrowing costs for servicing Britain’s national debt, which is now almost £3tn, are likely to have an effect on that headroom. Treasury sources say the impact may not be as much as feared, but with the strait of Hormuz remaining closed, growth is sluggish and inflation creeping upwards.
 4. Cost of living Burnham has made a number of popular early interventions to help ease the cost of living. Some, such as cutting VAT on energy bills, are ostensibly funded by cutting existing programmes such as the digital ID scheme, though, as the former minister Darren Jones pointed out, that was never properly costed in the first place. Healey has suggested there are no further plans to offer energy support at this October price cap, though prices have risen by 4%, wiping out the impact of the VAT cut. The Treasury will want a contingency plan in place in case more help is needed in January – probably a targeted scheme for more vulnerable households. The Resolution Foundation has suggested that even a targeted scheme for those earning under £25k would cost about £2bn.
 5. Defence targetsThe Treasury confirmed on Friday that it would delay setting out when the UK would meet the target of spending 3% of GDP on defence, until next year’s spending review. Burnham would have had to find an additional £4.7bn over five years for defence in October’s budget, after Starmer announced £15bn extra when he published the defence investment plan, without saying where the cash would come from. The remaining £10.3bn will also have to be raised by “reallocating budget” from across government departments. Healey resigned as defence secretary in June under Starmer’s leadership, accusing the then prime minister of being “unable” and the Treasury “unwilling” to “commit the resources that the nation needs to defend the country”. Labour has committed to spending 3.5% of GDP on defence by the middle of the next decade. But there will be endless pressure to go faster, putting more and more of a squeeze on other departmental budgets.
 6. Public controlBurnham promised he wanted to place life’s essentials “back under public control” – specifically Thames Water. In June, he told the Guardian he favoured public ownership for Thames Water, which is struggling with a £20bn debt. One possible solution is to use the forthcoming water bill to change the terms of the special administration regime, but it could still end up in costly legal action. Burnham told the FT recently that he had intentionally spoken in terms of more public control rather than nationalisation, but the budget is his first opportunity to set out a direction of travel that goes beyond local control of bus routes.
 7. WelfareTwo big reviews will come back this autumn. One is the second part of the Timms review, which will look at a new system to deliver personal independence payments to disabled people, where the bill is increasing substantially. The other is the Milburn review of youth unemployment and inactivity, also likely to require significant spending to try to solve the structural crisis that is costing the economy £125bn annually. Both are highly emotive and fraught with risk, including a potential backlash from Labour MPs. The Telegraph reported on Thursday that Burnham was likely to push the issue of welfare into the new year at the earliest, and would not be attempting to tackle it in the budget.

Vietnam’s move to end executions for drug trafficking sparks debate in region
The proposal has put a spotlight on the different legal approaches against drug trafficking offences in the region
The proposal, presented to lawmakers last week, would remove trafficking from Vietnam’s list of capital crimes. Last year, Hanoi kept the offence on the list during an earlier round of death penalty reforms.
If passed, the revised law would leave capital punishment for four crimes: treason, murder, terrorism and illegal narcotics production.
For years, several Southeast Asian governments have treated serious drug trafficking as a crime that warranted the death penalty. However, some countries have re-examined their laws, leading to amendments.
The issue has led to debates on whether capital punishment still has a place in society, whether judges should have the discretion in sentencing, and how governments can disrupt the drug trade without the death penalty.

“Several accidents and growing consumer complaints have spurred the regulators into action,” said Gao Shen, an independent analyst in Shanghai. “With improved oversight, carmakers will have to shift their focus from making their vehicles more intelligent to ensuring quality.”
