Psilocybin Might Make Your Brain Live in the Moment
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-29
09:00:00 UTC
18:00:00 KST

Under the influence of psychedelics, the usual organization of the human brain loosens. That's what scientists have generally thought, with several studies showing that when we take these substances, the signals pinging between our neurons become more diverse and unpredictable. This increased entropy in our gray matter may underlie the strange, random, and often memorable experiences of psychedelic trips.
But in one of the largest neuroimaging studies on the effects of psilocybin to date, researchers uncovered a hidden order in the apparent chaos. The study, published in Nature, indicates that while psilocybin blurs some of the boundaries within the brain, our neurological reactions to what we're experiencing in that moment become even more distinct.
The researchers tracked moment-by-moment changes across 332 regions of the brain using functional magnetic resonance imaging and electroencephalography, two methods of measuring brain activity. The 62 participants, who had no prior experience with psychedelics, took 19 milligrams of psilocybin in an oral capsule and then meditated, listened to music, or watched a movie.
With the help of artificial intelligence, the researchers identified patterns in the brain for each kind of activity the participants were engaged in. But surprisingly, the more intense the psilocybin experience, the clearer those neural signals were. Rather than becoming lost in the midst of an increasingly unpredictable trip, reality seemed to be leaving a more distinct imprint.
These findings weren't just apparent in the biological measurements but also in participants' personal experiences. Those who exhibited the most defined patterns of brain activity also tended to describe more intense experiences of immersion and unity with the world around them, the boundaries between themselves and the environment sometimes feeling blurred.
“Under psilocybin, brain networks that help us process our inner world and the world around us became less distinct, but reorganized into patterns that reflected what people were experiencing,” explained Devon Stoliker, the study’s lead author and a researcher at Monash University's School of Psychological Sciences in Melbourne, Australia.
In addition to providing a biological explanation for the sense of oneness that many people describe during a psychedelic trip, the findings also provide nuance to the idea that psilocybin simply makes the brain “chaotic.” This understanding is especially important in the emerging field of psychedelic therapy.
“This shows that context is not just background to the psychedelic experience,” Adeel Razi, a professor at Monash and the senior author of the study, emphasized in a press release. “For treatment, that reinforces why the environment and what a person does and experiences during the psychedelic session matter.”

Wildheuer: the gravity-defying haymakers above Lake Brienz
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-29
09:00:00 UTC
18:00:00 KST

Wildheuer: the gravity-defying haymakers above Lake Brienz
Scythes, whetstones, grass and sheer cliffs. Above Lake Brienz in canton Bern five friends return to Teni every summer to spend a few days in the footsteps of the Wildheuer – the haymakers who, for centuries, have braved the most inaccessible slopes to harvest wild hay. This activity has been enjoying a revival for almost three decades thanks to growing awareness of biodiversity and the Alpine landscape.
Outside, night is slowly giving way to day. The first light of dawn filters through the logs of the mountain hut. Silently, Reto, Thomas, Christof and Tom slip out of their sleeping bags and leave their beds on the hay. On the doorstep, they are greeted by the ring of mountains of the Bernese Oberland and, below, by the cobalt blue of Lake Brienz.
We are in Teni, above the municipality of Ringgenberg, in canton Bern. The simple mountain hut, at 1,600 metres above sea level, will be their home for the next five days. The four friends reached it the day before, weighed down by rucksacks laden with provisions and water. They climbed up there along a steep, winding path, passing through the Graaggetor – a natural gateway in the rock – and scaling the cliffs overlooking Lake Brienz. There is one detail that sets them apart from ordinary hikers: each of them is carrying a scythe.
Reto, Thomas, Christof, Tom and Fritz – who will be joining the group a little later this year – are haymakers, Wildheuer. For a few days, they step into the shoes of these legendary figures who, for centuries in Switzerland and other Alpine regions of Europe, have braved the steep, grassy slopes hanging over sheer cliffs to harvest wild hay (wild means wild and Heu means hay).
“What brings us back up here every year is the charm of tradition, direct contact with nature, the desire to leave the hectic pace of everyday life behind for a few days, and the friendship that has grown stronger through working together,” says Reto.
One false step can be fatal
Dawn looks promising in Teni. A few clouds linger in the sky after the previous evening’s rain. One by one, the four friends sling their scythes over their shoulders, clip their scythe holders to their trousers and set off along a short path to reach the meadow to be mown. They have attached crampons to their boots: slipping here could be fatal. Just below the grassy slope, in fact, lies a rock face nearly 100 metres high.
Over the past few weeks, the five friends have felt a growing sense of anticipation about returning up here: a sort of call to Teni.
At last, the sound of the whetstone on the scythe’s blade puts an end to the wait. Thomas sharpens the edge and, after a quick glance at the ground, begins. A swathe, a step, a swathe, a step. It feels as though we’re watching a dance between him and the scythe, interrupted now and then to sharpen the blade. Reto, Christof and Tom do the same.
They carry on like this until breakfast time and then until midday, when the morning dew has long since evaporated and the grass is too dry to mow.
They go back and forth along the slope. Like the shuttle of a loom, they weave a regular pattern across the now bare lawn, made up of long, horizontal mounds of grass. Sometimes they stop to look at the surrounding landscape and give their arms a rest. Their foreheads and backs are drenched in sweat.
Usually they sit in an office in front of a computer, perhaps with a steaming cup of coffee on their desk. Now the scent of wet grass and aromatic plants fills their noses; the sounds of Wildheuer cutting fill their ears.
“I’m moved by the steady tapping of the hammer on the scythe as the edge is re-sharpened, the sound of the grass being cut, and the sound of the whetstone when the blade is sharpened,” says Tom.
When hay was worth a fortune
What is now a hobby for Reto, Thomas, Christof, Tom and Fritz – and a way of preserving a centuries-old tradition – was once an essential activity for mountain farming families.
“In the first half of the 17th century, the production of hard cheeses, which were sold in Lombardy, became widespread. Hay, essential for feeding livestock during the winter, became such a precious resource that it sometimes took on the value of a genuine currency,” explains geographer and journalist Elsbeth Flüeler, author of a book on the Wildheuer of canton Nidwalden. “And so, although Wildheu was leaner than the hay from the meadows in the valley floor, it became increasingly valuable and sought-after.”
When the steep high-altitude meadows, the so-called Plangge, were not privately owned but belonged to guilds or cooperatives, their use was regulated very precisely: the plots could be auctioned off, allocated on a permanent basis, utilised under customary law, or allocated by lot. In some places, competition for the best meadows could even lead to conflicts.
“In the Erstfeld Valley, in canton Uri, these disputes have gone down in history as the ‘scythe wars’,” Flüeler says.
Between the late 19th and 20th centuries, the harvesting of wild hay gradually declined in importance, mainly due to the economic and social changes that were transforming Alpine agriculture.
“The advent of the railway, with the resulting access to markets and growing competition, put pressure on mountain economies,” Flüeler explains. Later, with industrialisation, many people left the agricultural sector for wage labour in factories. “As a result, there was a shortage of the labour needed for such a strenuous and demanding activity.”
A culture coming back to life
Since the end of the 20th century, wild haymaking has regained importance in several Alpine cantons, particularly in central Switzerland. This resurgence has been driven by the drastic decline in biodiversity and a growing awareness of the ecological value of these areas which, unlike those intensively farmed in the valley floor, are rich in insect and flower species.
Around 75 species of orchid grow wild in Switzerland, 58 of which are found in canton Bern. Many are rare or threatened and are highly sensitive to changes in their habitat. In the Bernese Oberland, around 25% of the orchid species originally found there are now extinct or under threat.
In nutrient-poor mountain meadows, the cessation of mowing leads to the formation of a thick layer of grass, which causes biodiversity to decline rapidly.
To preserve orchids, it is therefore important to continue mowing, but only after the seeds have been dispersed. In Teni, the areas are mown on a rotational basis, roughly once every three years, so as to encourage the growth of orchids.
Some of these areas have therefore been included in the federal inventory of dry grasslands and pastures of national importance. Their management to promote biodiversity is also supported by cantonal and federal grants, which provide a significant financial incentive to resume farming on these lands. Another reason is avalanche prevention: tall grass that is bent and flattened by the snow can, in fact, cause the snowpack to slide more easily.
“Wild haymaking is more than just a tradition: it is a culture, with its own language, practices and symbols. It is a defining feature of our identity,” Flüeler points out.
“This culture has also left a deep mark on the landscape. As well as species-rich meadows, there are infrastructure features such as the ropes suspended on the slopes to transport hay down to the valley, or the small huts hidden away in the countryside.”
Family rituals and customs have also developed around Wildheuen. And so this activity has become almost a communal ritual. “In many cases, friends and acquaintances take part in the cutting and harvesting,” Flüeler says.
Over the past 50 years, haymaking on uncultivated land has also become highly mechanised. The scythe has been supplemented by motorised mowers specially adapted for slopes. In addition, blowers and other machinery, such as Twister hay turners, are used, making hay harvesting easier and quicker than the traditional method using a rake and pitchfork.
Transport has also changed: large nets, capable of holding 15 or more bales of hay, are transported down to the valley by helicopter, replacing the traditional suspended ropes in many places.
The Wildheuer of Teni have chosen to do without mechanical mowers and blowers and not to transport the hay by helicopter. Their aim is to preserve this practice in its most traditional and original form.
Mountain farming families also appreciate the quality of this fodder, which is rich in fibre and aromatic herbs. “Livestock farmers use this hay in a targeted way during the winter: they feed it to the animals at the start to stimulate digestion and at the end, almost as if it were a dessert, partly because the animals are very fond of it.”
Meanwhile, in Teni, work has only just begun for Reto, Thomas, Christof, Tom and Fritz. They are also supported by Werner, the father of Reto and Thomas. He carries out various tasks around the mountain hut and takes care of the logistics, transporting food, water, hay nets and hooks up to the alp on the opposite side of the Brienzergrat.
Once mown, the grass must be left to dry in the sun. The five of them will turn it over once or twice, then the dried hay will be gathered into transport nets, known as Seiltücher.
The bales of hay weigh between 40 and 80 kilograms. The group will have to hoist around 20 of these heavy bales onto their shoulders and walk along the path to the mountain hut: a task that requires strength and agility.
Finally, the most spectacular part begins: transporting the hay down to the valley floor via wires suspended above the rock faces and the woodland. Once hooked onto the cable, the load will pick up speed and the wire will begin to vibrate, emitting a sort of song. For Reto, Thomas, Christof, Tom, Fritz and Werner, it will be one of the most intense and thrilling moments of their five days spent in the shoes of the Wildheuer. An experience that will draw them back to Teni again next year.

External auditing of sustainability reports reaches record level in Switzerland
More than 90% of Switzerland’s largest listed companies have had all or part of their sustainability reports for the 2025 financial year audited by an external body, according to a recent report by consultancy firm IRF.
The number of companies whose sustainability reports are externally audited has risen steadily in recent years. It increased from 21 in 2021 to 31 in 2023, before climbing to 35 in 2024 and 38 in 2025. This year, the figure reached a record high of 43 companies, accounting for around 91% of Switzerland’s largest listed companies.
The consultancy firm analysed 47 companies in the SMI Expanded Index that had published a report by the end of May 2026. The index includes Switzerland’s 50 largest listed companies.

Bipartisan US Lawmakers Take Aim At Serbia's Vucic Over Democracy, Russia Ties
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-29
08:59:33 UTC
17:59:33 KST

A bipartisan group of US lawmakers has taken aim at the government of longtime Serbian President Aleksandar Vucic, citing what it calls “serious setbacks” in democracy and the rule of law, as well as Belgrade’s ties with US adversaries Iran, Russia, and China.
Republican Representative Joe Wilson, a co-sponsor of the legislation, said that “under President Vucic, Serbia has deliberately moved further and further away from the rule of law and closer to enemies of freedom, such as the war criminal [Russian President Vladimir] Putin, the Communist Party of China, and the terrorist regime in Tehran.”
“Despite widespread protests against corruption, Vucic’s government threatens to destabilize the region and beyond. The people of Serbia deserve better,” Wilson said after submitting the bill on August 27.
The bill, also sponsored by Democrat Bill Keating, a fellow member of the House Foreign Affairs Committee, would impose visa bans and sanctions on individuals who undermine the stability of the Western Balkans or the territorial integrity of any state in the region.
It would also target individuals who take part in “undermining democratic processes and institutions, corruption, serious human rights violations, or actions that obstruct regional agreements and frameworks for security, peace, cooperation, or mutual recognition.”
The legislation, known as the Serbia Act, specifically calls out Vucic over what it describes as the excessive use of force against recent student-led protests and calls for an investigation into, and accountability for, the 2024 railway tragedy in Novi Sad that helped ignite the demonstrations.
The measure is not yet law. It would have to pass the full House and Senate before being sent to the president for signature.
US-Serbia Relations
Keating said that “democracy, rule of law, and anti-corruption must remain key pillars in the US-Serbia bilateral relationship.”
“The United States has an enduring interest in a stable, democratic, and sovereign Serbia that is committed to regional peace and security and firmly anchored in Euro-Atlantic institutions and free from malign external influence,” the bill text states.
The proposed legislation would also direct Secretary of State Marco Rubio to press Belgrade on ensuring free and fair elections, fighting corruption, strengthening the rule of law, and addressing Serbia’s ties with Iran, Russia, and China.
If those issues are not adequately addressed, Keating and Wilson said the United States should suspend its participation in the US-Serbia Strategic Dialogue.
The dialogue was held in Washington in July, with the two sides issuing a joint statement outlining areas of cooperation.
Vucic, who has been president of Serbia since 2017 after serving as prime minister for three years, has long sought to balance his country’s aspirations to join the European Union with its historically close ties to Russia.
He has faced nearly two years of student-led street protests, initially sparked by the collapse of a railway-station roof in Novi Sad in November 2024 that killed 16 people. The demonstrations later expanded into broader complaints about Vucic’s government and allegations of corruption.
Vucic and pro-government media have accused the students and their professors of working with unidentified Western security services in an effort to remove him from power. He has provided no evidence to support the claims.
Vucic's Next Move?
In July, Vucic said he would resign as Serbia’s president, despite having almost a year remaining in his term. Few expect that to mean he will leave Serbian politics, where he has been the dominant figure for more than a decade.
Vucic, 56, has already been elected president twice and is constitutionally barred from seeking a third term.
Analysts say that by stepping down, Vucic could potentially return as prime minister if his ruling Serbian Progressive Party (SNS) wins early parliamentary elections. Vucic has said the elections will be held in October, although they were not otherwise due until December 2027.
“His possible move to the position of prime minister would simply place him, constitutionally, where he already is -- the country’s key political figure who makes all the important decisions,” Dusan Spasojevic, a professor at the Faculty of Political Sciences at the University of Belgrade, told RFE/RL’s Balkan Service in July.
The bill also lays out conditions under which Washington could seek closer ties with Belgrade.
If the Serbian government takes steps to strengthen its Euro-Atlantic path, including through a credible and independent investigation into the Novi Sad railway collapse and accountability for the excessive use of force against peaceful protesters, the legislation says the US president should take steps to improve bilateral relations.
Those steps could include measures aimed at strengthening Serbia’s democratic institutions and its resilience to what the legislation describes as harmful foreign influence.

Austria Is Strengthening Its Defences Against russian Cyberattacks, Disinformation, and Espionage

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) – Tainan announced Friday that it has designated 49 hectares of land in Anding District as a new town, pending a review, according to a press release.
The city said it sent the proposal to the Ministry of the Interior in July to accommodate growth driven by Southern Taiwan Science Park. The new settlement is expected to attract up to 4,000 people.
The 49-hectare community will be established on farmland near Anding Junior High School, with approximately 30 hectares rezoned for residential and commercial use. The city plans to rezone an additional 8 hectares into a park, parking lot, and a recreation center.

Southern Taiwan Science Park, or the Semiconductor S-Corridor, is a major hub for high-tech industries such as semiconductor manufacturing that stretches from Chiayi to Pingtung.

EXPLAINER – Pacific Islands summit: Key issues to watch
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-29
08:56:39 UTC
17:56:39 KST

Leaders of Pacific island nations will gather in Palau from Aug. 30 to Sept. 4 for a summit that could test whether the region can maintain a common voice while major powers compete for strategic influence and access to its vast ocean resources.
The 55th Pacific Islands Forum Leaders Meeting will be held under the theme “Building Economies: Life. Action. Unity.”
The forum has 18 members: Australia, the Cook Islands, Fiji, French Polynesia, Kiribati, the Marshall Islands, the Federated States of Micronesia, Nauru, New Caledonia, New Zealand, Niue, Palau, Papua New Guinea, Samoa, the Solomon Islands, Tonga, Tuvalu and Vanuatu. American Samoa and Guam are associate members.
The US and China are the dialogue partners of the forum.
Although its members have small populations, the forum represents an immense expanse of the Pacific Ocean. Its decisions therefore carry significance far beyond the islands, particularly as competition intensifies among China, the US and Washington’s regional allies.
For Pacific governments, however, the central question is whether foreign attention can be converted into climate protection, infrastructure, economic opportunities and control over their own resources — without turning the region into an arena for strategic confrontation.
Pacific leaders have repeatedly described climate change as the greatest threat to the region’s security. Rising seas, coastal erosion, saltwater intrusion and stronger storms are already damaging homes, roads, freshwater supplies and traditional livelihoods.
The Palau summit is expected to move the Pacific Resilience Facility closer to becoming operational. Designed as a Pacific-owned financing mechanism, the facility aims to fund small community-level projects that often struggle to secure support from large international climate funds.
Leaders are expected to launch a call for pilot proposals in Palau. The initiative will test whether the region can build a financing system that is easier for vulnerable communities to access and less dependent on complicated international procedures.
Funding nevertheless remains a challenge. Pacific governments want wealthy countries — particularly major historical emitters — to provide grants rather than loans that would add to the debt burdens of small economies.
Energy security will also feature prominently. Most island nations rely heavily on imported fuel, leaving them exposed to global price shocks and supply disruptions. Palauese President Surangel Whipps Jr. has advocated a regional transition toward 100% renewable energy, while calls have emerged for the appointment of a Pacific energy commissioner.
Economic development is closely tied to the ocean. Fisheries generate vital public revenue, while tourism supports jobs across the region. Illegal and unregulated fishing, depleted stocks and marine degradation therefore constitute economic as well as environmental threats.
The most contentious resource question may be deep-sea mining. Mineral-rich nodules on the Pacific seabed contain metals sought for batteries, electronics and defense technology.
Palau supports a precautionary pause on extraction until its environmental consequences are better understood. Nauru, Kiribati and Tonga, however, have explored mining opportunities as a potential source of income. China and the US are also competing for access to critical minerals.
The summit comes amid growing concern about militarization. China’s test of a nuclear-capable ballistic missile into the Pacific in July exposed divisions among forum members.
Some governments criticized the test, while others with close relations with Beijing resisted a regional condemnation.
The disagreement illustrates the forum’s central diplomatic problem: members maintain different security partnerships and diplomatic alignments.
China has expanded its presence through infrastructure, policing and development agreements, including its security relationship with the Solomon Islands. Australia and the US have responded by increasing aid, defense cooperation and diplomatic engagement.
Fiji and Australia signed a defense treaty in July, while Solomon Islands Prime Minister Matthew Wale has promoted discussion of a broader Pacific security agreement.
Taiwan’s participation will provide another test of regional unity. Taiwanese Foreign Minister Lin Chia-lung is expected to attend dialogue sessions and related events, according to Taiwan’s Foreign Ministry.
Palau, the Marshall Islands and Tuvalu are Taiwan’s three remaining diplomatic partners in the Pacific. Beijing, which considers Taiwan part of China, opposes its presence at international gatherings.
Taiwan and other external partners were excluded from last year’s summit in the Solomon Islands. Its return in Palau reflects the host country’s close relationship with Taipei but could sharpen tensions with Beijing and forum members that recognize China.
The summit's outcome will show whether Pacific leaders can prioritize regional priorities over outside rivalries.

U.S. Navy tests land-based Harpoon missile system
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-29
08:56:19 UTC
17:56:19 KST

- The Harpoon Coastal Defense System successfully struck a target vessel during a developmental test at Point Mugu Sea Range in July.
- The land-based system fires the existing Harpoon anti-ship missile to defend coastal areas, according to the U.S. Navy.
The U.S. Navy’s Harpoon Coastal Defense System successfully launched a Harpoon missile from land and struck a target vessel in near-shore waters during a two-day test in late July at Point Mugu Sea Range, California, the Navy said.
The event, designated Developmental Test 1, brought together the Strike Weapons Program Office known as PMX-201, the Naval Air Weapons Station Technical Project Office, Point Mugu Sea Range personnel and Boeing, which builds the Harpoon missile.
The Harpoon Coastal Defense System is a land-based launcher built to fire the existing Harpoon anti-ship missile against maritime targets from shore, giving military planners a way to defend coastal areas and strategic waterways without relying solely on ships or aircraft.
“The flawless execution of this test is a direct testament to the unparalleled expertise and relentless dedication demonstrated by the entire team,” said Capt. Sarah Abbott, PMX-201 program manager. “In the face of complex technical requirements and tight schedules, the team’s cohesive effort and proactive problem-solving ensured that every critical parameter was met.”
“This represents a significant milestone in our mission to deliver a vital, high-priority defense capability to the field,” Abbott said. “An achievement of this scale is never the result of a single individual, it is the culmination of shared vision, rigorous discipline, and exhaustive preparation by everyone involved.”
Developmental testing is one stage in a broader evaluation process the Navy uses to check combat readiness before a system moves closer to fleet use, involving live-fire and tracking events at sea. The Navy did not disclose the number of missiles fired during DT-1, the specific type of target vessel used, or a date for the system’s next testing phase.
The Harpoon missile itself has been in U.S. Navy service since the late 1970s and has been adapted over the decades for launch from ships, aircraft and submarines. The Harpoon Coastal Defense System represents an additional, land-based launch option built around that same missile rather than a new weapon.
The test was overseen by PAE Munitions, a Department of the Navy organization that manages weapons programs including this one, according to the Navy’s announcement. The Navy has not announced a timeline for when the Harpoon Coastal Defense System might be fielded operationally.

Taiwan links foreign labor access to pay raises in bid to ease shortages
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-29
08:56:10 UTC
17:56:10 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — The Ministry of Labor has rolled out measures to ease deepening worker shortages by tying access to migrant labor to wage increases for local workers and expanding support for older and female job seekers.
The measures, announced Thursday, aim to address industry labor shortages that officials say reflect structural factors. Liberty Times reported that these measures include demographic changes, shifting work patterns and rising worker expectations, as well as ongoing industrial transformation.
Under a cross-border workforce enhancement scheme launched at the start of this year, manufacturing employers can gain additional migrant worker quotas by raising wages for Taiwanese employees. For each local worker given a monthly pay increase of at least NT$2,000, a company may hire one extra migrant worker, with the additional quota capped at 10% of its insured workforce. When combined with other mechanisms, the overall migrant worker ceiling can reach up to 45%.
The labor ministry noted that it is also treating middle-aged and older workers and women as key labor sources, using hiring subsidies to encourage employers to recruit unemployed people from these groups, Liberty Times reported.
It cited measures including subsidies for continuing to employ older workers, grants for employers that adjust working hours, and offer job redesign assistance. This will help companies improve work environments and tasks, thereby increasing employment opportunities for older workers and women re-entering the workforce.
The policy push comes as the National Development Council warned this week that Taiwan’s working-age population will shrink by about 10.67 million, or 67%, over the next 50 years, with more than half of workers aged 45–64 by 2037.
A recent Chinese National Federation of Industries white paper also urged further labor reforms, per UDN. These include extending the maximum stay for industrial migrant workers from 12 to 14 years and shifting migrant worker policy from a focus on “3K” (dangerous, dirty, difficult) industries to one guided by actual labor demand.

Hongkongers can use either ID or home return permit at revamped Huanggang Port
Security chief Chris Tang reveals arrangement after massive drill at border crossing, which could open next month
Hongkongers can present either their identity card or home return permit at the revamped Huanggang border checkpoint instead of both documents under the latest agreement with mainland Chinese authorities, the security minister has revealed.
Secretary for Security Chris Tang Ping-keung announced the measure after a drill at the crossing involving more than 20,000 civil servants on Saturday.
“Residents using e-channels to enter the mainland or return to Hong Kong can use the Hong Kong identity card or the home return permit, whichever they prefer,” Tang said.
Saturday’s drill was the largest so far, with more than 20,000 civil servants taking part to simulate peak stress on the building’s capacity.
Huanggang Port is expected to be able to handle 200,000 passenger trips per day and is the first checkpoint to use a “joint clearance” model.
Passengers only need to undergo departure and arrival clearance at a single checkpoint and present one travel document at either automatic or manual counters, instead of passing through separate counters.

Iran’s regime is at war with its own people - and executions are its weapon - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-29
08:54:20 UTC
17:54:20 KST

Early Sunday morning, the Islamic Republic executed Shahram Sadeghi, who had been arrested in connection with the nationwide protests that erupted in January. His death came just one day after an anniversary that, for my family, has marked the brutality of this regime for nearly half a century.
On August 15, 1980, the regime executed my grandfather, Yousef Khoshkish. He had spent decades serving Iran as the head of the country’s largest commercial bank, Bank Melli, and later as the last Pahlavi-era governor of the Central Bank of Iran, building institutions meant to serve generations of Iranians. I never had the chance to know him, but his execution has been part of my family’s story for as long as I can remember, and part of Iran’s story for even longer.
Forty-six years separate those two days, and almost nothing separates the logic behind them. From its earliest days, the Islamic Republic has relied on the gallows as its language of rule. It has spent nearly five decades at war with the Iranian people, directing its anger inward whenever it emerges bruised from its foreign adventurism or fractured within.
How Iran cracks down on mass uprisings
The response to a mass uprising is always the same: arrests, torture, forced “confessions,” closed-door sham trials, and executions. These are less acts of revenge than instruments of political survival, intended to convince a population with its sights set on freedom that challenging the state is futile.
As of August 18, at least 932 people have been executed in Iran since the beginning of 2026, and the true number is likely far higher. More than 100 others face death on bogus national security charges.
On July 19, Erfan Esfandiari and Gol-Mohammad Mohammadi were hanged for sheltering protesters fleeing security forces that were trying to kill them, two of 12 men sentenced to death in a single trial. Nine days later, Amir Hossein Safari and Abolfazl Sepahi were publicly hanged in Isfahan’s Alikhani Square.
This location was chosen to convey a message, because thousands had gathered there during January protests. Security forces surrounded the execution site and fired into crowds of locals who had gathered in an attempt to stop the state-sanctioned killing.
On August 1, authorities hanged 20-year-old Arvin Kheirkhah, convicted by a Revolutionary Court on charges including moharebeh, or “waging war against Allah.” His family had gathered outside the prison the night before, hoping the execution could still be stopped.
Charges such as moharebeh, “spreading corruption on earth,” and “collaboration with hostile states” reduce Iran’s judiciary to an instrument of ideology. The last is used to dress up its conspiratorial claims of connections between Iranian protesters and the United States, Israel, or other foreign powers. These accusations are designed to deny an obvious reality: Opposition to the Islamic Republic is organic and homegrown.
Eighteen-year-old Shervin Bagherian is one of the countless Iranians who remain at risk of execution. Security forces raided his home in the dead of night, beat him, and took him to an undisclosed location. Interrogators reportedly placed a noose around his neck and staged mock executions to force a confession for state television.
This wave of executions coincides with rising concern among the regime’s Basij and IRGC over the possibility of renewed protests. In a recently leaked internal meeting, officials discussed preparations for another round of unrest and ordered personnel to identify and track Iranians posting anti-regime content online.
The aim is to raise the cost of the next uprising before it begins. For a regime that claims to embody the Iranian nation, conceding that millions of Iranians reject it would be politically fatal. So protesters become “spies,” and critics online become “saboteurs.”
Meanwhile, the state cannot reliably provide electricity, water, or economic stability, yet its machinery of repression remains remarkably organized. That contrast is a statement of priorities, and it should shape how democratic governments approach the Islamic Republic.
The West treats nuclear negotiations, terrorism, regional militias, and human rights violations as separate policy files. To the Islamic Republic, they are a single file: survival. Which is why concessions purchased at the expense of Iranian lives purchase nothing durable.
No serious Iran policy can treat the Iranian people as an afterthought. They are the central strategic question, and they are the country’s engine of change. Millions have defied guns and bullets, detention and torture, internet blackouts and executions, and they will not stop until they reclaim their motherland and their future.
The Islamic Republic understands this better than many foreign governments do. It knows where the greatest threat to its survival resides. As champion wrestler and protester Navid Afkari said before his execution in 2020, as long as this regime remains in power, it will keep “searching for necks to hang from its gallows.” My grandfather’s was one. More than a hundred Iranians are waiting to learn whether they are next.
The author is deputy communications director at the National Union for Democracy in Iran.

Relocation of US arms from Europe may expose vulnerabilities in US global military posture - report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-29
08:54:15 UTC
17:54:15 KST

Military planners in Washington worry that dwindling munitions stores may reduce the US’s ability to defend against potential threats from Russia and China, according to a Friday Wall Street Journal report citing US officials familiar with the matter.
While the officials noted that Western military officials have assessed that full-scale attacks from Russia and China are not imminent, they told the WSJ that insufficient weapons stockpiles have left vulnerabilities in the US’s global military posture.
Some officials described the situation as “beyond critical,” with arms moved to the Middle East from stockpiles in Europe and Asia creating shortages that could take years to replenish.
Administration officials have reportedly assessed that due to weapons being moved out of Asia for use in the war with Iran, the US may not be able to fully carry out contingency plans to defend Taiwan in case of a Chinese invasion.
Low levels of Europe-based defense assets raise concerns over defense against Russia
The officials highlighted that European-based defense assets, including precision strike munitions and interceptors, have reached low levels.
Stockpiles of Patriot air defense interceptors, Terminal High Altitude Area Defense (THAAD) interceptors, and counter-drone systems are among the arms impacted by the shortage created by the relocation of munitions, the officials added.
US European Command, according to the WSJ report, has been forced to adjust its operational plans because of dwindling munitions inventories on the European continent.
Some lawmakers stated that they are increasingly concerned about Russian hybrid and drone attacks and a Pentagon review of US military posture in Europe that could lead to a reduction in American troops in the region.
Following intelligence assessments that Russian President Vladimir Putin may attempt to test NATO’s resolve within the next few years, US Senator Roger Wicker (R - Mississippi) urged the posture review to “account for a wounded Putin lashing out.”
As weapons have been used and relocated, the US has also reportedly struggled to produce enough munitions to replenish its own stockpiles, in addition to allegedly limiting the amount of arms sent to Ukraine and Washington’s allies in Europe.
White House, Pentagon deny concerns over weapons stocks
US President Donald Trump and his administration declined to discuss with the WSJ which weapons have been moved to the Middle East and how many remain in Europe and Asia.
The Trump administration has repeatedly denied reports regarding the arms shortages, insisting that the US has sufficient supplies to continue fighting Iran and to combat other global threats.
White House spokeswoman Anna Kelly told the WSJ that “the United States Military has more than enough munitions, ammo, and stockpiles to serve all of President Trump’s strategic goals and beyond.”
Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell also denied the reports, saying “claims of US munition shortages are false.”
Despite Washington’s insistence that there are no concerns regarding the stock levels of essential arms, the US has turned away from military strikes against Iran and has instead intensified efforts to force Tehran to make a deal through economic pressure.

Iranian leaders are acknowledging the economic toll of war with the United States, with the supreme leader calling on the government to address the hardship while the president reported foreign trade has shrunk by more than one-third due to the American sanctions and blockade.
Supreme Leader Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei, who was injured and has not been seen publicly since the February 28 attack that killed his father, former Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei, called on the government to tackle the economic hardship.
"There is the need to seriously address the chain of economic and livelihood challenges, such as inflation, unemployment, management of prices and the market for goods and services," said a written statement attributed to Khamenei.
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian told state media that Iranian exports and imports slumped nearly 35% because of US sanctions and a naval blockade of Iranian ports.
With the war now at the six-month mark, and negotiations at an impasse, President Donald Trump's administration has stepped up efforts to punish Iran financially with what it has billed as an "economic D-Day."
With the US focused on its economic pressure campaign, others have sought to revive diplomatic efforts to end the war. Qatari Prime Minister Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman Al Thani met with Iranian leaders in Tehran on Thursday. He said he had stressed during the meeting the importance of returning to the pre-war status of open shipping through the Strait of Hormuz.
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi on Friday described the talks with Al Thani as "creative." Qatar and Pakistan helped broker the June memorandum of understanding that led to a brief ceasefire before disagreements over the strait caused it to unravel.
Iran: 'Enemy' failed to achieve war goals, claims victory
Iranian army commander-in-chief Amir Hatami has claimed that the country emerged victorious from the war because the “enemy” failed to achieve its objectives.
Hatami said the “enemy” had sought to destroy Iran’s drone and missile capabilities, but that its missile stockpile continued to be fired at them with the “utmost intensity until the last moment”, according to the Fars news agency.
“In military logic, the aggressor and aggressor sides are considered victorious when they achieve their goals, but in defensive warfare, the failure of the enemy to achieve its goals means the victory of the defender,” he added.
Israeli strike kills three in rare West Bank strike
Israel's military said it carried out an airstrike in the West Bank on Friday that killed a Palestinian it described as a Hamas operative as well as two of his accomplices, in a rare use of deadly Israeli air power in the occupied territory.
Hamas condemned the strike but did not claim the person targeted — whom the Israeli military named as Qais Bitawi — as a member. The strike targeted a car in the area of Jenin in the northern West Bank, the military and medics said.
The West Bank has seen a surge in militant Israeli settler attacks on Palestinians as well as military raids into Palestinian towns. The northern West Bank, where Jenin sits, was the site of a major Israeli assault last year, which the military says was aimed at targeting militant strongholds.
In a statement, the military said Bitawi was involved in directing, funding and executing attacks on Israeli civilians and security forces. It said he maintained ties with Hamas members in Gaza, where the group is based, as well as abroad.
The Palestine Red Crescent ambulance service said Israeli ground troops raided the site of the drone strike, briefly detained medics and prevented them from transporting those wounded or killed to hospital.
Israel's military did not immediately provide comment on the ambulance service's statements.
Israel's 2025 operations in the northern West Bank forced thousands of Palestinians from their homes, with Israeli forces clearing out refugee camps and maintaining their longest presence in some West Bank cities for decades.
Human Rights Watch has accused Israel of war crimes and crimes against humanity over what it said were forced expulsions.
Russia, China, Iran leaders to attend summit in Kyrgyzstan
Russia's Vladimir Putin and China's Xi Jinping are expected in Central Asia's Kyrgyzstan Monday for a two-day summit, also attended by Iran's and India's leaders, of a regional bloc seeking to be a counter-influence to the West.
Around a dozen heads of states will head to the Kyrgyz capital Bishkek to mark 25 years of the Shanghai Cooperation Group (SCO).
The group brings together Russia, China, India, Pakistan, Iran, four Central Asian countries and Moscow-allied Belarus.
Putin and Xi have previously used SCO summits to promote their vision of a multipolar world and present a united front against the West.
It takes place four-and-a-half years into Moscow's Ukraine invasion and six months into the war between Washington and Tehran. Iran will be represented by its president, Masoud Pezeshkian.
Putin, Xi, Pezeshkian as well as India's Narendra Modi and Pakistan's Shehbaz Sharif are due to take part in a plenary session chaired by Kyrgyz leader Sadyr Japarov.
Putin is also expected to hold separate bilateral talks with Iran's Pezeshkian and China's Xi, among other leaders, Kremlin spokesman Yuri Ushakov said.
Russia and Iran -- among the most sanctioned states in the world -- have massively deepened their military and economic ties during the Ukraine war.
US President Donald Trump has warned Moscow and Beijing against arming Iran.
Putin's meeting with Pezeshkian comes days after the CIA's director John Ratcliffe made a rare trip to Moscow, with US media speculating he could have discussed Ukraine and Iran with his Russian counterparts.
Iran government says diplomacy and defence inseparable
The Iranian government pledged on Sunday to stand firm against U.S. sanctions and what it called US-Israeli "conspiracies," saying diplomacy and defence were "complementary, coordinated and inseparable" tools for protecting the country’s national interests, security and territorial integrity.
In a statement carried by state media, the government said it would pursue both tracks simultaneously and focus on curbing inflation, creating jobs, supporting domestic production and gradually reducing dependence on the dollar.
The Iran war has entered its sixth month, with the conflict continuing to fuel military tensions, diplomatic efforts and growing economic pressure.
Iran's president says foreign trade has fallen by nearly 35% under US sanctions and a naval blockade, while Tehran insists it remains in control of the Strait of Hormuz despite US claims that the key waterway is open to shipping.

Turkish presence in Syria poses threat to Israel due to Ankara’s NATO combat doctrine, expert warns
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-29
08:53:35 UTC
17:53:35 KST

The Turkish military presence in Syria constitutes a significant threat to Israel due to its NATO combat doctrine, expert Dr. Eitan Hai Cohen told 103FM's Prof. Aryeh Eldad and Ron Koffman in an interview on Friday.
Cohen discussed what he described as the strengthening of economic and strategic ties between Ankara and Washington in Syria and the potential implications for Israel.
According to Cohen, Turkey has become a central strategic player in the region since the fall of the Assad regime and has positioned itself as a mediator between Syria and the United States.
"Turkey began training [Syrian President] Ahmed al-Sharaa. They also approached the US to remove the American sanctions on Syria. What is the reason? To rebuild Syria," he explained.
Cohen said Turkey has a clear economic interest in Syria’s reconstruction, particularly because of its powerful construction sector.
"The construction industry in Turkey is very strong," he said. "They built in northern Syria; they are there as an occupying force, that is no secret. They are telling the Americans that we can share the profits together; we can make a lot of money here. The Europeans also support it because they want to get rid of the Syrian refugees."
Turkish takeover of Syrian oil coincided with Chevron deal, Cohen says
He also addressed what he described as a military development in northeastern Syria earlier this year.
"Last January, Syrian regime forces invaded northeastern Syria, the Kurdish region, and took control of the oil wells," said Cohen. "Immediately after the Syrian takeover, what did we see? An American company, Chevron, signed a cooperation agreement with the Syrian state oil company. This says a lot of things."
According to Cohen, these developments could provide the United States with a new type of foothold in Syria.
"For the first time in history, the US can penetrate Syria," Cohen explained. "Until 1918, there was a Turkish presence, then French, then communist, then Russian, then Iranian, and now, Turkey is returning there and telling the US: You were never able to enter Syria, and we can pave the way for you into Syria."
"From an American perspective, there is a matter here of political penetration," he added. "Erdogan is 'paying' [US President Donald] Trump in cash, and therefore Trump says every other day: He is a strong guy, a good guy and I like him."
Cohen also warned about the expansion of Turkey’s presence in Syria.
"If the US does not intervene, the Turks will continue," he warned. "They signed an agreement with the Syrian regime. They have the entire legal infrastructure. They have the ability to provide weapons, ammunition, including training."
He said Israel must also consider the capabilities of the Turkish military.
"Turkey's way of warfare is not that of some rickety Arab country, but rather NATO's way of warfare," Cohen noted. "We are talking about a very high standard, and we have to think about that."
Cohen also addressed growing tensions between Israel and Turkey and what he described as Washington’s approach to the issue.
"Before this needs to be absorbed in Ankara, it needs to be absorbed in Washington. The US thinks that the friction between Israel and Turkey is only verbal and that it will not lead to physical friction," he said.
Cohen: IDF's Syria strike sought to send message to Turkey
According to Cohen, Israeli strikes in Syria were intended to send a clear message to Ankara.
"What we saw about a week ago with the Israeli bombing, and also last year in April, is essentially a red line, an Israeli declaration that Israel does not want to see any kind of Turkish presence in central Syria," he emphasized. "We do not want to see them in southern Syria, Turkish penetration; we are not interested in seeing this."
He said he hopes the message will also be understood in Washington.
"The US is ignoring this, and I very much hope that after this bombing in the Idlib area, an area of Turkish influence, the Turks are also very surprised that Israel bombed northwestern Syria," he concluded.

The crisis began late Friday evening, Aug. 28, when a Russian drone struck an enterprise near the Kyiv-Chop highway at approximately 8:10 p.m local time. The strike triggered a massive fire and secondary detonations of materials stored at the facility.
The scale of the explosions forced the National Police to completely close sections of the M-06 Kyiv-Chop highway in both directions.
Prime Minister Serhiy Koretskyi issued a condemnation of the incident, demanding strict accountability for those responsible. He stated that a similar recent tragedy involving a massive detonation at a weapons depot in Vyshneve “did not serve as a lesson.”
“Making the same mistakes in the fifth year of a full-scale invasion is criminal negligence,” Koretskyi said on Telegram after receiving briefings from the Interior Minister and the head of the State Emergency Service. “Everyone responsible, without exception, must face severe punishment so that such situations do not happen again.”
The Prosecutor General’s Office has launched an investigation into the Myla incident to determine if explosive materials were legally stored at the enterprise and whether the necessary safety permits were in place.

Dutch institute issues 'red alert' over Trump-shaped ecstasy pills
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-29
09:48:34 BST
17:48:34 KST

Dutch institute issues 'red alert' over Trump-shaped ecstasy pills
- Published
A Dutch drug addiction and mental health institute has issued a "red alert" to users about potentially lethal ecstasy pills in the shape of US President Donald Trump's head.
The Utrecht-based Trimbos Institute said several of the pills had been handed in at testing centres in August and were found to contain a "very high" amount of the chemical PMMA.
"Do not use this pill under any circumstance," the institute said in its warning, cautioning that the drug could cause "overheating with potentially fatal consequences".
It issued images of the pills, which feature a depiction of Trump's head on one side and the words "Trump" and "NL" stamped on the other.
PMMA, or para-methoxymethamfetamine, is a substance similar to MDMA – the active ingredient in ecstasy pills.
"However, the effect occurs later, and the stimulating effect is often absent," the institute advised. "This increases the risk of overdose."
Users are being warned they could experience symptoms such as nausea, an increased heart rate and convulsions hours after ingesting the pills.
Trimbos Institute spokesperson Anniek Groothuis told the Associated Press that it had no reported cases of death or serious illness among possible users.
While producing, selling and using ecstasy is illegal in the Netherlands, a 2024 Dutch government report said the substance was "still quite popular as a party drug".
The report added that, in 2022, a "record 550,000 people" had taken the drug at least once.
This is not the first time Donald Trump's facial features appear to have been used as inspiration for the shape of ecstasy pills.
In 2017, German police confiscated about 5,000 carrot-coloured ecstasy tablets in the shape of the US president's head – which they believed had been promoted on the internet under the slogan "Trump makes partying great again".

U.S. Air Force taps small Alabama firm for AIM-120X missile parts deal
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-29
08:47:15 UTC
17:47:15 KST

- The U.S. Air Force awarded BK Manufacturing Co. a sole-source contract worth up to $28 million for AIM-120X and CATM-120X missile wings and fins.
- The contract runs through August 27, 2031, with no funds obligated at the time of the award.
Somebody has to build the little wings and fins that steer America’s main air-to-air missile, and this week that job went to a small manufacturer most people have never heard of.
BK Manufacturing, based in the small town of Arab, Alabama, just picked up a U.S. Air Force contract worth up to $28 million to build wing and fin components for the AIM-120X and CATM-120X, both part of the AMRAAM missile family. The Air Force didn’t put this out for competitive bidding. It went straight to BK Manufacturing as a sole-source deal, meaning no other company got a shot at it.
AMRAAM is the missile that’s been doing the heavy lifting for American fighter jets since the early 1990s. The whole point of it is beyond-visual-range combat: a pilot can fire before the enemy aircraft is even visible to the naked eye, and once the missile is away, it flies itself the rest of the way in using its own onboard radar. Pilots call that “fire and forget.” It’s flown in the Gulf War, Kosovo, the fight against ISIS, and more recently it’s shown up in the skies over Ukraine and during the 2025 incident when Russian drones crossed into Polish airspace.
Not every missile covered by this contract will ever be fired for real, though. The CATM-120X piece of the deal is for training rounds, essentially AMRAAMs with no explosive warhead, used so aircrews and ground crews can practice loading and handling procedures without burning through the expensive live weapons.
The contract itself runs all the way out to August 2031, but here’s the interesting part: as of right now, zero dollars have actually been spent. The Air Force set an upper spending limit of $28 million and will hand out individual orders as parts are actually needed, rather than committing to a bulk purchase up front. That’s a fairly standard way the Pentagon buys smaller components like this, spreading orders out over years instead of writing one big check.
The Air Force Life Cycle Management Center at Robins Air Force Base in Georgia is running the contract. So far, the Air Force hasn’t said how many sets of wings and fins it actually expects to buy under this deal.

The US has a secret plan for Libya. It will backfire
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-29
08:47:12 UTC
17:47:12 KST

The US has a secret plan for Libya. It will backfire
For nearly a year, Massad Boulos, US President Donald Trump’s senior advisor on Arab, Middle Eastern, and African Affairs, has aggressively pursued a diplomatic circuit connecting Tripoli, Benghazi, Paris, Rome, and Abu Dhabi. His primary objective is to push a transactional political settlement designed to resolve Libya’s administrative paralysis and the internal west-east divide by formalizing an alliance between the country’s rival power centers.
Taking shape behind closed doors since last September, first in Rome then across other capitals, the core mechanism of this US-brokered blueprint is a restructuring of the executive presidency: placing Saddam Haftar (Commander of Ground Forces in eastern Libya and deputy to his father) at the helm of a reformed Presidential Council, while keeping Abdul Hamid Dbeibeh as Prime Minister. Rather than fostering a democratic transition, the framework accepts state fragmentation as a permanent reality, securing the Dbeibeh administration in the west and the Haftar family network in the east as a dynastic duopoly.
To pave the way for such initiatives, Washington has leveraged preliminary milestones. In April, Boulos helped broker a record 190 billion dinar unified budget agreement – the first in Libya since 2014. At the same time, joint military maneuvers were executed in Sirte under AFRICOM’s Flintlock exercises, bringing together east and west forces alongside participation from Italy and over a dozen African nations.
Treating this unwritten transactional design as a national settlement fundamentally misreads the crisis.
Rather than establishing a legally grounded framework for general elections or dismantling entrenched militia networks, the arrangement codifies an elite duopoly. By relying on temporary financial distributions and supervised unified military drills to broker a top-down truce, Washington is mistaking a fragile pact between ruling families for actual state-building – guaranteeing that Libya’s hydrocarbon wealth continues to line the pockets of an entrenched cartel at the expense of its people.
Crucially, the Boulos initiative operates as an unwritten diplomatic push devoid of statutory grounding. By ignoring the foundational UN Security Council resolutions that grant legal mandate to external mediation, Washington’s ad-hoc gamble lacks the institutional backing required to bind local actors. Furthermore, the plan offers no long-term enforcement mechanisms. It relies on current US political backing and provides no protocol if the newly installed executives simply refuse to vacate power after the proposed two-to-three-year interim.
Without a universally accepted arbiter to compel compliance, the initiative risks becoming a dangerous power trap, leaving Libya vulnerable to renewed confrontation the moment external priorities shift.
This bilateral push also directly collides with the ongoing UN-led mediation process overseen by the UN Support Mission in Libya (UNSMIL). While the UN’s incremental track has certainly been slow and struggled to deliver a breakthrough, it remains anchored in UNSC mandates and operates through recognized, albeit heavily discredited, domestic institutions – such as the House of Representatives and the High Council of State. By attempting to bypass these constitutional bodies in favor of an elite shortcut, Washington risks completely undermining the delicate institutional consensus UNSMIL has spent years attempting to build. Replacing a broad-based, rules-driven process with a fast-tracked bargain creates a parallel route that further fragments international diplomatic efforts and deepens institutional paralysis.
The fundamental flaw of the American initiative lies in its false equivalence between the political dynamics of eastern and western Libya. While the eastern region serves as a traditional stronghold for the Haftar family, western Libya presents a fragmented power balance. Prime Minister Dbeibeh exercises no absolute command over the west, operating instead through fragile networks and pacts with autonomous armed factions, including within his own home city of Misrata.
This domestic resistance exploded into the open on July 5, when Misrata’s military and civic coalitions issued a condemnation of Washington’s plan, rejecting any settlement that involves the Haftar family. When Boulos visited the commercial hub on July 7 to smooth over opposition, local elders and municipal leaders refused to endorse an unwritten deal. Dbeibeh seems to lack the authority to deliver western compliance, and a pact struck in foreign capitals cannot override the deep-seated opposition of the ground forces and local communities required to sustain it.
Beyond its immediate political flaws, the broader framework is viewed domestically as a mechanism designed to help the Haftar and Dbeibeh networks establish a permanent political dynasty, dividing the country’s state apparatus and economic assets strictly between themselves. Crucially, the plan contains no timelines for when, or if, national legislative and presidential elections ever take place.
This omission ignores the aspirations of the more than 2.8 million registered Libyan voters who picked up their electoral cards for the shelved 2021 polls, eager to restore popular legitimacy to their governance institutions. Instead of creating a bridge toward a democratic transition, Washington’s framework codifies the status quo, deferring the Libyan people’s right to choose their own leaders.
Another major obstacle confronting Boulos’s initiative is that Libya remains a deeply contested theater for regional heavyweights – notably Ankara, Cairo, Abu Dhabi, and Moscow – who are navigating the proposed deal with extreme caution while protecting their security, military, and economic footholds. Türkiye maintains a military presence across key bases in the west alongside extensive commercial interests, Egypt views eastern Libya as a non-negotiable border security perimeter, the UAE manages influential financial and energy networks, and Russia retains military and diplomatic leverage across both divides. While Washington seeks to build momentum through parallel diplomatic and economic pressure, these actors seem to have signaled (based on fragmented media reports) a reluctance to reshape their strategies. Instead, they are maintaining a wait-and-see stance, preferring to withhold definitive positions until an official plan is formally presented.
Even if Washington succeeds in cobbling together a consensus between Tripoli and Benghazi, the Boulos framework faces a structural barrier: the UN Security Council. Because the initiative deliberately bypassed the UN-facilitated inter-Libyan tracks, any final arrangement must eventually seek international legitimacy and statutory backing through a new UN resolution to replace existing mandates. In the Security Council, however, Russia holds a permanent veto. By ignoring Russian interests and attempting to unilaterally reorder Libya’s security architecture, Washington has designed a blueprint that can be easily decapitated at the UN table, leaving its Libyan signatories legally unsanctioned.
The core failure of the Boulos initiative is that it approaches Libya like a corporate asset undergoing restructuring rather than a sovereign state in desperate need of constitutional legitimacy. Instead of fulfilling the transition to democracy promised in 2011, when the US and its NATO allies intervened only to trigger a relentless free fall ever since, this diplomatic blueprint manages the ruins. It substitutes a genuine political horizon with an arrangement among the ruling elite. For the Libyan public, abandoned without peace or popular sovereignty, it is a pause that leaves the country vulnerable to renewed warfare the instant the bargain fractures.

How bird flu could spread among Australia's mammals, and what it means for your pets
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-29
08:44:00 UTC
17:44:00 KST

In brief
- A seal, a dolphin and a fox have tested positive for H5 bird flu in South Australia.
- Experts share advice on protecting pets and wildlife as the outbreak grows.
Bird flu has begun its spread beyond birds in Australia, with cases confirmed in three different mammal species since last weekend.
On Friday, Australia's chief veterinary officer, Beth Cookson, said H5 bird flu had been confirmed in a red fox found in metropolitan Adelaide, marking the first in a land mammal in Australia.
A dead dolphin found on South Australia's Fleurieu Peninsula also tested positive this week, days after a long-nosed fur seal found dead at Beachport became the country's first mainland mammal case.
How does bird flu spread in mammals?
Bird flu has been detected in many different mammals on other continents, including cats and dogs, farm animals, dolphins, seals, foxes, tigers, leopards and polar bears.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
Infected birds spread the virus through droppings, feathers and other bodily fluids. It can also be transmitted via contaminated clothing, footwear, equipment and vehicles.
Under favourable conditions, the virus can survive in the environment for months, Australian government authorities have said.
While the virus primarily spreads from infected birds, there is evidence it can also spread between some mammals, including during outbreaks in seals and dairy cattle overseas.
Among scavengers like foxes and cats, infections have been linked to eating or interacting with bird carcasses.
Cookson said there was no evidence of mammal-to-mammal transmission of the virus in Australia.
"This detection in a fox is a good reminder that people and their pets should avoid sick or dead wildlife," Cookson said on Friday.
"Although this is a concerning development, it is not unexpected given that H5 bird flu has been detected in other wildlife in areas where there are high levels of infection in wild birds."
She said the risk to human health remains low.
Which Australian mammals are most at risk?
The government's H5 bird flu risk assessment ranks multiple dolphin, seal and sea lion species among Australia's most vulnerable native mammals, and experts fear the virus could have devastating consequences for endangered species such as the Australian sea lion.
Seal populations around the world have proved particularly vulnerable to bird flu outbreaks.
The virus decimated southern elephant seal populations on Heard Island after reaching the Australian sub-antarctic territory last year, killing an estimated 75 per cent of pups.
Jane Younger, senior lecturer in Southern Ocean vertebrate ecology at the University of Tasmania, said it was "devastating news for wildlife" that bird flu had been detected in a mainland Australian mammal.
"My biggest concern now is the endangered Australian sea lion, which is found nowhere else in the world," she said.
"Infected and dying seabirds have already been found at important sea lion breeding sites around Kangaroo Island. If the virus enters a breeding colony, there is no way to stop it spreading."
She called for intensive surveillance of seal and sea lion colonies, rapid genome sequencing of mammal cases and an urgent investigation of whether targeted vaccinations could help protect certain populations.
South Australian Environment Minister Emily Bourke said last week that her state would assess the possibility of importing an experimental US vaccine for use among mammals in Australia, but warned that vaccines for mammals such as cattle and cats being developed overseas are yet to be approved by authorities.
The use of vaccines in birds is further advanced, with Australian officials saying last year that a H5 vaccine had been procured and authorised for use in particular rare, protected or valuable bird populations.
Victoria is currently vaccinating thousands of little penguins, which are a popular tourist attraction.
Should we be worried about our cats and dogs?
Bird flu infections have been reported in domestic cats and dogs overseas, though the Australian government says such infections are uncommon and usually occur through contact with infected birds.
Symptoms may include fever, lethargy, decreased appetite, red or inflamed eyes, discharge from eyes and nose, coughing and sneezing, and tremors.
Cat owners should be particularly mindful, Robyn Alders, an animal influenza expert and honorary professor at the Australian National University's Crawford School of Public Health, told SBS News.
Overseas, cats infected with the virus have experienced a high mortality rate.
She suggests keeping cats indoors, especially in areas where bird flu cases have been confirmed, and keeping dogs on a leash when walking.
The virus can also be spread through contaminated food and water, so experts recommend keeping pets' bowls inside or out of reach of wild birds.
Australians visiting wetlands, beaches, farms or wildlife areas are advised to observe wildlife from a distance, avoid contact with sick or dead animals, and to clean footwear and equipment with detergent or disinfectant.
Alders suggests that pet owners who go for walks in areas where sick or dead animals have been found could consider keeping a separate pair of walking shoes that they always disinfect.

Himalayan flood sparks concern among Nepalese and Tibetans in Switzerland

Himalayan flood sparks concern among Nepalese and Tibetans in Switzerland
The flash flood in the Himalayas has caused widespread distress among Nepalese and Tibetan communities in Switzerland, representatives of the two communities told the Keystone-SDA news agency on Friday.
The images of the devastating flash flood offered little cause for hope, Markus Ruckstuhl, president of the Swiss-Nepalese Society (SNS), told Keystone-SDA.
More
Nepal and the Himalayas, the agony of glaciers on the roof of the world
On Wednesday, a huge surge of mud and rock carved a path of destruction along the Bhotekoshi River. Bridges were swept away, dams damaged and homes engulfed by mud within seconds, dramatic video footage showed.
Waiting for news of loved ones
The wider community has also been left in shock. The Nepalese community in Switzerland is small and close-knit, with many people knowing one another, Ruckstuhl said on Friday. In his view, those ties are a source of strength. “People look out for each other,” he said, “even in difficult times.”
+ Himalayan nations can no longer ignore an environmental time bomb
Ruckstuhl said he personally knows around five people living in Switzerland who have been affected by the floods, either directly or indirectly. “We know people from the region,” he said. “Some have lost family members, friends or their homes, while others are still waiting for news of loved ones.”
Emergency relief efforts in Nepal appear to have begun swiftly and professionally, according to Ruckstuhl. The SNS plans to launch a fundraising appeal in the coming days.
Shockwaves through the Tibetan community
The news has also sent shockwaves through the Tibetan community, Nyma Schneider of the Tibetan Youth Association in Europe told Keystone-SDA. “There are people in Switzerland who come from the affected area,” said the organisation’s co-president.
More
Why the Swiss are leading efforts to track melting glaciers
Alongside the personal losses, there is also deep uncertainty. Unlike in Nepal, very little information is emerging from the Tibetan side of the border. While relatives in Nepal can be contacted, there has been virtually no news from Tibet. “Information isn’t getting out and aid isn’t getting in,” Schneider said. “That’s frightening.”
The morning prayer service at the Tibetan Buddhist monastery in Rikon, near Zurich, took on particular significance as it was held just hours after the disaster. During the ceremony, prayers were offered for the swift and safe rebirth of those who died in the floods.
No way home after floods
Schneider said he has been in touch with Tibetans in the affected area. One of his friends is currently stranded in Nepal and unable to return home. “The main road he had planned to take by bus simply no longer exists,” he said. The flight to India cost his friend his entire savings.
More
Why melting glaciers affect us all
Schneider attributes the scale of the disaster to what he says has been insufficient environmental protection by the Chinese state in Tibetan regions since 1959.
“Climate-related disasters like this keep happening in Tibet,” Schneider said. He called for an urgent monitoring programme and an effective early warning system under Tibetan sovereignty.

08:40:00 UTC
17:40:00 KST

Ain Hanschmidt: The economy's glass is half full
Not long ago it seemed that the economic downturn and high cost of living had no intention of easing, and that the most painful and bleak records in the economy would soon be set. Now, fresh statistics inject a measure of optimism, writes Ain Hanschmidt in a commentary originally published in the Employers' Manifesto 2026.
The economy grew faster in the first half of 2026 than the euro area average, inflation is calming, and investors have become more confident than before — they are no longer quick to sell their businesses and leave. For the first time in a long while, dialogue has re‑emerged between the government and entrepreneurs.
Thus, several proposals formulated four years ago in the Estonian Employers' Confederation manifesto have already been implemented or are in the process of being implemented.
For example, the state is rapidly reducing bureaucracy that suffocates entrepreneurship; the shortage of workers with necessary skills is being eased by more flexible employment relationships and simpler hiring of foreign workers. There is now a responsible party for ensuring a competitive electricity price — crucial for business — and the state has accelerated planning procedures. These are critically important and commendable changes for economic development.
It is equally true that government spending continues to grow faster than the economy. There is no alternative: the state must bring its expenditures under control as quickly as possible and declare a period of tax peace — no new taxes or increases in the tax burden for the next four years. Tax hikes made during a shrinking economy produced the opposite result: they raised prices and reduced the competitiveness of our companies.
We need a longer view and greater ambition: Estonia's economic policy must be as bold, radical, and pragmatic as it was in the 1990s. Fine‑tuning will not take us forward, and in recent years we have lost much of the success and competitive advantages we once gained.
The state's long‑term strategy Estonia 2035 sets the goal of raising productivity to 110 percent of the EU average. As employers, we support this, because Estonia's future success depends on productivity growth. But to achieve this goal, we must begin developing twice as fast — what has been done so far, and simply continuing it, will not get us there. We must set a clear target and begin working toward it both in business and in government, and cooperate effectively.
At the same time, we must improve our position in the international investor community. It may sound unbelievable, but for investors Estonia still sits in the lowest category — a frontier market. This means that a large share of global investment capital never reaches us.
Although the country's credit rating is good — A+ — our aim must be the highest rating, AAA, and a place among developed markets. This sends a signal that it is safe to operate here long‑term, makes borrowing cheaper for companies and individuals, and as the economy grows, wages rise as well.
These issues are not merely economic questions, because only a successful, growing, and competitive economic environment can fulfill the main purpose of the Constitution — to ensure the preservation of the Estonian nation, language, and culture.
Eighty‑five percent of the state's revenues come from consumption and labor taxes. The collection of these taxes into the state budget depends on how high the wages paid by Estonian companies can be. That, in turn, depends on how competitive our companies and economic environment are.
On 7 March 2027, Estonians will again elect members of parliament whose choices and decisions will determine our future success. Leaders who will bear responsibility for setting direction and driving bold change.
We expect the newly mandated politicians to answer questions such as: What is the plan for fixing the state's finances? How will we solve the labor shortage crisis in a society with an aging and shrinking working‑age population? How can we turn educational knowledge into business competitiveness? How can we fund healthcare in a way that is affordable for society and increases healthy life years? How can we support companies' innovation leap? And what conditions can we offer in Estonia to create a competitive environment that drives economic growth?
The Employers' Manifesto helps answer these questions through the views of Estonia's top economic leaders and specialists, outlining not only the challenges ahead but also a set of solutions and proposals.
Their goal is singular: to improve the well‑being of Estonian people through a better economic environment.
Decisive choices lie ahead, and action must be taken with statesmanship. The Employers' Confederation is ready for this — in both words and deeds.
We await a new government and parliament that understand the importance of the decisions to be made in the coming years and are ready to take responsibility for putting Estonia's economy and people's well‑being on a firm path of growth. Employers stand ready for cooperation and joint effort.
--
