China Focus: Waste to wonder: Porcelain's second life in Jingdezhen
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-29
11:22:40 CST
12:22:40 KST

NANCHANG, Aug. 29 (Xinhua) -- Sleek, colorful, and artfully crafted, the ceramics lining the shelves of a shop in Jingdezhen's Taoxichuan art district reveal little about their surprising beginnings: piles of broken porcelain once bound for the landfill.
The brand, XUN, which means "recycling," turns discarded porcelain into vases, planters, tableware and other ceramic products by sorting, crushing and purifying the waste before reformulating and firing it into new ceramic material.
"We started the brand because we wanted to give waste porcelain a second life," said Lan Lan, the shop's owner and a co-partner in the brand. "Once it is made into a new product, you can hardly tell it was recycled. It's safe, durable and even adds a distinctive touch by retaining some porcelain particles in the finished pieces."
XUN also uses sand-mold 3D printing to shape recycled material into larger decorative pieces. Its products are showcased annually at the China International Import Expo and Canton Fair, with strong sales in Europe and the Americas.
"We aim to tackle the problem of ceramic waste by shifting from taking more from nature to making better use of what we already have," she said. The brand showcases an approach that addresses the problem at its root while giving the porcelain industry a new lease on life.
This shift may be modern, but the impulse behind it taps into a much older instinct. In Jingdezhen, China's porcelain capital, giving broken porcelain a second use is a habit centuries in the making.
For generations, broken porcelain shards, spent saggers and worn-out kiln bricks were used to fill waterways, raise ground levels and build walls and foundations, turning waste from the kilns into part of the city's infrastructure.
Even the city's street names still carry the memory. Xianong, or "lower alley," marks the ground that was once reclaimed from the river using discarded porcelain -- a linguistic fossil of how waste once shaped the land beneath people's feet.
Ceramic waste was also packed beneath streets to create porous layers that allowed rainwater to seep into underground channels, helping the flood-prone city manage runoff.
By 1990, Jingdezhen had more than 90,000 meters of sewers, including over 6,000 meters of arched channels built with discarded kiln bricks. One drainage channel laid in 1914 remains in use today.
The city's centuries-old porcelain landscape gained global recognition in July, when Jingdezhen Handicraft Porcelain Industry Sites were inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List, becoming China's 61st World Heritage site.
That tradition of reuse now faces a new challenge. Official data shows that Jingdezhen produces up to 90,000 tonnes of discarded porcelain each year, much of which ends up dumped or buried.
"Ceramic waste does not readily decompose and can pose long-term environmental risks if not properly handled," said Zhang Jingjing, vice president of Jingdezhen Ceramic University. "Recycling the waste into new materials through crushing and reformulation is currently the most effective way to reduce its environmental impact."
A growing number of businesses and designers are doing just that.
Yi Design, a startup, turns discarded ceramics into reusable materials for architecture and art design. Its permeable brick, made from more than 90 percent recycled porcelain, is well-suited to "sponge city" projects designed to ease urban flooding and heat. The brick won an iF Design Gold Award in 2022.
Such practices are now finding institutional backing. In 2024, Jingdezhen launched a "zero-waste city" initiative, urging ceramic makers to cut waste at the source through technological upgrades while pushing for broader, higher-value uses of discarded porcelain.
"Waste porcelain has long been a bottleneck to the green development of the ceramic industry," said Tong Xiwei, an official with the ecology and environment bureau of Jingdezhen. "We are working to reduce, recycle and safely manage solid waste while fostering new zero-waste models across Jingdezhen's ceramic industry."
Tong added that the effort extends beyond factory walls, encouraging businesses, communities and residents to embrace greener ways of producing and living.
In July, China released a plan to advance the development of the country's circular economy during the 15th Five-Year Plan period (2026-2030), aiming to basically establish a high-quality development system for the recycling economy by 2035. As part of the efforts, the plan calls for stronger waste collection and recycling networks, as well as technological upgrading and industrial innovation.
For Lan Lan, the momentum feels like something Jingdezhen has been doing all along: finding a place for what its kilns leave behind.
She hopes that every piece of waste porcelain -- like the shards once packed beneath Jingdezhen's streets a century ago -- eventually finds its way home. "Nothing is truly discarded. It's simply waiting for its next form." ■

Multipolar Eurasia? Here is why India sticks with the SCO
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-29
02:57:52 UTC
11:57:52 KST

Multipolar Eurasia? Here is why India sticks with the SCO
Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi will be attending the Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) summit in Bishkek starting Sunday as the bloc enters its 25th year in 2026. It marks a significant milestone for an institution that has evolved from a narrowly defined regional security grouping into one of the important multilateral platforms across Eurasia.
Established in 2001 by China, Russia and four Central Asian states (Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan and Uzbekistan), the SCO was initially driven by concerns regarding ‘Three Evils’ – terrorism, separatism and extremism.
However, its agenda later expanded to encompass trade, connectivity, energy, development, digital cooperation and people-to-people exchanges. Its geographical and political weight has also increased substantially, particularly following the admission of India and Pakistan as full members in 2017 and the subsequent inclusion of Iran and Belarus.
The 25-year milestone, therefore, provides an opportunity to assess the SCO not merely in terms of its institutional longevity, but from the perspective of India’s evolving Eurasian strategy.
From observer to member
When the SCO was just established, India was an outsider to the organization and New Delhi initially viewed the emerging Eurasian grouping from the margins. However, in early 2000s, India was increasingly concerned about terrorism, the Afghanistan crisis, energy security, Eurasian connectivity and engagement with the newly independent Central Asian republics.
India subsequently moved from cautious distance to institutional engagement with the SCO. India, Iran and Pakistan were given observer status at the 2005 Astana Summit. In 2005, Indian External Affairs Minister Natwar Singh framed India’s interests in the SCO as anti-terrorism efforts, greater economic cooperation and people-to-people contacts like the ancient Silk Route era, while also emphasizing a shared Asian identity.
Later, India formally applied for full SCO membership in 2014 and was admitted in 2017.
Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi, while speaking at the 2017 SCO Summit, highlighted that the fight against terrorism, climate change, connectivity, peace, and stability in Afghanistan were India’s priorities within the SCO.
The fact that both of India’s two major milestones in the SCO, observer status in 2005 and full membership in 2017 were formalized at Astana summits does provide an interesting indicator of the special place Kazakhstan occupies in India’s SCO journey, which has been symbolically significant and diplomatically supportive. Astana marked both the beginning and the culmination of India’s institutional journey in the SCO.
India’s SCO engagement became considerably more regular following full membership in 2017. PM Modi has personally participated in nine SCO Heads of State summits, including three virtual participations in 2020, 2021 and 2023.
India has hosted the SCO Heads of State Summit only once, in July 2023, in a virtual format. This decision reflected the difficult political environment surrounding the SCO at that time. With India simultaneously managing tensions with China and Pakistan and navigating the diplomatic complications surrounding the Russia-Ukraine conflict, New Delhi chose to minimize the risks of a potentially contentious leaders’ meeting.
During India’s presidency, New Delhi attempted to broaden the SCO’s agenda by promoting cooperation in areas such as start-ups and innovation, digital transformation, traditional medicine, science and technology, youth empowerment and shared Buddhist heritage. This reflects India’s desire to prevent the SCO from becoming a mere security organization and transform it into a platform for developmental and technological cooperation among Eurasian countries.
Why India is at the SCO
India remains committed to the SCO institutionally, while calibrating the level of political engagement according to its broader strategic interests. It uses the organization as one platform within a larger network of partnerships.
India simultaneously participates in the SCO, BRICS, QUAD, G20, I2U2 and other mechanisms. Consequently, its SCO engagement is best understood through the lens of strategic autonomy and multi-alignment, rather than bloc politics.
For New Delhi, the SCO is primarily a pragmatic platform for engaging continental Eurasia, managing security challenges, preserving strategic autonomy and ensuring India’s presence in Central Asia. The biggest attraction of the SCO for India is geographical. It brings India into a forum with Russia, China and the Central Asian republics, alongside Iran, Pakistan and Belarus. Some of these countries play an important role in defining New Delhi’s economic and strategic engagement with Eurasia.
India does not want Eurasia to become the exclusive sphere of influence of any single power, and thus, a multipolar Eurasia suits New Delhi. Participation in the SCO allows India to remain politically present in a region where its physical connectivity remains relatively limited.
The SCO is the only multilateral platform which can facilitate India’s engagement with its two foremost security challenges – Pakistan and China. However, the degree of success in both cases has been different for New Delhi.
The SCO forced India and Pakistan into the same room, but institutional proximity has not produced meaningful bilateral rapprochement. The 2025 SCO defense ministers’ meeting illustrated this sharply. India objected to the failure of the joint statement to adequately address terrorism and the Pahalgam terror attack, and the meeting ended without consensus on the statement. The SCO has enabled contact but not reconciliation between India and Pakistan.
Engaging with neighbors
One of the expectations from India’s SCO membership was to dilute China’s power through a multilateral mechanism. The SCO, on different occasions, proved to be a platform for India-China crisis management and political signaling, even when the relationship remains largely competitive.
In October 2024, during the BRICS summit in Kazan, Russia, India and China firmed up a border pact in eastern Ladakh. It paved the way for Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi to travel to Tianjin, China, in August 2025 to attend the 25th annual SCO Summit, where he and Chinese President Xi Jinping held extensive discussions.
A similar diplomatic pattern occurred years prior. In September 2022, just one week before the SCO Summit in Samarkand, Uzbekistan, both militaries eased tensions in eastern Ladakh. The SCO has repeatedly provided a diplomatic setting in which India-China tensions have been managed or temporarily de-escalated.
However, India has not succeeded in using the SCO to overcome the China-Pakistan strategic partnership. China remains Pakistan’s main strategic partner and continues to support it on the issue of terrorism, the main bone of contention between India and Pakistan. The SCO, however, helps India to prevent Pakistan from monopolizing the regional diplomatic narrative and to ensure that China and Pakistan are not in an uncontested position to define the SCO agenda entirely on their own terms.
India has also used the SCO to deepen its engagement with the Central Asian countries, in line with its Connect Central Asia policy announced in 2012. The SCO provides India with regular interaction with Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan, Kyrgyzstan and Tajikistan at the leaders’, ministerial and bureaucratic levels. This is important because India’s bilateral engagement with Central Asia is otherwise constrained by the absence of a direct land corridor.
India-Russia Partnership
India–Russia relations are important for understanding how the SCO works, because Russia has traditionally acted as a balancing and moderating force between India and China, while India has used the SCO to pursue its Eurasian interests without accepting a China-dominated regional order.
India did not join the SCO simply because it wanted to enter a China-led organization. Its longstanding strategic partnership with Russia provided an important bridge into the SCO. Moscow has supported India’s participation in Eurasian multilateral institutions, including the SCO, BRICS and RIC. For India, presence of Russia reduces the perception that the SCO is merely an instrument of Chinese influence, as Moscow gives diplomatic space to India vis-à-vis Beijing.
India’s close relationship with Russia, therefore, contributes to a multipolar rather than a bipolar China–Russia structure within the SCO. This is particularly important for New Delhi because India would want to maintain the SCO as a forum in which states with differing interests can coexist without the dominance of any country.
Doubts over India’s SCO Membership
Critics have often raised doubts over India’s membership in the SCO, arguing that it offers India limited gains. India’s increasing focus on the Indo-Pacific, maritime security, supply chains and the Indian Ocean are also sometimes seen as working against its Eurasian strategy.
However, India has many reasons to stay in the SCO rather than depart the organization.
India’s exit from the SCO would surrender diplomatic space to China and further strengthen the China-Pakistan partnership against India in Eurasia, especially with regards to the issue of terrorism. Such a move could allow both Pakistan and China to dominate the narrative on regional security to India’s disadvantage. India’s current SCO engagement continues to emphasize counterterrorism and fighting extremism as its main interests in the organization.
The Central Asian countries have welcomed India’s presence in the region, as part of their multi-vector foreign policy. India’s SCO exit would harm their foreign policy balance and impact India’s engagement with them.
The SCO is also one of the institutional spaces where India can interact with Russia despite the growing complexity of the international system. Exiting the SCO could, therefore, unintentionally reduce one of the platforms through which India manages its simultaneously important but increasingly complicated relationships with Russia and China.
New Delhi’s foreign policy is increasingly characterized by multi-alignment and strategic autonomy. Leaving the SCO could be interpreted as India moving closer to the West. That would unnecessarily constrain its diplomatic flexibility.
What has India missed at the SCO so far?
India joined the SCO partly because it wanted greater access to Central Asia. But after 25 years, India’s physical connectivity with the region remains weak. Meanwhile, China’s Belt and Road Initiative has created extensive infrastructure connecting China with Central Asia and Pakistan. India has achieved institutional connectivity with Central Asia, but not physical connectivity.
India initially hoped that SCO membership would create an institutional mechanism through which terrorism could be addressed collectively. But Pakistan’s membership has made this difficult, as both India and Pakistan have fundamentally different positions on terrorism.
Afghanistan is arguably the area where the SCO could have enormous relevance. However, it has struggled to develop a coherent common policy after the Taliban’s return to power due to differences among member states.
India has an interest in using the SCO to address the Afghanistan–Central Asia–South Asia narcotics corridor, but India–Pakistan tensions and the absence of Afghanistan from effective SCO mechanisms have prevented the organization from becoming a truly effective regional counter-narcotics platform. The SCO has Afghanistan at the center of its security agenda, but Afghanistan remains at the periphery of its institutional architecture.
The Taliban government has expressed a keen interest in full SCO membership. India should consider supporting Afghanistan’s membership if Kabul meets the organization’s security and political requirements. This would not endorse the Taliban but serve India’s strategic interests by embedding Afghanistan in a broader Eurasian framework and preventing its future from being shaped predominantly by Pakistan.
The defense agreement signed on August 7, 2026 by Saudi Arabia, Türkiye and Pakistan has implications for the SCO, even though the pact is not an SCO initiative. The so-called Mecca Pact, which treats an armed attack on one party as an attack on all three, creates a security triangle involving one SCO member (Pakistan) and two SCO partners. This could increasingly influence discussions on terrorism, West Asian security, energy and connectivity within the broader SCO ecosystem.
The Mecca Pact does not directly threaten the SCO, but it could make the SCO’s internal geopolitics more complicated by bringing a Pakistan-led security alignment into an organization where India and Iran are already major stakeholders, negatively impacting the SCO’s consensus-based politics.
Bottom line
As the SCO completes 25 years, India’s experience demonstrates that the organization remains more useful as a platform for strategic engagement than as an instrument for achieving transformative outcomes. India has gained institutional access to continental Eurasia, maintained regular interaction with member states and used the SCO to advance counterterrorism, connectivity and development-oriented cooperation.
Yet, its limitations are equally evident: India has been unable to overcome the China-Pakistan strategic partnership, translate institutional connectivity into physical connectivity with Central Asia, or build a coherent collective response on Afghanistan and terrorism.
Nevertheless, these shortcomings do not make withdrawal attractive. For India, leaving would create diplomatic space for China and Pakistan while reducing one of the few forums where New Delhi can simultaneously engage Beijing, Moscow and Central Asia. The SCO, hence, remains relevant to India, not simply as a geopolitical bloc, but strategically – as an instrument to work towards a multipolar Eurasian order.

Judge deals blow to Trump moves to deport pro-Palestinian activists
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-29
02:49:27 UTC
11:49:27 KST

Judge deals blow to Trump moves to deport pro-Palestinian activists
- A federal judge ruled that the Trump administration’s use of immigration laws to deport pro-Palestinian student activists is unconstitutional and violates free speech rights.
- The judge criticised the State Department and DHS for targeting non-citizens based on their political views, emphasising the importance of free speech for all.
- The ruling follows similar cases and warns that suppressing speech disliked by the government threatens democracy and could affect anyone expressing dissenting opinions.
AI generated
A federal judge on Aug 28 ruled that laws that US President Donald Trump’s administration used to cancel visas and initiate deportation proceedings against non-citizen college students based on their pro-Palestinian advocacy and criticism of Israel are unconstitutional.
US District Judge Noel Wise in San Jose, California, in a blistering ruling chastised the US State Department and US Department of Homeland Security (DHS) for how they had deployed provisions of federal immigration law to target non-citizens for deportation for expressing views they wanted to suppress.
The judge, an appointee of Democratic president Joe Biden, said in the United States, free speech, including the freedom to criticise the government and its leaders, was evidence of the strength of the country’s democracy.
“That strength is diminished when members of our society – citizens and non-citizens alike – must self-censor and ‘behave’ or suffer the government’s retaliation,” she said.
The State Department and DHS did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
Wise’s ruling focused on how the Trump administration, from March 2025, began revoking visas and detaining non-citizens who engaged in pro-Palestinian advocacy on campus, starting with the arrest of Columbia University graduate Mahmoud Khalil, who is fighting separately to avoid being deported.
Those arrests formed the basis of a lawsuit that was filed in August 2025 by Stanford University’s student newspaper, The Stanford Daily, which alleged that some of its writers with student visas had refrained from covering pro-Palestinian student protests and topics related to the Middle East conflict as a result of the administration’s policies.
The newspaper’s lawyers argued that two provisions of the Immigration and Nationality Act that the administration relied upon to cancel student visas and initiate deportation proceedings violated the US Constitution’s First and Fifth Amendments as applied to constitutionally protected speech.
Those laws allowed Secretary of State Marco Rubio to render non-citizens deportable if he personally determined someone’s action “compromises a compelling foreign policy interest” and allowed him to revoke someone’s visa at his discretion.
Wise agreed with the newspaper, saying that when a non-citizen’s speech is the reason behind a visa revocation and deportation determination, “the government is singling out that speech for disfavoured treatment based on its viewpoint or content”.
Conor Fitzpatrick, whose group Foundation for Individual Rights and Expression represented the student newspaper, in a statement said the ruling “proves that free speech isn’t a privilege, but the inalienable right of every man, woman, and child”.
The ruling was similar to a decision in 2025 by Boston-based US District Judge William Young, who similarly found the administration had acted unconstitutionally by adopting a policy of revoking visas, arresting, detaining and deporting foreign students and faculty engaged in pro-Palestinian advocacy.
Wise in her ruling expressed concern the administration had moved on to target people for expressing other types of views it disfavoured, saying eventually the “targets may include anyone in the United States who exercises their freedom of speech to simply express opinions the government does not like”.
“This downward spiral is antithetical to our Constitution that recognises our right to speak freely,” she wrote. “Here you can simultaneously hate the content of a person’s speech and love the country that cherishes the freedom to allow it.” REUTERS

Europe only fourth on US security priority list – NATO envoy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-29
02:47:59 UTC
11:47:59 KST

Europe only fourth on US security priority list – NATO envoy
Europe only ranks fourth among Washington’s global security priorities, US envoy to NATO Matthew Whitaker has said, as President Donald Trump pushes the bloc’s members to take greater responsibility for their own defense.
Speaking to Newsmax on Thursday, Whitaker outlined Washington’s priorities under Trump’s national security strategy.
”The defense of the homeland is number one... The Western Hemisphere, where we live, [is] obviously equally important,” he said, followed by the Pacific. “Defending Europe is also a priority, but it’s in fourth place.”
Whitaker said the changing division of responsibilities within NATO would also benefit the US economically.
”Our European allies are taking over the conventional defense of the European continent,” Whitaker said. “And I think that’s good for the American taxpayers.”
The ambassador described NATO as being on a “new trajectory” under Trump, crediting the US president with pressuring other members of the US-led military bloc to dramatically increase defense spending.
Whitaker said European NATO members and Canada have spent an additional $139 billion on defense, including $60 billion on US-made equipment and ammunition.
At last year’s NATO summit in The Hague, members agreed to raise defense and security-related expenditure to 5% of GDP by 2035. Whitaker contrasted the new commitment with the bloc’s previous 2% target, which many members failed to meet.
”For 77 years our NATO allies have taken advantage of the United States’ strength,” Whitaker told Newsmax. “But now we’re going to be all equally strong.”
The Trump administration has repeatedly demanded that European NATO members shoulder a greater share of their own defense costs. The Pentagon is also reviewing the roughly 80,000 US troops currently stationed in Europe, with officials considering different options for Washington’s future military presence on the continent.

Muslim police recruits decline sharply under National Security Minister Ben-Gvir
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-29
02:41:47 UTC
11:41:47 KST

The number of Arab citizens, particularly Muslims and excluding Druze, joining the Israel Police has declined sharply during National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir’s four years in the position, according to police recruitment data obtained by Walla on Monday.
The decline comes despite an overall increase in police recruitment during the same period, according to data from the Ministry of National Security and the Israel Police.
This decline in Arab recruitment comes as violence in these communities, during the four years that Ben-Gvir has served as national security minister, has continued to reach new highs almost daily.
The Arab sector in Israel makes up about 21% of the country’s population, with Muslims accounting for more than 18%.
The figures indicate significant underrepresentation of a sector that makes up more than one-fifth of Israel’s population.
Officials in the Ministry of National Security attributed the decline to a directive issued by Ben-Gvir requiring all police candidates to meet the same minimum recruitment standards, including a Dapar score, a military aptitude rating, usually requiring a score of 4 out of 9, and knowledge of Hebrew.
According to ministry officials, an affirmative action policy introduced before Ben-Gvir took office was intended to increase Arab representation in the Israel Police and promote greater integration into the state. The policy allowed Arab candidates to be accepted even if their Dapar score was below the standard threshold or if they lacked Hebrew proficiency.
The officials said the policy was abolished after Ben-Gvir took over the ministry.
Police recruitment rises as Arab enlistment declines
According to police data, the Israel Police had 36,856 officers in 2025. That year, 3,294 new officers joined the force, including only 96 Muslims, two Bedouins and 12 Arab Christians.
This means that only 0.26% of police recruits in 2025 were Muslim, Bedouin or Arab Christian, a figure roughly 70 times lower than their share of the population.
The vast majority of new recruits joined the regular police force rather than the Border Police.
The Ministry of National Security has highlighted an increase in police recruitment over the past four years, attributing the rise to improved conditions for officers and a large-scale recruitment campaign on social media and other platforms.
The overall increase in recruitment has been driven by a rise in Jewish recruits, alongside a decline in the number of Arab recruits, excluding Druze, joining the police.
After a decline in Arab recruitment in 2019, and signs of recovery between 2020 and 2022, the trend has reversed again over the past four years.
According to police and Ministry of National Security data, 2,109 new officers joined the police in 2022, including 135 Muslims, six Bedouins and 48 Arab Christians.
In 2023, 2,778 new officers joined the force, including 165 Muslims, seven Bedouins and 59 Arab Christians.
In 2024, 3,814 new officers joined, including 143 Muslims, two Bedouins and 15 Arab Christians.
In 2025, 3,294 new officers joined, including 96 Muslims, two Bedouins and 12 Arab Christians.
During the first half of 2026, 2,276 people joined the police, indicating continued growth in overall recruitment. However, only 64 were Muslims, two were Bedouins, and seven were Arab Christians.
The figures do not include recruitment data from the Druze community, where enlistment rates are higher and have generally remained stable.
Ben-Gvir: 'You will continue talking, and we will continue working'
The shift in recruitment trends comes amid rising violence in Arab communities, as the government cancels dedicated budgets for the Arab sector and redirects funding toward other priorities and sectors. It also comes as Israeli society becomes increasingly polarized and calls against integrating Arabs into key state positions grow, particularly as elections approach.
Ben-Gvir’s office responded to the data by saying:
"Even when the number of recruited police officers has risen significantly, and thousands of new officers have been added, the media still has criticism. You will continue talking, and we will continue working."

US President Donald Trump said Friday that Washington finalized an agreement with Venezuela to secure majority control of more than 65 billion barrels of proven oil reserves.
 
“The United States of America has just entered into an agreement with the country of Venezuela on the biggest oil deal in world history,” he wrote on his social media platform Truth Social.
 
He credited Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth for working alongside Venezuelan Acting President Delcy Rodriguez to finalize the transaction. Rodriguez assumed the interim presidency in January after a US military operation captured President Nicolas Maduro.
 
Trump asserted that the deal was achieved through a partnership with private industry and would involve no cost to American taxpayers. He claimed the transaction more than doubles existing US oil reserves and will "substantially lower gas prices" for Americans in the long term, while promoting prosperity in the South American nation.
 
The deal will strengthen the rapidly evolving relationship between Washington and Caracas, said Trump.
 
Rubio said the deal is a "huge win" for both nations, and that it will bring nearly $100 billion in private investment to Venezuela.
Venezuelan 'revival'
 
Rodriguez characterized the agreement as a “historic milestone” that will catalyze the “nation's revival.”
 
She said in a statement that the initiative is a direct result of strengthening ties with Washington and will facilitate a massive flow of capital for the “recovery and reconstruction of strategic infrastructure” in the hydrocarbons industry.
 
Rodriguez said the pact involves the development of 17 strategic fields with a proven potential of 65 billion barrels. She projected that the deal would secure an investment of more than $100 billion and generate more than $209 billion in taxes for the country. The acting leader asserted that the contributions will promote "the energy security of our hemisphere" and provide "greater balance in international markets."
 
The Washington Post reported earlier that the administration is targeting a stake in 17 specific oil fields, several of which have suffered from years of neglect and lack necessary transport infrastructure.
 
Transferring control of natural resources to Washington could require changes to Venezuela’s Constitution due to strong domestic opposition, according to the report.
 
Despite the administration’s efforts to attract investment in the post-January status quo, Venezuelan oil production has increased by only about 200,000 barrels per day in the last year, according to The Washington Post.
 
US Energy Secretary Chris Wright is expected to travel to Venezuela next week.

High Court freezes legal proceedings against former IDF legal chief Tomer-Yerushalmi
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-29
02:41:28 UTC
11:41:28 KST

The Supreme Court temporarily froze the legal proceedings against the former Military Advocate General Maj.-Gen. (res.) Yifat Tomer-Yerushalmi, regarding her role in leaking a video alleging abuse of Palestinian prisoners at Sde Teman prison, after Likud MK Avichai Boaron and the right-wing Lavi organization requested an additional hearing on the matter.
This new ruling follows a ruling from three weeks ago in which the court said that there were no grounds for judicial intervention in the investigation into the affair and also ruled that there was no basis to intervene in the decision allowing the state attorney to decide on the charges in the case against Tomer-Yerushalmi.
The court further ruled that there was no reason to grant Justice Minister Yariv Levin additional time to appoint an oversight official for the investigation, which had recently concluded. The ruling cleared the way for the prosecution, led by State Attorney Amit Isman, to advance toward a decision in the case.
However, on Thursday, MK Boaron and Lavi submitted a request for an additional Supreme Court hearing, asking the court to reconsider its decision not to intervene.
The request for an additional hearing is based, among other arguments, on the minority opinion in the original petition, in which Supreme Court Justice David Mintz argued that the petition should have been partially accepted.
Judicial opinion: Initial investigation required oversight
Mintz argued that the clear underlying premise of the previous ruling was that the investigation required the appointment of an oversight and accompanying official due to the extraordinary sensitivity of the affair. The case involves allegations that the head of the IDF’s law enforcement system was involved in leaking investigative materials and providing false information to the court.
Mintz argued that as long as the investigation had not been conducted under proper oversight, it could not be said that the basis for determining the state attorney’s inability to handle the case had changed, and therefore the time had not yet come to reconsider the issue.
He also argued that the fact that police had exhausted, in their view, their investigative actions did not justify continuing the proceedings without examining whether the process was valid, even retroactively.
Justice Mintz emphasized that he was not ignoring the fact that his conclusion could open the door to prolonging the investigation process. However, he argued that the solution was not to disregard the previous ruling, but rather to issue an order requiring the minister to exercise his authority.
The petition stated: "This request extends far beyond the boundaries of the affair: In the Boaron case, it was determined that oversight of a sensitive criminal investigation such as this one is mandatory, and from this derived the recognition of the minister’s authority, the limitations on its exercise and the operative instruction that was issued with the agreement of the entire panel; the ruling that is the subject of this request determined that oversight is only an 'option.'"
"The two legal principles cannot coexist side by side; at the very least, the ruling raises fundamental and important questions that the honorable court itself has already found worthy of being examined by an expanded panel."
Grounds for an expanded panel of judges
The High Court must now decide whether to hold another hearing before an expanded panel of judges or determine that there are no grounds for one. Until that decision is made, Justice Dafna Barak-Erez temporarily froze the handling of the investigation file.
In a brief decision issued Friday, Barak-Erez wrote: "The request for a further hearing was transferred to my handling yesterday, Thursday evening. For the sake of caution and without taking a position at this stage, I order a stay of execution of the ruling that is the subject of the request, by freezing the current situation regarding the handling of the investigation file by the state attorney, until another decision is issued."
Until the High Court issues another ruling, proceedings in the military prosecutor affair remain frozen. No decision will be made on whether to file indictments in the case until then.

Seven ancient Parthian tombs unearthed in Iraq’s Kurdistan region amid survey of 6,500 sites

02:41:26 UTC
11:41:26 KST

Seven tombs dating back to the ancient Parthian Empire were discovered during a two-month-long excavation in Koy Sanjaq (Koya), Kurdish media network Rudaw reported earlier this month, citing the Kurdistan Region’s antiquities authorities.
The discoveries were reportedly made in the Khazna area, along the new Erbil-Koya road, carried out between late April and late June.
"One of the [tombs] contained a clay coffin with a small headless figurine of a pregnant woman,” Muhammad Lashkri, director of antiquities and heritage affairs in the Kurdistan Region of Iraq, told Rudaw.
Bracelets, earrings, and cosmetic items had been found alongside the figurine, according to Lashkri.
He added that the artifacts are now being stored at the antiquities and heritage directorate in Koya.
The Parthian Empire, also known as the Arsacid Empire, was centered in ancient Iran between 247 BCE and 224 CE. At the height of its power, the empire stretched from central-eastern Turkey to present-day Afghanistan and western Pakistan.
According to Lashkri, since 2009, around 6,500 archaeological sites have been recorded in over half of the Kurdistan region, with the help of foreign archaeological teams.
“Forty-five percent remains,” he told Rudaw, explaining that the delay in identifying more sites cocmes primarily due to political issues, and sites being located in border areas and disputed territories.
Lashkri described the technology used by the directorate to “accurately identify 75 percent of the sites,” including geographic information systems (GIS) and satellite imagery.
Many foreign missions unable to return due to US-Iran war
He explained that typically there are between 25 and 35 foreign archaeological missions surveying and excavating the region.
The missions include teams from France, Germany, the UK, the Czech Republic, the Netherlands, and Japan, and one from Harvard University that has been working at a site for over a decade, according to Lashkri.
He noted that many of the archaeological missions were unable to return in 2026 due to the war between Iran and the United States, and that “some teams are taking on new work, while others are completing their projects.”
“We need to turn our archaeological sites into a source of tourism revenue,” Lashkri told Rudaw, explaining the need for greater documentation of ancient landmarks and databases for long-term heritage management in the region.

Egypt unearths three previously unknown tombs from different eras at Bahariya Oasis cemetery
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-29
02:41:26 UTC
11:41:26 KST

Three previously unknown tombs were unearthed by an Egyptian archaeological mission during excavations at the Sheikh Soby site in the Bahariya Oasis, alongside a collection of ancient artifacts.
The tombs, whose discovery was announced earlier this month by the Egyptian Tourism and Antiquities Ministry, date to different periods of Egyptian history, including the Roman and Late periods.
The first tomb, dating back to the Late Period of Egypt (664 BCE until 332 BCE), is a rock-cut tomb carved into sandstone, believed to have been dedicated to a single family unit consisting of five individuals.
It is made up of a square-shaped shaft, approximately three meters deep, that leads to two burial chambers on its western and northern sides.
Inside the western, which itself is small and rectangular, archaeologists discovered a limestone sarcophagus resting in a recess on the chamber floor, containing a mummy covered in linen wrappings.
The placement of the sarcophagi in the chamber is consistent with the method of placing sarcophagi in Late Period tombs at the site, explained Mohamed Abdel Badi, head of the Egyptian Antiquities Sector at the Supreme Council of Antiquities.
In the larger northern chamber, archaeologists found four limestone sarcophagi, each containing a mummy covered with linen wrappings.
Two tombs date back to Roman period
The second tomb found at the site by the mission is an undecorated, staircase-style tomb and believed to date back the Roman period.
Badi noted that it consists of a small tunnel leading to a staircase made up of three steps, which end in a burial chamber. However, current archaeological evidence suggests that it had not actually been used for burial.
The third tomb, also thought to date to the Roman period, is a shaft-style tomb, made up of a tunnel leading to small, roofless hall that then breaks off into two chambers on its southern and eastern sides.
The hall is thought to have been used as a receiving room for the mummy before it was taken to its final resting place inside one of the tomb’s chambers, according to common burial practices during the Roman period.
Fragments of a ceramic coffin were found within the tomb’s southern chamber, while a limestone sarcophagus with parts of its lid missing was found in the eastern chamber.
Archaeologists also discovered four entrances set into the tomb’s entry tunnel, located on its astern, northern, and western sides.
Excavations at the eastern entrance revealed a side burial, where the deceased is interred in a lateral position, and an oval-shaped ceramic coffin that had been broken into several pieces.
The coffin’s lid was decorated with a raised depiction of a human face with clearly defined features.
Several other artifacts were found at the site, explained Professor Qutb Fawzi, head of the Central Administration of Cairo and Giza Antiquities, including a collection of pottery vessels, small bottles, and plates of various shapes and sizes, in addition to a number of offering tables made of limestone and sandstone.
A number of small terracotta statues used in religious practices as offerings (votives) and depicting motherly figures and stylized animal forms were also discovered at the site.
The discoveries provide new evidence on the history of the Bahariya Oasis, said Tourism and Antiquities Minister Sherif Fathy, who praised the ongoing efforts of both Egyptian and foreign archaeological missions operating in the region.
Uncovering more of Bahariya Oasis' history
Dr. Sabri Farag, who heads the archaeological mission at the site and serves as Bahariya Oasis’ director general of antiquities, confirmed that excavations at the site will continue in future seasons.
The hope, Farag explained, is to uncover more tombs that could reveal ongoing settlement of the site in antiquity and shed further light on the oasis’ inhabitants.
Notably, the Sheikh Soby site is home to a Late Period cemetery containing the tombs of Bahariya Oasis rulers and priests from that period, including the Temple of El-Bawiti.
The temple was built by the ruler of the Bahariya Oasis during the 26th Dynasty in honor of Pharoah Ahmose II (also known as Amasis II) who reigned between 570 - 526 BCE.
In 570 BCE, Ahmose II conquered Cyprus, the first pharoah do so since Thutmose III’s Bronze Age campaign. His reign there, however, was brief, as Cyrus the Great took the Mediterranean island from him in 545 BCE.

Guinea-Bissau votes on a stronger presidency: What’s at stake?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-29
02:38:27 UTC
11:38:27 KST

Guinea-Bissau votes on a stronger presidency: What’s at stake?
The proposed constitution would give the president more power and reshape parliament and elections.
Voters in Guinea-Bissau will decide on August 30 whether to approve a new constitution that would significantly strengthen the presidency and reshape the country’s electoral system.
The vote comes nine months after the military seized power and installed General Horta Inta-A Na Man as transitional president, and just more than three months before presidential and legislative elections scheduled for December 6.
Supporters of the reform say it would provide clearer lines of authority and help address years of political instability and disputes between state institutions. Critics argue that it would concentrate too much power in the presidency and have questioned the process through which the draft was produced.
The African Party for the Independence of Guinea and Cape Verde (PAIGC), one of Guinea-Bissau’s main opposition parties, has rejected the referendum and called for a boycott.
The referendum will determine whether the constitution approved by the National Transitional Council (CNT) enters into force and provides the framework for the country’s return to elected government.
Why is Guinea-Bissau changing its constitution?
The process began after the November 26, 2025, military coup.
Presidential and legislative elections had been held three days earlier. The military seized power while the electoral process was still under way, one day before the electoral commission was due to announce the presidential results.
Horta, then army chief of staff, became transitional president.
The transition charter established a National Transitional Council (CNT), which was given legislative powers during the transition. The council approved the proposed constitutional text on January 13, 2026.
Guinea-Bissau is a small Portuguese-speaking country on the West African coast, bordered by Senegal to the north and Guinea to the east and south. It gained independence from Portugal in 1974 and has experienced repeated coups and political crises since independence.
Under the existing constitution, Guinea-Bissau operates a semi-presidential system in which executive authority is shared between the president and prime minister.
The proposed constitution would substantially alter Guinea-Bissau’s existing semi-presidential system, giving the president significantly greater executive authority and reducing the prime minister’s role in government.
What would change?
Under the proposed constitution, the president would have greater control over the government, including the appointment and dismissal of the prime minister and members of the government.
The president would also chair the Council of Ministers and have the power to create or abolish ministries.
The proposed constitution would reduce parliament from 102 seats to 65 and cut the number of electoral constituencies from 29 to 12.
It would also introduce new requirements for presidential candidates.
Candidates would have to have lived permanently in Guinea-Bissau for the five years preceding an election. They would also have to pay a 50 million West African CFA franc deposit, or approximately $90,000.
Political parties sponsoring presidential candidates would need at least 5,000 members, including at least 300 in each region.
The proposed constitution would also establish a Constitutional Court.
Why is a stronger presidency controversial?
Guinea-Bissau’s political system has repeatedly been marked by disputes between presidents, prime ministers and parliament.
Supporters of the reform argue that giving the president clearer authority over the government could reduce institutional conflicts and make decision-making more effective.
Critics fear that concentrating executive authority in the presidency would weaken parliament and other checks on government, significantly altering the balance between the executive and legislature.
Critics have also raised concerns about the proposed reduction in the number of electoral constituencies, arguing that it could affect political representation and weaken parties that rely on strong local support.
The new financial and membership requirements have likewise drawn criticism from those who argue that they could make it harder for smaller political movements to contest presidential elections.
There is a separate dispute over how the constitution was produced.
The draft was prepared during a military-led transition rather than by a restored elected parliament. Opposition parties and civil society groups have criticised the process and questioned whether the drafting process was sufficiently inclusive.
Is the referendum about Horta Inta-A Na Man?
Horta has led the transition since the coup, but the referendum is not simply a vote on his political future.
The transition framework bars the transitional president and prime minister from running in the elections at the end of the transition.
The immediate issue is therefore what powers the next elected president will have.
If the constitution passes, the president elected in December would have considerably greater authority over the government than under the existing constitutional system.
Why does the timing matter?
The referendum comes before the presidential and legislative elections scheduled for December 6.
Voters will therefore decide the proposed constitutional framework before choosing the leaders who are expected to govern under it.
That means the next president and parliament could take office under rules drawn up during the military-led transition.
For the transitional authorities, the referendum is part of the process leading to a return to elected government.
For opponents, the timing raises the question of whether a military-led authority should determine fundamental political rules before elected institutions are restored.
What would a yes or no vote mean?
A yes vote would bring the proposed constitution into force, including stronger presidential powers, a smaller parliament, fewer electoral constituencies and new requirements for presidential candidates.
A no vote would reject the proposed constitution, leaving the question of constitutional reform unresolved.
At stake is not simply whether Guinea-Bissau adopts a new constitution, but how much power the presidency should hold when the country returns to elected government.

Security forces along the Line of Control (LoC) in Jammu and Kashmir have been put on high alert after fresh aerial activity originating from across the border was detected in the Poonch district.According to inputs from Army sources cited by news agency ANI, an unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) from Pakistan was detected at around 8:05 pm on Friday.
The drone was spotted hovering over the general area of Behrooti village in the Balakote area of Poonch's Mendhar sector, which falls under the operational area of responsibility of the 22 Jammu and Kashmir Rifles (22 JAK RIF).
Drone tracked towards Mangalnar-Dabrote axis
Military personnel tracked the UAV as it manoeuvred towards the Mangalnar-Dabrote side near the border before returning to Pakistan.Alert troops immediately logged the intrusion, following which the entire forward sector was placed under tight aerial and ground surveillance.Security forces launched the search operation at first light on Saturday in adjoining forward areas to check for any possible dropping of contraband or arms.Monitoring along the border remains active, and further official updates are awaited.
Similar drone sightings reported along border
The latest incident comes amid heightened security concerns along the India-Pakistan border and follows other suspected drone sightings reported in Jammu and Kashmir in recent weeks.
Earlier this month, security forces launched a search operation after a suspected Pakistani drone was spotted over forward villages along the International Border in Jammu and Kashmir's Kathua district.The BSF and Jammu and Kashmir Police conducted searches to ensure that no weapons, explosives or other material had been dropped.A suspected Pakistani drone was also spotted in Rajouri's Sunderbani sector last month, after which security forces carried out a search operation but found nothing suspicious.Earlier in June, Army personnel opened fire after spotting a Pakistani drone over forward posts in the Balakote sector of Poonch, forcing it to retreat towards Pakistan-occupied Kashmir.
Turkish military flights raise concerns
Notably, the latest incident also comes days after an unusual increase in Turkish military transport flights to Pakistan raised concerns in Indian defence circles.Open-source flight trackers recorded a surge in Turkish C-130 Hercules and A400M aircraft flights between August 19 and 21, with the planes landing at Pakistani air bases, including Nur Khan, Masroor and Murid.There was speculation in defence circles that the flights may have carried military hardware, including unmanned aerial systems and air-defence equipment, although neither Pakistan nor Turkey officially confirmed the nature or cargo of the operations.
Search operations underway in Udhampur, Kathua and Rajouri
Separately, security forces are carrying out massive search operations in the forested districts of Udhampur, Kathua and Rajouri following information about suspicious movement, according to news agency PTI.In Rajouri, another search operation was launched in Gaibas, Mithiyani, Mogla and Narla after villagers reported the movement of two suspected armed persons, believed to be terrorists.No contact with any suspected persons had been established so far, officials said.The latest incident in Poonch comes as security forces continue to maintain heightened surveillance along forward areas of Jammu and Kashmir.

The United States has struck a deal with Caracas that would give them control of some 65 billion barrels of Venezuela’s proven oil reserves, President Donald Trump has announced, while reviving the OPEC nation’s battered energy industry.
In a post on Truth Social, Trump said the “historic transaction more than doubles American oil reserves” and “will substantially lower gas prices for all Americans”.

TOKYO, Aug. 29 (Xinhua) -- Japan has officially entered the influenza season, the health ministry said Friday, marking the second-earliest start since record-keeping began in 1999.
In the week through Aug. 23, as many as 4,094 flu patients were reported by some 3,000 monitoring institutions nationwide. The average number per institution came to 1.11, topping the benchmark of 1 that indicates the onset of the flu season, according to the ministry.
By region, the southern prefecture of Okinawa logged the highest number of cases in the reporting week, at an average rate of 4.43 per institution, followed by Iwate and Aomori in the northeast with 2.10 and 2.08, respectively.
Except for 2023, when the number of flu cases was high all year round, 2009 saw the earliest start of the season, with cases exceeding the threshold in the week of Aug. 10-16.
The ministry called for people to take precautions against flu, such as washing hands, wearing masks and getting vaccinated. ■

Chinese researchers complete Earth-Moon two-way laser link test
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-29
10:31:09 CST
11:31:09 KST

BEIJING, Aug. 29 (Xinhua) -- Researchers have completed a laser communications test between Earth and the Moon, successfully verifying two-way high-speed laser link capabilities in orbit, the Technology and Engineering Center for Space Utilization (CSU) of the Chinese Academy of Sciences said on Friday.
After more than a year of in-orbit testing, the team established a two-way laser communication link across a distance of over 400,000 km, marking the expansion of China's space laser communications from near-Earth orbit to deep space.
Compared with traditional microwave communications, laser communications offer faster speeds, greater bandwidth, stronger security and more compact hardware. However, enabling laser communications across the Earth-Moon distance required overcoming three major challenges: beam alignment, signal weakness and transmission speed.
"Earth-Moon communication is like threading a needle from a thousand miles away," said Yang Lei, a researcher at the CSU and head of the laser communication test team. Given the extreme distance, minor satellite wobbles or ground atmospheric turbulence can cause laser beams to drift. A tiny angular deviation could translate into a kilometer-scale miss at the Moon's distance.
The team developed an innovative acquisition and tracking scheme that integrates corrections for orbital, atmospheric, and optical propagation delays, enabling ground and spaceborne equipment to maintain precise alignment while in motion.
After traveling 400,000 km back to Earth, the laser signal becomes so faint that ground telescopes receive only a few photons at a time. Moonlight, starlight and urban lighting add further interference -- akin to hearing the sound of a falling pin in a bustling market, the CSU said.
The researchers developed high-speed superconducting single-photon detection technology and high-sensitivity algorithms to extract valid communication signals from background noise.
To tackle the speed bottleneck, the team developed high-bandwidth signal processing technology and adopted special coding schemes to counter noise. The test achieved two-way communication rates of 1.25 Mbps uplink and 100 Mbps downlink.
With manned lunar landings and lunar research station construction on the horizon, future lunar exploration will generate massive volumes of observation images and scientific data that traditional communications bandwidth can no longer support. This Earth-Moon laser "information highway" will provide a new high-speed data transmission route for upcoming lunar missions, the CSU said. ■

China Focus: South China's Greater Bay Area deepens integration through tech collaboration
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-29
10:31:00 CST
11:31:00 KST

GUANGZHOU, Aug. 29 (Xinhua) -- About 30 years ago, when Hong Kong businessmen came to Dongguan, less than 100 kilometers away in the Pearl River Delta, they invested in the production of toys, clothing, and other low-value-added items that earned the city the nickname "world factory."
Today, scientists and young entrepreneurs in Hong Kong are once again heading to Dongguan, now an emerging innovative hub in south China's Guangdong Province, in search of research equipment and experienced talent.
This is more than a story of Dongguan's industrial upgrading. Across China's nine Pearl River Delta cities and two special administrative regions, which make up the Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao Greater Bay Area, collaboration among enterprises, universities, and research facilities has grown at an unprecedented pace. It has been fueled by technological innovation needs and supportive policies.
RESEARCH COOPERATION
Since the term of Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao Greater Bay Area was first mentioned in China's government work report in 2017, a series of experimental facilities and research institutions have been put into operation in the Pearl River Delta, enabling easier access for Hong Kong and Macao researchers to resources that were previously less available.
In Dongguan, one of the most iconic facilities is the China Spallation Neutron Source (CSNS) owned by the Institute of High Energy Physics of the Chinese Academy of Sciences, located near Songshan Lake on the city's outskirts.
Following Britain, the United States and Japan, the CSNS is the world's fourth pulsed neutron source facility, and the first in China. Spallation Neutron Source (SNS) is regarded as a more efficient and safe way to produce neutrons -- which are highly useful to material probes -- by using a process that sends high-energy ions into a heavy metal target.
For researchers based in Hong Kong and Macao, the CSNS has also become the closest facility to carry out material-related experiments since it began operation in 2018.
"We have cooperated with the University of Hong Kong, the City University of Hong Kong (CityUHK), the University of Macau and several other universities in the two regions, which followed the same process as mainland institutions in applying to use the facility," said Tong Xin, deputy director of the Spallation Neutron Source Science Center.
According to the center, researchers with seven Hong Kong and Macao universities have so far used the CSNS to conduct 131 research projects in fields such as high-entropy alloys, lithium-battery materials, polymer films and biomedicine.
The center also worked with Dongguan University of Technology and CityUHK to build China's first multi-physics spectrometer, which began operation in 2021 for use in various fields of materials science. In 2024, it signed agreements with eight universities in Hong Kong and Macao to jointly build the Southern Advanced Light Source. This synchrotron radiation light source can produce intense beams of light that enable detailed material probing.
"We expect to see the Southern Advanced Light Source operate complementarily with the CSNS in micro material probing, better serving the development of the Greater Bay Area," Tong said.
TECHNOLOGY COMMERCIALIZATION
As a close partner of the CSNS, CityUHK has worked with the Dongguan government to set up a new university near the facility in the Songshan Lake area. City University of Hong Kong (Dongguan), or CityUHK (Dongguan), was officially established in 2024.
One reason behind CityUHK's cooperation with Dongguan is the city's exceptional capacity to commercialize technologies from its strong manufacturing base, said Chiu Chi-yue, vice president of CityUHK (Dongguan).
"CityUHK has been leading Hong Kong universities in terms of the number of patents. At the same time, the commercialization of patents is not always easy in Hong Kong, but is relatively convenient here in Dongguan," he said.
Chiu noted that CityUHK (Dongguan) currently offers five undergraduate programs and 10 master's programs, including materials science and engineering, artificial intelligence (AI), and data science. All are of strategic importance for the development of the Greater Bay Area and the country.
Compared with traditional universities, CityUHK (Dongguan) places particular emphasis on fostering innovation and entrepreneurship, encouraging students to participate in faculty-led research early in their university studies.
Nearby, the university has found a perfect partnership with Xbot Park, a startup incubator in the Songshan Lake area, which has developed into an industrial cluster spanning research and commercialization.
Drawing on the Greater Bay Area's integrated supply chain, Xbot Park, established in 2014, has set up a so-called "shared factory." It collaborates with supply-chain service providers to offer startups support in trial production, project management, and other stages from an initial idea to mass production.
"The shared factory helps address core challenges facing startups, such as limited access to supply chains and weak bargaining power," said Yu Chunhua, who is in charge of Xbot Park's supply chain division.
The incubator has attracted innovative startups and companies across the Greater Bay Area. CYC Group, a Hong Kong company that develops electronic bikes, opened an office there in 2023.
Founder and CEO Jon Chan said the Dongguan office puts the company's supply chain close at hand and makes it possible to hire experienced engineers from the mainland -- talent that is now hard to find in Hong Kong.
According to Gao Min, dean of the Guangzhou HKUST Fok Ying Tung Research Institute, professional experimental laboratories and an abundant pool of skilled engineers are among the mainland's key advantages in helping Hong Kong and Macao commercialize technologies.
Founded by the Hong Kong University of Science and Technology in Nansha in 2007, the institute was Guangzhou's first scientific research institution with a Hong Kong background. It is currently the university's major mainland-based platform for technology innovation and commercialization.
"Only on the mainland can we find highly capable, yet not prohibitively expensive, engineers, who are demanded in large numbers for turning an original technology into an outstanding product," Gao said.
OVERSEAS CONNECTION
Meanwhile, research and production collaboration with partners in Hong Kong and Macao is helping enterprises in the Pearl River Delta expand more smoothly into overseas markets, according to local business leaders.
Guangzhou Pharmaceutical Holdings Limited, a leading traditional Chinese medicine (TCM) manufacturer, has set up a joint laboratory with the University of Macau and a factory in Macao. It also plans to build a modern TCM manufacturing center on Hengqin island in Zhuhai adjacent to Macao.
"The Hengqin facility will apply the most advanced international production standards to ensure its products are qualified for Hong Kong and Macao markets, and we hope they can subsequently reach Portuguese-speaking countries and other overseas markets," said Chen Jiehui, vice chairperson and general manager of the enterprise.
PCI Technology Group Co., LTD. (PCITECH), a Guangzhou-based enterprise that provides AI solutions for urban traffic management, established an R&D center in Hong Kong at the beginning of this year.
Wang Yuemiao, executive director of PCITECH's central research institute, said the center will be responsible for their products' adaptation to international technical standards and development for overseas markets, and serve as a platform to connect cooperation resources and expand markets.
Wang said that for mainland companies, Hong Kong can help them connect with overseas markets more efficiently with its mature international business networks and well-developed services in areas such as law, finance, and accounting.
Hong Kong also has the strength in helping companies adapt technologies and solutions already proven in China to international standards as well as regulations and business models in foreign markets, he said. "This will help projects realize long-term operations after entering overseas markets."
Yet Wang believes that mainland enterprises should see Hong Kong as more than a gateway. Instead, they should bring in the technological, industrial and application capabilities they have developed on the mainland and combine them with Hong Kong's strengths in research, internationalization and professional services.
"The goal is to actually integrate the mainland's industrial strengths with Hong Kong's international advantages, so that we can jointly build innovation capacity for global markets," he said. ■

BEIJING, Aug. 29 (Xinhua) -- A fast-moving chain mudslide, triggered by a high-altitude glacier collapse on the Nepalese side, has caused heavy casualties and left many missing at a port on the China-Nepal border in southwest China's Xizang Autonomous Region.
Rescuers immediately launched an all-out effort to reach the mudslide-hit port and search for the missing. Here is what we know about the deadly mudslide and the latest rescue and relief progress there:
-- As of 1 a.m. on Saturday, seven people were confirmed dead and 554 others remained missing at Gyirong Port, according to Xizang's emergency management department.
-- Xi Jinping, general secretary of the Communist Party of China Central Committee, Chinese president and chairman of the Central Military Commission, on Friday chaired a Party leadership meeting to deliberate and make arrangements on rescue and relief efforts.
Every effort should be made to search for and rescue all missing Chinese and foreign nationals, the meeting stressed, adding that China will provide emergency aid to the disaster-hit area in Nepal and carry out international rescue cooperation.
-- Premier Li Qiang inspected the damage and met with rescue workers. He called for swift repairs to damaged infrastructure, including roads, communications and power facilities, to restore access for rescue operations as soon as possible.
-- At about 4:30 p.m. on Friday, a six-member team from the Xizang Fire and Rescue Corps and a group of 15 members with a search dog from the Sichuan Fire and Rescue Corps arrived at Gyirong Port, becoming the first professional rescue teams to reach the core rescue area, the National Fire and Rescue Administration said.
-- More than 500 personnel from the Chinese People's Liberation Army (PLA) and the People's Armed Police Force, along with vehicles and military helicopters, have been deployed in the rescue operations. The first supply truck from the PLA Xizang Military Command has transported more than 9,000 items, including cotton tents, folding beds, and moisture-proof mats, to Gyirong Township.
-- China Anneng, a state-owned engineering and rescue enterprise, sent out a 15-member team on Friday with reconnaissance drones, portable satellite stations and mobile surveillance cameras to conduct on-site surveys of the blockage and surrounding roads to provide accurate data for efforts to address the barrier lake.
-- Relief operations remain severely hampered by complex and dangerous conditions on the ground, including dangers posed by an upstream barrier lake, heavy downpour, and cut-off roads and communication to the core area.
Xinhua reporters at the scene said the mudslide has devastated the river valley below. The silt layer in the core disaster area is more than 1.5 meters deep, posing a high risk of trapping anyone caught in it.
-- A total of 499 villagers and construction workers have been properly accommodated. Meanwhile, 555 affected tourists were evacuated and transferred under the coordination of cultural and tourism authorities. No tourists remain stranded.
-- The National Commission for Disaster Prevention, Reduction and Relief, together with the Ministry of Emergency Management (MEM), helped allocate 30,000 central relief supplies, including tents, stoves, clothing, quilts, folding beds and moisture-proof mats, to support evacuation, resettlement and relief work.
-- The Ministry of Finance and the MEM also allocated 120 million yuan (about 17.7 million U.S. dollars) in central natural disaster relief funds to support Xizang in carrying out emergency rescue and disaster relief operations. ■

Bayern makes flying start to Bundesliga title defense
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-29
10:30:24 CST
11:30:24 KST

BERLIN, Aug. 28 (Xinhua) -- Bayern Munich opened the 2026-27 Bundesliga season in commanding fashion as the defending champions beat VfB Stuttgart 5-1 at home on Friday.
Bayern broke the deadlock in the 21st minute when Joshua Kimmich delivered a corner into the area and Dayot Upamecano escaped Josha Vagnoman to head home.
Luis Diaz then had an opportunity to double the lead after Harry Kane, who was honored as Germany's Footballer of the Year before kickoff, sent him through, but Stuttgart goalkeeper Fabian Bredlow produced a strong save.
The visitors continued to threaten, and their persistence was rewarded seven minutes after the restart. After goalkeeper Manuel Neuer saved Jeff Chabot's header, Vagnoman met the rebound with a volley from 12 meters to make it 1-1.
Kimmich released Michael Olise with a pass through the Stuttgart defense and the Frenchman calmly restored Bayern's lead in the 55th minute.
Three minutes later, Vagnoman slipped while attempting to clear Alphonso Davies' delivery and inadvertently turned the ball into his own net.
Substitute Ismael Saibari then helped Bayern put the match beyond doubt, setting up Aleksandar Pavlovic in the 82nd minute before providing Diaz with the pass for the fifth in stoppage time.
"We gave everything from start to finish. Against Stuttgart, it is often the case that they start to tire midway through the second half. I'm very happy to have scored," said Pavlovic.
"Bayern had enough chances. If Fabian hadn't had such a good day in goal, we could have lost by an even bigger margin. Bayern just didn't stop. Unfortunately, the result ended up being so clear," said Stuttgart forward Deniz Undav.
Stuttgart hosts Cologne next Friday, while Bayern visits Schalke the following day. ■

How the Philippines missed a Korean gambling racket worth US$3.8 billion
Recent arrests expose a long-running crime network that flourished in the shadow of the nation’s Pogo scandal
But all the while, and with far less scrutiny, South Korean syndicates were building a parallel industry worth billions of US dollars – one that a spate of recent arrests suggests is still very much intact.
The most recent involved a 29-year-old Korean woman named Kim Young-sun, who authorities allege ran a network of 23 illegal online betting websites out of offices in Pasay and Quezon City that raked in an estimated 5.33 trillion won (US$3.8 billion) between November 2018 and this year.
But while investigators trained their attention on those operations, an analogous Korean criminal economy was expanding largely unnoticed. Kim’s arrest and a related case unsealed by police in Seoul just weeks earlier suggest this economy had grown far larger than most realised.

The senators, led by Arizona Sen. Ruben Gallego, said in a joint statement that development in E1 would sever East Jerusalem from major Palestinian population centers and make a contiguous Palestinian state harder to achieve. The statement also linked the move to rising settler violence in the West Bank, including against Palestinian Americans, and called on Israel to halt settlement expansion and take urgent action against settler violence.

The senators urged the Trump administration to use existing authorities, including targeted sanctions against individuals and entities, to address settlement expansion and violence.

Is Israel Really 'One Step Away' From Total Victory in Gaza?
Since the October 7 disaster and throughout two years of war, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has repeatedly declared that Israel was on the verge of achieving "total victory" over Hamas.
He has insisted not only that such a victory was attainable, but that Israeli forces were just weeks away from completing the mission.
Time and again, reality has proved otherwise.
Two months into the war, at a Hanukkah candle-lighting ceremony held at the Western Wall on December 7, 2023, Netanyahu declared: "We will soon achieve total victory over the forces of evil and restore security not only to the south but also to the north."
In August 2025, Netanyahu and his security cabinet set five objectives that had to be achieved before the war could end: disarming Hamas, securing the return of all the hostages, the complete demilitarization of Gaza, permanent Israeli security control including the perimeter zone, and the establishment of an alternative civilian administration that would be neither Hamas nor the Palestinian Authority.
A cease-fire agreement was signed last October, but as of August 2026, Hamas has not been defeated. The group has yet to disarm, and Israel continues to control a significant portion of the Gaza Strip – beyond the Yellow Line set out to separate the sides in the agreement – while striking Hamas targets and operatives almost daily, with dozens of Palestinians killed every month.
The IDF also assesses that Hamas has used the recent period to rebuild its capabilities.

Here are Friday's latest updates:
■ The IDF and Shin Bet said three Palestinians were killed in an airstrike near West Bank's Jenin, including Qais Bitawi, identified as a senior Hamas operative in the Jenin refugee camp. Palestinian reports said Israeli forces surrounded the strike site and delayed Red Crescent medics, confiscating medical equipment and ordering them to leave without evacuating the wounded.
