====================================================================================================

What will happen if Iran, Egypt, Bangladesh join Mecca Joint Defense Agreement? - analysis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
21:52:34 UTC
06:52:34 KST

Less than three weeks after Saudi Arabia, Turkey, and Pakistan signed the Mecca Joint Defense Agreement, attention is shifting from the pact’s collective defense pledge to a more consequential question: Who else might join it?
For more stories from The Media Line go to themedialine.org
Bangladesh has publicly expressed interest, Egypt says it is studying the prospect, and Iran, arguably the most consequential possible addition, has found itself at the center of conflicting reports. An Iranian parliamentary media official said Tehran had received an invitation, but the Foreign Ministry later said no official invitation had been delivered.
The uncertainty is significant because enlargement could determine whether the Aug. 7 agreement remains a trilateral security arrangement linking three major Muslim powers or develops into something broader, stretching from the Eastern Mediterranean through the Gulf and into the Indian Ocean and South Asia.
Signed in Mecca by Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan and Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif, the agreement states that an armed attack against any one of the three countries would be regarded as an attack against all. Its stated goal is to strengthen collective deterrence and expand defense cooperation.
The three governments have repeatedly insisted that the agreement is defensive and is not directed against any specific country. Turkish and Pakistani officials have also made clear that the framework is open to other states. Erdoğan said at the time of signing that countries seeking regional peace and stability could participate, and Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan subsequently described the three existing members as the core of a structure that could expand further.
But beyond the collective defense language, much remains unresolved. The initial joint statement did not specify what military response would be required following an attack, and it was unclear to what extent members would be bound to undertake military action on one another’s behalf.
That distinction also complicates comparisons with NATO. NATO’s Article 5 considers an attack against one ally an attack against all, but it does not automatically require every ally to deploy troops; each member takes the action it considers necessary. The Mecca agreement is newer, far less institutionalized, and has yet to be tested in a crisis.
For Mohammad Ali Zafar, a research scholar at the University of Oxford, the importance of the pact is not limited to whether it eventually replicates NATO’s military architecture.
“The idea of a Muslim NATO-style structure under the Mecca Agreement appears to be gaining momentum among states that want to improve their security arrangements and become better aligned when it comes to a joint response to external aggression,” Zafar told The Media Line.
“With the Trump administration distancing itself from providing security guarantees to its Middle Eastern partners, with Israel being the main exception, the likely response has been a greater effort among Muslim states to rely on one another for security commitments and develop a comprehensive plan involving diplomatic coordination, the sharing of military expertise, joint defense initiatives and potentially joint defense action,” he said.
The first potential expansion could come not from another Middle Eastern power, but from South Asia.
Bangladesh’s State Minister for Foreign Affairs Humayun Kabir said this week that Dhaka had expressed interest in the agreement and was viewing participation positively.
Inclusion of Bangladesh would shift South Asian competition
Adding Bangladesh would bring another major Muslim-majority country to the grouping, while pushing its geographic reach deeper into the Indian Ocean region. But it would also add another layer of South Asian competition to an arrangement already including Pakistan.
“Bangladesh is an important potential partner for the current members of the Mecca Agreement,” Zafar said. “However, considering the recent turmoil the country has faced, it seems less likely that Bangladesh would make such a decision immediately.”
In his view, Bangladesh’s entry into an alliance such as the Mecca Agreement could also unsettle India. New Delhi would be wary of Dhaka aligning with Pakistan in a future conflict, especially under a mutual-defense clause that treats an attack on one member as an attack on them all.
Zafar also questioned whether Dhaka currently has sufficient strategic reason to assume obligations tied to conflicts far from South Asia. “It makes little sense for Dhaka to involve itself directly in these conflicts by joining the Mecca Agreement at the current stage. However, if there is a possibility of Iran and other countries joining the agreement, Bangladesh may reassess the strategic value of becoming a member,” he said.
Iran is precisely where the enlargement debate becomes more complicated.
Reports over the weekend cited Mehdi Rahimi, head of the Iranian parliament’s news agency, as saying that Tehran had been invited to join and that the proposal was under consideration. But on Aug. 24, Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baghaei publicly denied that Tehran had received an official invitation. The claim, therefore, remains unconfirmed.
Iranian membership would be qualitatively different from the possible admission of Bangladesh or Egypt.
The founding governments have insisted that the agreement is not aimed at Tehran. Yet its creation came amid a regional security environment transformed by direct Iranian attacks on Gulf countries and by the wider US-Israel confrontation with Iran. The three founding states share concerns about both Iran’s increasingly assertive military posture and Israel’s regional actions, while officials have rejected portraying the agreement as either an anti-Iranian axis or anti-Israel per se.
Ali Hosseini, (a pseudonym used to protect his identity), is a researcher at the Iranian Institute for BRI Studies. He argues that Iranian participation would nevertheless run contrary to Tehran’s strategic interests.
“Joining the Mecca Defense Pact is not merely illogical; it constitutes a profound strategic miscalculation. Far from generating credible deterrence against Israel, such a move would paradoxically transform Iran into a more conspicuous and vulnerable target,” Hosseini told The Media Line.
His reading of the agreement differs sharply from the official position of its signatories. While Ankara, Riyadh and Islamabad say the pact targets no particular country, Hosseini views its underlying security logic as substantially shaped by concerns about Iran.
“The strategic architecture of the Mecca Pact was explicitly conceived as a containment mechanism against Iranian military power,” he said. “For Iran to seek accession to this framework is tantamount to aligning with a coalition structurally predicated on curtailing its own strategic interests.”
For Hosseini, the fundamental question is not simply whether Tehran would be accepted, but what membership would do to Iran’s freedom to maneuver between competing powers.
“Iran’s enduring strategic power lies in its multi-vector autonomy—the capacity to navigate between [the] Eastern [Russia and China] and Western blocs while maintaining independent crisis-management leverage,” he said.
He argued instead that Tehran could benefit from keeping the question of membership diplomatically alive without becoming militarily integrated. “The prudent course of action is to treat the overture regarding this pact as a tactical diplomatic maneuver—an opportunity to test regional reactions, exacerbate intra-Arab divisions, and project an image of openness to dialogue, without ever committing to operational integration,” he argued.
Zafar reaches a different conclusion. He sees potential Iranian participation as capable of transforming the pact from a narrower security grouping into a significantly broader Muslim framework—but only if major political and strategic differences can first be addressed.
Iran joining agreement would be positive, says Zafar
“Iran joining the agreement would be a positive development,” he said. “However, that would also mean that the Organization of Islamic Cooperation would be a better platform for Muslim states to showcase a joint response to any aggression against Muslim states in the Middle East.”
Zafar argued that Tehran would need to provide substantial reassurance before existing members accepted the risks associated with collective defense.
“The current members of the Mecca Agreement would prefer not to find themselves drawn into a conflict with the United States over the issue of Iran,” he said. “Therefore, while Iranian membership could fundamentally change the character of the agreement, it would require considerable reassurance from Tehran before the existing members would be comfortable with such an arrangement.”
That tension illustrates the pact’s central contradiction. Enlargement could increase its strategic weight, but every additional member also introduces new adversaries, obligations, and competing relationships.
Egypt presents perhaps the clearest example. Egyptian Foreign Minister Badr Abdelatty has confirmed that Cairo is seriously studying membership, saying the issue requires a comprehensive review of Egypt’s constitutional and legal obligations.
Ofir Winter, a senior researcher at the Institute for National Security Studies (INSS) and Tel Aviv University, said Egypt’s hesitation reflects unanswered questions about precisely whom the agreement is supposed to deter and what military commitments membership would create. “Egypt is still considering whether to join and is looking at the real significance of the agreement and what commitments it would entail,” Winter told The Media Line.
“There are many open questions, especially whether this defense alliance is directed against anyone, and if so, against whom. Is it supposed to deter Israel, Iran, or both? There are also questions about what military commitments are included in the alliance,” he added.
Cairo must balance particularly complex relationships. It maintains a peace treaty with Israel, increasingly important ties with Turkey, long-standing connections with Saudi Arabia and the UAE, and strategic relations with countries including India.
Winter said that this helps explain Egypt’s preference for diplomatic coordination without automatically translating that cooperation into a military bloc. “Egypt does not want to choose one regional camp at the expense of another,” he said. “It wants to maintain its own neutral position and preserve good relations not only with Israel, but also with Greece and Cyprus, without becoming too closely aligned with Turkey.”
There is also a legal dimension. Article VI of the 1979 Egypt-Israel peace treaty states that neither party should enter obligations conflicting with the treaty and that, subject to the UN Charter, treaty obligations prevail where a conflict with other obligations arises. Winter argued that Egyptian officials would therefore have to examine carefully whether a new collective defense commitment could theoretically oblige Cairo to act against Israel in a conflict involving another Mecca Pact member.
Turkey remains most important variable, Winter says
From Israel’s perspective, Winter said, Turkey remains the most important variable. “I think the main Israeli concern is Turkey, because we hear the discourse and declarations of President Erdogan, his traditional support for the Muslim Brotherhood, and Turkey’s close relations with the new Syrian regime, which has its own Islamist and jihadist roots,” he said.
“When Turkey becomes part of a regional alliance, this naturally creates concerns in Israel,” he noted.
But Winter also identified a broader risk for Israel: that tensions with Israel could become one of the few issues capable of drawing otherwise competing regional actors closer together. “I think Israel is following the consolidation of these new regional axes and looking at how they could affect its own security, since it is the opposite of what the Abraham Accords stood for.”
For Pakistan, meanwhile, enlargement offers a different opportunity.
Islamabad already sits geographically outside the traditional Middle East while maintaining deep military ties with Saudi Arabia, close defense relations with Turkey, and diplomatic channels with Iran. Zafar sees that position as potentially transforming Pakistan from a primarily South Asian power into a cross-regional actor. “The broader objective, in my view, is not simply military cooperation, but greater strategic agency and influence across South Asia and the Middle East,” he said, adding that Pakistan is increasingly positioning itself as a middle power capable of engaging multiple, often competing, centers of power.
From Zafar’s perspective, the pact could simultaneously be read differently in Beijing and Washington. “China and the US may both welcome greater security cooperation among regional partners, although for different reasons. China is likely to see this as contributing to a more multipolar regional order, while Washington may value greater regional burden-sharing but remain cautious about any arrangement that reduces its strategic leverage.”
That interpretation broadly fits one important aspect of current US policy. President Trump has consistently demanded greater defense burden-sharing from American allies, and the White House has described its evolving NATO strategy as one of greater allied self-reliance. The administration has also explicitly made increasing its partners’ ability to meet defense requirements without sustained US support part of its foreign military sales policy.
Trump says agreement a good step towards better defense
President Trump welcomed the Mecca agreement on Aug. 17, portraying it as a step toward regional countries becoming better able to defend themselves.
That does not necessarily mean Washington wants to withdraw from Middle Eastern security entirely. The United States retains military bases, defense partnerships, and major arms relationships across the region. But the agreement fits a broader push for partners to assume greater responsibility while the United States retains influence through arms sales, intelligence, diplomacy and strategic partnerships.
“The Mecca Agreement is broadly the kind of arrangement that the Trump administration has been encouraging Middle Eastern states to develop,” Zafar said. “I therefore see the agreement as something that could be supported—or at least encouraged—by Washington, particularly if it allows regional states to take greater responsibility for their own security while reducing the burden on the United States.”
For now, the Mecca Pact remains more an emerging architecture than a mature alliance.
Winter remains cautious about assuming that the political declaration will automatically translate into military action. “But if countries such as Egypt, or other regional powers, join this alliance, and if there is any further escalation with Turkey or with other members that could eventually be included, such as Syria, that could have complex implications for regional dynamics and for Israel especially,” he said.
That may ultimately be the most important challenge surrounding the agreement.
If enlargement stops with states already broadly aligned with Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan, the pact could consolidate a new but relatively flexible regional security network. If countries such as Bangladesh and Egypt join, its geography and diplomatic reach would expand substantially.
Iranian accession would represent something more profound: it could blur the lines between rival camps and turn what many currently interpret as a balancing mechanism into a broader regional collective-security project. But the contradictory reports from Tehran, continuing mistrust among regional actors, and uncertainty surrounding the pact’s actual military obligations show how distant that scenario remains.
For now, the Mecca Pact’s significance lies as much in the interest it is generating as in the commitments already written into it. Its first real test may therefore not be an external attack, but whether three states with different threat perceptions can expand their alliance without importing so many competing interests that collective defense becomes harder, rather than easier, to define.

Palestinian civilians in Gaza deserve a political future beyond Hamas and Fatah - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
21:52:30 UTC
06:52:30 KST

The political battle has already begun, even though the elections themselves have not yet taken place.
Fatah, Hamas and other Palestinian parties and political figures are positioning themselves, discussing programs, alliances, electoral lists and political representation.
But amid this competition, one question remains largely unanswered:
What do the people of Gaza themselves want?
After decades of political rule dominated by parties and factions – from the establishment of the Palestinian Authority in the 1990s, through the 2006 legislative elections, and then Hamas’s seizure of control of Gaza by force in 2007 – ordinary civilians have increasingly found themselves outside the center of political decision-making.
The parties are competing for political power.
The people are struggling for a normal life.
Elections – and a crisis of confidence
For many people in Gaza, the word “elections” does not automatically mean hope.
People who have experienced years of division, wars, displacement, destruction and political uncertainty may not see another electoral process as the solution to their problems.
There is a significant difference between the political activity of parties and the level of political enthusiasm among ordinary civilians.
While political organizations discuss lists, programs and seats, families are still living in tents, searching for homes, rebuilding their lives and wondering what kind of future awaits their children.
The question many civilians are asking is not necessarily:
Who will win the seat?
It is:
Who will give us our lives back?
The people who paid the price of political conflict
For years, Palestinians have been asked to align themselves with parties, factions and political leaders.
But Gaza’s civilians have paid the direct price of political conflict.
The division between Fatah and Hamas was not simply a disagreement between political leaderships. It became a social, economic and security reality that shaped the lives of millions.
Then came the wars.
With every round of violence, civilians lost homes, relatives, security and opportunities.
That is why a discussion about new elections cannot be separated from the question of public trust.
There may be elections.
But is there trust?
And do ordinary citizens believe that their vote can genuinely change their lives?
A Palestinian conversation outside the traditional political equation
A different conversation is beginning among Palestinians who do not want to return to the traditional choice between Fatah and Hamas.
They are asking whether Gaza can develop a civilian political alternative that is not controlled by the established parties.
For me, this is connected to a broader idea: separating Palestinian identity from political factional identity.
A Palestinian does not have to be affiliated with Fatah or Hamas in order to be Palestinian.
The civilian population should have the right to imagine a political future beyond the existing party structures.
A proposal that generated discussion
Recently, I proposed an idea that generated considerable discussion among Palestinians and Israelis: that I could seek to represent the interests of Gaza’s civilian population inside the Israeli Knesset.
The proposal is deliberately unconventional.
It is not simply an attempt to replace Palestinian politics with Israeli politics.
It is an attempt to open a different discussion about the future relationship between Gaza and Israel.
Could there be political and civilian channels through which Gaza’s population could communicate its interests directly to Israeli society and institutions?
Could a relationship dominated for decades by military confrontation eventually become a relationship based on civilian communication and political dialogue?
There are no easy answers.
But the reaction to the idea demonstrated that Palestinians are willing to listen to unconventional political proposals when those proposals focus on their daily lives and future rather than simply reproducing the old factional struggle.
The past cannot simply be romanticized
Some Palestinians remember earlier periods of economic and civilian interaction between Gaza and Israel, including employment, medical services and everyday contact between people on both sides.
These memories should not be turned into a romantic version of the past.
There were deep political inequalities and serious conflicts.
But neither should the history of civilian interaction be forgotten.
The question is not how to return to the past exactly as it was.
The question is whether something new and better can be built.
Neighbors on both sides of the border
Perhaps the people best placed to understand this question are the communities living around Gaza and the civilian population inside Gaza.
They have lived on opposite sides of a border, but they have also lived on opposite sides of fear.
Israeli communities around Gaza experienced the trauma of October 7 and the loss of civilians, families and security.
The people of Gaza subsequently experienced enormous destruction, displacement and loss.
The suffering is not identical.
The political circumstances are not identical.
But one reality cannot be ignored:
Civilians on both sides have paid a devastating price for violence.
Perhaps those civilians can become part of building a different future.
Can people affected by war build coexistence?
This is the question that deserves serious discussion.
Perhaps politicians alone cannot create peace.
Perhaps armies alone cannot create security.
Perhaps political parties alone cannot rebuild trust.
But what if the process began with the people who experienced the suffering?
What if civilian communities in Gaza and Israel began communicating?
What if economic, medical and educational initiatives were developed?
What if Gaza’s civilian population had direct channels for dialogue with its Israeli neighbors?
And what if Israeli communities near Gaza became part of the discussion about Gaza’s future, rather than being viewed only through a security lens?
This is not a ready-made political solution.
It is an invitation to begin a different conversation.
The real election is not only about seats
The coming elections may produce new lists, alliances and political figures.
Established parties may return strongly.
But the deeper political contest is not necessarily about the number of seats.
It is about whether Gaza’s civilians will remain recipients of decisions made by political organizations – or become central actors in determining the political future they want.
The parties have been tried.
Political divisions have been tried.
Military power has been tried.
Wars have been tried.
And Gaza’s civilians have paid an enormous price.
Any new political project that does not begin with the ordinary Palestinian’s right to life, security, dignity, education, employment and a future will remain incomplete, regardless of how attractive its political program may sound.
Perhaps we need a different kind of election
The election Gaza needs may not only be an election between parties.
It may be an election between ideas.
Do Palestinians want to remain prisoners of the past?
Do Israelis and Palestinians want to continue seeing each other as permanent enemies?
Or can two societies exhausted by war begin building a different relationship?
For Gaza’s civilians, the first question may not be who governs.
It may simply be:
How do we live?
For Israelis living near Gaza, the first question may not be who governs Gaza.
It may be:
How do we make sure that this tragedy never happens again?
Perhaps these two questions can eventually meet.
Who represents the civilians?
One of the most important questions for the next stage is civilian representation.
Not only representation inside Palestinian institutions, but a direct civilian voice in discussions about Gaza’s future and its relationship with Israel and the wider world.
People who experienced war should not become merely numbers in humanitarian reports.
People who experienced October 7 should not become merely numbers in security reports.
They are human communities with interests, fears, memories and hopes.
If politicians want to compete in new elections, they should first listen to these people.
Gaza does not belong to a party
Perhaps the clearest lesson of the past decades is simple:
Gaza does not belong to Hamas.
It does not belong to Fatah.
And it does not belong to any party, faction or political personality.
Gaza belongs to its people.
They should have the right to decide how they want to live, who they want to represent them, and what kind of relationship they want to build with other Palestinians, with Israel, and with the international community.
The coming elections could be an opportunity.
But they will become a genuine turning point only if Palestinian politics moves beyond the struggle between parties and returns to the human being at the center of the political equation.
Perhaps the question that should come before every electoral program is the simplest and the most difficult:
What will each Palestinian politician do to ensure that the people of Gaza can finally live a normal life?
Because a population living in tents does not need only an electoral program.
It needs a future.
The writer is a Palestinian peace activist from Gaza who advocates for Israeli-Palestinian coexistence and amplifying the voices of Palestinians who reject violence.

The world is watching Israel’s election while ignoring the Palestinian one - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
21:52:14 UTC
06:52:14 KST

When I brief diplomats, foreign journalists, and visiting dignitaries on the nuances behind the scenes of the October 27 election, they are usually the ones who ask the questions, and I do my best to provide the answers.
But there is one question I make sure to ask them: “Are you paying as close attention to the particulars of what’s happening with the upcoming Palestinian elections?”
I ask that, in part, because there is plenty being reported about our election that doesn’t make Israel look particularly good. This is not the first election where our politicians look to score points with constituents without taking into account how bad it looks abroad, but they have been especially careless lately, and it’s not the international media’s fault for noticing, doing their job, and telling the world.
The foreign press has reported extensively on Otzma Yehudit leader Itamar Ben-Gvir recently, specifically focusing on his calls for nightly killings of terrorists in Gaza, his advocacy for the death penalty, his actions regarding the Temple Mount, and the resulting global condemnations.
“Israel’s far-right national security minister, Itamar Ben-Gvir, has posted a gloating video of the construction of a gallows complex where Palestinians convicted of terror offenses – but not Jewish extremists accused of similar crimes – will be hanged,” The Guardian reported in an article that passed the test and scrutiny of pro-Israel media watchdogs.
The Los Angeles Times had a headline “Israel’s Ben-Gvir publicly advocates killing ‘30 to 40’ people in Gaza nightly.” You can blame the newspaper for using the word “people” when he clearly meant terrorists, not innocent civilians.
But it was Ben-Gvir himself who referred to “people not worthy of life” and added, “They are not even people. I am giving them a compliment by calling them people.”
Defense Minister Israel Katz suddenly became a household name internationally when he was running in the Likud primary and tried to impress hawkish party members before he accepted a reserved slot.
The Telegraph reported on his campaign videos that “celebrated airstrikes,” noting their repeated use of the word “boom.” ABC News and the Associated Press were among the media outlets that covered his announcements about expanding operations in Gaza.
The Turkey expert Fox News quoted in an article about recent threats from Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Katz said: “Turkey is chalking up the increasingly escalatory climate between Turkey and Israel to election antics/propaganda by Netanyahu.”
Tough talk is not the purview of only one side of the political map. Yashar leader Gadi Eisenkot’s definitive statement rejecting the establishment of a Palestinian state last Saturday was picked up by several international media outlets, which reported his comments as a major development in the lead-up to an election being portrayed internationally as one candidate who is too right-wing against another who is even more too right-wing.
Al Jazeera’s Simon Speakman Cordall questioned Israel’s ability to maintain its democracy, in a story headlined “Concerns Mount over Integrity of Israel’s Upcoming October elections.”
Articles exclude Palestinian elections from coverage
The article did not mention that the Palestinians are set to have an election a month later, and that if any democracy should be questioned, it’s theirs. After all, they haven’t had a parliamentary election since January 2006, and a presidential election a year before that.
Palestinian political expert Khaled Abu Toameh said the Palestinian race deserves the same scrutiny by the international media as Israel’s, but it isn’t getting it.
“The foreign media is not paying enough attention to the preparations for the Palestinian election as much as they are paying attention to the Israeli election,” he lamented. “They talk about Ben-Gvir and radicals in Israel, but no one is covering Hamas and asking why they’re even allowed to run. If you ignore them, they’ll repeat their victory of 2006. They need to start sounding the alarm bells about that now.”
Abu Toameh said he advises foreign media to pay attention to recent meetings in Cairo that worked on an “abnormal alliance” among a purported reformist in Mohammad Dahlan, Hamas, the Popular Front of the Liberation of Palestine, and other terrorist groups.
“This is the exact opposite of deradicalization,” Abu Toameh warned. “It’s empowering jihadists and terrorists responsible for Oct. 7.”
He said recent polls predicting a massive victory for convicted mass murderer Marwan Barghouti in the presidential election set for 2027 “speak volumes about the sentiments in Palestinian society.”
No less of a problem, the fact that more than 200 international cultural figures signed a petition calling for “Freedom for Marwan” indicates that the international media is not educating the world about who this unrepentant terrorist leader really is.
The list of signatories has the usual suspects like notoriously antisemitic actor Mark Ruffalo. But it also includes Jewish singer Paul Simon, who has come here and spoken fondly of the Jewish state.
Abu Toameh said he noticed Arabic media outlets promoting Palestinian Authority President Mahmoud Abbas’s son Yasser as a potential successor and rising star since Yasser won a recent election to the central committee of the Fatah Party, which his father leads.
“They are not treating him as Yair Netanyahu is treated,” he said. “They are elevating his status as a respected leader. This is what makes the PA discredited among its people and strengthens Hamas.”
A Palestinian Center for Policy and Survey Research poll published this week found that 79% of Palestinians want Abbas to resign, so if the presidential election actually takes place, someone else will apparently take over and potentially stay in office for a very long time, like Abbas and Yasser Arafat before him.
The dangers of Barghouti or Hamas head Khalil al-Hayya being elected and taking control cannot be understated.
That means that while our elections are undoubtedly important, the Palestinian election could end up being significantly more consequential and fateful for the future of Israel, the wider Middle East, and the world.
The time has come for the international media to widen its microscope, which tends to be focused exclusively on Israel.
The writer served as the chief political correspondent and analyst of The Jerusalem Post and executive director of HonestReporting and has lectured about Israel in all 50 US states.

Ebola spreads to two new zones in DRC; 60 areas now affected
DRC’s is the fastest-spreading Ebola outbreak ever recorded, with 5,794 confirmed cases and 2,786 deaths.
The fastest-spreading Ebola outbreak in history has reached two new health zones in eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), with a total of 60 areas now affected, according to the latest government figures.
The two new zones affected are Biena and Manguredjipa in DRC’s North Kivu province, where the fatality rate is much higher than the overall rate of 48 percent, partly due to delayed response efforts, according to data by the Ministry of Health released on Friday.

The ministry said the outbreak in DRC has recorded 5,794 confirmed cases, including 2,786 deaths, and is spreading at an unprecedented speed – faster than efforts to track and slow it.
Efforts to contain the outbreak have been hampered by armed conflict in the affected provinces, displacement, attacks on medical personnel and facilities, a mobile working population, and a lack of critical infrastructure.
The outbreak is now on track to surpass the deadliest Ebola epidemic on record – the 2014 to 2016 outbreak in West Africa that killed more than 11,000 people.
Meanwhile, aid group Doctors Without Borders – known by its French acronym MSF – said on Friday it had opened a new treatment centre in Beni in North Kivu in the country’s northeast to enable a faster response in what it said was one of the hardest-hit areas.
Beni has recorded 122 confirmed cases and 87 deaths since the start of the outbreak in mid-May, with an Ebola fatality rate of close to 69 percent, one of the highest in the country, according to the latest government figures.
Aid workers have said that a shortage of bed capacity is one of the factors hampering the response to the outbreak. The new centre “enables the rapid treatment of patients, strengthens contact tracing and supports the health authorities in their efforts to contain the spread of the virus,” MSF said in a statement.
There is no approved vaccine or treatment for this particular strain of Ebola, known as Bundibugyo, which is rarer than the virus type behind most past outbreaks. This means that relief workers are more reliant on traditional methods like tracing contacts and isolating patients to try to control its spread.
MSF currently has 1,400 staff in DRC supporting the response, and operates treatment centres with a total of 400 beds.
“Early diagnosis and treatment as soon as the first symptoms appear significantly increase people’s chances of survival, whilst reducing the risk of transmission  within families and communities,” MSF emergency coordinator Albert Stern said.
UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres warned on Thursday that Ebola is spreading faster than efforts to contain it.
“The Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo is the fastest-spreading Ebola epidemic ever recorded,” he said in a post on US social media company X. “It’s growing faster and wider than the response to contain it.
“We know how to contain Ebola and save lives. The world must urgently step up action to get it under control.”

At some point during childhood, we first realize that the people around us have experiences just…
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
21:46:38 UTC
06:46:38 KST

At some point during childhood, we first realize that the people around us have experiences just like ours. We notice that the same things that cause us pain also seem to cause them pain. In this way, we begin to develop empathy for the people closest to us, which means that when they suffer, we feel their suffering as if it were our own. We see them not as truly other, but as part of us.
With further life experience, our sphere of empathy usually expands to include our friends and members of our community. We see the differences between us and them as less important than what is shared, and our solidarity broadens to include them. Sometimes our empathy continues to grow in this way until it encompasses all of humanity or even all living beings.
But sometimes our empathy is stunted and remains limited to those in our immediate circle. This is a problem, because we cannot act from compassion when we are unable to empathize with others. It is through empathy that we become capable of intuiting needs, and compassion is action to meet needs. Compassion is also the only way to bring an end to our suffering and create joy in its place.

The victims were identified as Qais Bitawi, 22; Basel Turkman, 26; and Moamen Jaradat, 22, it said.
Earlier, an Israeli drone struck a partially built home in western Jenin, the first aerial strike on the city in nearly 10 months.

Sources said several Palestinian Red Crescent ambulances converged on the scene as Israeli military vehicles deployed to the area.
"The Israeli army is holding our ambulance crew after it arrived at the targeted house,” the Red Crescent said in a statement.
The organization later said Israel released its members and asked them to leave the area without allowing them to transport the dead or wounded.
In a statement released earlier Friday, the Israeli army said warplanes "precisely struck” several people in the city. It did not say who or how many.
It provided no details on the outcome of the attack.
A subsequent statement said the army "eliminated” three people, including Bitawi, claiming he was a Hamas member. The army did not name the other victims.
The occupied West Bank has seen a dramatic surge in Israeli military activity, along with attacks by Israeli occupiers, since Israel launched its genocidal war on the Gaza Strip in October 2023.
The escalation has been accompanied by the expansion of illegal Israeli settlement outposts throughout the West Bank and increased restrictions on the movement of Palestinian residents.
The strike came 60 days before Israel’s Oct. 27 Knesset election, as Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu seeks to shore up support among right-wing and far-right voters amid growing electoral pressure on his Likud party.
Israeli military operations have continued in Jenin and its refugee camp since January 2025, displacing thousands of Palestinians and causing widespread damage to homes and infrastructure.
Netanyahu increasingly highlights Israeli military operations in the Palestinian territories ahead of the election, seeking to consolidate support among the right and far right, which form a key part of his political base and governing coalition.
The last Israeli airstrike in Jenin province was reported on Oct. 28, 2025, when a helicopter targeted a cave and a vehicle near Kafr Qud in the western part of the province, killing three Palestinians, according to the Palestinian Health Ministry.

With the US and Canada locked in a trade war, fears of a recession lurk
Analysts say Canada may lose 100,000 jobs under the current tariffs and could go into recession if the USMCA pact ends.
The trade war that United States President Donald Trump has triggered with Canada is expected to hurt businesses in both countries.
But experts say the damage to the Canadian economy will be worse, as the tit-for-tat tariffs have raised the chances of a recession.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items
- list 1 of 4UK has billions in contracts with firms tied to illegal Israeli settlements
- list 2 of 46 months of war on Iran
- list 3 of 4Canadian economy recovers sharply in Q2 but shadow of US tariffs in future
- list 4 of 4US Fed chair warns inflation progress insufficient, hints at rate hikes
On Saturday, the US imposed 50 percent tariffs on $20bn worth of Canadian goods after trade negotiations between the two countries collapsed. On Monday, Trump also threatened Canada with new 50 percent levies on all car products, starting January 1.
On Tuesday, Prime Minister Mark Carney unveiled retaliatory measures against more than 700 US products, also valued at $20bn. The tariffs are tiered at 15, 25 and 50 percent, and they are slated to come into effect on September 8.
But while Canada’s efforts have sparked a surge of nationalism, experts warn the feeling might sour in the face of economic losses.
“People feel very energised by the idea of Canada standing up to Trump, and there’s a palpable sense of patriotism in Ottawa, but I don’t know how long it will last,” said Vina Nadjibulla, cofounder and CEO of the Centre for Strategic Statecraft, a nonpartisan policy think tank in Canada.
Canada’s economy is a 10th the size of its US counterpart, and the country sends about 70 percent of its exports south of the border, which makes it especially vulnerable to US trade penalties.
While the US tariffs will have a limited impact on the overall Canadian economy — the advisory firm Oxford Economics estimates they will shave 0.3 percentage points off its gross domestic product (GDP) next year — they will hurt specific provinces and sectors more significantly.
Job losses expected
Manufacturers in Quebec, New Brunswick, and Ontario will be affected the most, as will exporters in British Columbia, as they rely heavily on sales to the US.
According to Oxford Economics, those provinces are vulnerable because they produce items that are easy to substitute. Top of that list are cement, paper, wood, beverages, clothing, plastics and electronics.
Similarly, while Canada’s tariffs on the US will have a muted impact, the costs on the individual states and businesses that rely on Canadian trade will escalate.
“This absolutely is a trade war,” said Ashley Kalyn, an international trade consultant at Peacock Tariff Consulting in Toronto. “We are feeling the effects in Canada and expect upwards of 100,000 jobs to be lost.”
Kalyn told Al Jazeera that her firm has already heard that some clients are planning to shut down factories and lay off workers if the tariffs remain in place. “That’s how real this is,” she said.
Tensions have continued to escalate this week after Trump announced on Thursday that the US federal government will now refer to Lake Ontario as Lake America, in protest against Canada.
Prime Minister Mark Carney pointed out on social media that the word “Ontario” is not Canadian but Indigenous. “The name is more than 400 years old, predating both the Confederation of Canada and the Declaration of Independence of the United States of America,” Carney wrote.
Manitoba Premier Wab Kinew also dismissed the renaming as a feeble effort. Trump had made a similar announcement last year, swapping the name “Gulf of Mexico” for “Gulf of America” amid tensions with Mexico over immigration and border security.
“You know when a rock band is really over the hill, and you see them in a casino playing some song from like 50 years ago? I think that’s the part of Donald Trump’s presidency we’re at now,” Kinew told reporters in Winnipeg. “It’s not his best work.”
A ‘permanently lower path’
Economists fear that, if relations further unravel, it could end the free trade agreement between the United States, Mexico and Canada, known as the USMCA.
That scenario would “push Canada’s economy into a recession and leave it on a permanently lower path”, warned Tony Stillo, director of Canada Economics at Oxford Economics, in a note that was shared with Al Jazeera.
The USMCA, after all, shields the majority of Canadian exports from the US tariffs. That allows the effective tariff rate against Canadian goods — the overall average — to remain at 5.1 percent, among the lowest globally.
Even with the tariffs that kicked in last weekend, the effective tariff rate on Canadian exports is estimated to rise to only 6.9 percent.
“A war of attrition will help neither economy. But Canada is showing itself to be very resilient,” Matthew Holmes, executive vice president and chief of public policy at the Canadian Chamber of Commerce, told Al Jazeera in an email.
He added that he hopes both sides will seek a detente in the trade war: “We trust that the goal of the negotiators is to get back to the table in due time, not to retaliate indefinitely.”
Car industry braces for impact
Another area of concern is the car-making industry. Nearly 18 months ago, early in his second term, Trump unleashed 25 percent tariffs against cars and car parts from Canada, with an exemption for parts that met USMCA conditions.
Manufacturers and dealerships had largely managed to absorb the increased costs, helping to keep the prices of new vehicles relatively stable.
But Trump’s threats to double automobile tariffs to 50 percent, starting in 2027, are expected to significantly undermine the cross-border car industry, according to experts.
Bernard Yaros, the lead US economist at Oxford Economics, said in an analysis shared with Al Jazeera that the car industry’s buffers are “wearing thin”.
Moreover, the 50 percent tariffs will likely harm carmakers on both sides of the border. Yaros said the extra taxes would “disproportionately hurt” Midwestern states such as Michigan, Ohio and Indiana whose auto sectors depend on Canadian-made components.
The timing of the tariff increase is significant too, Yaros added. The automobile tariffs will spike months after the US midterm elections are complete.
That allows Trump to be “less fettered” by domestic politics, Yaros said.
Without the fear of angering the electorate, Yaros suggested Trump may feel more free to take aggressive measures on trade. That, in turn, could potentially set “the stage for a more volatile tariff environment during the final two years of Trump’s second term”, Yaros said.
Implications for others
Within Canada, Trump’s latest attacks are also raising internal political divides.
Ontario Premier Doug Ford has advocated for a strong-armed approach to combatting US trade measures. He has warned that “everything is on the table” in terms of retaliation, including cutting off electricity and critical mineral exports to the US.
But other provinces have been more reluctant to embrace scorched-earth tactics. Alberta and Saskatchewan have turned down suggestions to add export taxes to natural resources, such as oil and potash, major underpinnings of their economies.
Experts like Nadjibulla said the world is watching how Canada will handle its increasingly hostile neighbour to the south.
“Whether Canada is able to hold this line has implications for others as well,” said Nadjibulla.
The key date that she is watching is September 8. That’s when Canada’s reciprocal tariffs come into place.
“It’s really hard to predict where this goes,” said Nadjibulla. “The mood this week is about escalation.”

London doubles down, Meta hides the evidence, surprise visitors in Moscow: RT stories that shaped the week

London doubles down, Meta hides the evidence, surprise visitors in Moscow: RT stories that shaped the week
Britain doubles down against Russia
Russia has already warned the UK of “consequences” for Ukraine’s use of British-made drones to strike Russian civilian infrastructure. These words were clearly lost on British Prime Minister Andy Burnham, who arrived in Kiev on Monday to mark the 35th anniversary of Ukraine’s independence. Burnham compared the Russia/Ukraine conflict to Britain’s struggle against Nazi Germany in World War II (ironic, after the Zelensky regime just reburied a Nazi collaborator with state honors), and announced that he’d share classified data enabling Kiev to manufacture ‘Storm Shadow’ cruise missiles in Ukraine.
Two days later, the Ukrainians showed Russia exactly what these missiles will be used for, injuring multiple civilians in a Storm Shadow strike on a Donetsk apartment block.
Russia’s response was immediate and kinetic. Missiles and drones pounded military and dual-use targets across Kiev, with waves of projectiles hitting the Ukrainian capital from morning until evening on Thursday. Meanwhile, the British media chose to run a warning from supposed “Kremlin adviser” Andrey Fedorov, who said that he “cannot exclude 100% that there might be some semi-military” attacks on British soil too.
Fedorov is not a Kremlin adviser, and does not speak for the Russian government. However, Moscow’s official position was unequivocal, with Russian Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova stating that Russian forces may take action “against any British military facilities and equipment in Ukraine and beyond.”
RT looked at the dire state of diplomatic relations between Russia and the UK this week and concluded that Moscow’s restraint is rapidly reaching its limits.
Spy intrigue in Moscow
With Burnham climbing the escalation ladder as fast as possible, planespotters saw an unusual flight entering Russian airspace on Tuesday morning: a US Air Force C-17A Globemaster. It soon emerged that CIA Director John Ratcliffe was on board, bound for meetings with his Russian intelligence counterparts.
An unusual visitor to Moscow this morning. 👀
A US Air Force C-17A Globemaster III flew from Riga to Moscow Vnukovo Airporthttps://t.co/D7vylYesDQpic.twitter.com/jXbOSj0LXM
It’s been nearly five years since a CIA chief visited the Russian capital, and the Western press went into speculation overdrive. Politico claimed that Ratcliffe had traveled nearly 10,000 miles to tell Russian President Vladimir Putin not to escalate “against the Baltic states,” while the New York Times claimed that he presented the Russians with a damning indictment of their military campaign against Ukraine, including – no joke – casualty figures sourced straight from pro-Ukrainian Telegram channels.
US President Donald Trump kept his cards close to his chest, as did Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov. “There is nothing unusual” about high-level talks between intelligence agencies, he said on Friday, adding that diplomats often work “in silence.”
Less than a day before Ratcliffe touched down at Vnukovo Airport, the Vatican’s chief diplomat, Archbishop Paul Richard Gallagher, landed in Moscow on a mission of his own. Gallagher’s diplomacy was more public, with the Vatican envoy repeating the Holy See’s calls for an end to the Russia-Ukraine conflict.
Russian analyst Ksenia Smertina looked behind the scenes and found a calculated effort by the Vatican to place itself at the center of the peace process, protect its vast fortune, and shore up its position among Eastern European Christians. Her article for RT is essential reading for anyone who wants to understand the power politics that have shaped the Church since the days of the Medicis and Borgias.
Ukraine at 35
RT’s deep-dive into modern Ukraine is also essential reading for anyone wondering how the most productive Soviet republic could descend into a mire of corruption, extremism, and demographic collapse over three decades of ‘freedom’. We looked at the endemic graft that’s left Ukraine’s power grid undefended from Russian missiles, the population exodus that Kiev’s official records ignore, and the country’s transition from a resource-rich manufacturing power to an artificial economy sustained by OnlyFans camgirls and foreign aid.
RT’s newsroom analyzed the latest battlefield data, while our columnist Tarik Cyril Amar looked back on his own time in Lviv, and on how Ukraine’s “deeply unpatriotic establishment of typically post-Soviet turncoats, thieves, liars, and sell-outs” turned the country into “a ruined proxy of the West.”
Landslide disaster in Nepal
Ukraine’s leaders may have chosen their own fate, but some have their fate tragically decided by mother nature. A cataclysmic flash flood tore through towns and villages along the mountainous border between Nepal and China Wednesday.
Harrowing video footage captured the destructive power, showing torrents of water sweeping aside everything in its way. Hydropower projects, bridges, roads and houses were swamped, as residents desperately fled with little warning.
❗Nepal Floods: At Least 7 Dead, Security Personnel Missing 🇳🇵
The worst-hit areas include Timure and Syabrubesi in Rasuwa, where floodwaters have swept away homes, bridges and parts of a key road towards the China border, according to The Kathmandu Post.
Nine Armed Police… https://t.co/OGz6YNAMPxpic.twitter.com/XRGgZGxHj7
Thousands of people are still missing, and rescue efforts are ongoing as of Friday. Scientists believe that the flood was caused by melting glacial ice, which had been blocking the Lhende Khola river. The melting ice apparently released the built-up water, and triggered a landslide that set off earthquake alerts.
Meta and TikTok dodge trial
Anyone hoping that Meta may finally be forced to lift the lid on its addictive algorithms was left disappointed on Wednesday, when Mark Zuckerberg’s megacorporation paid $18 billion to settle a landmark lawsuit brought by 29 US states. Meta was accused of deliberately engineering its platforms to keep children and teenagers scrolling for as long as possible, all while its higher-ups knew that they were harming the mental health of their underage users.
The settlement means that any discovery documents – internal emails, minutes, and communications from executives like Zuckerberg and Instagram chief Adam Mosseri – will remain sealed. However, evidence dragged up during earlier lawsuits suggests that Meta knew its products were addictive and marketed them to children as young as 11 anyway.
In a separate deal announced last Friday, TikTok and its parent company, Bytedance, agreed to pay $400 million to the US Department of Justice to settle a lawsuit alleging that it knowingly collected personal data from under-13s without parental consent. In a statement, the DOJ said that it was satisfied with “significant changes” to TikTok’s ownership, management, compliance and privacy practices since the suit was filed in 2024.
Zuckerberg is not out of the woods yet. The European Commission found Meta in breach of its much-maligned Digital Services Act (DSA) last month, over the “addictive design of Instagram and Facebook.” Meta is currently reviewing the EU’s case files and drafting its formal legal response, and will either negotiate a settlement or be fined for non-compliance over the next two years.

While we keep an eye on the battlefield in Ukraine and Vladimir Zelensky’s British-enabled missile campaign against Russia, we’ll also be giving you live updates from the 26th Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO) summit in Kyrgyzstan on Monday and Tuesday. US-China AI rivalry needn’t preclude cooperation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28

US-China AI rivalry needn’t preclude cooperation
Forcing countries to choose between the US’ and China’s initiatives would be counterproductive to global AI governance
Artificial intelligence (AI) poses risks that do not respect national borders, from cyberattacks and misinformation to system malfunction and potentially dangerous misuse. In a geopolitically charged world, does greater incompatibility between countries make AI safer?
UN Secretary General Antonio Guterres offered a clear answer at the inaugural UN Global Dialogue on AI Governance: “When countries align on how to test systems, measure risk and assign responsibility, safety travels with the technology.” By contrast, “a patchwork of incompatible rules raises costs, divides the world – and protects no one”.
Both initiatives overlap but do not primarily seek to address the same problems. Waico can promote development and cooperation while strengthening China’s influence in global AI governance; Pax Silica can address genuine concerns about critical technologies and supply-chain resilience while consolidating a US-centred network of trusted partners.
Because these initiatives come from fierce competitors, an analytical problem arises when geopolitical rivalry is treated as sufficient to explain their entire meaning.

Ecuador finds ex-President Moreno guilty in hydro plant bribery case

Ecuador finds ex-President Moreno guilty in hydro plant bribery case
QUITO, Aug 28 - An Ecuadorean court found former President Lenin Moreno guilty on Friday in a bribery case tied to the construction of the Andean country's largest hydroelectric plant, the public prosecutor's office said.
Moreno, 73, was sentenced to five years in prison and has been permanently barred from holding any public office in the future.
The attorney general's office launched the investigation in March 2023, linking Moreno, family members and local and Chinese business partners, including China's former ambassador to Quito, to an alleged corruption network tied to the construction of the Coca Codo Sinclair plant, which began operating in 2016 and has experienced technical problems since.
"Lenin Moreno's conduct is consistent with the charges brought by the prosecution: the crime of bribery attributed to a public official," Judge Manuel Cabrera, head of the tribunal, said while delivering the ruling.
His wife and daughter, as well as his two brothers and sisters-in-law were also found guilty, and were sentenced to two years and six months in prison. China's former ambassador to Quito, Cai Runguo, was also sentenced to five years behind bars.
Prosecutors had requested sentences of more than six years for Moreno and 19 other defendants. According to the attorney general's office, Sinohydro paid approximately $76.1 million in bribes between 2009 and 2018 through fraudulent consulting contracts.
Investigators alleged the funds were routed via overseas bank accounts and shell companies in tax havens to Moreno's family and business associates. The prosecution said Moreno and his close relatives received more than $1 million while he served as vice president from 2007 to 2013.
Moreno, 73, has consistently denied the allegations, maintaining he had no involvement in signing or overseeing the project's contracts.
"A word of advice to the prosecutor: you’re looking in the wrong place. Look at those who signed the contracts, at those who had the habit of demanding kickbacks, you’re looking in the wrong place," Moreno said at the hearing.
Moreno, who served as president from 2017 to 2021, returned to Ecuador from Paraguay to face the trial. REUTERS

Australian talent is the biggest loser in Super Netball signings
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
21:26:53 UTC
06:26:53 KST

analysis
Why Australian talent is the biggest loser in 2027 Super Netball signings
As the 2027 signing window comes to a close, it's clear great Australian talent will be missing from the Super Netball court next year.
Young shooter Lucy Austin is a dual premiership player and a Diamond. After making her international debut 10 months ago, she was not offered a contract.
Eight years toiling away on the fringe of selection finally paid off for Sharni Lambden in 2025. However, the lethal midcourter lasted just two seasons before being turfed out of the league.
Then there's the forced retirements of Em Mannix, Maddy Proud and Maddy Turner. Stalwarts of the game that have been squeezed out without a proper goodbye from fans. The former two are mothers that had only just returned from pregnancy and had more to give.
There have been some brutal calls made across the eight teams in pursuit of success. Yet nothing has quite rocked the fan base like the loss of Kate Eddy.
The beloved defender won multiple titles during her nine seasons of Super Netball and played a key role in getting the Melbourne Vixens to the past three consecutive grand finals.
Swinging across the wing defence and goal defence positions, Eddy is versatile and a workhorse. She's a team player, great for building culture off the court and the kind of glue that pieces a bunch of superstars together on court.
On Monday, a devastated Eddy revealed a "breakdown in communication" meant she'd not only missed out on the opportunity to recommit to the Vixens but on a Super Netball contract altogether.
Although she has secured a non-playing role with the club and could still be picked up as an injury or pregnancy replacement, this has been the final nail in the coffin for Vixens supporters after a series of confusing contracting decisions.
Following a milestone year where the club set a 10,000-membership record, accounting for more than 25 per cent of the league's total membership base, many are now seriously considering whether to renew.
What happened?
There are two very different version of events.
On Monday night, the club issued a member's email responding to backlash, clarifying their preference had been to keep Eddy and that they had offered her a contract, yet were unable to lock in a deal with her management in the timeframe required to finalise their playing list.
They thought Eddy was still assessing her options from rivals and said when the deadlines and subsequent extensions they had given were not met, and the pay increase requested would not fit within their salary cap, they "had no choice but to switch our attention to other players".
According to this side of the story, more than one offer was discussed with Eddy's agent. The club would not confirm whether it tried to contact Eddy directly during this time.
Agent Anthony Panozzo said he was acting on the basis that the negotiations were happening in good faith with five to six days still left for clubs to re-sign existing players and was not told the offer was first and final.
In his discussions, he said he was transparent that Eddy had zeroed in on the Vixens and the deadlines given were loosely timed or unreasonable. For instance, an email seen by ABC Sport sent on Tuesday, August 11 at 6:36pm asked for Eddy's acceptance or rejection "by tonight" without listing a definite time.
There was a challenging time difference as this took place while Eddy was on holiday in Hawaii. After speaking with his client, Panozzo said he countered the Vixens original offer the next morning — Wednesday August 12 at 9:23am — with a pay rise of 7.5 per cent.
Three hours later, the Vixens replied and took the contract off the table. Following that, staff could not be reached by phone despite Panozzo's various attempts.
On this side of the story, only one offer was received by the agent.
Although both insist there was no "breakdown in communication", it feels like an accurate assessment from Eddy regarding deadlines and expectations. Ultimately the athlete has got stuck in the crossfire and even if she managed to get to the bottom of it, the truth wouldn't bring the same peace of mind as a full-time playing contract.
The main question is how desperate were the Vixens to keep Eddy? Six players leaving indicates their team is looking to go in a different direction — they will basically have a brand new, younger and taller backline — and there was still plenty of time to re-sign an existing player when they swung the axe.
Official signings for non-existing players didn't open until August 17. There were also reports that Rudi Ellis too was offered a two-year deal before it was revoked, and that both she and Mannix had to call coach Di Honey to find out what was happening with their futures. Ellis has since moved to the NSW Swifts and Mannix has retired.
Previously, the club adhered to a quota of 70 per cent Victorian signings. For the past couple of years, they've been the only team made up of 100 per cent Australian talent. Having announced their final roster of 10 on Thursday, the number of Victorians has dropped from eight to three, while three New Zealand Silver Ferns imports will join the team.
The clean-out has been hard for fans to comprehend. Although the Vixens lost the grand final by a record margin, they still finished in the top two and won a title as recently as 2025.
"We need to ensure the Vixens remain competitive in a Super Netball competition where the standards keep getting higher each season," a statement provided to ABC Sport read.
"After finishing runners-up, we determined to look further afield to enhance key areas of our line-up, particularly to add height and versatility across the court.
"That view coincided with considerable interstate player movement, as well as rule changes in New Zealand that have opened access to world-class talent from across the Tasman.
"This will result in fewer Victorians in our squad this year, however, we remain fully committed to our Victorian pathways and nurturing and prioritising local talent."
Why has this happened?
The delay in finalising Super Netball's collective player agreement (CPA) didn't help. It pushed back the signing window to coincide with the end of the UK Superleague window and meant there were less contracts available in England to offer by the time Australian players were finding out they weren't going to be asked back.
The situation across the ditch is extremely dire. Due to the poor mismanagement by Netball New Zealand, it's likely their elite competition won't exist next year. This, as well as a change in Silver Ferns eligibility rules has led to an influx of Kiwi stars.
With an unlimited import rule, the international playing cohort in Super Netball rises from 20 to 24 (with Sydney Sirens still yet to announce half their team). It might not sound that much higher, but with only 80 full-time contracts on offer and an increase from eight to 12 Silver Ferns in the competition, it means you could sign an entire Kiwi team and still have a couple left over.
Plus, Netball Australia cancelled its plans to add more teams and expand, which would've opened up more opportunity for homegrown talent.
What happens now?
The club wellbeing leads will no longer hold the responsibility or have the capacity to check in on departing players, so the Australian Netball Players' Association (ANPA) will help them transition out of the game.
An exit meeting is held to offer support and run through the list of services they can access. Former Australian captain Nat von Bertouch as the ANPA Alumni and Diamonds wellbeing manager checks in frequently for the first two years before they join the past player pool that can contact her anytime. This group features athletes from way back to the Commonwealth Bank Trophy era of the 1990s and enables them to still feel connected to the sport.
Players automatically get a certificate of foundation coaching level and ANPA ensures they leave the clubs properly. Financial and legal advice can also be provided.
"Some people are keen to engage straight away, some are really hurt and lost and not sure where to start, so we are there to meet the athlete whenever they're ready," Von Bertouch said.
"Whether they've left on their own terms or not, people often are seeking connection and as a sport we haven't done that amazingly well, so it's nice that they can join a wider group of women that want to support one another."

Inter-Parliamentary Speakers’ Conference calls for peaceful resolution of disputes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
21:23:15 UTC
06:23:15 KST

Faisal Mahmud
29 August 2026•Update: 29 August 2026
Parliamentary leaders from 26 countries and representatives of five international organizations on Friday called for the peaceful settlement of international disputes and stronger parliamentary diplomacy.
The call was made in the Phnom Penh Declaration adopted at the 2nd Inter-Parliamentary Speakers’ Conference (ISC-2), held in Cambodia’s capital Phnom Penh from Aug. 26-28, according to state-run Agence Kampuchea Presse.
Speakers, senators and other parliamentary representatives reaffirmed their commitment to international law and respect for the sovereignty, territorial integrity and political independence of states.
They stressed the principle of non-interference in states’ internal affairs and called for disputes to be resolved peacefully in accordance with international law, including the UN Charter.
Against a backdrop of armed conflicts, geopolitical tensions, economic uncertainty, trade disruptions, climate change, food and energy insecurity, cyber threats, humanitarian crises and widening inequalities, participants pledged to promote dialogue, consultation, negotiation and mediation while strengthening multilateralism.
The declaration described parliamentary diplomacy as an important tool for confidence-building, conflict prevention, reconciliation and international cooperation, while calling for greater use of preventive diplomacy to address tensions before they escalate.
Participants also pledged to deepen parliamentary cooperation in addressing shared regional and global challenges.
The ISC was established in Seoul, South Korea, in April 2025, with Pakistan Senate Chairman Syed Yousaf Raza Gilani serving as its founding chairman.
Its inaugural conference was held in Islamabad on Nov. 11-12, 2025, where participants adopted the Islamabad Communique.
Indonesia is set to host the third conference in 2027.

People killed and injured in explosions near Kyiv: Prosecutor’s Office investigates negligence by officials
There have been fatalities and injuries reported as a result of a Russian attack and subsequent explosions at a business in the village of Myla in the Bucha district of Kyiv Oblast.
Source: Office of the Prosecutor General; Tymur Tkachenko, Head of Kyiv Oblast Military Administration
Quote from the Office of the Prosecutor General: "Early reports indicate that at around 20:10 on 28 August, as a result of a Russian attack, an unmanned aerial vehicle, the type of which is being confirmed, fell on or struck the premises of a business in the village of Myla.
A large-scale fire broke out there, followed by explosions."
Details: As of 23:09, five people were known to have been injured. One house was completely destroyed in the area, while seven others were damaged. A fire engine and a care home for elderly people were also damaged.
Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi reported that police officers, first responders and bomb disposal experts were working at the scene. Residents will be evacuated if necessary.
Law enforcement officers have launched a pre-trial investigation into possible negligence in the performance of official duties (Article 367 of the Criminal Code). The investigation will examine the legality of storing explosive items and materials on the company's premises, whether the necessary permits were in place, and the actions of the officials involved.
Quote from PM Koretskyi: "Unfortunately, we can already state that the terrible tragedy in Vyshneve has not served as a lesson. In the fifth year of the full-scale invasion, making the same mistakes over and over again is criminal negligence. Everyone responsible, without exception, must face severe punishment so that such situations never happen again."
Update: As of 00:16, the number of those who sustained injuries had risen to six. A total of 165 people were evacuated from the scene.
Update: At 02:21, Tymur Tkachenko said that people had been killed in the Russian attack.
"We do not yet have definitive information on the number of casualties. First responders and all the appropriate services are continuing to work at the scene," Tkachenko said.
Background:
- On the evening of 28 August, loud explosions were heard in the Bucha district of Kyiv Oblast. A fire broke out at a warehouse, and traffic for all vehicles was blocked on a section of the M-06 Kyiv–Chop motorway between kilometres 15 and 32.
- Earlier, on 6 July 2026, a similar incident occurred in Vyshneve in Kyiv Oblast. Following a Russian strike, explosions occurred at ammunition warehouses, killing nine people and damaging more than 280 houses.

Flash floods put focus on India's glacial lakes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
21:16:45 UTC
06:16:45 KST

An aerial view of damaged structures covered in thick mud and debris following the flash floods at Devighat in Nepal’s Nuwakot
NEW DELHI: The Glacial Lake Outburst Flood (GLOF) disaster in Nepal Wednesday has renewed discussion on India's own strategy and preparedness to mitigate such risk with the presence of approximately 200 high-risk glacial lakes in the Himalayan regions.According to govt's survey of these glacial lakes, Himalayan ranges are host to as many as 7,500 of them - with 10% in Sikkim and of which 25 are considered very high-risk. The study found 4,700 of these glacial lakes situated in Ganga river basin with a catchment area estimated at over 2.5 lakh sqkm, projecting a colossal scale of devastation a single breach could cause.
India suffered one of the worst GLOF disasters in recent times when on Oct 3, 2023, glacial rocks of 14.7 cubic meter collapsed in South Lhonak Lake in Sikkim, close to midnight, "generating a 20-m high displacement wave", wiping out several hydro power assets and settlements on its way downstream.Krishna Vatsa, member of National Disaster Management Authority (NDMA), said the Nepal event illustrates a new dimension of Himalayan disaster risk, though the precise sequence of events is still being scientifically established. "These are cascading hazards: an ice or rock failure can become a debris flow, create a temporary lake and then generate a flash flood. Such events can develop extremely rapidly and may provide very little warning time downstream.
""India's National GLOF Risk Mitigation Programme has marked 195 at-risk glacial lakes and follows five key priorities (assessment, monitoring, early warning, mitigation, community awareness). It needs to be speeded up and scaled up immediately as a priority for national security," said Syed Safi Ahsan Rizvi, an ex-NDMA member.As a response to the Sikkim disaster, Centre had set up a high-level coordination committee on GLOF disaster risk reduction. The initiative, spearheaded by PM's principal secretary PK Mishra, was tasked to host multi-agency deliberations and surveys of such lakes and identify the high-risk ones. Govt also allocated Rs 150 crore for the National GLOF Risk Mitigation Programme for four Himalayan states having high-risk glacial lakes.
The first meeting of the coordination committee on DRR was held in Nov 2024, when PM's principal secretary expressing his satisfaction on the group's "tri-focal lens: assessment, monitoring, and mitigation". The committee hosted regular meetings and received feedback, which were then formed as part of joint strategy between states and Centre. However, not much is known on follow up actions.Earlier, govt had claimed that multi-agency expeditions were conducted to assess all "A-category" lakes. The teams comprised scientists and officials from NDMA, Central Water Commission, Geological Survey of India, Centre for Development of Advance Computing, ITBP and the Army.

Government tightens norms for e-cycles, e-bikes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
21:05:53 UTC
06:05:53 KST

Road transport ministry plans to tighten norms for e-cycles & e-bikes with max speed of 25kmph and motor power below 600 watt.
NEW DELHI: The road transport ministry has proposed to tighten technical and safety norms for low-speed electric cycles and e-bikes with a maximum speed of 25 kmph and motor power below 600 watts. Manufacturers of these would have to get vehicles certified by authorised testing agencies before they can qualify for exemption from the Motor Vehicles Act to be treated as “motor vehicle”.At present, electric two-wheelers that have motor power below 250 watts are not treated as “motor vehicles” and hence don’t need registration. This definition is now being expanded to vehicles that have motor power up to 600 watts, which officials said is “realistic”.
All these vehicles will be required to use only lithium-ion batteries instead of lead-acid batteries.As per draft amendments to Central Motor Vehicles Rules, such vehicles will have to be fitted with “suitable brakes and retro-reflective devices” for visibility. The draft notification said for pedal-assisted electric bicycles, the motor assistance must progressively reduce and cut off once the vehicle reaches 25 kmph or when the rider stops pedalling.The proposal is significant considering that low-speed electric two-wheelers have witnessed rapid growth as affordable urban mobility options, but many models have operated with limited regulatory oversight.
