Junk foods will soon have labels warning of high salt, sugar and fat
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
20:59:44 UTC
05:59:44 KST

Junk foods will soon have labels warning of high salt, sugar and fat
Anuja Jaiswal / TNN / Updated: Aug 29, 2026, 03:42 IST
Comments
Share
AA
Text Size
Small
Medium
Large
FSSAI agrees to red hexagonal warning labels on junk food packages for high salt, sugar and fat content.
NEW DELHI: Junk foods will soon carry warning labels highlighting high levels of salt, sugar and fat, with the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) telling Supreme Court on Friday that it has agreed to red-coloured hexagonal warnings on the front of food packages to help consumers identify products high in specified nutrients of concern.FSSAI conveyed its position through a compliance affidavit filed before Supreme Court in response to the court's Aug 13 order on front-of-pack labelling (FoPL).The move comes after the court pushed Centre to act on the issue, saying, "If the Union does it on its own, well and good, otherwise we shall proceed to pass further directions."Under the framework, products high in specified nutrients would carry prominent red hexagonal warnings reading "HIGH FAT", "HIGH SALT" and/or "HIGH SUGAR", as applicable.FSSAI has agreed to exempt single-ingredient foods such as ghee, edible oil, salt, sugar, jaggery and honey from the proposed warnings, subject to applicable food safety and labelling regulations.The regulator has agreed to implement FoPL in phases, giving the industry time to reformulate products. Phase I would cover products high in two or more specified nutrients, while Phase II would extend warnings to products high in any one specified nutrient.
Do warning labels work?
The framework is based on nutrient thresholds specified under the Dietary Guidelines for Indians, 2024, issued by ICMR-NIN. The affidavit follows the Supreme Court’s observations on public health, particularly amid concerns over the rising prevalence of childhood obesity. The court said front-of-pack labelling could help consumers make informed purchasing decisions.
The case stems from a PIL filed by NGO 3S and Our Health Society, which approached Supreme Court through advocate Rajiv Shankar Dwivedi, seeking front-of-pack labelling to help consumers make informed choices.FSSAI said the system is intended to provide a “simple, prominent and easily comprehensible warning” to consumers about food products high in specified nutrients of concern. It also cited international examples, including Chile and Canada, where front-of-pack labelling has been adopted.Supreme Court had considered options including coloured indicators, interpretative words, numbers, letters, symbols and percentages for front-of-pack labelling and directed Centre to take a decision and place it on record.
Anuja Jaiswal is a Senior Assistant Editor at The Times of India, with an impressive 18-year career in narrative journalism. She specializes in health and heritage reporting, expertly simplifying complex health information to make it engaging and understandable for readers. Her deep dives into heritage topics are well-researched, resulting in captivating narratives that resonate with her audience. Over the years, she has worked in Chandigarh, Chhattisgarh and West UP, gaining diverse on-ground experience that shapes her storytelling.

Clean energy push unfair on developing nations: CJI Surya Kant
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
20:58:56 UTC
05:58:56 KST

CJI Surya Kant said clean energy push unfair on developing nations
NEW DELHI: CJI Surya Kant on Friday told Commonwealth Countries that it is unfair that the industrialised countries, who took two centuries to adopt clean energy, are asking the nations in the process of industrialisation to move towards renewable energy within decades.Speaking at the Commonwealth Secretariat in London, CJI Kant said, “Countries that are finally industrialising are being asked to move rapidly towards renewable power, and often made to bear the brunt of criticism when they cannot move fast enough. In comparison, the nations urging that transition spent two centuries building their own strength on coal and oil,” he said.
Addressing the common platform for 56 countries on “Policy dialogue on climate justice”, the CJI said the cumulative shift of commonwealth countries to clean energy depends on copper, cobalt and lithium, extraction of which carries environmental and social consequences.Developing countries facing myriad challenges depending on their geographical locations and pushing them towards clean energy at an unrealistic pace could create more challenges than solutions, he warned.Justice Kant said, “The challenge, therefore, is to reconcile the urgency of the clean energy transition with the principles of fairness and shared responsibility that must underpin it.”He said the Supreme Court of India and the HCs have played a significant role in protecting the environment, ecology and its endangered species.
He recounted the Zambian HC making a copper mining company liable for polluting water. Commonwealth countries can learn from each other’s experience to bolster efforts towards smoother transition towards clean energy without making their populations pay a heavy price, he said.“We need not develop a separate jurisprudential vocabulary in every country where a climate question reaches the Courts. Rather, the Courts should be open to borrowing ideas, approaches, and solutions that have proved useful elsewhere in the Commonwealth, while adapting them carefully to their own constitutional, social, and environmental circumstances,” he said.“Courts must be willing to search for solutions that protect the environment without losing sight of the legitimate needs of development, and to recognise that the two need not always be cast as choices in which one must defeat the other,” CJI Kant said.
He cited the case before SC where the officials were accused of felling many trees to widen a road for access to a super specialty hospital for wounded para-military forces. “We had no wish to reward officials who had cut trees; equally, we had no wish to deny wounded soldiers an ambulance route,” he said.Instead of halting the widening of roads, the SC had ordered extensive compensatory afforestation. “We still monitoring that afforestation today… development and preservation do not always have to stand on opposite sides of the scales. Sometimes, the task of a Court is to find the third way to promote both routes through judicial creativity,” he said.

Nilekani committee seeks public ideas to fix exams
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
20:55:09 UTC
05:55:09 KST

The panel, headed by Infosys co-founder Nandan Nilekani, was announced by PM Modi last month.
NEW DELHI: The high-powered task force set up by Centre to overhaul India’s public examination system opened a nationwide consultation on Friday, seeking suggestions from students, parents, teachers and other stakeholders on making high-stakes tests more secure, transparent and student-friendly.The panel, headed by Infosys co-founder and technology expert Nandan Nilekani, was announced by Prime Minister Narendra Modi last month amid heightened scrutiny of the examination system following NEET-UG paper leak controversy and youth protests over alleged lapses in the test’s conduct.
The announcement had come a day after Centre accepted the demands raised by the youth-led CJP, whose protests over NEET leak included calls for then education minister Dharmendra Pradhan’s resignation and withdrawal of FIRs against protesters. “The High-Powered Task Force (HPTF) on Reforms in Public Examinations wants to hear from students, parents, teachers — every citizen,” a senior official said on Friday.The task force’s mandate “to examine and recommend comprehensive reforms relating to conduct, security, design and governance of public examinations, including examinations conducted by National Testing Agency (NTA), the ministry of personnel said.
HPTF, which seeks “to benefit from the experience, knowledge and perspectives of stakeholders”, said the suggestions may dwell on the conduct and security of public exams as well as the examination design and assessment methodology.Stakeholders may give inputs on better governance, accountability and institutional arrangements; as also systems to prevent, detect and redress examination malpractices, the ministry said. The public consultation will remain open till Sept 13, with citizens allowed to send suggestions through WhatsApp, a dedicated website, email and a toll-free number.Officials said the task force is examining reforms across the examination chain — from institutional processes and question-paper security to use of technology and strengthening of examination infrastructure.It will also look at measures to improve accessibility and inclusion, while factoring in student well-being during the examination process.“The objective is to develop a public examination system that is robust, secure, transparent, equitable and future-ready,” the official said. The exercise assumes significance after repeated controversies surrounding national-level entrance and eligibility examinations raised questions over paper security, examination management and the ability of testing agencies to respond quickly to irregularities.
Apart from Nilekani, the task force includes former Isro chairperson S Somanath, former Intelligence bureau director Tapan Deka, IIT Madras director V Kamakoti, former education secretary Anita Karwal and logistics expert Amrit Lal Meena.The panel is expected to recommend both immediate safeguards and longer-term structural changes in the way public examinations are designed, administered and secured.

Forced birth control in Greenland violated women’s rights, experts find
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
20:54:35 UTC
05:54:35 KST

Forced birth control in Greenland violated women’s rights, experts find
Truth commission to be established after two expert reports failed to agree whether scheme constituted genocide.
Greenland is establishing a truth and reconciliation commission surrounding a decades-long forced contraceptive scheme against Indigenous girls and women, after two expert reports failed to agree whether it constituted genocide.
From the 1960s to the 1990s, at least 4,000 Greenlandic Inuits – including girls as young as 12 – received intrauterine devices (IUDs) or contraceptive injections, often without their consent or knowledge, a joint Danish-Greenlandic inquiry found last year.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items
- list 1 of 4Massive iceberg capsizes off the coast of Greenland
- list 2 of 4A US territory? Trump unveils proposal to control Strait of Hormuz
- list 3 of 4Can Trump really make Strait of Hormuz a US territory?
- list 4 of 4Can China’s new Arctic sea route to Europe replace Middle East chokepoints?
That inquiry found the practice was intended to reduce birth rates and family sizes, which Danish authorities at the time viewed as a way to improve living standards and social and health conditions in Greenland, an Arctic island and semi-sovereign territory of Denmark, with a population of 57,000.
Greenland’s government tasked a four-member commission in 2024 with investigating the campaign, which led some victims to suffer serious infections, scarring of the fallopian tubes or removal of the uterus. Some were later unable to have children.
But the experts could not reach a unanimous conclusion, Greenland’s Justice Minister Marianne Paviasen told reporters on Friday, with one report stating there was no genocide and the other saying the extent of the violations could not be established.
“We cannot say, on behalf of the government, whether there was genocide. This is something we can continue to debate,” Paviasen said.
Greenland’s Prime Minister Jens-Frederik Nielsen said the reconciliation commission would “not be about assigning blame, but about uncovering the truth with a view to genuine reconciliation”.
Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen said Copenhagen would “handle the political process together with the government of Greenland”.
The Greenlandic Siumut Party, however, urged the genocide question to be settled by “a competent and independent international court”.
“Today we could have been far more Greenlanders,” the party added.
‘Treated like animals’
Victims have questioned why no Greenlandic Inuit were appointed as experts while recounting painful histories dug up by the panel.
“For me, this is not just about history or politics. It’s my body, my life, and my right to self-determination,” Henriette Berthelsen told the AFP news agency.
“And once again, I see that it is others who will investigate and define what was done to me and to other Inuit women,” she added.
Inger Platou, 70, told Reuters she had woken up from what she had been told was a minor operation only to discover an IUD had been inserted without her consent.
“It turns out we were treated like animals,” she said. “Without consent, they just wanted to stop women from giving birth or having children. It was a very inhumane act.”
Complications from the coil left her unable to become pregnant, she said.
Denmark apologised for the scheme last year, with Frederiksen describing “systematic discrimination” against Greenlanders.
On Thursday, the Danish parliament agreed that women affected by the forced contraception campaign can claim compensation of up to 300,000 Danish crowns ($46,758) each.

'A line has to be drawn': The trade-off we're making without really noticing
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
20:40:40 UTC
05:40:40 KST

in brief
- Experts warn that expanding AI surveillance in Australian policing poses serious civil liberties risks.
- Privacy advocates have called for stronger laws to prevent unchecked algorithmic overreach in public spaces.
Artificial intelligence is increasingly used by police departments across Australia, with experts warning that lines must be drawn over the technology's use, invoking the dystopian world depicted in George Orwell's novel Nineteen Eighty-Four as a potential future to avoid.
Police departments are starting to trial the use of AI technology for "various forms of surveillance" and "predictive policing", professor Toby Walsh, chief scientist at the UNSW AI Institute, told SBS News.
In WA, police have been trialling AI facial recognition software to scan pedestrians on the street and compare their faces against watchlists. In the trial's first week, 130,000 people were scanned, leading to 18 arrests.
Walsh said that while most people would be "pleased" with the result, he believes such public surveillance is "an erosion of the things that we used to value".
"The question is, how much are we willing to trade those values for the benefits that the technology is bringing?"
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
Overseas, the rise of AI in surveillance technology has become an increasingly contested topic.
In the United States, citizens have been taking action against the surveillance cameras of the AI company Flock Safety, which has tens of thousands of devices across the country. Videos of people destroying the cameras have gone viral on social media.
Tom Sulston, head of policy at the advocacy group Digital Rights Watch, told SBS News that, while Flock cameras are not currently used outside of the US, "plenty" of companies in Australia are doing "similar things".
Palantir, the US data analytics firm contracted by military and US immigration forces, and Cellebrite, an Israeli digital forensics company working with law enforcement, both have tens of millions of dollars in government and private contracts in Australia.
"We should be concerned," Sulston said. "We have a right to go out in public without being surveilled, without having our biometric data uploaded to the cloud, and without it being used for purposes we don't really know."
Both have said that governments across the country need to rapidly turn their focus to expanding individual privacy laws, particularly as wearable surveillance technology like smart glasses become more widespread.
"We do have some legislation that covers public surveillance, but the more companies that get into that market, the more pressure there will be to relax them," Sulston said.
Walsh argues that a line between privacy and security "has to be drawn" as AI has made previously impossible levels of surveillance mundane.
"The one thing that George Orwell got wrong: it wasn't people watching people. It was computers, particularly artificial intelligence, watching people," he said.
What do Flock cameras do?
Flock's 120,000 cameras across the US mainly record licence plate and vehicle information for a searchable database.
The company states it is not in the business of mass surveillance, only in targeted crime prevention and response. Data is encrypted, held by the company for 30 days, and access to it is only available to customers who are logged.
Sulston notes that the information captured can be layered with other datasets from companies like Palantir to "produce really rich surveillance data of practically everyone that goes out in public".
"They have been doing that, and they've been using that to create pre-crime systems that try to predict where crimes will happen and inform police of where they think a crime is going to happen," he said.
Such systems, like many AI tools, frequently demonstrate bias in their responses and serve to further disempower "traditionally overpoliced people, whether that's immigrants or non-white people," Sulston said.
"There are real civil liberties issues".
While the company has yet to make any international moves, Flock chief executive Garrett Langley referenced Australia's relatively centralised police — spread across just eight forces — as an example of a potentially lucrative overseas market.
AI policing in Australia
While Australia doesn't have anything matching the Flock network's capabilities, police forces are increasingly using AI in their operations.
NSW Police notes on its website that they are primarily interested in using AI for "the automatic processing of high volumes of data for the identification of relevant laws, procedures, and precedents" but that they are also looking into "novel ways in which artificial intelligence can be used to prevent/reduce crime."
At present, high-volume data processing such as mobile phone detection or seatbelt offences are managed by machine learning throughout Australia. Victorian police note that, while AI flags potential offences, humans review and issue fines.
Walsh argues that a slow normalisation of AI into everyday policing could lead to social changes in which police develop a "tendency to defer to the machine".
More broadly, he argues that the law and its human application has been superseded in this area by AI, which operates in a much stricter fashion.
"I'm not so sure that we actually have the public's buy-in," he said.
In the US, the Washington Post reported that at least 50 law enforcement officers had been charged with misusing data access — including Flock information — to monitor romantic partners or ex-partners. In Australia, dozens of police officers have been charged with similar offences.
"We have to be really careful about the data we collect and the oversight that we have of the people who have access to that data," Sulston said.
'We need the government to step in'
The use of AI in surveillance technology is not limited to policing.
In 2024, Coles signed a three-year contract with Palantir to optimise its workforce and streamline its supply chains across 840 supermarkets in Australia.
Bunnings uses AI-driven facial recognition technology to monitor customers in their stores.
Sulston said the rising popularity of AI is supercharging already existing privacy concerns and that present laws "aren't really working for us".
"We need the government to step in, prioritise privacy reform, and ensure that the laws available to us can handle these new threats that we're facing," he said.
Walsh argues that the country needs to handle the rise of AI with caution and should learn lessons from the retroactive regulation of social media.
"We need transparency, he said. "The public needs to be assured of where and when it's being used and not being used, and under what circumstances and under what limits".
"There's still the social licence here, but I suspect if we're not careful, it will disappear very rapidly."

The big retirement question hiding in Australia's housing crisis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
20:39:48 UTC
05:39:48 KST

This audio is voiced by AI and may occasionally mispronounce words.
Share your feedback and help us improve this feature. Read more about how we use AI at SBS here.
Damian Hole's last mortgage repayment is due when he's 80.
The 52-year-old bought his first home about a decade ago and refinanced it in 2024, locking in a new 30-year loan term just before he turned 50.
He's among a growing cohort of Australians buying their first home later in life. People over the age of 40 accounted for nearly one in five first-home buyers last year (18.7 per cent), according to data from one of Australia's largest mortgage brokers, Aussie Home Loans.
That's up from just over 5.5 per cent in 2005.
At the other end, people under the age of 20 made up around a quarter of first-home buyers in 2005, compared with less than 0.5 per cent in 2025.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
As housing affordability pressures make it harder for young Australians to enter the market, solutions designed to ease the path to home ownership have increasingly focused on expanding access to credit — allowing buyers to borrow more, with smaller deposits or longer mortgage terms.
Low-deposit loans can be accessed through the federal government's 5 per cent deposit scheme, while family guarantor loans allow first-time buyers to borrow up to 100 per cent of the purchase price.
Meanwhile, more lenders are offering 40-year mortgage terms, meaning some borrowers could be signing up to make repayments well into their later years.
If a growing number of Australians are buying homes later while taking on larger loans for longer, what happens when they reach retirement still saddled with mortgage debt?
'A cat and mouse game'
Making it easier for people to borrow can fuel higher house prices.
According to James Graham, a housing economics expert at the University of Sydney, without massively expanding housing supply, broadening access to credit alone is not a sustainable solution.
"It's just sort of a cat-and-mouse game," Graham tells SBS News.
"The prices go up, so we change mortgage credit. That pushes prices up further.
People are just borrowing more to buy more expensive houses, and they're not really any better off.
When the government introduced its 5 per cent deposit scheme last year, designed to help first-home buyers, the Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA) predicted the measure would likely "put at least some further upward pressure" on housing price growth.
By March, the value of new loans taken out by first-home buyers was around 11 per cent higher than before the scheme was expanded in October, with the increase largely reflecting bigger average loan sizes, according to the RBA.
The costs of delayed home ownership
Graham says buying a first home later in life could have consequences beyond carrying mortgage debt into retirement. Entering the market at 40 or 50 leaves less time to build housing wealth and can reduce people's ability to move as their lives change.
"People are likely to be locked in for longer," he explains, warning that some buyers may end up remaining in homes that were intended as a first step into the market rather than a last stop.
"Less moving has its own social consequences," he adds.
"It means that people can't move back to communities that they wanted to be part of; they're further away from their children than they wanted to be; they're not near jobs that they want to be near.
"Maybe they've moved far out of the city because that's the only place they could buy. But now they're away from amenities and doctors."
Delayed home ownership and larger mortgages could also have implications for the aged care sector. Traditionally, many older Australians have relied on accessing housing equity (the portion of a property that is owned outright) to help fund retirement living or aged care, often through selling the family home. Unsettled mortgage debt could affect this transition, reducing the overall equity available.
Another concern is long-term mortgage stress, which can reduce the wellbeing of older Australians and may lead retirees to draw down their superannuation to pay off housing debt, according to 2019 research from the Australian Housing and Urban Research Institute (AHURI).
This, in turn, could place additional pressure on the pension system.
Currently, the Age Pension excludes the primary home from its assets test.
Paying down mortgage debt on a primary home with super can, therefore, reduce a person's assessable assets and potentially make them eligible for the pension.
"We have an ageing population in Australia, so the fiscal pressure on government will increase with that if government is supporting people through the pension system," AHURI managing director Tom Alves tells SBS News.
"The compulsory superannuation system is designed to address that issue, and if people are not having enough income through their super because they've used it to pay off their mortgage, obviously that's an issue."
AHURI's research notes that mortgage debt was uncommon among people aged 55-64 as early as the 1990s. Between 1996 and 2013, however, the proportion of Australians in that age bracket still paying off a mortgage rose from under 20 per cent to 45 per cent.
Home ownership has long underpinned Australia's retirement system, with policies, including the Age Pension, built on the assumption that most retirees own their home.
Widely used superannuation savings targets typically assume that people will own their homes outright by the time they reach retirement. While some modelling also considers renters, retirees still paying off a mortgage are largely left out of the picture.
"They do assume that people own their home," Susan Thorp, a retirement finance specialist at Monash University, tells SBS News.
"They're not allowing for the idea that someone may have, say, $150,000 of mortgage debt at the time they're retiring."
Yet a growing share of Australians may not fit those assumptions. In a January survey of 1,020 people by Loan Market Group, 58 per cent said they planned to own their home before retirement.
The rise of the 40-year mortgage
A small but growing number of Australian lenders have started offering 40-year mortgage terms, which can give borrowers access to loans they might not otherwise have been able to afford — but can add staggering extra interest costs over the life of the loan.
Richard Brown, a Mortgage Choice broker in the Sydney suburb of Epping, says many of his clients are eager to find ways to maximise their borrowing power, which is increasing their appetite for longer loan terms despite the downsides.
"There's an appetite for borrowers to get access to the money they need to buy the property they want," he says.
"They don't care what it is."
Sebastian Watkins, CEO and co-founder of mortgage broking giant Lendi Group, says relying on borrowing innovations like longer loan terms risks overlooking the underlying issue of unaffordable housing prices.
"We can't simply respond to people taking longer to save by giving them longer to pay off their loan," he tells SBS News.
If current trends continue, in a decade or two, Watkins expects the average Australian mortgage to be "larger, held later in life and managed much more dynamically".
We are likely to see longer loan terms, more family-supported or multi-generational borrowing and products that adapt as a customer's income, family circumstances and property needs change.
Japan offers an extreme historical example of intergenerational borrowing. Amid soaring housing costs in the 1980s, it experimented with 100-year mortgages designed to be repaid across multiple generations. Researchers who later modelled the loans concluded they did little to improve housing affordability.
What happens when debt stretches beyond careers?
Lenders assessing older applicants will typically look for a credible exit strategy demonstrating the loan can be comfortably managed in retirement, Watkins says.
"They may look at the expected loan balance at retirement age and consider the borrower's projected superannuation and other assets. Another potential strategy could be downsizing, where the borrower could sell the property and purchase a lower-value home," he says.
Hole, who bought his first home at 42, says his bank requested his superannuation balance before approving his mortgage.
"It was almost done, and then they requested my super balance, and then I realised, because my age will go beyond retirement, they're just seeing if I've got enough super to pay off the loan."
He says he should be able to comfortably repay the remainder of his mortgage with a lump sum from his super when he reaches retirement age, at which point he intends to access the Age Pension.
The retirement debt challenge
Alves says there is no single policy fix, but governments need to consider both retirement and housing policy together.
Potential approaches include adjusting Age Pension settings to better reflect the differences between homeowners and non-homeowners, as well as expanding affordable housing options for older Australians, he says.
More broadly, he says improving access to home ownership earlier in life and increasing the supply of affordable rental housing could help reduce the number of Australians entering retirement with housing stress.
Thorp says there are fundamental questions that remain unanswered about what happens when more Australians enter retirement with housing debt.
"The question of how housing policy merges with superannuation and retirement policy is not fully worked out," she says.

"Escalating rates of sexual violence, particularly amongst young people, are a huge concern that we need to address," Social Services Minister Tanya Plibersek said in parliament.
"Almost 40 per cent of victims of sexual assault are between the ages of 10 and 17, and we know that online harms are spilling into real-life harm."
Plibersek said "sexual strangulation is becoming more commonplace" due to children being exposed to "violent and degrading pornography".
"It's where they're getting their sex education from."
According to the Breathless Campaign, 57 per cent of young Australians have been strangled by a partner during sex and 51 per cent have strangled a partner during sex.
Ralston is the Queensland and Northern Territory projects executive manager and facilitator trainer for a primary prevention program called Love Bites.
She told SBS News about what actually works.
What is the Love Bites program?
Operated by the National Association for Prevention of Child Abuse and Neglect, Love Bites is a trauma-informed and evidence-based respectful relationships program teaching young people across Australia since 2003.
A national network of grassroots facilitators delivers it to young people aged 11 to 17.
Designed in line with Australia's consent curriculum, it's "scaffolded according to their developmental needs" and addresses topics like consent, technology-facilitated abuse, pornography and coercive control.
"It's a universal program that really challenges the drivers of violence ... we unpack what the attitudes and beliefs are that form somebody's actions or behaviours," said Ralston.
What do young people know about sex?
In 2022, almost 40 per cent of young people had already encountered online pornography by the age of 13.
Ralston said pornography and its effects are so pervasive that the Love Bites senior program is now being delivered to the youngest cohort.
"We're now having these conversations in the younger years around coercive control, around consent and more explicit consent conversations," she said.
"We're hearing about the impact of AI, sextortion, sexual images, technology-facilitated abuse — all of these conversations that we didn't even have words for a few years ago."
She said there's been a significant rise in language and content associated with the "manosphere" — and it's happening in primary schools.
Manosphere is an umbrella term for a mix of online spaces that talk about men, masculinity and gender relations. Such spaces frequently advocate narrow and rigid ideas about what it means to be a "real" man.
But most Love Bites graduates are pushing back.
"We see so many incredible young men in our Love Bite programs that are genuinely trying to navigate their way through this harmful space and they're asking really great questions, they're showing respect in relationships and in their actions," said Ralston.
"We can't pretend this isn't happening at all, but we can highlight the incredible young people, men and women, who are really recognising harm and standing by each other."
How do you challenge a harmful sexual behaviour or attitude in a young person?
When a concerning opinion or behaviour is identified in the Love Bites program, it's met with "curious questioning".
She said facilitators are trained to "provide opportunities to have conversations around how things could look different".
The approach varies by age.
"When we're working with little kids, up to 10 years old, developmentally they need us to be their manager. We can run the program and feed the information to them," Ralston said.
"When we work with adolescents, 11 years and up ... we're hired as a contractor ... we come into the room with a perspective, tell them what we know, and they can choose if they want to contract our services."
She said it's a method that has enabled complex and progressive conversations and helped young people self-determine what safe, respectful sex is.
What's the right way to talk to young people about sex?
Ralston said being delicate isn't necessary when talking to young people about sex.
She said many young people in the Love Bites program have expressed a desire to be able to talk to the adults in their lives about sex and relationships.
"It's just providing that safe space and beginning the conversation," she said.
"The really important thing is being curious and having solid, informed, evidence-based research."
What to do if a young person needs help?
Conversations about sex can feel shameful at any age, Ralston said it's important to "get comfortable and confident".
"If we are not comfortable having a conversation about some explicit materials, we need to start with ourselves," she said.
"We've done really well in Australia to normalise conversations around the prevention of domestic and family violence. We need to get that with sexual violence and sexual abuse."
Consent education can cause some to reflect on experiences they deemed healthy — and realise otherwise.
Ralston said it's a common occurrence.
She said when a young person discloses an experience of sexual assault, believing them is crucial.
If a young person has recognised they've perpetrated harmful sexual behaviour, they must be met with support.
"We need to help them understand that everybody has capability to change," Ralston said.
"The first step in understanding how to change is understanding that your behaviour has crossed the line."
Readers seeking support can ring Lifeline crisis support on 13 11 14 or text 0477 13 11 14, Suicide Call Back Service on 1300 659 467 and Kids Helpline on 1800 55 1800 (for young people aged 5 to 25). More information is available at beyondblue.org.au and lifeline.org.au.
Anyone seeking information or support relating to sexual abuse can contact Bravehearts on 1800 272 831 or Blue Knot on 1300 657 380.
If you or someone you know is impacted by sexual assault, call 1800RESPECT on 1800 737 732, text 0458 737 732, or visit 1800RESPECT.org.au. In an emergency, call 000.
The Men's Referral Service, operated by No to Violence, can be contacted on 1300 766 491.

broken ladders, bird sculptures, and hidden faces shape ricardo luevanos’ tokyo exhibition

Unknown Publisher

THE SKY PROMISED NOTHING exhibition explores human hope
Based in Guadalajara, Mexico, artist Ricardo Luevanos presents The Sky Promised Nothing, his first solo exhibition in Asia, at Diesel Art Gallery in Tokyo from July 25th to September 23rd, 2026. Working across digital drawing, mixed media, painting, sculpture, and installation, Luevanos creates poetic visual narratives that explore longing, nostalgia, hope, and the enduring human desire to transcend perceived limitations. His work has been presented in solo museum exhibitions in Mexico and has expanded into the country’s broader cultural landscape through projects including official artwork for international film festivals.
all images courtesy of Ricardo Luevanos and Diesel Art Gallery
RICARDO LUEVANOS BUILDS A PATH TOWARD THE UNREACHABLE
The exhibition explores the inner landscape of human emotion through installation, sculpture, painting, and text-based works. At the center of the gallery is a site-specific installation featuring a broken ladder rising from the ground. Its first steps are missing, making the initial ascent impossible. Around this absence, a chair, suspended platform, and pedestal become alternative steps, suggesting new possibilities beyond limitation. Bird sculptures remain suspended throughout the space, representing both contrast and reflection. While birds can physically reach the sky, for humans the sky exists as a symbol of longing, aspiration, and possibility. Portraits with hidden faces and hand-painted text works further explore themes of memory, identity, and hope.
Presented by Diesel Art Gallery, the exhibition reflects the gallery’s commitment to introducing internationally recognized contemporary artists while creating a platform where art, fashion, and culture intersect. Located within DIESEL SHIBUYA in Tokyo, the gallery continues to present exhibitions that connect contemporary art with a global audience. The Sky Promised Nothing reflects on the tension between impossibility and hope. As artist Ricardo Luevanos writes, ‘The sky promised nothing. Still, we reached for it.’

UN envoy urges stronger security response as Haiti gangs expand grip
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
20:35:10 UTC
05:35:10 KST

Berk Kutay Gokmen
28 August 2026•Update: 28 August 2026
The UN secretary-general’s special representative for Haiti on Friday called for stronger international support for Haiti’s security institutions after a gang attack in Kenscoff killed at least 47 people and left dozens abducted.
Addressing an urgent UN Security Council meeting, Carlos Ruiz Massieu condemned the assault on the commune in the hills overlooking Port-au-Prince as a “horrific” atrocity and demanded the immediate and unconditional release of those kidnapped, including women and children.
The attack, which occurred overnight on Aug. 23-24, also left dozens injured, displaced residents and destroyed homes, said Massieu. Gang members are said to have attacked people seeking refuge at a church, where some were killed while others attempted to flee.
Massieu said the attack was the latest in a series of attacks in Kenscoff since early 2025, demonstrating gangs’ “continued capacity and determination” expand beyond the capital and challenge state authority.
He cited UN documentation showing that more than 1,400 people were killed and over 600 injured between April and June 2026 alone.
Massieu welcomed a decision by Haitian authorities on Aug. 26 to coordinate the Haitian National Police, armed forces and the Gang Suppression Force (GSF). He said the GSF would strengthen its presence in the Port-au-Prince area, while national security forces would reinforce their deployment in Kenscoff.
“National security institutions cannot be left to confront this threat without adequate support,” he said, stressing that the GSF’s full deployment was essential.
However, Massieu warned that security operations alone would not deliver lasting stability. He called for efforts to restore state authority and basic services, reopen schools and health facilities, create livelihoods and provide pathways for young people to leave gangs.
He also urged accountability for those responsible for the Kenscoff attack and those financing and enabling gang violence, saying breaking the cycle of impunity was critical to restoring confidence in state institutions.
UN humanitarian coordinator Indrika Ratwatte separately warned the Security Council that Haiti’s violence was fueling a severe humanitarian crisis, with more than half of the country’s 6.4 million people requiring humanitarian assistance and nearly 1.5 million internally displaced.
Haiti has not held elections since 2016, and its last President Jovenel Moise was assassinated in 2021 shortly after postponing a vote. 
Last month, the Provisional Electoral Council announced that a first-round presidential and general election will be held on Dec. 13, with a second round and local-level elections on Feb. 21.

Attacks on Zaporozhye NPP’s SNF storage site create threats to nuclear safety
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
20:21:31 UTC
05:21:31 KST

MELITOPOL, August 28. /TASS/. Ukraine’s attacks on the Zaporozhye Nuclear Power Plant’s (ZNPP) dry spent nuclear fuel (SNF) storage facility pose a threat to nuclear security, the plant’s said.
A Ukrainian drone attacked the ZNPP’s dry SNF storage site on August 26. No serious damage was done, no casualties were reported. The radiation background is within the normal levels, the plant said.
"Any attacks in the vicinity of such a facility are inadmissible as they pose a potential threat to nuclear security. An attack on the dry SNF storage site is dangerous primarily due to the potential damage to the complex’s infrastructure and containers holding spent nuclear fuel. The consequences of such actions cannot be ignored - they could create additional risks and require complex measures to ensure the facility’s security," according to a post on the ZNPP’s channel in messaging app Max.
The dry SNF storage site is a "reliable and unique facility, built with a large safety margin and designed for the long-term safe storage of fuel," it said. August 24 marked the 25th anniversary of the installation of the first container of spent nuclear fuel at the storage site and the start of pilot operation of this ZNPP facility.
Currently, the facility holds 173 containers. The site is designed to safely store up to 380 containers for 50 years, the ZNPP said, adding that the site is regularly checked by specialists and International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) inspectors deployed to the nuclear plant.
Earlier in the day, IAEA Director General Rafael Grossi called for the utmost restraint following three Ukrainian drone attacks on the ZNPP on August 25 and 26. On August 25, a drone exploded near the plant’s cooling pond. Two Zaporozhye NPP employees were injured in the incident. The next day, another drone exploded on the grounds of the plant’s dry spent nuclear fuel storage facility. On the same day, a third drone struck a sprinkler system at the plant’s power units. On August 27, Russian Foreign Ministry Spokeswoman Maria Zakharova said that Russian calls on the IAEA to take measures against the Kiev regime in connection with the strikes on the Zaporozhye NPP.

US condemns ‘savage’ gang attacks in Haiti, urges swift deployment of suppression force
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
20:21:01 UTC
05:21:01 KST

Berk Kutay Gokmen
28 August 2026•Update: 28 August 2026
The US on Friday condemned “in the strongest terms” a deadly gang attack in Haiti's Kenscoff community, calling for stronger security efforts to protect civilians and prevent armed groups from undermining the country's democratic future.
Addressing an UN Security Council meeting, Jennifer Locetta, the US alternative representative for special political affairs to the UN, described the attacks by “terrorist gangs” as “savage” and that Washington mourned the innocent lives lost.
Her remarks came after a gang attack in Kenscoff killed at least 47 people and left dozens abducted.
The attack, which followed months of deadly violence, was another indication of the “dire state” of Haiti's security crisis, Locetta said, accusing gangs of murdering civilians, terrorizing communities, burning homes and destroying families.
Locetta warned that gang coalitions were seeking to prevent Haitians from exercising their right to elect their representatives in future elections.
“Terrorists cannot take democracy hostage for their own selfish and violent ends,” she said, stressing that civilians must be protected from gang violence.
She said the US stood firmly with Haitian authorities seeking to hold perpetrators accountable, end gang impunity, restore state authority and allow Haitians to choose their leaders.
Washington remains committed to supporting Haitian-led security efforts to end gang violence, Locetta said, describing the Kenscoff attack as evidence of why the UN-authorized Gang Suppression Force (GSF) mission is needed.
“The GSF was not created to issue statements from within a compound wall, or spend our money while Haiti suffers,” she said, urging the force to actively confront armed groups.
Locetta called on troop- and police-contributing countries to deploy personnel to the GSF as quickly as possible and urged UN member states to contribute to its trust fund.
“The GSF needs equipment, resources, and political will to do and finish this job,” she said.
She called on Security Council members to renew the GSF mandate next month, saying the US looked forward to working with Panama, the council's co-penholder, on the renewal.
However, Locetta acknowledged that security operations alone would not deliver lasting stability in Haiti.
She called for credible alternatives to gang violence, accountable governance and greater international investment in infrastructure, capital and job creation to provide opportunities for younger generations.
“The United States stands with Haiti and will continue to work with Haitians and international partners to end this crisis and restore Haiti's stability,” she said.
Haiti is scheduled to hold general elections for the first time in more than a decade on Dec. 13.

====================================================================================================

Q&A: The Future of Air Force Cyber Systems and Warfighter Comms
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
20:01:49 UTC
05:01:49 KST

Just over a year ago, in July 2025, the Air Force established a dedicated office on the Air Staff for communications/cyber functions, separate from the intelligence directorate it had long been attached to. The new Warfighter Communications and Cyber Systems directorate now focuses on secure communications, cyber operations, and information technology systems as they support the frontline Airman or Guardian.
The move, leaders said at the time, was a major shakeup necessary to support the service’s need for resilient, reliable communications and cyber operations, and the equipment and personnel associated with those capabilities.
In June, Brig. Gen. Jeffrey A. Phillips took over as Deputy Chief of Staff for Warfighter Communications and Cyber Systems from interim deputy chief Brig. Gen. Joy Kaczor, who filled the role following the retirement of Maj. Gen. Michele C. Edmondson.
Phillips, a prior-enlisted Airman, started his career as a computer programmer and serving six years wearing stripes before commissioning through Officer Training School at Maxwell Air Force Base, Ala., in 1999. He previously commanded the 67th Cyberspace Wing at Joint Base San Antonio-Lackland, Texas, and served as Director of Cyberspace and Warfighting Communications at the headquarters of Air Combat Command at Joint Base Langley-Eustis, Va.
The one-star now serves a community of about 30,000 enlisted, 3,000 officers, and nearly 100 newly minted warrant officers. He recently sat down with Air & Space Forces Magazine for an interview about where the office stands after a year in operation and his priorities moving forward for the position, the equipment, and the people involved in vital communications and cyber work for the Air Force.
Editor’s Note: The following Q&A has been edited for length and clarity.
Q: What is your office doing to modernize both the equipment and support the Airmen in communications and cyber jobs?
A: We have to stop getting stuck in five-year acquisition cycles that end up delivering a product that’s outdated by the time we put it on the battlefield, and so that’s my number one priority. And we’re doing that through a few different lines of effort. Theater deployable communications, or TDC, is really important. We learned in operations like Operation Epic Fury that when we’re out in the field at several locations, we need to be connected at all those locations. So, we need to get that equipment out to the people who need to be connected, and we need to have Airmen out there who know how to operate it or make it simple enough for anyone to operate.
And there’s enterprise communications; those are the foundational networks that we connect back into from the edge, and a lot of those have been underinvested in over the past 30 years, so we’re playing a catch-up game. A big focus for Chief Information Officer Ashley Devoto and me is making sure we can modernize that enterprise network, so I came in with that as my number one priority.
My second priority is the continued evolution of our talent management processes. I think we’ve come a long way in the time that I’ve been part of it, and we need to do that for our enlisted Airmen, our warrant officers, and our officers. In the last few years, we created an executive development forum that all the cyber general officers sit on. It’s really a development team for our colonels. Now all of our general officers mentor all of our colonels.
This year we had what we call our Champions Initiative, and the colonels who were part of our development team were mentors to each O5 and below that we’re meeting on that development team. On the enlisted side, our 1D7 [Cyber Defense Operations] career field has obviously been in a state of flux and change for probably the last 10-plus years, we’ve changed those AFSCs and what they represented several times over that time period, and I kind of put a chalk line in the sand and I said we’re not going to make any more changes until we figure out what’s right, what’s wrong. We get the Airmen the career development courses that they need and then get them the education they need so they can test for promotions on their specialty knowledge tests. So that’s the number two priority.
There are a lot of key partners and stakeholders that we need to work with, so my goal is to rebuild those bridges because we can’t do anything alone. We have to partner with organizations like the Secretariat of the Air Force, the Office of the CIO, and DAF CIO Devoto. We have to partner with our acquisition organization, primarily under Air Force Life Cycle Management Center, and we work with the [Command, Control, Intelligence and Networks Directorate] within AFLCMC primarily for our theater deployable communication and our enterprise IT.
Q: What are some of the key technologies or equipment that your office is helping roll out, use, or upgrade across the communications and cyber areas of the Air Force?
A: Our legacy communication equipment is our Flexible Communication Package, or FCP. It’s been around probably for about the last decade. When you deploy an FCP, the only way a combatant commander can task it is through a unit type code that requires 10 pallet positions on an aircraft, about 40 people, and about 20 short tons to move. It includes things like bulldozers and huge satellite dishes, and it’s been modernized to the point that we don’t need such a big footprint anymore. Our new deployable comm kits—we have two of them: the ACP, the Agile Communications Package, and the Fly-Away Communications Terminal. They’re similar equipment, but a Fly-Away Comm Terminal supports fewer users than an ACP would. So, if we deploy somewhere we need to run command and control applications, we might need more compute and storage power. We can put that on the ACP. If we go someplace where we don’t have terrestrial internet, we can attach a satellite, our commercial satellite comm terminal. So agnostic transport is really big. We can set up a 5G bubble and use that as our transport. That gives us modular equipment so we can reduce our footprint and deploy with a couple of Airmen who know how to use it, providing connectivity for a whole mission-generation force element versus 10 pallet positions and, you know, 20 short tons.
We are in the midst of fielding ACPs. We have a lot of FACTs that are fielded. Now we’re working toward our next-generation ACPs. This technology changes very rapidly, and so keeping up with it is very challenging.
Q: You mentioned work to develop officers; what is your office trying to do for the enlisted and new warrant officers in the ranks?
The 1D7 Cyber Defense Operations career field, for example, has five “shreds.” At different points in time, there have been more or fewer shreds. Those shreds have meant different things, and so you could ask an Airman, or you could ask some senior leaders, “Hey, you know, what’s the definition of a 1D7X1 today? And unless you’re keeping up with the change, which was constant, it was very hard to define it clearly. So, freezing any further changes for Airmen in that career field is crucial because they want that stability, so they can develop more technical expertise and depth.
With warrant officers, we’re not asking them to lead people, we’re asking them to lead efforts. We’re asking them to become technical experts. We’ve put warrant officers in our cyberspace operations career field at the 67th Cyberspace Wing, and we’re starting to put them in the 688th [Cyberspace Wing] and get them into some staff positions as advisors to senior leaders who might not have the technical depth warrant officers have.
Q: How has working in Air Forces Cyber, and the cyber officer’s role, changed over the course of your time in uniform?
A: When I came in, we were support officers. Now we’re operations officers, and I think that’s a huge difference. I was proud of being a support officer. I had a great boss when I was a second lieutenant who pulled me in at Shaw Air Force Base, and he said, “Hey, Munster, this is your role as a communications officer at this base. You’re supporting the SEAD mission.” I said, “Sir. What’s the SEAD mission? He explained it as Suppression of Enemy Air Defenses, and I started to link my service to that mission, and I was very proud of that. As we transitioned to a more of an operational community, I got to lead a cyberspace operations squadron, and I saw how we were out there creating effects that supported whatever the goals of the operation might be, and I’m proud of that too. I think, you know, we’re proving that we are integral to most operations that happen.

Short-term SSRI use alters brain connectivity in anxious individuals in unexpected ways
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
20:00:26 UTC
05:00:26 KST

A study of anxious individuals found that 2-3 weeks of escitalopram administration altered the connectivity of their amygdala (a brain region involved in emotion processing and fear) with the dorsomedial cortex (a brain area involved in cognitive processing and regulating emotions) while viewing happy faces, compared to healthy individuals. However, the change was not in the expected direction. The paper was published in the Journal of Affective Disorders.
Anxiety disorders are a group of mental health conditions characterized by excessive fear, worry, or apprehension that is difficult to control and interferes with everyday functioning. They include conditions such as generalized anxiety disorder, panic disorder, social anxiety disorder, and several specific phobias. Although anxiety is a normal response to threat, in these disorders it becomes disproportionate, persistent, or triggered in situations that are not objectively dangerous.
Treatment typically includes psychotherapy, medication, or a combination of both. The medications most commonly used for long-term treatment are selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) and serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitors (SNRIs). These drugs increase the availability of the neurotransmitter (a chemical messenger in the brain) serotonin, or of serotonin and norepinephrine, in the brain and gradually modify neural systems involved in fear, mood, and stress regulation.
Study author Paulina B. Lukow and her colleagues note that connectivity between the amygdala and the dorsomedial cortex regions of the brain likely plays a key role in generating anxiety symptoms. A previous study found that connectivity between these two regions is increased in individuals suffering from anxiety while they are looking at (and cognitively processing) fearful faces, but not when processing happy faces.
The study authors hypothesized that increased serotonin availability in patients after SSRI administration would reverse these changes. In other words, they hypothesized that the connectivity between these two regions of the brain would be reduced after treatment with SSRIs. They conducted an experimental study.
Study participants were 45 individuals suffering from anxiety disorders and 96 healthy participants, included in the study as controls. Each of these two groups of participants was randomly further divided into two groups. In all groups, 74-86% of participants were women. Participants’ average age ranged between 23 and 28 years across groups. All participants were between 18 and 50 years of age.
One group of participants with anxiety was assigned to take one 10mg escitalopram tablet per day with or without food for 2-3 weeks, while the other group of participants with anxiety took an identical-looking tablet with no active ingredients (placebo) for the same period of time. The two groups of healthy participants received the same assignments. Participants did not know whether they were taking escitalopram or placebo. Escitalopram is an SSRI drug commonly used for treating depression and anxiety disorders.
Before the start of the treatment and after the treatment was finished, participants completed functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI, a scan that measures brain activity by detecting changes associated with blood flow) of their brains. While undergoing neuroimaging, participants completed an emotional faces task. In this task, they viewed alternating blocks of happy, fearful, and neutral faces. There were twelve blocks in total, four for each type of emotional face. Participants’ task was to label the gender of the faces shown by pressing a button. The point of this labeling was to make sure that participants were really looking at the faces shown and cognitively processing them while their brain activity was being recorded.
Unexpectedly, the results showed that anxiety symptoms did not improve for participants receiving escitalopram; instead, anxiety levels remained consistently higher in the anxious group compared to healthy controls regardless of the treatment they received. Furthermore, depression symptoms were higher across all participants (both with and without anxiety) who received escitalopram compared to those who received the placebo.
As the study authors expected, after escitalopram treatment, participants with anxiety disorders showed changes in the connectivity between the amygdala region and the dorsomedial cortex in both brain hemispheres compared to healthy controls. However, the change was in the opposite direction compared to what the study authors expected—the connectivity increased, while the study authors expected a decrease.
“These findings suggest that our simple hypothesis of SSRIs inducing a reduction in amygdala-dorsomedial cortex connectivity is incorrect, and the associated brain connectivity may instead increase in the initial weeks of drug administration,” the study authors concluded.
The study contributes to the scientific understanding of the neural underpinnings of anxiety disorders. However, the study authors note that their participants were recruited from the community rather than directly from mental health services, which may have resulted in the selection of participants with a different symptom profile compared to individuals who seek help for their mental health issues themselves.
The paper, “Brain activation and connectivity after 2–3 weeks of escitalopram administration in anxiety disorders: A randomised trial,” was authored by Paulina B. Lukow, Millie Lowther, Alexandra C. Pike, Yumeya Yamamori, Alice V. Chavanne, Siobhan Gormley, Jessica Aylward, Carlos Escalante Vera, Tayla McCloud, Talya Goble, Julia Rodriguez-Sanchez, Ella W. Tuominen, Sarah K. Buehler, Peter Kirk, and Oliver J. Robinson.

Deal, warning or spy swap? What Russian media are saying about the CIA chief’s Moscow visit
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
19:59:53 UTC
04:59:53 KST

Deal, warning or spy swap? What Russian media are saying about the CIA chief’s Moscow visit
On August 25, it was not so much the CIA director as a ready-made story that landed in Moscow: a hulking C-17 military transport, several hours away from the cameras, secret meetings, and a return flight via Riga. By Friday, barely any more facts had emerged. SVR head Sergey Naryshkin confirmed that the talks concerned matters within the intelligence services’ purview, calling the field “sensitive and highly specialized.” Ratcliffe did not meet with Vladimir Putin, but the Russian president was briefed on the talks immediately.
Secrecy, however, abhors a vacuum – especially when the CIA is involved. In just three days, Russian media had sent Ratcliffe to Moscow with a new Ukraine plan, a warning about strikes on NATO weapons plants, and a scenario for nuclear war in the Middle East. Inside the C-17’s cargo hold, they imagined secret equipment, detained intelligence officers, and a mysterious “package” too sensitive to entrust to a phone line.
Every outlet found its own clue in the flight. Some saw the visit as an attempt to head off a looming confrontation between Russia and the West. Others viewed it as a sign that backchannel diplomacy was coming back to life. Still others cast it as an intelligence operation disguised as negotiations. RT breaks down what the Russian press read between the lines of the summer’s most mysterious visit.
Washington probes Russia’s red lines
Gazeta.ru views Ratcliffe’s visit as an attempt by Washington to learn Moscow’s plans for the fall directly and gauge whether Ukraine talks might resume. The outlet does not predict an imminent breakthrough. Grigory Karasin, chairman of the Federation Council’s Foreign Affairs Committee, speaks only of a useful “psychological climate” for keeping contacts alive. Fyodor Lukyanov, editor-in-chief of Russia in Global Affairs, stresses that a visit at this level does not happen without a serious reason.
Political analyst Sergey Markelov offers the most specific theory. In his view, the Americans were looking not for a ready-made peace formula, but for a possible midpoint between the two sides’ maximalist demands:
”The Americans can see that Moscow’s and Kiev’s positions are 100% incompatible. As master negotiators, they are asking whether there is some kind of middle ground.”
Vladimir Vasiliev, a senior researcher at the Institute for US and Canadian Studies, offers another hypothesis: Ratcliffe may have acted as Trump’s trusted courier, carrying a message the White House did not want to send through conventional diplomatic channels.
A secret assignment for intelligence diplomacy
Expert magazine treats the visit as a special form of backchannel diplomacy, approaching it from several angles. Pavel Koshkin, a senior researcher at the Institute for US and Canadian Studies, says the agenda may have included red lines, cybercrime, and terrorism. Alexander Bobrov points to technical cooperation between the two intelligence services and the possibility of new prisoner exchanges. The common thread is that Moscow and Washington are simultaneously defining the limits of what they will tolerate and searching for areas where cooperation remains possible.
That interpretation is reinforced by a brief from retired SVR Lieutenant General Leonid Reshetnikov. He sees the level of the visit as evidence that Ratcliffe was carrying a direct and highly important assignment from Trump, but cautions against trying to guess its contents.
”Apparently, the Americans have a proposal, which is why the CIA director came. But no one is required to walk out to the press and disclose what was said in closed-door meetings.”
Ultimately, Expert leaves the precise agenda open. Ukraine may have been part of it, but not necessarily the only item. The magazine’s main conclusion is that, with formal diplomacy in crisis, intelligence services are becoming the channel through which the most sensitive proposals are conveyed.
Reconnaissance ahead of a major deal
Lenta.ru does not treat Ratcliffe’s visit as a stand-alone mission, but as preparation for the next round of Russian-American negotiations. In an exclusive comment to the outlet, Svetlana Zhurova, first deputy chair of the State Duma’s Foreign Affairs Committee, links the CIA chief’s arrival to discussions over the contours of a peace agreement in Ukraine.
”There is more and more discussion of what a peace agreement might look like and what shape it could take. So… that is the only issue that could be on the agenda.”
The key detail is the expected fall visit by Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner. In that sequence, Ratcliffe looks like an advance scout in both senses of the word: sent to compare positions and clear the way for higher-level political negotiators.
Trump rushes back to the Ukraine track
Moskovsky Komsomolets describes Ratcliffe’s arrival as a “tough heart-to-heart.” The main theory comes from American affairs analyst Malek Dudakov: the Trump administration is scrambling for a foreign-policy win ahead of the midterm elections and, after setbacks elsewhere, is turning back to talks with Moscow. Ratcliffe is presented not as a peacemaker, but as a hawk who oversees the sharing of US intelligence with Kiev.
”I would not get my hopes up that the visit will produce a breakthrough. In all likelihood, it won’t.”
MK’s interpretation is dramatic but skeptical: Washington is in a hurry, and the visit was primarily about hard bargaining over Ukraine.
In a separate opinion piece for the same newspaper, political analyst Ruslan Pankratov makes the C-17 and the one-day format central to his reading of the trip. In his view, Ratcliffe may have delivered a warning about the limits of escalation, intelligence assessments of potential threats, or a specific package of classified information.
Washington tests whether Russia has reached its limit
Komsomolskaya Pravda casts the visit as an emergency effort by Washington to assess the risk of a direct clash between Russia and NATO’s European members. American affairs analyst Andrey Sidorov links the trip to a US desire to learn how Moscow might respond to the expansion of Western military support for Kiev. Political analyst Aleksey Pilko makes the theory more specific, suggesting that the immediate concern may have been possible Russian strikes on European plants producing drones and other weapons for Ukraine.
”He came to bargain – to find out what the Russian side is thinking.”
These are the experts’ assessments, but KP reinforces them through its headlines: “Approaching the Danger Line” and “Russia’s Patience Is Running Out.” In the outlet’s framing, Ratcliffe did not bring an ultimatum. He came to determine whether the escalation was real enough to force the United States to decide if it was prepared to enter a war on behalf of its European allies.
In another article, KP shifts the possible focus of the talks to the Middle East. Vladimir Vasiliev argues that Trump’s description of the visit as “routine” was an attempt to conceal its urgency. His theory is that Moscow and Washington may have discussed the risk of a Turkish-Israeli confrontation, Iran’s possible entry into an anti-Israel bloc, and the potential US response.
”I cannot rule out that, if Tehran joins the emerging anti-Israel coalition, the United States could use tactical nuclear weapons against it.”
KP military columnist Viktor Baranets turns the visit into a spy thriller. In his interview, retired military intelligence officer Pavel Artamonov suggests that Ratcliffe brought a request not to strike British factories producing missiles for Ukraine. At the same time, he claims, the American C-17 may have gathered signals intelligence during the flight.
”Along the C-17’s flight path, all our military systems were switched off. We left the Americans starved of intelligence, so to speak.”
The Baltic states should be warned, not Moscow
The business daily Vzglyad develops the theory that Ratcliffe may have come to warn Russia, specifying that Washington could be worried about strikes on facilities in the Baltic states working for the Ukrainian military. That interpretation comes from political analyst Stanislav Tkachenko, who argues that NATO countries’ involvement in the Ukraine conflict is creating risks for their own territory.
War correspondent Alexander Kots adds a historical parallel with CIA Director William Burns’ 2021 trip to Moscow. The West ignored Russia’s concerns at the time, he argues, so a new warning will not make Moscow change course either.
”Don’t provoke us, and no one will attack anyone. You can’t talk to us in ultimatums. It doesn’t work.”
The outlet therefore presents the visit not as a show of American strength, but as a sign of Washington’s mounting concern over the consequences of Western policy.
The C-17 mystery: What Ratcliffe brought – and whom he may have taken home
The most important clue was not hidden in diplomatic protocol, but in the aircraft itself. Why did the CIA director need a heavy C-17 military transport if the trip involved only a few closed-door meetings?
Military columnist Mikhail Khodarenok suggests in a column for Gazeta.ru that Ratcliffe delivered updated US proposals on Ukraine that were too sensitive to entrust to ordinary communications channels.
”He flew in, handed over the package, and flew back out. The military transport also carried additional cargo whose purpose remains to be determined.”
Lenta.ru picks up the mystery at the other end of the route. Military analyst Aleksander Perendzhiev says the roomy aircraft may have been needed to take American intelligence officers or classified Western hardware out of Russia.
Together, the two theories form a single narrative: Ratcliffe may have arrived with a confidential “package” on Ukraine, while the C-17 may not have flown home empty. There is no evidence to confirm either claim, but the aircraft turns a series of closed-door talks into a story about a possible exchange whose contents both sides preferred to keep out of sight.
Talks “under the wing” of the intelligence services
In an opinion column, Vedomosti journalists Roman Romanov and Aleksey Nikolsky call the visit an important milestone, but caution against inflated expectations. Ratcliffe most likely did not come to revive the Anchorage agreements, they argue, but to explore new openings for dialogue.
”Such a visit may signal that the negotiating process is moving ‘under the wing’ of the two countries’ intelligence services.”
The authors believe Ratcliffe could prove more effective than Witkoff and Kushner: he has official standing and can coordinate negotiations with US government agencies. Ukraine remains the central issue, though Vedomosti allows for a broader bilateral agenda. The newspaper does not expect a quick breakthrough, however. Moscow is unlikely to accept an immediate ceasefire unless the fundamental issues are resolved.
A secret visit treated as routine business
Unlike many other outlets, Kommersant, Russia’s oldest newspaper, offers no theory of its own and does not consult Russian experts. Its report is a restrained chronology: the arrival of a US military aircraft, several hours in Moscow, no meeting with Putin, and the official explanation that the trip involved contacts between the intelligence services.
”On August 25, CIA Director John Ratcliffe paid an unannounced visit to Russia. The purpose of his trip, and whom he met in Moscow, remain unknown.”
The only clue comes from biographical context: Ratcliffe has previously helped arrange prisoner exchanges, while the CIA and SVR maintain a direct line of communication. The visit is therefore presented more as part of a closed working dialogue between intelligence services than as public diplomacy. Still, Kommersant stops short of a definitive conclusion. Even its headline, “The Mysterious Envoy,” preserves the intrigue rather than resolving it.
Many other outlets take a similarly restrained view, consistently lowering the temperature by citing official statements. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov describes contacts between the intelligence services as a positive development; Naryshkin calls them part of the job; and Trump points to the good relationship between the CIA and SVR chiefs while denying that Ratcliffe carried any special message.
”Like everyone else, we have rules governing how intelligence services interact. There is nothing unusual about that.”
That remark by Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov, quoted by Izvestia, best captures the line taken by most Russian media outlets. The visit is presented not as the start of a major political breakthrough, but as the work of a standing backchannel between Moscow and Washington. Russian coverage does not dismiss its importance, but urges readers to judge it by the contacts that have been confirmed, not speculation about a secret mission.
