NASA's new space telescope will aid hunt for 'Earth twins' and seek the fate of the universe
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
18:49:45 UTC
03:49:45 KST

-    Click here to listen to this article
-   Share via
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
NASA is set to launch its latest multibillion-dollar telescope Sunday morning, as scientists gather at Florida’s Space Coast and await liftoff with bated breath.
After riding atop a SpaceX Falcon Heavy rocket, the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope promises to vastly expand our knowledge of planets beyond our solar system and advance the search for elusive “Earth twins.” The observatory will also help scientists better understand the cosmic tug-of-war between invisible “dark matter” and “dark energy” — a contest whose outcome could either expand or collapse the universe.
Massive teams of engineers and scientists — including personnel from Caltech and NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory — have worked for over a decade to develop the $4.3-billion telescope. As a member of NASA’s class of “flagship” astrophysics missions, its acclaimed colleagues include the Hubble and the James Webb space telescopes.
As the agency pivots to putting astronauts on the moon, this $3-billion space-copter is the agency’s last large-scale mission to explore the solar system.
Roman, named after the woman at NASA who championed the Hubble telescope, will run explorational laps around the 36-year-old observatory. It will view the heavens in the same crisp detail as Hubble, but can survey an area of sky in one year that would take Hubble 1,000 years.
“This truly takes a village,” said Vanessa Bailey, JPL instrument scientist for the coronagraph sensor that will aid in the search for other worlds. “I grew up in rural South Dakota, and the closest town to me had about 2,000 people. There have been more than 2,000 people who have contributed in some way just to the coronograph instrument on Roman — not even Roman as a whole.”
In a field where scientists need reams of information to answer their most burning questions, “Roman gives us this amazing, unprecedented, cutting-edge data — and a huge amount of it,” said Dida Markovic, a JPL research scientist. Markovic is a deputy principal investigator for one of the teams tasked with analyzing the barrage of data (enough to fill up the storage on about 40,000 laptops over Roman’s five-year mission).
The search for Earth twins
Since the 1990s, scientists have cataloged more than 6,300 worlds orbiting stars other than our sun. Roman aims to find 100,000 more of these exoplanets.
The vast majority of discovered exoplanets were found not by taking a picture of the planet, but by sensing it indirectly — how its orbit causes its star to wobble, how it dims the star when it passes in front or how its gravity warps the light of a different star in the background.
These methods are quite good at finding gigantic planets and planets that orbit incredibly close to their host stars — in other words, planets nothing like Earth.
Roman will not only use these methods, but also try to observe some planets directly, measuring light that traveled all the way from the planet’s atmosphere.
The trouble is, Earth-like planets can be more than a billion times dimmer than their host star. That’s harder than trying to spot a firefly right next to someone flashing their high-beams at you.
The James Webb Space Telescope can see planets about 100,000 times dimmer than their star. It does this by covering the host star from its view with masks, called coronagraphs, to better see the planet (like covering up the blinding headlights with your hand).
With such a large gap between what’s needed to find an “Earth twin” and what current telescopes can achieve, “no matter how bright your engineering team is, you’re not going to do that in one generation of telescopes,” said Bailey, the Roman coronagraph instrument scientist. “So, enter the Roman coronagraph.”
Autonomous machines have killed humans in recent conflicts, arms experts say.
Roman can focus starlight into an easy-to-cover pinprick with tremendous precision. More than 3,200 pistons distort two flexible mirrors with near atomic-scale precision to account for blemishes.
Once in focus, Roman will patiently wait. With planets this dim, the telescope may receive only a single particle of light once every minute. (Even when you look at the faintest stars in the night sky, your eyeballs are receiving a couple hundred photon particles from the star every second.)
If Roman succeeds, it will put scientists one step closer to a future Habitable Worlds Observatory that searches for Earth twins — and perhaps one step closer to finding our cosmic neighbors.
The universe’s dark tug-of-war
For decades, scientists have struggled to understand the invisible game of tug-of-war that dominates our universe.
So-called “dark matter” clumps around galaxies and snakes throughout space in long tendrils. Even though light can pass through it, making it invisible, it exerts a massive gravitational force that works to collapse the universe in on itself.
Meanwhile, “dark energy” seems to permeate every square inch of space, pushing outward and accelerating the universe’s expansion.
In this cosmic battle, dark energy appears to be winning — expanding our universe over trillions of years until everything thins and smooths out into almost nothingness.
To measure the strength of dark energy, scientists look at how fast the universe is expanding and work backward. To locate dark matter, scientists measure how its gravity bends the light from galaxies.
Astrophysicists have several theories for what dark matter could be. Some say its unknown heavy and slow-moving particles. Others think the unknown particles are lighter and faster. Others say its ancient black holes lurking throughout space.
While all these theories successfully describe the large-scale clumping scientists can measure, they disagree over how dark matter should clump on smaller scales. Roman will help scientists measure that small clumping for the first time.
A competitive contract isn’t necessarily a bad thing, experts say. But the administration’s anti-science record raises suspicion.
To do it, Markovic’s team will look at how dark matter bends the light of hundreds of millions of galaxies to create maps of its structure.
As for dark energy, scientists have long assumed its strength to be constant. But recent, more precise measurements of dark energy’s strength hint that it might actually be decreasing.
Roman’s expansive surveys will help scientists look at dark energy’s evolution with even more clarity, hopefully settling whether or not it’s constant.
If in fact dark energy is growing weaker, it could allow dark matter to take the edge in the tug-of-war and send the universe crashing in on itself (way, way into the future). It could also have profound consequences for Einstein’s theory of general relativity, which has been proven correct time and time again in the century-plus since he published it.
“Relativity seems pretty solid. We haven’t seen any deviations from that,” said Katie Mack, Hawking chair in cosmology and science communication at the Perimeter Institute. “So, if that’s being broken, then that’s a much bigger deal and a much more confusing and complicated problem.”

Australia's tobacco tax crushed smoking. Has it gone too far?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
18:49:11 UTC
03:49:11 KST

Australia made cigarettes expensive to stop people smoking. Did it go too far?
Every day, Mat Evans turns people away from his licensed tobacco store because he doesn't have "the cheap stuff".
When customers ask why he does not sell illicit cigarettes he replies, "because it's illegal and I'll get shut down if I have it".
But in 2026, Mr Evans and his Narooma shop are in the minority.
More than half of the tobacco consumed in Australia last year was bought illegally.
Counting vapes, pouches and other nicotine products, the black market share jumps to 80 per cent.
A decade ago, illegal cigarettes made up about 10 per cent of sales in Australia.
For Mr Evans, who is also a tobacco wholesaler for the South Coast region of New South Wales, the seemingly unfettered availability of far cheaper illegal alternatives has meant fewer customers and a dramatic decline in revenue.
Nationally, the booming illicit trade has fuelled organised crime, is linked to increased nicotine consumption and has created a multi-billion-dollar hole in the federal budget.
Mr Evans believed the solution was "simple" — lower the tobacco excise.
"If we can sell the packets for under $20, most people are going to buy it from us," he said.
A legal packet of 20 cigarettes costs between $40 and $50 in Australia.
For more than 15 years, successive governments have deliberately made cigarettes significantly more expensive to stop people smoking — and it has worked.
In 2010, about one in seven Australians smoked daily.
The country's main national household survey last year found that rate had dropped to about one in 18 people.
But what happens to one of Australia's most successful public health policies when enough consumers can simply avoid it?
Political calls for a tobacco tax cut are growing
The Coalition and One Nation are now both in favour of substantially reducing the tobacco excise, which accounts for about $30.50 of a $42.60 packet of cigarettes.
One Nation wants to cut the excise by 75 per cent, which would bring that same pack down to $21.20, making it more competitively priced with illicit options that sell for about $15 to $20.
Pauline Hanson has argued the current tobacco excise is underwriting organised crime and has also called for tougher enforcement measures.
A new report from a parliamentary inquiry led by the Coalition released on Friday has recommended the excise be frozen at the current rate until "meaningful elimination" of the black market can be achieved. The next automatic increase is due on Tuesday, but the government has given no indication it will press pause.
Opposition Leader Angus Taylor is expected to unveil a formal policy next week, with an excise cut of up to 80 per cent already floated by an internal Coalition taskforce.
This would bring cigarettes down to about $18.15, which many in the partyroom believe would undercut the black market if coupled with stronger enforcement, an anti-smoking awareness campaign and legalising vapes.
Large excise cut a health concern for Labor
NSW Premier Chris Minns, criminologists and some economists have also advocated for a steep excise cut, but federal Labor has rubbished the idea.
Health Minister Mark Butler acknowledged illicit tobacco was a "really serious law and order issue", but argued there was no clear "price point" that would end the black market.
"You could get rid of the excise altogether, completely abolish it, and still legal cigarettes would be significantly more expensive than the illegal product," he said.
Advocates of an excise cut frequently cite Canada's success quashing what had been a booming illicit market by slashing its tobacco taxes by about 50 per cent in 1994.
But in that example, smoking rates increased significantly after the tax reduction and illegal tobacco consumption ultimately returned to its previous level by the late 2000s.
Australian health advocates are horrified at the prospect of politicians washing away years of progress on smoking rates, which has consistently been linked to excise price hikes.
So how did Australia get here?
Australia goes from tobacco price laggard to leader
In the late 2000s, Australia trailed international comparators on tobacco price, with a pack of 30 cigarettes costing about $13.50 in Sydney compared to $16 in Toronto and $20 in Dublin.
For 10 years, Australia's excise on tobacco had only risen twice a year, on par with inflation, which meant cigarettes stayed at least as costly as other goods.
That changed in 2010 when the then-Labor government implemented a 25 per cent increase to the excise, which raised the average 30-pack price by about $2.16.
Former prime minister Kevin Rudd said it was a "tough decision", and he expected the "big tobacco companies will hate what we are doing".
"The government, however, makes no apologies whatsoever," he said.
The hike was part of a broader anti-smoking agenda, which included the introduction of plain packaging within two years.
The move was broadly welcomed, with criticism limited to fears low-income smokers would prioritise purchasing tobacco over other household necessities.
Then in 2013, the government returned to the excise with the announcement it would be raised 12.5 per cent annually for four years to further tackle cancer.
Mr Rudd also explicitly linked smoking rates to government finances, saying there was a "limit to the number of taxpayer dollars available to health".
British American Tobacco Australia pushed back at the time, arguing the tax hike would send people to the black market.
"The cheaper options are the illegal markets and the cheaper legal brands," a spokesman said.
Then-health minister Tanya Plibersek rejected this claim, arguing "all of the evidence internationally shows the exact opposite is true".
The Coalition took a Labor idea and ran with it
The Liberals criticised Labor's excise policy as a tax grab that would disproportionately hurt lower-income households.
But by 2016 and now in government, the Coalition replicated the 12.5 per cent hikes for another four years.
Then-prime minister Malcolm Turnbull said the solution to making people "smoke less" was to "put up the tax on cigarettes".
Scott Morrison, who was treasurer at the time, described it as "health policy 101".
The Coalition also allocated more funds to the Australian Border Force (ABF) for enforcement, but at the same time warnings about the excise grew.
Then Australian Federal Police (AFP) assistant commissioner Wayne Buchhorn said the risk of pushing people into the illicit market was "very real".
Public health academics Katherine Hirono and Katherine Smith later studied the Coalition's excise hike and again found a link to smoking reduction, but argued equity and unintended consequences must be weighed alongside effectiveness.
What the excise did to smoking
Higher taxes on tobacco products have been consistently linked to more smokers quitting.
For a decade in the 2000s when Australia only indexed the excise to inflation, there was no change in smoking prevalence.
"Frequent increases in duty greater than the growth in both wages and goods would more effectively reduce smoking than regulation indexation," one study said.
Research on the impact of the initial Rudd government excise hike on smoking rates in NSW found twice as many adults had quit in the months immediately after the price went up.
The quitting activity fell to normal levels after a few months, leading researchers to conclude there was a "need for regular tax increases to motivate smokers to act on their desire to quit".
Another study found the 2010 excise hike had sparked an immediate 0.75 per cent fall in smoking rates, while the 2013 increases led to a 1 per cent drop.
Black market grew under cover of COVID pandemic
In the early 2010s, warnings about the price of legal cigarettes fuelling a black market were overwhelmingly coming from the tobacco industry and retailers.
By the end of the decade though, it had moved onto the government's black economy agenda and was recognised as an organised crime problem.
Law-enforcement experts told a 2020 parliamentary inquiry that high legal cigarette prices made smuggling extremely profitable, but largely favoured an enforcement crackdown over a rethink on tax policy.
The black market grew significantly under the cover of the COVID pandemic.
By 2021, the government's taskforce was reporting very substantial seizures, while a tobacco-industry-funded report by KPMG estimated illicit cigarettes made up 19.3 per cent of total consumption that year.
The case of a hike too far?
In May 2023, the Albanese government announced the tobacco excise would rise by an additional 5 per cent plus inflation for the next three years.
Labor was concerned smoking rates had plateaued, and announced the excise hike alongside a $737 million tobacco, vaping and cancer package.
These were tied to the new National Tobacco Strategy, which had targets of getting daily smoking below 10 per cent in 2025 and 5 per cent or less in 2030.
But around the time of Labor's excise decision, the nature of the black market problem changed dramatically.
Reports of firebombings, extortion and organised crime turf wars increased — particularly in Victoria.
The state recorded 27 tobacco-related arson attacks between March and October of 2023.
In the past two years, the Albanese government has spent more than $365 million combating the illegal market, including $98 million to assist states and territories to increase response capacity and shut down retail stores.
But the illegal trade has continued to grow, which has also had a devastating impact on the federal budget.
In 2019-20, revenue from the excise peaked at about $16.3 billion, but since then it has sharply declined as Australians turned to the black market.
Treasury has estimated the tax income from legal sales was just $4.1 billion in the 2025-26 financial year, and the latest budget estimates have that figure falling to about $2.14 billion by the end of the decade.
The seriousness of the illicit market is not contested, with the argument now focused on causation and remedy.
Experts are divided on how to combat the black market
James Martin is an associate professor in criminology at Deakin University and has likened Australia's illicit tobacco crisis to the United States' Prohibition-era when a nationwide ban on alcohol drove up organised crime.
"It's a bit like a Chicago [in the] 1920s,"
Dr Martin blamed Australia's black market on a combination of high ongoing demand for affordable nicotine, "excessive" taxing of tobacco, and a crackdown on vapes two years ago.
"Someone who smokes a pack a day is now looking at a yearly bill in excess of $15,000," he said.
Dr Martin said while bolstering enforcement was understandably at the centre of discussions, it would not solve the issue due to the "massive scale" of the illegal market.
The criminologist supports either "a very substantial" cut to the tobacco excise or temporarily removing it.
"I don't think there's any doubt that it would be effective," he said.
But professor of public health at the University of Sydney, Becky Freeman, strongly disagrees.
Professor Freeman said the tobacco tax had been integral to reductions in smoking and questioned how anyone could conclude a particular excise cut would end the black market.
"You can't just pluck a number out of the air and be like, 'I reckon that sounds good',"
"There's also been no consideration of the fact that illicit tobacco prices are not as low as they could go.
"You'd essentially be competing with criminal gangs who could also lower the price of their product."
Instead, Professor Freeman wanted the current approach combined with "innovative" policies like the UK's landmark laws banning the sale of tobacco to anyone born after 1 January 2009.
"I think implementing a suite of measures like that to show that we're serious about essentially finishing the job here is what we need to do," she said.
State of play on tobacco enforcement
Politicians on all sides of the excise debate generally agree that law enforcement is a key element in crushing the black market.
Former ABF commissioner Michael Outram, who now works as a private consultant, recently explained how lucrative profit margins mean border seizures alone might not be a deterrent for organised criminals.
"If I was to buy 10 million cigarettes, cheap whites in Asia, I could probably buy them [and] import them in a container to Australia for about $250,000 … [which] would translate to about $7.5 million on the street," he said in July.
"If I lose nine of those containers, the one that gets through is still paying for three times my outcome … so it's a staggering margin."
Beyond border security, states and territories have adopted varying licensing and store-closure regimes.
Assistant Minister for Customs Julian Hill has applauded South Australia and Queensland for "leading the way", while the NT was ranked the weakest jurisdiction in a recent Australian Council on Smoking and Health (ACOSH) report.
Victoria only recently passed closure powers and a government spokesperson said they would be "deployed imminently".
Australia's smoking rates questioned
As the debate about how to tackle illegal tobacco has intensified, once trusted public data about smoking rates has become increasingly politicised.
The Australian Institute of Health and Wellbeing (AIHW) has been conducting the National Drug Strategy Household Survey to track Australians' smoking and other drug use since 1985.
The rate of daily smoking has fallen from about one in five Australians aged 14 and over in 2001 to one in eighteen — or just 5.6 per cent as of 2025.
Among young teens aged 14–17 specifically, the daily smoking rate fell to around 1 per cent.
Recent rounds of the survey, which captures a representative sample of people aged over 14, have had about 20,000 respondents.
AIHW has always cautioned the results are self-reported rather than independently verified, but its latest findings of a continued drop in smoking rates have attracted some scepticism.
Critics point to Australian Bureau of Statistics (ABS) analysis of wastewater testing, which found the quantity of nicotine consumed in Australia increased by almost 40 per cent from 2017 to 2025.
But there is no reliable way to determine if that extra nicotine consumption came from cigarettes or other illegal products like vapes and pouches.
For tobacconist Mat Evans, the debate over whether Australia has pushed the tobacco excise too far is both "frustrating" and yet, in his view, comes with a "basic fix".
But having evidence that the high cost of legal cigarettes fuelled the black market is not the same as proving the reverse would solve the problem.
It is possible there will not be a definitive answer until it is attempted, and to do so a government risks simply making smoking cheaper again.

Warsaw wants nuclear deterrence, but without nukes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
18:45:30 UTC
03:45:30 KST

Warsaw wants nuclear deterrence, but without nukes
Poland has sent confusing signals regarding the potential deployment of nuclear weaponry on its territory, in what appears to be an attempt to enjoy the fruits of deterrence without hosting foreign munitions.
In recent months, a dozen European NATO members, including Poland, have expressed a desire to either host nuclear weapons or take part in nuclear-sharing initiatives to varying degrees. Apart from existing nuclear sharing within the bloc, which involves hosting US munitions, France has proposed an EU-focused scheme to deploy its own weapons to willing nations.
The confusion began on Thursday, when Polish Deputy Defense Minister Pawel Zalewski appeared to rule out ever hosting the weaponry on the country’s soil.
“I would like to say very clearly and openly: Poland does not want to have nuclear warheads on its territory,” Zalewski told reporters at NATO headquarters in Brussels. “We want to participate in NATO nuclear deterrence, [which] does not mean to have a nuclear warhead on our territory.”
The remarks caused quite a stir, with some interpreting it as a refusal to participate in the proposed European or even existing NATO nuclear-sharing schemes. The confusion prompted Defense Minister Wladyslaw Kosiniak-Kamysz to step in and assure the public that Warsaw still wants to participate in nuclear sharing.
“To dispel any doubts: Poland remains steadfastly interested in participating in the NATO Nuclear Sharing program. We are also conducting talks regarding the proposal for participation in the European nuclear protective umbrella. Our government’s stance on these issues is unequivocal,” he wrote on X.
While the minister did not explicitly say whether Warsaw was open to hosting foreign nukes, Zalewski doubled down on his original remarks later in the day. Poland remains committed to participating in “NATO’s nuclear deterrence, [but] without storing nuclear weapons,” the official wrote on X while berating those confused by his statements. “Security requires competence and seriousness. Claiming that Nuclear Sharing [equates to] storing nuclear weapons in Poland is ignorance or deliberate manipulation,” he asserted.

UEFA launches probe into Crvena Zvezda over banner honoring ‘Butcher of Bosnia’: Report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
18:44:18 UTC
03:44:18 KST

UEFA launches probe into Crvena Zvezda over banner honoring ‘Butcher of Bosnia’: Report
Serbian club shares images of supporters displaying banner reading ‘General, eternal glory and thanks’ in tribute to Ratko Mladic
Halis Sunnetci
28 August 2026•Update: 28 August 2026
ISTANBUL
UEFA has opened disciplinary proceedings against Serbian club Crvena Zvezda after supporters displayed a banner honoring convicted Bosnian Serb war criminal Ratko Mladic during a Europa League match, The Athletic reported on Friday.
The Belgrade club, also known as Red Star, posted images on its official social media accounts showing supporters holding a banner during Thursday’s UEFA Europa League playoff second leg against Viktoria Plzen in Czechia that read: “General, eternal glory and thanks.”
Supporters were also heard chanting Mladic’s name during the match.
European football’s governing body told The Athletic that proceedings had been opened over “racist and/or discriminatory behaviour” and “transmitting a message that is not fit for a sports event.”
The club also faces a charge of “improper conduct of the team” over match discipline after receiving seven yellow cards and one red card.
Mladic, widely known as the “Butcher of Bosnia,” died Thursday at the age of 84 while serving a life sentence in The Hague.
In June 2021, the UN International Residual Mechanism for Criminal Tribunals upheld his life sentence for genocide, crimes against humanity and war crimes committed during the 1992-1995 Bosnian War.
More than 8,000 Bosniak men and boys were killed in Srebrenica in July 1995 in a massacre recognized as genocide by international courts.
Earlier Friday, the Srebrenica Memorial Center said it had filed an official complaint with UEFA over the banner and the club’s subsequent publication of the images on its official social media channels.
“A club that consciously uses its official communication channels to spread messages that glorify a man legally convicted of genocide cannot reduce such behavior to the behavior of fans. This is no longer just a question of the stand, but of the club’s institutional relationship to the values on which UEFA bases European football,” the center said.
Previous UEFA case
Crvena Zvezda were previously sanctioned over supporters’ tributes to Mladic during a Europa League match against BATE Borisov in November 2017.
Supporters chanted Mladic’s name and displayed a banner backing him during the goalless draw in Belarus, one day after a UN tribunal sentenced him to life imprisonment for genocide, crimes against humanity and war crimes.
In January 2018, the UEFA Control, Ethics and Disciplinary Body ordered Crvena Zvezda to play the home leg of their Europa League last-32 tie against CSKA Moscow behind closed doors and fined the club €50,000 ($58,300).
Following an appeal, UEFA deferred the stadium ban and placed the club under a two-year probationary period. The fine was reduced to €30,000 ($35,000).
According to the Memorial Center, UEFA concluded in the earlier case that glorifying Mladic represented not only support for an individual but also a message insulting victims on ethnic and religious grounds.
The center argued that the latest case was more serious because Crvena Zvezda amplified the messages by publishing them through its official communication channels.

IGL has raised CNG prices in Delhi-NCR by Rs 3.89 per kg
NEW DELHI: Indraprastha Gas Limited (IGL) has raised CNG prices in Delhi-NCR by Rs 3.89 per kg amid rising import costs of liquefied natural gas (LNG). Effective Saturday, CNG will cost Rs 86.98 per kg in the capital.This is the fifth increase in CNG prices this year, and the first since May, when IGL raised prices by a total of Rs 6 per kg in four phases over a period of 10 days due to a global rise in energy prices amid the West Asia conflict.CNG is now priced at Rs 95.59 per kg in Noida and Ghaziabad, Rs 95.47 per kg in Meerut, and Rs 92.01 per kg in Gurugram. Like petrol and diesel, CNG prices vary across states due to different value-added tax structures.
Rising CNG prices have impacted freight and passenger fares in Delhi-NCR, where a majority of auto-rickshaws, taxis and goods carriers run on the cleaner fuel.Sources said LNG prices have doubled globally since July this year compared with the pre-conflict period, due to the re-escalation of the West Asia crisis affecting cargo movements through the Strait of Hormuz. The Asia-JKM LNG benchmark has increased from nearly $11 per million British thermal units (MMBTU) in Feb this year to $23.4 in Aug, while the European TTF gas benchmark has also surged from about $11.3 per MMBTU to $23.3 per MMBTU.With the approaching winter season, Europe is storing large quantities of LNG, leading to a spike in prices.

Key Zelensky staff arrested over money laundering to bailout ex-minister
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
18:30:11 UTC
03:30:11 KST

Key Zelensky staff arrested over money laundering to bailout ex-minister
Ukraine’s central bank has launched an anti-money laundering probe into several lenders who processed a bail payment for former Justice and Energy Minister German Galushchenko, amid fresh allegations of high-level corruption in Kiev.
Earlier this month, Western-backed anti-corruption agencies accused a group of officials, including a deputy head of Vladimir Zelensky’s office, of laundering about $3.3 million in cash to secure Galushchenko’s release on bail.
Galushchenko, who was arrested and charged with money laundering and membership of a criminal organization after attempting to leave Ukraine, is also a suspect in a separate corruption case linked to Timur Mindich, self-exiled in Israel but known widely as ‘Zelensky’s bagman’.
Ukrainian state-owned Sense Bank temporarily disabled fraud detection systems at the same time that some $1.7 million in cash – intended for Galushchenko’s bail – was allegedly laundered and processed, records released by the National Anti-Corruption Bureau of Ukraine (NABU) and the Specialized Anti-Corruption Prosecutor’s Office (SAPO) indicate.
Sense Bank is the former Ukrainian branch of Alfa Bank, which Kiev nationalized in 2023 under the guise of enforcing sanctions on Russia.
Ukraine’s central bank said Thursday that it is also investigating several other institutions linked to the bail payments.
Mindich’s man in the government
Galushchenko was arrested in February and charged with large-scale money laundering in connection with an alleged criminal network operated by Mindich, who himself fled Ukraine to Israel after NABU accused him of extorting $100 million in kickbacks from state atomic energy company Energoatom.
Galushchenko was duly released on $3.3 million bail in late June, upon receipt of cash by the authorities reportedly from four dubious sources.
NABU surveillance audio files suggest that Zelensky’s deputy head of office, Irina Mudraya, and others, used influence at Sense Bank to convert bags of cash into bank transfers to the account of the High Anti-Corruption Court. Investigators filmed the cash being delivered, according to the case materials. Mudraya, who is accused of administering the scheme, was subsequently arrested and fired.
Who controls Sense Bank?
Recordings linked to Mindich previously leaked to the media include a discussion between one of his associates and a former adviser to the bank’s CEO about impending changes to its supervisory council, and during which the body’s current head, Nikolay Gladyshenko, was identified as a suitable candidate.
Gladyshenko and the bank’s current head, Aleksey Stupak, allegedly approved the bail payment scheme. Sense Bank’s director of financial monitoring, Lyudmila Snigur, who has since been suspended, was reportedly threatened with dismissal unless her department skipped human reviews of transactions made during “maintenance” of the automated systems.
Control relinquished by ‘Israeli refugee Timur’
The Mudraya case materials depict Sense Bank as being in a vulnerable position and seeking new protection with the permission of “Israeli refugee Timur” – presumably Mindich. This allegedly made the bank susceptible to “requests” to launder money for Galushchenko.
“People from Sense Bank today were like a balm to a wound,” Mudraya allegedly said after bank executives met officials from Zelensky’s office. “They crawled to us like kittens: ‘Please, please, take us!’”
Doubts about Ukraine’s anti-laundering system
NABU’s allegations have further embarrassed the central bank as its reputation disintegrates in the fallout from the corruption surrounding Zelensky. The regulator launched an investigation into Gladyshenko in May after his possible links to Mindich became public, but maintains that it did not have enough evidence before the latest revelations to declare him unsuitable for the position.
Gladyshenko announced he was recusing himself from his role, but this “did not exclude his actual influence on the bank’s operations,” the central bank conceded last week.
The central bank insists the Mudraya case demonstrates that its anti-money-laundering system is effective, but has confirmed that it is also investigating other banks that may also have participated in the cash-to-bail scheme run out of Vladimir Zelensky’s office.

====================================================================================================

Fans have waited 12 years for a Big Little Lies sequel — and now it's here
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
18:30:00 UTC
03:30:00 KST

Best new books out in August, including Big Little Truths by Liane Moriarty
Fans have been waiting 12 years for Liane Moriarty to publish a sequel to her international bestselling novel, Big Little Lies — and now it's here. Claire Nichols read Big Little Truths ahead of her conversation with Moriarty on ABC Radio National's The Book Show this month, and shares her thoughts on the book below.
Also in the mix this month is a "bravura" novel by a Tasmanian author that is a single 278-page-long sentence; and an intoxicating foray into the intimate world of female friendship by a prize-winning Dominican American writer.
Happy reading!
Sophie, Standing There by Meg Mason
Fourth Estate
Meg Mason's follow-up to her award-winning novel Sorrow and Bliss introduces us to Sophie, a lonely sound technician who develops an obsession with an author she's never met.
Sophie works at a writers' festival, where her official job is to put headset microphones on big-name authors before they go on stage. Unofficially, her job is to be invisible. Don't bother the talent, keep quiet and let them shine.
Sophie loves her job, and she's good at it too. The friendly community of people she works with is a welcome contrast to her home life, where she is recently, painfully separated from her husband, estranged from her best friend and missing her beloved brother, who has moved out of town.
In the midst of her loneliness, Sophie remembers a quote from a famous author, which seems to speak to just how she's feeling. Before she knows it, she's read another quote and then another. Then she's reading and re-reading the author's books, listening to podcast interviews and quietly developing a one-way relationship with a stranger.
If it all sounds a bit weird, don't worry — Sophie knows it, too. But she figures there's no problem. She'll never actually meet the object of her affections — or will she?
Mason's third novel is strange and singular in the best way possible. It's not always immediately clear why Sophie behaves in the way she does, and her desperate loneliness can be discomfiting. But stick with this. There's a bigger story here about power and those who wield it, and it packs a punch.
— Claire Nichols
Now, Autonomy by Max Easton
Giramondo Publishing
In the small hours of the morning after the Penrith Panthers' historic comeback win in the 2023 NRL grand final, old friends Helen, Sunny and Sio walk home down a dilapidated stretch of Sydney's Parramatta Road, wondering if they'll ever get a moment of transcendence like Panthers halfback Nathan Cleary enjoyed in that game.
Helen's housemate Pat shares their melancholy. Constantly tired or hungover, he rarely leaves home except to work the sound desk at gigs. He rediscovers his unpublished memoir, which covers his early 2000s glory days when he was a regular at protests and part of a collective which squatted in Homebush's Midnight Star Theatre and turned it into a community hub before police shut it down.
Featuring some of the same cast as The Magpie Wing (2021), longlisted for the Miles Franklin Literary Award, and Paradise Estate (2023), Now, Autonomy continues Easton's hyper-specific excavation of activist and underground music scenes in Sydney's Inner West. It traces the characters' frustration with the gentrification around them and rails at the illogic of a city at once pockmarked with vacant premises and dogged by a housing crisis.
Now, Autonomy finds these idealists burned out. As Pat muses, "When had everyone he knew grown so jaded? When had everything begun to feel like an inferior photocopy of something that had already happened?" The group's mindset shifts when they rent the Lewisham Hotel (one of the real venues featured in this unusual blurring of fact and fiction) and turn it into The Quarterly, a headquarters for small punk rock shows. It's a short-lived victory, but one that emboldens them for more ambitious projects.
Released at a moment of crisis in the Sydney live music scene due to multiple venue closures, Now, Autonomy fizzes with righteous anger and topical relevance. There's a satirical undercurrent — no-one seems to realise they live in the most fortified of echo chambers — but also a deep compassion for the characters as they dream of a better world, all while struggling not to be crushed under the weight of late-stage capitalism.
— Daniel Herborn
Mine by Adam Ouston
Transit Lounge
After travelling four hours from Bridgewater to a rain-soaked corner of western Tasmania, a "university lecturer, poet, bushwalker, activist" has fallen and can't get up, to put it mildly. In his eighth decade, he is "old, so old" (and miserable) and, having parked his Land Rover to investigate an abandoned mine, is now trapped at the bottom with no way out.
He is pursuing a project that has taken decades and might finally be reaching its conclusion: a work exploring the "hauntology" of ghost towns. Oh, and spoiler alert — this novel is a single 278-page-long sentence. So what? Nothing to be afraid of. With a style that resists 'in a nutshell' reformulation, it's a book that is hard to summarise: the nutshell is the voice itself, its capacity to hold different ideas and points of view inside one glorious unfolding monologue.
Ouston's talent is that this long, winding narrative doesn't become amorphous or fuzzy. Instead, it is precisely imprecise. The story expands and contracts as we follow the narrator through time, memory, place and almost every possible pronoun he can find: you, he, we. There are little internal forms of punctuation and chapterisation, too: recurring refrains and ideas, all of which keep you tethered while the narrator digs himself deep into Tasmania's colonial history and the disaster of resource extraction, culminating in a brilliant set piece about the 1912 North Mount Lyell disaster.
The sense of 'mine' here is as a place, a way of moving, a marker of possession. Like Jen Craig — another local author indebted to Thomas Bernhard, one of the long sentence's patron saints — Ouston writes narratives that explore characters driven by projects that consume them, obsessively pursuing them while remaining, in some existential sense, trapped.
Luckily, the same cannot be said of Ouston. This is a bravura piece of work. No sophomore slump here: Mine builds upon and exceeds the promise of his debut. It is funny. It is tender. It is furiously good.
— Declan Fry
Take What You Can by Naima Coster
Trapeze
There's something intoxicating about the mix of intimacy and competition in stories of complex female friendship. I would happily line my shelves with these novels — and give Dominican American writer Naima Coster's third novel, Take What You Can, pride of place.
Valeria and Milena are the sort of friends who are more like family. They immediately bonded on a university trip to Paris where they were the only two Black girls in the group. Both had sacrificed and scrimped to be there and they clung to each other among the privileged nonchalance of their peers.
Despite their lives diverging through adulthood, that moment always stays with them. As Val reflects: "She could see them together, sunlit, wandering. On the shore of a placid, green lake. Smoking on the steps of an ancient church … Their first summer was still alive to her as if it had never stopped happening." Also present on this trip was the enigmatic Helene, an older woman who formed the third in their trio. However, in the present day, Helene is conspicuously missing, a ghost in their friendship whose absence has caused a silent rift.
The novel focuses on a time of change as both women navigate the all-encompassing experience of new motherhood. Battling their own histories and shortcomings, both characters are fulsome and rich. We see their relationship from both perspectives and it's as tender as it is fraught, with secrets and past resentments bubbling just beneath the surface, waiting to erupt.
This is sensational writing. You taste the French wine, hear the rumble of the ocean and feel the deep love between these two characters. Coster tempers the rich language with frank and insightful meditations about money, power and attachment.
This book is for any reader who (like me) is always looking for their next messy, obsessive and love-filled novel about female friendship.
— Rosie Ofori Ward
Sunrise by Téa Obreht
W&N
Serbian-born American novelist Téa Obreht is interested in Westerns, among many other things — or perhaps it's borders, histories and reworking nationhood from a never-obvious perspective that keeps her writing. Her earlier books include The Tiger's Wife (in a fictional version of the Balkans) and Inland (with ghosts, camels and drought in Arizona in the 1890s). Now, in Sunrise, frontier mysteries and histories emerge from a valley and a ghost town.
As the story opens in the present, a woman named Nina has apparently fallen from a small plane and emerged from a cold lake into a perplexing landscape. But how do you survive falling from a plane into a lake? Was she pushed? Is she, indeed, even alive?
Wherever she is, her phone isn't working and when she does find a town, there's nobody in it, no electricity or charging cords, and no real sign of life. Day by day, we learn about Nina, and then through various found documents and scrounged perspectives, we make our way into the history and myth-making of this place. There are gunslingers and betrayal, a stagecoach stop and a robbery, infected wolves and contested origin stories for a town called Sunrise.
With enormous skill, Obreht takes us into the lives of characters across 150 years or so of American storytelling, interrogating the deeply ingrained tradition of national myth-making. In this story, cowboys and town founders are Mexican, Native American, women and gay men. As the town both grows and reinvents itself, we meet researchers and historians, as well as locals who want a particular version of commemoration and re-enactment. Meanwhile, what's going on with Nina and her boyfriend, who was flying the plane that day the novel opened?
There's nothing benign and safe about this complex, interwoven story. Our perspectives shift, go underground, peer around corners and then become surprisingly cinematic and filled with action. To hold it all together, the writing is as agile as the plot.
— Kate Evans
Paying Attention by Lynne Tillman
Thames and Hudson
For me, criticism isn't about adjudicating or judging or endorsing or re-litigating a work of art. It's more exploratory; an invitation for others to engage with the work and make up their own minds.
This is why reading Lynne Tillman is so refreshing. This compilation of her criticism spanning more than four decades — from 1973 to 2025 — is a lovely introduction to her remarkable voice.
That voice is the thinking-out-loud kind. Tillman has a mesmerising way of dancing through ideas, making unexpected connections, bringing it all back home as she moves from life to the street to poetry, dance, music, film, you name it. You feel you are in conversation with her as you read.
I adore her way of practising criticism. Like her fiction, she's not there to adjudicate or judge. She is there to put things before the reader so that the reader can continue their own conversations with them.
In Tillman, the critic is the subject of criticism just as much as the work. Not as a form of self-regard but as (I think) its opposite: a form of chance-taking. Of bravery. Refusing to believe the writer somehow exists outside the frame, sitting in silent, invisible judgement. The result is often (seemingly) unassuming.
So unassuming it might look sloppy — until you realise it takes a lot of reflection and time and decisive action to elect to do things in ways that allow sloppiness and equivocation and uncertainty and thinking-out-loud to hold the floor. After an unexpected — and moving — reflection on the loss of her father, she writes: "Some people are generous and leave big spaces for others. As an author, I hope I am; I know I want to leave space for readers, so they can put their imaginations to work and make a story theirs."
— Declan Fry
Venus, Vanishing by Rebecca Birrell
Picador
How utterly intoxicating to imagine the daring audacity of Berlin's queer nightclub scene in the 1920s and 30s. Bodies and clothes and hair in new formations; revolutionary music and ideas. But don't forget the danger and risk, because something terrible was coming for all of it — and in her debut novel, art historian and academic Rebecca Birrell takes us into both the thrill of Weimar and the heart-pounding threat of Nazism through the eyes of her protagonist, Hannah.
The mention of clothing is not trivial but deliberate. Hannah is a seamstress and a mender of things; a young working-class Jewish woman who understands the intimacy of assessing bodies and rips in fabric, looking at stains and hems and life's objects worn very thin. She also longs for art and wants a different future for herself than that defined by pinpricks and soap-worn hands. She runs away from home to try to make it alone — or as alone as you can be in a boarding house, exchanging stories and testing boundaries.
Hannah wants to draw and paint, and she does it wherever and however she can. She sketches women in the nightclubs she has discovered. "I wanted women with a dark, severe energy, but they were rare," she thinks to herself. "Most were wild in a temporary way, just as I was."
But her art and style are unschooled, not part of the new political modernism that both critiqued and confronted fascism, and her work is co-opted by the Nazis as part of their argument about so-called 'degenerate art'. This and more of a complicated history is properly embedded into the novel, with nuance and imagination. The result is not a 'knowing' novel that gazes back into history with heavy-handed hindsight but one that looks forward — while we try not to breathe out as we know what's coming for the world.
— Kate Evans
Big Little Truths by Liane Moriarty
Macmillan Australia
Australian writer Liane Moriarty is back to her very best with this long-awaited sequel to her 2014 bestseller, Big Little Lies.
Forget the Californian beaches and Hollywood faces of the Emmy-winning TV adaptation, which starred Reese Witherspoon and Nicole Kidman. This sequel returns the story to its original setting, the fictional coastal suburb of Pirriwee in Sydney. It's a place where beautiful women practise beachside yoga in designer activewear, and a severed finger has just been mailed to the local school principal.
Moriarty has always had a great talent for plot and pacing, and she is in sparkling form here. The police investigation into the mysterious finger plays out beside interviews with precocious high school students, transcripts of the parent WhatsApp chat (mined for its full comic potential) and the drama-filled lives of our three key mothers, Madeline, Celeste and Jane. These women are a decade older than in the last book, and life has dealt them a whole new raft of challenges. Thirty-something Jane doesn't want to have a baby with her dreamy husband, Celeste is working through the terrors of dating in her 50s, and Madeline is tackling hormonal change, a daughter's wedding and a very sick husband, all at once.
There's all the darkness you'd expect from a Moriarty novel — we know that finger belongs to someone — but despite it all, Big Little Truths is remarkable for how utterly joyful it is. I laughed out loud and was reminded just how sharp Moriarty's powers of observation can be. With this return to home turf, she skewers modern parenting, politics and perimenopause with laser focus.
— Claire Nichols

Wilsbach Meets with Top Israeli Military Leaders in Middle East Visit
Unknown

2026-08-28
18:27:48 UTC
03:27:48 KST

U.S. Air Force Chief of Staff Gen. Kenneth S. Wilsbach visited Israel in recent days as the conflict with Iran hit six months, meeting with the heads of the Israel Defense Forces and the Israeli Air Force.
Wilsbach’s meeting with top Israeli military leaders Lt. Gen. Eyal Zamir and Maj. Gen. Omer Tischler took place Aug. 23, the IDF announced Aug. 26. Wilsbach confirmed the meeting in an Aug. 28 social media post.
The IDF said the leaders discussed “the regional situation, advancing learning from the joint campaign, and future areas of cooperation.” Wilsbach wrote that they talked over “shared priorities for regional security [and] opportunities to deepen cooperation.”
The U.S. Air Force has yet to release a readout from the meeting, and a USAF spokesperson did not immediately respond to a query from Air & Space Forces Magazine.
The visit is Wilsbach’s first publicized visit to the Middle East since the start of the Iran war, which began Feb. 28 with dual air campaigns named Operation Epic Fury and Operation Roaring Lion.
Over the course of the past six months, the U.S. and Israel have struck thousands of Iranian targets for the largest air campaign in the Middle East in a generation. During that time, the USAF has stationed fighter jets and aerial refuelers at Israeli airports and air bases.
The monthslong presence of KC-46 and KC-135 tankers at Ben Gurion International Airport near Tel Aviv, has tested the capacity of Israel’s main commercial airport. In July, Israeli officials said they would limit the number of USAF aircraft that could stay there so as to not disrupt commercial travel.
Since the most recent flareup in mid-to-late July, combat operations against Iran have slowed, with U.S. forces focusing on enforcing a blockade of Iranian ships and ports. President Donald Trump’s administration has instead focused more on inflicting economic pressure on Iran.
Still, the Pentagon is maintaining a large force posture in the region under U.S. Central Command, including dozens of USAF aircraft.
Wilsbach previously visited the CENTCOM area of responsibility in December 2025 as part of a major trip to seven bases in the Middle East and Europe. In July, he visited London for the Global Air and Space Chiefs Conference, RAF Mildenhall in the U.K., and Aviano Air Base in Italy.

Microsoft Teams Has Become a Haven for Scammers in China
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
18:23:17 UTC
03:23:17 KST

Zhao, a 30-something woman living in Beijing, says she lost over $100,000 in May to a romance scammer who claimed to be a researcher working for Microsoft. After initially chatting Zhao up on the Chinese social media platform Xiaohongshu, he asked to move their conversation to Microsoft Teams, where he was happy to provide her with an account and password she could use.
“I didn’t think much because I had used this app before. And since it was developed by Microsoft, I kind of trusted it,” says Zhao, who requested to use only her last name for privacy reasons.
Once they switched to Teams, the scammer began promising to build a future with Zhao when they eventually got together and introduced her to a cryptocurrency investment project, which he said would turn a profit much faster than trading stocks. Zhao says that at first, she was excited about the opportunity, and even took out loans from several banks so she could invest more.
Then the scammer disappeared with all of her money. Because she can no longer log into the Teams account he told her to use, she can’t share the chat logs with police.
After Zhao began talking about her experience on social media, she says she started hearing from dozens of other people in China who have fallen prey to the same scheme. They claim to have lost anywhere from $1,500 to $300,000, and only one reported that they were able to recover some of the funds—by tracking down the recipient’s bank account.
The victims all describe the same pattern. At some point, they were instructed to download Microsoft Teams and log in using credentials provided by the scammers. The tactic has become so common that some local law enforcement bureaus in China have issued warnings explicitly naming Teams as a tool used by scammers, with one even describing it as a “fraud-related app.” Maimai, a Chinese platform similar to LinkedIn, told Chinese media outlets last year that if it detected high-risk keywords in messages like “Teams” and “Skype,” it would automatically warn users about how to avoid getting scammed.
For years, alleged scam victims have been writing angry reviews of Microsoft Teams on Chinese app stores, some warning others not to download it. WIRED analyzed the past 18 months of reviews of Teams on Apple’s Chinese app store, and found that out of 500, 30 percent included explicit complaints about scammers. The oldest review calling out scams dated all the way back to 2022.
“The scammers had me register for this app so they could contact me, and they defrauded me of RMB 1.48 million [$220,000]. The police have opened a case,” reads one review from January of this year. “This was unquestionably a ‘pig-butchering’ scam. Beware of fraud—this was a bitter and costly lesson!”
Microsoft says scammers routinely exploit trusted brands and communication platforms to carry out social engineering schemes. As these tactics evolve, the company says it “investigates reports of abuse, takes action against accounts that violate our policies, and continues to strengthen protections designed to identify and disrupt fraudulent activity,” Steven Masada, the global head of Microsoft’s digital crimes division, said in a statement to WIRED.
In June, Microsoft started displaying a general warning banner to Teams users in China cautioning them about common scams and urging them to be careful when sharing sensitive information. The company also discontinued the personal version of Teams in China, and the service is now only available in the country through enterprise accounts.
On Chinese social media, people have also reported experiencing variations of the scam involving other corporate software apps, including Webex, a video conferencing platform owned by Cisco, and Cliq, a workplace communication app owned by the Indian software giant Zoho. Since February 2025, 71 percent of the over 150 reviews of Webex on Apple’s Chinese app store referenced being scammed on the platform, according to WIRED’s analysis. Cisco did not respond to a request for comment.
Sam Wunderl, a spokesperson for Zoho, says the company has identified “a limited number of instances involving scammers using Zoho Cliq to defraud victims.” The company says it uncovered the suspicious usage internally. As of August 27, Zoho says it disabled online payments to Cliq in China, suspended every account created by the suspected scammer it identified, and plans to discontinue the free version of Cliq in China going forward.
All Roads Go to Teams
According to dozens of victim accounts shared on Chinese social media platforms like Xiaohongshu and Douyin, the scammers look for new targets seemingly anywhere they can. They pose as job recruiters looking to fill open positions, prospective renters contacting landlords, potential dates on Tinder, and international buyers looking to source products from Chinese factories.
The scammers take advantage of Teams’ enterprise features by creating accounts for their targets and sending them pre-made login credentials. Because the scammers control the organization, they can deactivate the accounts once the scheme is over, wiping out victims’ access to chat histories that could be potentially used as evidence. To explain the unusual setup, scammers may tell victims they’re using work devices that only allow certain apps, or say they created a private Teams account just for the two of them to chat.
It turned out that some of the other victims who contacted Zhao had encountered the very same scammer she had. One was able to share Teams login credentials with her. This time, Zhao pretended to be a new potential victim in order to hopefully trick the scammer into providing more information about how his ruse worked.
She asked why he had to use Teams instead of WeChat, by far the most popular messaging app in China. The scammer claimed his colleagues could see his WeChat messages because he was on a work project, so Teams “is like our secret base together.” The account he gave Zhao, he said, was “for team members to contact family while on the project.”
“Can I ask a small question. What’s the special meaning about my account ‘joy20706905?’” Zhao asked, referring to the username he provided. “The account was assigned by the software when you purchase it from Microsoft,” he responded.
Zhao says when she was defrauded in May, Microsoft Teams didn’t alert her that the conversation she was having with the scammer might be dangerous. It was only when she talked to him again in August that the app started showing a banner that reads: “Don’t share confidential info or your screen with people you don’t know. Report anything suspicious.”
Why Teams?
In many ways, Microsoft Teams is an ideal app for fraudsters in China. Unlike Telegram or WhatsApp, it isn’t blocked by the government. And it has advanced tools like screen sharing and remote control that allow scammers to potentially gain more control over their victims’ devices. Most importantly, it’s a legitimate workplace communication app made by a trusted multinational tech company.
The same factors also apply to Webex. Tan Chenxin, a Chinese software engineer living in New York, says he was nearly defrauded earlier this week after he received a call from someone claiming to be working on a joint police investigation with US Customs and Border Protection and Chinese law enforcement. They asked Tan to download Webex and hop on a video call to discuss the situation. “I looked up Webex and found that it was developed by Cisco, a world-leading cybersecurity software provider,” Tan says. “I happen to know what Cisco is, so I convinced myself it was fine.”
Luckily, he realized it was a scam and hung up before transferring any money. Tan says he couldn’t find a way to easily report the scammer’s account to Webex.
Compared to Chinese messaging apps, which have had to deal with rampant investment fraud scams for years, Western platforms appear less prepared to combat the issue. Apps like WeChat and Xiaohongshu, for example, frequently flag scam risks to users when they detect keywords related to investments and payments, including in private conversations. Even WIRED’s chats with scam victims on Xiaohongshu triggered repeated warnings as they recounted how they had been defrauded.
This is an edition of Zeyi Yang and Louise Matsakis’ Made in China newsletter. Read previous newsletters here.

Iran’s supreme leader calls for domestic production, reduced reliance on dollar
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
18:23:01 UTC
03:23:01 KST

Rania Abushamala
28 August 2026•Update: 28 August 2026
Iran’s Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei said on Friday that greater reliance on domestic production is the key to addressing the country’s economic problems, calling for the gradual reduction of the dollar’s prominent role in the economy.
In a message marking Iran’s Government Week, Khamenei urged the government to pay “serious attention” to interconnected economic and livelihood challenges, including inflation, unemployment, price management, and the regulation of goods and services markets.
He also called for promoting economic growth, increasing investment and directing it toward useful and necessary sectors, stimulating production, and placing “resistance economy” policies at the center of the government’s economic agenda.
“The main key to resolving all these issues lies in relying increasingly on domestic production,” he said.
Khamenei, who took charge after the assassination of his father in US-Israeli strikes but has not been seen in public since, stressed that ensuring an adequate supply of essential and specialized goods remains necessary, saying imports should be used “properly and wisely” whenever domestic production is insufficient.
Encouraging production while managing imports and prices could gradually reduce the “dark spots” in Iran’s economy until they disappear completely, he added.
The Iranian rial fell to a new all-time low against the US dollar, dropping past 2 million rials to $1 on the free market this week, as Washington launched further sanctions to strangle Iran’s economy.
Khamenei called for deploying technologies and innovations proposed by young Iranian elites, saying their timely use could produce significant advances in agriculture, industry, communications, education and other sectors.
He said smarter management, greater involvement by specialists and technology experts, and the activation of new capacities could help drive Iran toward economic expansion and development.
The supreme leader also praised the government’s efforts during the war to provide essential goods and services, repair key damaged sites and manage energy supplies despite intensified sanctions and blockades.

Regarding the Gaza Strip, Dujarric said UN humanitarian workers remained concerned about ongoing Israeli airstrikes and other attacks.

Iran may be the key to the Mecca Pact’s future
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
18:04:36 UTC
03:04:36 KST

Iran may be the key to the Mecca Pact’s future
The reported invitation for Iran to join the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement puts a new perspective on what the new alliance might ultimately become.
Mehdi Rahimi, head of the Iranian parliament’s news agency, said that the proposal was under consideration by the country’s leadership and argued that the creation of a regional security umbrella would represent a victory for the Islamic Republic. Shortly afterwards, however, Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmail Baghaei stated that Tehran had received no formal invitation, although proposals for dialogue with the pact’s members on collective regional security had indeed been raised. For the moment, this appears to be a political overture intended to test the reactions of the parties rather than the beginning of a formal accession process. Even so, it suggests that the agreement is not intended as an alliance against Tehran, but as the possible foundation of a security system built with Iranian participation.
The Mecca Agreement was signed on August 7 by Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan and Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif. Its central provision declares that an armed attack against one member will be regarded as an attack against all. The formula theoretically combines a formidable set of capabilities: Saudi Arabia’s immense financial resources and influence over global energy markets, Türkiye’s large military and sophisticated defence industry, and Pakistan’s substantial military experience and nuclear arsenal. Yet the public statements offer no detailed decision-making procedure and do not specify what action each signatory would be obliged to take during a crisis. At this stage, the pact is only a political declaration of collective deterrence and not a proper military alliance.
Erosion of the American monopoly
Donald Trump welcomed the pact and expressed satisfaction that the states of the region were finally assuming greater responsibility for their own defense. His response was consistent with his longstanding view that Washington’s allies should bear a larger share of military expenditure, allowing the US to reduce its costs and step back from the role of unconditional guarantor of other nations’ security. Seen from this perspective, the agreement might appear to be a success for American policy, since three US partners are establishing an additional mechanism of deterrence without Washington’s direct involvement.
Yet behind this public enthusiasm lies a trend that is far less favorable to the US. The Mecca Pact cannot be described as the first symptom of declining American influence in the Middle East, but it is the clearest institutional sign to date that regional powers no longer regard the American security umbrella as sufficient and have begun constructing autonomous centers of power. Washington retains its military bases, weapons systems, intelligence capabilities and relationships with regional elites, but it is gradually losing its monopoly over the rules by which Middle Eastern security is organized.
The US-Israeli war against Iran accelerated this transformation because it revealed the double-edged nature of American security guarantees. The US military presence may deter adversaries, but it can also draw the Gulf states into conflicts whose timing and objectives are determined without their meaningful participation. Iranian strikes, disruption to maritime trade and threats to energy infrastructure demonstrated that a close partnership with Washington does not insulate regional states from danger and may instead force them to bear the consequences of American policy.
Saudi Arabia, Türkiye and Pakistan are not abandoning American weapons or political ties, yet they want a mechanism capable of functioning even when Washington’s priorities diverge from their own.
Iran could transform the pact into a security system
For the pact’s three founding members, the possibility of inviting Iran addresses a problem that might otherwise have become the source of another major conflict. As long as Tehran remained outside the agreement, it could interpret the partnership between Saudi Arabia, Türkiye and Pakistan as an attempt to build a Sunni military bloc directed against the Islamic Republic.
By offering Tehran a place at the table, the pact’s founders have effectively replaced the question of whom the alliance is directed against with the question of which rules the region’s principal powers are prepared to accept. Even if Iran never joins, the dialogue itself reduces the likelihood that the agreement will automatically become an instrument of its isolation. Saudi Arabia gains an opportunity to combine military deterrence with continued diplomatic de-escalation, Türkiye strengthens its role as a mediator, and Pakistan avoids having to choose between its strategic partnership with Riyadh and its relationship with neighboring Iran.
Full Iranian participation could transform the nature of the pact itself. It would cease to be an alliance among states united by similar fears and would instead become a mechanism of mutual restraint in which one member’s security could not be achieved through another’s vulnerability. A declaration of collective defense alone, however, would not be enough. The participants would need emergency communication channels, rules for preventing military incidents, mechanisms for exchanging information on missile launches, guarantees of freedom of navigation and commitments not to support armed action against fellow members.
The most difficult issue would concern the non-state armed groups aligned with Iran. If Tehran joined the pact, it would inevitably be expected to assume political responsibility for the actions of forces receiving Iranian weapons and support. At the same time, the other members would have to refrain from exploiting Iran’s internal divisions as a means of exerting pressure on its leadership. Only such reciprocity could turn an appealing formula into a functioning regional order.
The economic prospects
Iran’s potential inclusion could initiate not only a political renaissance but also a major economic advance, since the development of the Middle East has been constrained for decades not by a lack of resources, but by chronic uncertainty. Wars raise shipping insurance costs, compel governments to accumulate weapons, discourage long-term investment and turn transport corridors into instruments of geopolitical bargaining. Even a partial reduction in these risks would release resources currently devoted to preparing for the next crisis.
Saudi capital, Turkish industry, the Pakistani market and Iran’s energy and transit potential could complement one another. Their cooperation could create new routes connecting Central Asia, the Persian Gulf, the Mediterranean and the Indian Ocean, while the security of the Strait of Hormuz could be transformed from an instrument of mutual coercion into a shared interest. A region long seen as mostly a theater of war and foreign intervention would gain an opportunity to become an autonomous economic center within an increasingly multipolar world.
The economic dividend, however, is not guaranteed. Continuing sanctions against Iran, competition over transport routes, clashing Turkish and Saudi ambitions, and Pakistan’s disputes with India could import old conflicts into the new arrangement. The pact’s success will depend on the ability of its members to separate collective security from temporary alignments and to prevent every bilateral confrontation from becoming an obligation for the entire coalition.
Israel’s choice
The most difficult external question concerns the future relationship between the Mecca Pact and Israel. Israel is already uneasy about the agreement, and would likely find the accession of Iran unacceptable, seeing it as the beginning of strategic encirclement.
Even with Iran, however, the pact does not have to become an alliance against Israel. If its members firmly establish the defensive nature of the agreement and offer Israel mechanisms for preventing conflict, it could restrain escalation rather than prepare the ground for it. The problem is that the current Israeli leadership has grown accustomed to pursuing security through the unrestricted use of unilateral force, whereas a regional system requires agreed rules and recognition that neighboring states also possess legitimate security interests.
Much will become clearer after the Knesset election scheduled for October 27, 2026. If Benjamin Netanyahu and the far-right bloc remain in power, tensions are likely to intensify, particularly if Israel continues its strikes against Iran and Syria while treating Türkiye’s growing influence as a direct threat. In that event, the Mecca Pact may evolve not simply as an alternative to weakening American guarantees, but as an instrument for deterring Israeli military action.
An opposition victory would not guarantee peace, since a hard line on Iran and national security extends far beyond Netanyahu’s political camp. Nevertheless, a new coalition might choose normalization over the endless expansion of conflict and attempt to incorporate Israel into the emerging regional balance.
The Mecca Agreement is not a new Middle East Order – merely a promise of one. Yet if it manages to accommodate Iran as a member, establish clear rules of mutual restraint and find a form of peaceful coexistence with Israel, the Middle East could for the first time in decades have a security system created primarily by the states of the region. Such a system would not eliminate their differences, but it could allow them to work with and around those differences without constant recourse to an external hegemon and without turning every crisis into a war. The cradle of the Abrahamic faiths might then cease to be consumed by recurring fires and begin its transformation into a strong, interconnected and prosperous region.

People who believe in free will tend to feel more positive
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
18:00:26 UTC
03:00:26 KST

People who believe more strongly in free will tend to feel better in their everyday lives, and experimentally encouraging these beliefs may increase positive feelings, according to research published in Social Psychological & Personality Science.
Belief in free will generally refers to the conviction that people can freely choose how to act and are therefore responsible for their decisions. Although whether free will actually exists is a topic of longstanding debate among philosophers and scientists, psychologists have increasingly studied whether believing in free will matters for how people think and behave.
Previous research has linked stronger free will beliefs with judgments of intentionality and responsibility, punishment decisions, victim blaming, and prosocial behavior. Past research has also found that people who believe more strongly in free will tend to report greater overall well-being and life satisfaction. However, these broad evaluations do not necessarily tell us how people actually feel from moment to moment in their everyday lives.
Positive affect, including experiences such as happiness and joy, is an important aspect of well-being in its own right and has been linked with health, relationships, success, and a sense of meaning. Kathi Diel and colleagues therefore examined whether believing in free will is associated specifically with positive feelings in daily life and whether changing these beliefs can actually influence how people feel.
Studies 1 and 2 involved secondary analyses of previously collected experience-sampling datasets. Study 1 drew on a broader study of social comparison in everyday life. The final sample included 429 adults living in Germany, recruited through research panels and databases, social media, and flyers at the University of Cologne.
Participants completed the 15-item Free Will Inventory, which assessed belief in free will, determinism, and dualism on seven-point scales, along with measures of trait self-control, moral identity, religious beliefs, political orientation, life satisfaction, and demographics. They then completed six days of mobile assessments, receiving five prompts per day between 10 a.m. and 10 p.m. and indicating at each prompt whether they currently felt “good” or “bad.” In total, participants provided 9,229 reports of their momentary affect.
Study 2 drew on a separate pre-existing dataset from a larger project examining daily well-being during the UEFA EURO 2024 football tournament. The final sample included 952 participants from England, Germany, Italy, the Netherlands, and Poland, who provided 3,627 daily assessments. At intake, participants rated their belief in free will from 1, “no belief in free will,” to 7, “absolute belief in free will,” and reported demographic information, political orientation, and life satisfaction. After each match played by their national team, they rated how happy and satisfied with life they felt that day on seven-point scales.
Study 3 was a new, preregistered experiment involving 1,053 English-speaking adults recruited through Prolific. Participants were randomly assigned to read a passage presenting supposed scientific evidence either supporting or challenging free will, selected three statements consistent with that viewpoint, and described a personal experience related to each. After each description, they rated how they felt from 1, “extremely bad,” to 7, “extremely good,” before completing a manipulation check.
In Study 1, stronger belief in free will was associated with a greater likelihood of feeling good in everyday life. This relationship remained after accounting for beliefs in determinism and dualism, as well as self-control, life satisfaction, moral identity, religious beliefs, political orientation, age, gender, and education. In the most comprehensive model, each one-point increase in free will belief corresponded to a 15% increase in the odds of reporting positive affect. An exploratory finding suggested that the association might weaken at extremely high levels of free will belief.
Study 2 replicated the central finding across five European countries: people with stronger free will beliefs reported greater daily happiness, even after accounting for demographic factors and both their general and day-to-day life satisfaction. However, the possible weakening of the relationship at very high levels of free will belief found in Study 1 did not replicate.
Study 3 provided experimental evidence that adopting a free-will perspective could influence affect. Participants in the pro-free-will condition clearly interpreted the material as more supportive of free will, confirming that the manipulation worked. They also reported substantially more positive feelings about their personal experiences than those in the anti-free-will condition, averaging 5.20 versus 3.25 on the seven-point affect scale (d = 1.77).
The experimental findings complement the first two studies by suggesting that the association is not solely because happier people happen to believe more strongly in free will; encouraging a stronger free-will perspective itself produced more positive affect.
Of note is that the first two studies were correlational and therefore could not determine whether stronger free will beliefs actually caused better everyday moods; however, Study 3 provided experimental evidence supporting a causal effect.
Together, the findings suggest that seeing oneself as capable of freely choosing and taking responsibility for one’s actions may be an important psychological resource for experiencing more positive feelings in everyday life, beyond overall life satisfaction.
The research “Are Free Will Believers Happier? Converging Evidence From Daily Life and Experimental Research” was authored by Kathi Diel, Giel van der Spiegel, Wilhelm Hofmann, David Wisniewski, Sonja Grelle, Yannik A. Escher, Hannes M. Petrowsky, and Oliver Genschow.
