Free-falling atoms in space put a new twist on Galileo’s gravity test
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
18:00:00 UTC
03:00:00 KST

An experiment made famous by Galileo has been shrunk down to the atomic level and shipped off to space.
To show that objects of different masses fall at the same rate, the 17th century Italian scientist is said — perhaps apocryphally — to have dropped weights off the Leaning Tower of Pisa. Now, scientists have re-created that experiment with atoms falling while orbiting Earth. Two clouds of atoms on China’s Tiangong space station fell with nearly identical accelerations, researchers report August 28 in Science Advances.
The researchers measured the relative accelerations of two clouds of cold rubidium atoms. The atoms in each cloud had different masses, due to a difference in the number of neutrons in their atomic nuclei. Yet the accelerations of the two clouds matched with a precision of 0.05 thousandths of a percent.
The matching accelerations confirm that two different ways of defining mass are equivalent. One, called gravitational mass, determines how an object responds to the pull of gravity. Another, called inertial mass, determines how much an object accelerates when pushed with a given amount of force. If the two definitions are equivalent, the effect of the mass cancels out in equations, and objects of different masses will fall at the same rate in a vacuum. The concept is known as the weak equivalence principle, and it’s a foundation of Albert Einstein’s general theory of relativity, which describes gravity as the warping of spacetime.
Scientists have tested the weak equivalence principle by dropping objects on Earth, including atoms. But objects on Earth can fall only so far, limiting the tests’ precision. In orbit, free fall can go on indefinitely. Space-based tests of falling metal cylinders on a satellite have previously confirmed the weak equivalence principle. But atoms, unlike larger objects, obey the rules of quantum physics, and it’s worth checking to see if they behave differently. Atoms in orbit take the weak equivalence principle to a whole new level.

US judge rejects Trump bid to toss hush money conviction
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
17:58:00 UTC
02:58:00 KST

A U.S. federal judge on Friday dealt another setback to President Donald Trump’s attempt to overturn his hush money conviction, rejecting his request to shift the New York state case to federal court and dismiss it on presidential immunity grounds.
Judge Alvin K. Hellerstein reiterated his earlier finding against Trump, saying that the reasons Trump cited for renewing his request were "neither new nor legally sufficient.”
The judge added: "He has failed to show good cause and diligence.”
It is the third time Hellerstein has blocked Trump from having the U.S. District Court in Manhattan seize control of the case from the New York court where he was tried and convicted.
And, like before, Trump will appeal, according to a spokesperson for his legal team who called Hellerstein's ruling "baseless and lawless.”
"The Supreme Court’s historic decision on Immunity, the Federal and New York State Constitutions, and other established legal precedent mandate that the Witch Hunt perpetrated by the Manhattan DA be removed to federal court, and immediately overturned and dismissed,” a statement issued on behalf of the legal team said. "President Trump will be filing a powerful appeal, and will continue defeating Democrat weaponization at every turn.”
The guilty verdict, reached in May 2024 while Trump was between terms, made him the first former - and now current - U.S. president to be convicted of a crime. Trump is also challenging his conviction through the state court appellate process, which is pending.
Hellerstein’s decision came after a federal appeals court last year ordered him to reconsider his prior denial. The judge previewed his ruling during oral arguments in February, slamming Trump’s lawyers for legal maneuvers that amounted to taking "two bites at the apple.”
State prosecutors did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Trump was convicted in May 2024 of 34 felony counts of falsifying business records to conceal a $130,000 hush money payment to adult film actor Stormy Daniels, whose claim of a sexual encounter with Trump a decade earlier had threatened to upend his 2016 presidential campaign.
Trump was sentenced to an unconditional discharge, which left his conviction intact but spared him any punishment. He had long denied Daniels’ claim and said he did nothing wrong. He has sought to get the conviction overturned both by attempting to move the case to federal court and through the appeals process in state court, which is pending.
Hellerstein rejected Trump’s requests to move the case twice before. The first was after Trump’s March 2023 indictment. The second was after Trump’s trial, as his lawyers sought to nix his conviction in the wake of the Supreme Court’s July 2024 ruling that presidents and ex-presidents can’t be prosecuted for official acts and prosecutors can’t use official acts as evidence that unofficial actions were illegal.
Trump appealed Hellerstein’s post-trial ruling and, last November, the 2nd U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals ordered the judge to reconsider his decision, finding that he had failed to consider "important issues relevant” to the president’s request to move the case.
A three-judge appellate panel said it expressed no view on how he should rule but instructed Hellerstein to closely review evidence that Trump claimed was related to official acts and whether Trump could argue those actions were taken as part of his White House duties.
The judges also instructed Hellerstein to determine if Trump had "diligently sought” to have the case moved to federal court and whether the case can even be moved to federal court now that Trump has been convicted and sentenced in state court.
During oral arguments in February, Hellerstein took issue with the Trump legal team’s decision-making after the Supreme Court ruling.
Instead of immediately seeking to move the case to federal court, he noted, Trump’s lawyers first asked the trial judge in state court, Juan Merchan, to throw out the verdict on immunity grounds. Normally, such a request must be made within 30 days of an arraignment, but a federal appeals court in Washington, D.C. has ruled that exceptions can be made if "good cause” is shown.
Trump, a Republican, did not attend the arguments.
Trump lawyer Jeffrey Wall argued that prosecutors rushed to trial instead of waiting for the Supreme Court’s presidential immunity decision and that Trump’s legal team was crunched for time after the high court’s ruling because his sentencing was scheduled for just 10 days later.
Trump’s lawyers did not ask Hellerstein to intervene until nearly two months later, while their request to Merchan was still pending. The judge called that a "strategic decision” and suggested that by going to the state court first, Trump’s lawyers cost him the right to pursue remedies in federal court.
"No, your honor,” Wall replied. "It is what any sensible litigant would do” in that situation.
"Not so,” Hellerstein replied.
"That is a decision on your part,” the judge added. "You didn’t have to do that. You could have come right to the federal court. Just by filing a notice of removal, there would be no sentencing.”
Trump’s lawyers "made a choice,” Hellerstein said, "and you sought two bites at the apple.”
In his written ruling Friday, Hellerstein said Trump was asking for a "'second bite at the apple,' a result the law disfavors.”
The judge added that "Trump’s delay in filing for removal constitutes a ‘quintessential strategic decision,’ and the ‘fact that he later came to view that decision as a poor one is not sufficient, by itself, to establish cause.’”

A Conservative MP has questioned the use of Royal Navy assets to support security arrangements around an informal meeting of European defence ministers in Ireland, arguing that restrictions associated with Irish neutrality could limit the usefulness of any British deployment, the UK Defence Journal understands.
John Cooper, MP for Dumfries and Galloway, raised the issue in a letter dated 28 August to Defence Secretary Wes Streeting, after reports that Dublin had requested Royal Navy support for the meeting in Wicklow.
Cooper wrote: “I am aghast at media reports from Dublin that their Government has requested support from the Royal Navy for security, but that any vessel involved must stay outside their 12-mile territorial-waters limit.”
In a social media post accompanying the letter, he said: “Neutral Ireland portrays their gunboat George Bernard Shaw protecting an EU defence event there next week… but they’ve asked for help from the Royal Navy… who must get close enough to be much use! I’ve asked the Defence Secretary why we’re paying for this idiocy.”
The meeting is due to take place in Wicklow as Ireland holds the rotating presidency of the European Union. Cooper’s letter asks whether the Defence Secretary will attend and whether the UK will reconsider the deployment of British forces in support of the event.
He linked his concerns to a reported incident near Dublin Airport in December, when uncrewed aerial vehicles were detected close to the airport as Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy arrived.
Cooper wrote: “While the Irish Defence Forces spotted the UAVs, they had no ability to interdict, lacking any meaningful air-to-air or surface-to-air capability.”
He acknowledged that Ireland possesses a small number of RBS Bolide short-range air-defence missiles, but argued that these would provide only limited coverage against fast-moving or higher-altitude threats.
The MP also questioned the value of positioning foreign warships outside Irish territorial waters. He wrote: “This insistence that foreign warships remain outside Irish limits hampers their effectiveness. The Royal Navy is being asked to do a bad job. To add insult to injury, British taxpayers are footing the bill for this bodge.”
Cooper went on to argue that Ireland’s long-standing policy of military neutrality has not been matched by sufficient investment in its own defence capabilities, despite recent moves to increase spending.
He said: “The Republic makes great play of its neutrality but has for too long not funded this in the way that, for example, Switzerland does.”
The letter also refers to expected French involvement in security arrangements around the Wicklow meeting. Cooper said the French frigate Aquitaine was expected to remain 12 miles from the Irish coast and questioned how useful its air-defence missile system would be from that position against small or fast uncrewed aircraft.
He wrote: “Her Aster surface-to-air missiles will have the range to cover Carlow, but against low and fast UAVs may be a sledgehammer when a scalpel is required.”
Cooper suggested that smaller-calibre naval weapons might be more suitable against some uncrewed aerial threats, adding that foreign ships would still have to be positioned sufficiently close to be effective.
The MP also raised the broader question of military cooperation between Britain and Ireland, asking the Defence Secretary whether the UK should reconsider the current relationship.
He wrote: “Will you look again at the deployment of any British forces for this ‘informal’ chit-chat next week? It is both an affront to Britain and unaffordable expense, especially when our involvement is subject to damaging caveats?”
Cooper then asked: “More substantially, will you bring to the House details of a reset of our military relations with Ireland?”
The letter ends with a broader criticism of Ireland’s defence posture and the degree to which British forces might be expected to assist during an emergency.
Cooper wrote: “We can no longer afford to let the Irish walk on our cane. Will the Marine Nationale bear the cost of protecting those cables and pipelines? Do you agree that rather than RAF Typhoons and F-35 Lightning IIs scrambling – at gulping expense – to intercept anything airborne in the Republic’s airspace, it should be over to the Armée de l’air et de l’espace to cover IDF blushes?”
He concluded: “Ireland must accept neutrality without funding is simply freeloading.”

Iran’s Leader: Any action undermining social cohesion is prohibited
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
17:53:54 UTC
02:53:54 KST

Iran’s Leader: Any action undermining social cohesion is prohibited
TEHRAN- Iran’s Leader, Ayatollah Seyyed Mojtaba Khamenei, has stressed the importance of preserving national unity and social cohesion, saying that any action or statement that undermines social cohesion is prohibited.
The leader made the remarks in a message marking Iran’s Government Week, while praising the administration's performance and emphasizing the need to highlight Iran’s capabilities, support domestic production, harness the potential of young innovators, and give strategic attention to culture and education.
Ayatollah Khamenei commended the government for its efforts to secure essential goods and services, repair key damaged infrastructure, and manage energy supplies despite the 'third imposed war,' intensified sanctions, and various actions by the US-Israeli enemy.
Describing public service and the pursuit of the Islamic Republic’s objectives as a valuable blessing, the leader said one of the requirements for building a 'stronger Iran' was to explain and highlight the country’s strength and capabilities, alongside sustained efforts and innovation.
He said weaknesses and shortcomings should be addressed through planning and practical measures rather than being unnecessarily highlighted. According to the leader, openly discussing certain domestic weaknesses at a time when the country’s adversaries are seeking to undermine public morale could strengthen the enemy and cause concern and confusion among Iran’s friends and supporters.
By contrast, he stressed the importance of highlighting the country’s strengths and achievements.
The leader also called for serious action to address economic and livelihood challenges, including inflation, unemployment, price management and the regulation of goods and services markets. He identified economic growth, increased investment, stronger domestic production and reducing the dollar’s role (dedollarization) in the economy as other important priorities.
He described greater reliance on domestic production as a key to addressing the country’s economic challenges, while stressing that imports should be used properly and prudently where domestic production is insufficient to meet national needs.
Supporting domestic production while managing imports and prices, he said, could gradually reduce the economic difficulties facing the country.
Ayatollah Khamenei also called for greater use of technologies and innovations proposed by young experts, saying the timely adoption of new capabilities and a departure from established (traditional) practices could generate significant advances in the country’s development.
In another part of his message, the leader identified national unity and social cohesion as fundamental issues that must remain at the center of attention for the government and all state institutions.
He said all major measures in the cultural, social, political, security and economic spheres should be carried out with due consideration for their impact on social cohesion.
Some measures, he noted, may appear to have support among certain segments of society, but if their implications for social cohesion are not properly assessed, or if safeguards designed to protect cohesion are ignored in practice, they could ultimately harm those same groups as well as other sections of society.
The leader also warned against statements that undermine hope and weaken national and public motivation, as well as 'false dichotomies,' citing examples such as “war or negotiations,” “consensus or extremism” and “compromise or warmongering.”
“I categorically declare that committing any act that harms social cohesion is prohibited,” he said.
Ayatollah Khamenei further described culture, education and upbringing as 'supra-strategic' issues, arguing that other national strategies should be formulated with due consideration for these areas.
He highlighted the role of teachers, university professors, religious scholars, doctors and nurses, as well as homemakers, in shaping the country’s future cultural environment.
The leader expressed hope that implementing these priorities and other government programs would help move the country toward building a 'stronger Iran.'

====================================================================================================

Israel’s next government must save the country before it is too late - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
17:52:59 UTC
02:52:59 KST

I began my foreign correspondent career in 1990 in Romania, just weeks after its communist dictator, Nicolae Ceausescu, was overthrown. The new government called itself the National Salvation Front.
Romania truly did need saving. The communists had left behind an impoverished economy, shattered institutions, and a demoralized population.
There are moments when ordinary politics are not enough, and salvation is required. Israel has reached such a moment.
If Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu wins in October, Israel will be heading toward catastrophe. But if the polls are right and the opposition wins, it will be inheriting a traumatized country, with weakened institutions and international isolation threatening its very existence.
In such an eventuality, the opposition must then think in terms of national salvation, as it will need that level of motivation to succeed.
Everything is connected. The occupation, settlements, and wars fuel isolation; isolation damages the economy and security; and internal societal distortions further weaken the country.
It is a self-reinforcing cycle – and the next government must break it. Given that the haredi (ultra-Orthodox) birth rate, under the current incentive structure, will not decline quickly enough, there is no time to spare before the whole enterprise collapses. I therefore propose a dozen immediate tasks for Israel’s “National Salvation Front.”
Accountability and democracy
First, establish a state commission of inquiry that investigates the October 7 catastrophe without games or evasions.
Then, repeal the judicial and constitutional changes imposed by the Netanyahu coalition. In this regard, undo the legislative blitz of its final months, including the law weakening the attorney-general and the measures that undermined the independence of the courts, legal advisers, and institutional gatekeepers.
Make clear that ministers, like everyone else, will obey court rulings. Israel can one day debate judicial reform – calmly and with broad consensus.
And from here, look outward. It is time to turn military power into diplomatic gains.
Say ‘yes’ to Trump Gaza plan – and mean it
Declare that Israel accepts the framework in full and will implement it in good faith. If Hamas genuinely disarms, Israel will withdraw as agreed, cooperate fully with the international stabilization force and the Board of Peace, and accept the new Palestinian governing authority.
Israel should enthusiastically assist in rebuilding Gaza and help raise funds from Arab states and international donors.
End Jewish terrorism in West Bank
End the de facto immunity enjoyed by violent Jewish extremists. Outlaw organizations involved in terrorism, confiscate illegal weapons, dismantle violent outposts, and establish a dedicated apparatus for securing convictions.
The IDF must receive unequivocal orders that protecting Palestinians from Israeli attackers is part of its mission. Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich’s charade is over.
Freeze settlement expansion beyond security barrier
Halt construction in settlements deep inside the West Bank and preserve the territorial possibility of future partition – because without it, there can be no Jewish state.
A Palestinian state is inconceivable as long as Hamas remains armed and the Palestinian Authority has not undergone reform, but Israel must stop making the notion of such a state impossible.
It can declare that major blocs such as Alfei Menashe, Ma’aleh Adumim, and Gush Etzion are expected to remain in Israeli hands under a future agreement, while offering generous incentives to Israelis living beyond the barrier to come home.
Rebuild a regional strategy
Offer Lebanon and Syria a fresh start. Declare that Israel has no territorial ambitions in either country beyond the Golan Heights, and offer non-belligerency pacts.
Test whether the Syrian government of Ahmed al-Sharaa genuinely wants peace, and if so, welcome it. Offer Lebanon whatever assistance it needs to confront Hezbollah.
As for Iran, replace a war of attrition with a long-term strategy coordinated with the US and its allies, combining military deterrence with diplomacy and economic pressure. End attacks carried out without coordination, explanation, or a clear objective.
And reach out to Saudi Arabia based on US President Donald Trump’s plan, which includes agreement in principle to some form of Palestinian state in the future, with the India-Middle East-Europe Economic Corridor in mind.
Thank Egypt and Jordan
Acknowledge these countries for maintaining peace through decades of difficulty, and make strengthening relations with them a national priority. Listen seriously to Cairo and Amman, and seek ways to deepen economic, security, and even cultural ties with both.
All of this will be relatively easy compared to the real challenge at home.
Embrace Arab society
Declare organized crime in Arab communities a national emergency. Triple the police presence where necessary, target the financing of criminal organizations and illegal weapons networks, and hold commanders accountable.
Every murder of an Arab citizen should be publicly treated as an Israeli tragedy. Amend the 1992 Basic Law: Human Dignity and Liberty to explicitly guarantee equality.
Establish transparent formulas for equal funding of Arab municipalities and launch a national project to repair neglected infrastructure and services. Then begin a serious dialogue with Arab community leaders about national service.
Declare state of emergency in education
Israeli students lag behind in mathematics and science, and the gaps between the strongest and weakest students are among the largest in the developed world.
A country that wants to remain a technological powerhouse cannot continue like this. Israel must massively invest in state education, teachers, mathematics, science, English, and civics.
At the same time, it must introduce an equation: No core curriculum? No state funding. Every school receiving state money or recognition must teach the full core curriculum, employ qualified teachers, and submit to supervision and standardized assessment. This includes the haredi and Arab education systems. If anyone goes berserk over this, let them.
Overhaul incentives
Gradually eliminate child allowances beginning after the third child. Restore yeshiva budgets to their previous, lower levels. Eliminate unnecessary publicly funded rabbinical and kashrut-supervision positions (and reinstate the Bennett-Lapid government’s kashrut reform).
Simultaneously, establish a national integration authority that offers adult education involving the completion of core studies, university preparation, vocational and technological training, employment assistance, and pathways into military or national service for anyone who wishes to enter the Israeli mainstream, whether haredi or Arab.
Military or national service
Yeshiva study or religion in general should no longer exempt a fit young person from military service or legally recognized national service. Israel should enact a universal service law, introduced sensitively and gradually.
Haredi draft evaders should face the same consequences as other draft evaders. Benefits can be withdrawn, and institutions that systematically facilitate evasion should lose state funding.
Initially, this will not be possible by consensus, because there are currently no partners for such an agreement – although determined implementation may eventually create them.
It is time to redirect the money, energy and national ambition back to Israel and Israelis without compromising genuine security.
Make the Negev, Galilee new national project
Radically reorder economic priorities: less money for isolated settlements, sectoral mechanisms, and political needs, and more for infrastructure, housing, transportation, healthcare and education inside sovereign Israel.
Redirect the energy and money that have been squandered to the Negev and Galilee instead. Invest in roads, railways, housing, hospitals, universities and industry, alongside aggressive tax incentives for businesses and families. In the North, build a genuine transportation network to turbocharge its economy.
Amend Basic Law
A person indicted on serious corruption charges should not be allowed to form a government. The Basic Law should be amended so that this cannot happen again.
There will be furious opposition to such an amendment, but a national salvation government cannot afford to recoil. Its mission is to confront the country’s burning structural problems, repair the damage of the past, reconnect Israel with the democratic world, and offer hope.
If these steps are not taken, the country may not survive to its centenary in 2048. Entanglement with a hostile Palestinian population combined with the rapid demographic growth of the haredi sector without radical reform will destroy Israel’s alliances and access to global markets, driving out its productive sector. What will remain is an impoverished, embattled ghetto.
But if Israel does these things with a sense of mission and urgency, perhaps the phrase I encountered in Romania all those years ago can apply in this case as well. There is much in Israel worth saving, and worth the effort. There is still a chance for national salvation.
Dan Perry is a former Cairo-based Middle East editor and London-based Europe/Africa editor of the Associated Press. He served as chairman of the Foreign Press Association in Jerusalem and authored two books about Israel.

Georgia Sen. Jon Ossoff distanced himself from left-wing streamer Hasan Piker, who has called Ossoff a “dark-horse” presidential candidate, citing Piker’s “reckless and dangerous rhetoric” about American Jews.
Ossoff is facing criticism from some of his state’s local Jewish community over his votes to block certain arms sales to Israel. He has joined a chorus of Democrats who criticized Piker this week over recent comments that many interpreted as justifying threats to American Jews, including a number of Democratic politicians.
Speaking on a Twitch livestream on Aug. 20, Piker stated, “If Jews in America keep putting this idea out there that they are singularly invested in Israel, eventually someone’s going to come around and take action.” Piker added, “Not against the state of Israel, mind you, but against American Jews.”
An Ossoff spokesperson told the Atlanta Journal-Constitution on Thursday that he “unreservedly rejects reckless and dangerous rhetoric suggesting that policy advocacy invites violence against the Jewish community or any community.”
“American Jews and all Americans must have the freedom and security to speak out and petition their government without fear of reprisal,” the spokesperson added.
Ossoff’s politics and sharp criticism of US President Donald Trump have generated buzz about him potentially running for president in 2028, and have attracted some left-wing figures who have lauded his messaging.
Piker was initially among those figures, telling the Jewish Telegraphic Agency in April that he was “intrigued” by Ossoff.
“I think he’s very charismatic, and he’s done things that I’ve found to be interesting, given his position in Georgia, when he was one of the first lone voices in the Senate that actually was critical about sending aid to Israel early on,” Piker said at the time. “I was like, that’s a unique position for - he’s Jewish as well - for a young American Jew to take in Georgia.”
Piker said that he heard from young Georgian Jews in his online community who “could not believe that their synagogues and their rabbis and their organizations in their communities took out like a full page ad yelling at Jon Ossoff for taking a stance against arming the State of Israel.”
Several Democrats condemn Piker's comments
Ossoff’s campaign had never responded to requests for comment about Piker until Thursday, as a slew of Democrats condemned the anti-Israel streamer’s comments.
Later that day, Piker was decidedly less enthusiastic about Ossoff when speaking on his stream.
“I don’t like Jon Ossoff,” Piker said, adding that he had “wanted to see if he had the right instincts” before declaring himself a full-fledged supporter.
“This is a moment where it’s very clear that he does not have the right instincts,” he added.
Piker: Ossoff’s Israel stance sparked my interest in him as a Senator
In a post on X/Twitter, Piker also explained how Ossoff’s Israel stance was what sparked his initial excitement about the senator.
“i think jon ossoff’s best strengths came from his lack of interest in attacking his left flank & focusing on trump’s corruption & scandals instead,” Piker wrote. “i said he was a dark horse because he’s been smart enough to back restrictions on weapons transfers to israel at times regardless of his incredibly conservative voting track record otherwise.”
The clash between Ossoff and Piker comes as members of the Jewish community in Atlanta have criticized the Jewish Democrat, largely over his votes to block certain arms sales to Israel. Ossoff is running for reelection in November in a high-profile battle against Republican Rep. Mike Collins that could determine which party controls the Senate.
Ossoff first voted to block weapons sales to Israel in November 2024, spurring a critical open letter from several Georgia Jewish organizations, including synagogues, Jewish schools, the local Anti-Defamation League chapter, and other groups. His vote also drew the attention of AIPAC, which released 30-second ads attacking US senators - including Ossoff - who had voted to block weapons sales.
Michael Morris, publisher of the Atlanta Jewish Times, penned an open letter earlier this month blasting Ossoff for voting to block weapons sales to Israel again in July 2025 and April 2026.
“I hear you claim, over and over again, that you support Israel - that your support is ‘ironclad,’” Morris wrote. “It is not.”
Morris accused Ossoff in the letter of “lying to me and your constituents” about his support for Israel. Days later, Republican former house speaker Newt Gingrich appeared to run with that accusation in a post that attacked Ossoff, in response to the Senator’s remark about Trump and his aide Natalie Harp.
“Ossoff routinely lies as the Jewish leaders in Atlanta pointed out recently, and we should accept that he is a profoundly dishonest politician with no sense of honor,” Gingrich wrote.
Asked about Ossoff’s comments on Piker, Morris told JTA he agreed with the statement, but that it wasn’t enough to win his support.
“It’s better than him supporting Piker - absolutely, 100%,” Morris said. “But, you know, talk is cheap, and trying to push one extremist a little bit out of the envelope - it’s one little step forward. Very little.”

Medical coexistence: As Israel faces a physician crisis, Arab Israeli doctors fill the gap
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
17:52:32 UTC
02:52:32 KST

Israel is in dire need of doctors. Many serving today are nearing retirement age, which could lead to major problems within the health service and the population it serves.
A disturbing reality is that 58% of all practicing doctors in Israel received their initial medical degrees abroad primarily due to the shortage of places in medical schools here. Israel has one of the highest rates of foreign-trained doctors in the OECD.
The Arab community in Israel represents 21% of the total population, yet within Israel’s health system, the percentage of Arab Israelis increases across the medical spectrum.
In 2010, Arab physicians numbered 8% of the total number. Today, 25% of all physicians working in Israel are Arab Israelis; nurses number 27% and dentists 27%. Arab Israeli pharmacists are virtually 50% of those working within the health system. Without doubt, this participation is of paramount significance.
An Arab doctor’s perspective on Israel’s medical future
To receive the perspective of an Arab Israeli doctor, the Magazine spoke with Israeli-born Mustafa Sarhan, a 58-year-old family doctor who has been practicing family medicine since 2004.
What motivated you to enter the medical field?
From an early age, I loved helping others and saw the medical profession as a place where I could meaningfully give support to those in need. As I progressed through my school days, it became clear that medicine was the subject I wanted to study. While I was not accepted in a medical school here in Israel, I managed to obtain a place in a Bulgarian medical school; however, this meant that I could not qualify for a subsidy toward the tuition fees given to Israelis studying in Israel.
Following your return to Israel, what challenges did you confront during your initial training period?
One of the biggest hurdles to cross on returning to Israel was the Israeli Medical Licensing Examination (IMLE) – testing for many – which, fortunately, I succeeded in passing. I did my stage – medical internship – at Jerusalem’s Hadassah-University Medical Center based in Ein Kerem and Mount Scopus. The training involved varied aspects of medicine, all of which helped me acclimatize to the Israeli health system.
The most difficult part of the journey began with my choice of specialization – namely, family medicine, and being accepted for an internship; fortunately, Maccabi Healthcare Services provided this opportunity in 2001, and I have remained part of Maccabi up until today.
What aspects of medicine does your professional role embrace?
As a senior physician in the system, my role encompasses several aspects of family medicine. I am a family physician, a diabetologist, and an administrative physician. Fortunately, while at times demanding, I succeed in fulfilling my role.
How do you view Israel’s health system in comparison to other countries?
I see Israel as one of the best health systems in the world. This is a unique country because every citizen is assured of receiving full health coverage via the various kupot cholim (health maintenance organizations).
Our community health service system is a world leader. Many countries come here to see how our health service works in the hope of emulating the Israeli concept. Compared to Europe and the United States, Israel is a shining example of a system that works for all.
As an Arab Israeli doctor working within the Israeli system, have you experienced any personal negativity?
Contrary to the negative bias against Arab Israeli doctors – as projected by the press, TV, and radio – the reality is somewhat different. There is an outstanding coexistence – at every level – between Arab and Jewish doctors. We work together, we assist one another professionally and otherwise, and we celebrate together.
You have four children, three daughters and a son, all of whom have chosen medicine as a career. This is a great compliment to their father – as well as their mother, who is a dentist. Did they study abroad, and where are they today?
Yes, they all studied abroad as it was impossible to enter a medical school here. The eldest, a girl, returned to Israel to complete her medical studies and now is a gynecologist working in Nazareth.
Our son, who has completed his formal studies, is currently carrying out his stage in Nahariya; he aims to become a family doctor – just like his father.
Another daughter, having completed her initial medical studies in Russia, has now returned to Israel and is preparing for the IMLE – possibly in January – a prerequisite prior to beginning the period of stage. Her aim is to become an ophthalmologist.
The youngest daughter is currently studying medicine in Istanbul.
There can be little doubt that Israel requires far more medical schools, enabling Israeli students – both Jew and Arab – the opportunity of studying in Israel rather than abroad. The acceptance rate in Israel’s medical schools, where tuition fees are subsidized, is roughly 20% to 30%, meaning that 70% to 80% of applicants either give up the idea of studying medicine or are forced to study abroad, where the entire high cost of tuition falls on the student.
The disturbing reality is that a number of those studying abroad do not return to Israel. Percentages vary, but the Health Ministry projected that 30% might choose to stay abroad.
A July 2025 survey – publicized by Ynet – on 233 Israeli medical students in Europe and the US found that close to three-quarters said they are weighing staying abroad, not only for financial reasons but also due to better working conditions and career advancement opportunities.
What is abundantly clear is that Israel’s health service would be unable to function without the professional input of its Arab Israeli participants. The health service provides proof that Arabs and Jews can work successfully together. We can but wish that this positive reality of coexistence could be emulated – not only elsewhere in Israel but throughout the entire world.
The Magazine expresses its sincere appreciation to Dr. Sarhan for his valued contribution to this article. We wish him and his family continued success, not only within their professional careers but in all aspects of life.■

US Treasury revokes 'critical node' of Iranian access to US dollars in latest Tehran sanctions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
17:52:22 UTC
02:52:22 KST

The US Treasury Department proposed on Friday to revoke Banque Misr UAE’s correspondent banking access to US financial institutions, calling it a “critical node” in the Iranian regime’s access to US dollars.
The proposal is part of Operation Economic Outcast, a broader effort by the US government to sever remaining “financial lifelines” sustaining the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC).
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said that the department had “promised to sever every economic lifeline Tehran has left and finally end the threat of the Iranian regime.”
“We also warned that Iran’s enablers cannot continue to enjoy access to the US dollar and the global financial system,” he continued. “Banque Misr UAE decided to find out the hard way, and today, we are taking the first step in holding it accountable for its continued, egregious support of the Iranian regime.”
The US Treasury estimates that Banque Misr UAE processed “approximately $1.8 billion for 103 companies that are potentially part of Iranian shadow banking networks,” the statement said, an avenue that Iran has taken following direct US sanctions on the regime.
Shadow networks provide “key access to US dollar correspondent banking relationships,” the Treasury said. “Iran uses these shadow banking networks to launder funds, procure weapons, and bankroll its regional terrorist proxy groups.”
Banque Misr is one of Egypt’s oldest and largest banks, founded in 1920 to facilitate trade between Egypt and the UAE and serve Egyptian expatriates in the Gulf.
Treasury: Front companies include those used by IRGC, Iran's Defense Ministry
Its customers, according to the US Treasury, include “apparent front companies used by Iran’s Ministry of Defense and the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps to evade US sanctions, as well as to launder money on behalf of Iranian Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei.”
A Treasury official said the action only applies to Banque Misr's UAE branches, allowing the bank to continue dollar transactions through its head office in Cairo and other foreign branches. These include Paris, Frankfurt, Riyadh, Beirut and Djibouti, according to Banque Misr's website.
Egypt's central bank said on Friday that the US action only affected Banque Misr's UAE branches and did not extend to any other Egyptian banks. The Central Bank of Egypt said in a statement that it and Egypt's Ministry of Foreign Affairs were in contact with the US authorities about the measures.
The Treasury also announced on Friday new sanctions against Bank Melli, alleging it has facilitated “billions of dollars’ worth of transactions through accounts controlled by the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps Qods Force (IRGC-QF)” and has “allowed the IRGC-QF and its parent organization, the IRGC, to move funds inside and outside of Iran.”
Additionally, the bank has funded Iranian-aligned proxies and partners such as Iraq, the statement added.
Reza Mohammad Taeedi, the general manager of the bank’s Dubai branch, was identified as a Specially Designated Global Terrorist “for having acted or purported to act for or on behalf of, directly or indirectly, Bank Melli,” according to the statement.
Hong Kong-based Kameng Trading Limited was also sanctioned on Friday for helping sanctioned Iranians access the international financial system, the Treasury said.
Sanctions follow crackdown on 'far-left terrorist networks'
The sanctions come two days after the Treasury cracked down on what it called “far-left terrorist networks,” with a new wave of sanctions against Italy’s Autistici Inventati, Palestine Action, a UK-based organization designated by the British government as a terrorist group in 2025, and transnational group Masar Badil.
The Treasury accused Autistici Inventati of supplying “specialized digital architecture, tools, and services for Antifa cells and other violent far-left extremists, including a foreign terrorist organization” and Masar Badil of operating “as a front for the Popular Front for the Liberation of Palestine, a designated Foreign Terrorist Organization.”
“Far-left extremists, their fronts, and their enablers should be on notice: We will bring the full weight of our economic tools to bear,” said Bessent. “Political terrorism has no place in our society, and we will continue to cut the financial lifelines of these groups until they are eliminated.”
The US identified far-left terrorist groups as one of the three major terrorist threats that the country faces today.
In July, Bessent warned of far-left terrorists “increasingly embracing organized, deadly violence in pursuit of their objectives,” and said that the Treasury’s actions reinforce the US’s commitment to disrupting the groups’ infrastructure.
Reuters contributed to this report.

====================================================================================================

No politician has the right to risk Israel’s national security - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
17:52:10 UTC
02:52:10 KST

For some time, I have argued that the cognitive war being waged against Israel must be recognized for what it has become: A national-security threat.
I have written about it, as well as invited Knesset Foreign Affairs and Defense Committee chairman Boaz Bismuth to discuss its importance on TV with me. If the campaign to delegitimize Israel, isolate it from allies, influence American politics, radicalize university campuses, and endanger Jews worldwide constitutes what many now call an “eighth front,” then cognitive warfare cannot remain a secondary priority.
It is a national security issue.
But accepting this proposition has consequences. Actions capable of materially damaging Israel on the cognitive battlefield must be judged as national-security events, even when the person taking them believes passionately that he is defending Israel.
That is why what troubles me most about MK Zvi Sukkot’s recent sledgehammer episode is no longer Sukkot himself.
It is the Israeli government’s response.
How Israel fails to take cognitive warfare seriously
Sukkot entered Kafr Madama near Nablus under IDF protection and participated in demolishing a Palestinian monument that appeared to honor terrorists.
The IDF said soldiers had been diverted from operational duties for what they understood to be an authorized tour and that Sukkot then acted outside the approved framework and “without authority.”
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu condemned the incident. Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich reportedly reprimanded Sukkot and told him not to do it again.
Not to do it again?
If cognitive warfare really is national security, is that remotely sufficient?
Consider an admittedly uncomfortable comparison: Peace activist Mordechai Vanunu.
Vanunu believed Israel’s nuclear policy was morally wrong. He decided that his own judgment entitled him to disclose extraordinarily sensitive information about Israel’s nuclear program.
Israel concluded that no individual had the right to make such a national-security decision for the country. He was convicted of grave offenses and sentenced to 18 years in prison, 11 of them in solitary confinement.
Obviously, Sukkot did not reveal nuclear secrets. He did not commit espionage, and I am not suggesting his statutory offenses are equivalent to Vanunu’s.
But the distinction may be more one of degree than kind than we are comfortable acknowledging.
Imagine an IDF soldier selling several M4 rifles to an enemy. Another person sells Iran plans for upgrades to an Israeli missile defense system. The consequences are radically different, and therefore the punishments should be radically different.
But the underlying violation belongs to the same family: an individual has taken something entrusted to him within Israel’s national-security establishment and assigned to himself the right to decide how it will be used.
That principle must apply to cognitive security as well.
Sukkot effectively decided this, given that he believed the monument glorified terrorism. This argument may have merit; he believed he was entitled to decide when, where, and how Israeli power would be exercised to destroy it.
He was not.
That decision belongs to the State of Israel.
No Israeli civilian gets to walk into an air force command center and select tomorrow’s targets in Iran, Lebanon, or Gaza because he believes a particular target must be destroyed.
Why, then, should any Israeli citizen, particularly an elected official, believe he has the authority to select targets on the cognitive battlefield when his actions can affect Israel’s relationship with Washington, its diplomatic standing, Jewish communities abroad, and its global legitimization?
And this is not confined to one political camp.
In May 2025, Yair Golan, the head of the Democrats Party, declared that Israel was on the way to becoming a pariah state and said that “a sane country does not fight against civilians, does not kill children as a hobby.”
Whatever his intention, language of that kind from a senior Israeli political figure and former general in the IDF is immediately weaponized by those seeking to portray Israel as criminal and immoral.
Yet Golan is still being rewarded by the Israeli public with support and remains a major political actor with a potential 11 seats in the upcoming elections.
IN APRIL, an Israeli soldier was photographed striking a statue of Jesus with a sledgehammer in a Christian village in southern Lebanon. The image generated international outrage. The IDF investigated. Two soldiers were removed from combat duty and sentenced to 30 days in military detention.
Why?
Because one soldier’s hammer did not merely strike a statue.
It struck Israel’s strategic interests, but others who have struck Israel’s strategic interests go unpunished and even rewarded. This means the system is failing.
The same principle applies when senior politicians create unnecessary friction with Israel’s most important ally.
US Vice President JD Vance publicly rebuked Israeli ministers after they clashed over American diplomatic policy, asking in frustration: “What is your exact proposal? You’re a country of 9 million people. You can’t just kill your way out of solving every single national security problem that you have.”
A potential future president of the United States felt compelled to publicly admonish senior Israeli leaders. If the management of that relationship is not a national-security issue, what is?
The question is simple: Who has the right to jeopardize a strategic relationship, at a strategically sensitive moment, in pursuit of his own political objective?
That question is urgent now.
Israel is approaching elections. America is approaching midterm elections. Iran remains a critical strategic challenge, and Turkey is fast approaching as our next serious challenge. The relationship with Washington remains indispensable. Global antisemitism has increased dramatically. At the same time, Israel is investing unprecedented resources in public diplomacy and communications.
Yet Israelis continue to behave as though cognitive damage can be created by politicians today and repaired by hasbara (public diplomacy) professionals tomorrow.
It cannot.
A photograph travels around the world before an Israeli spokesperson has finished writing the first sentence of an explanation.
Sukkot swinging a sledgehammer beside Israeli soldiers is instantly internalized. Explaining that the monument apparently glorified terrorists, that Palestinian incitement is real, that Sukkot had previously requested its removal, and that the IDF did not authorize what happened takes several paragraphs.
Our enemies get the photograph.
We get the explanation.
That is the asymmetry of cognitive warfare.
Which brings me back to what I find more disturbing than Sukkot’s behavior: The absence of consequences commensurate with the national-security principle supposedly at stake.
A condemnation is not deterrence.
A reprimand is not doctrine.
“Don’t do it again” tells the next politician that the potential reward – headlines, social-media engagement, and support from a political base – may exceed the cost.
That is an extraordinarily dangerous message for a country fighting a cognitive war.
This government understandably sees an election only weeks away. Coalition politics matter. Political constituencies matter. But national-security leadership requires looking beyond the next election.
The government’s responsibility is not merely to survive October 27. It is to establish rules of behavior that protect Israel on October 28 and for years afterward.
If Israel wants the world, the IDF and its own citizens to take cognitive warfare seriously, then deliberately creating unauthorized strategic liabilities must carry meaningful consequences.
This principle cannot depend on whether the unauthorized national-security decision came from the Left or the Right, from a nuclear technician or an MK, or from someone leaking secrets, wielding a sledgehammer, or a former IDF general making a statement that hands Israel’s enemies a propaganda victory.
No individual gets to privatize Israel’s national security.
The elected government determines Israel’s military strategy. It determines which risks to take with Iran. It manages our relationship with the US. And it must ultimately determine how Israel conducts itself on the cognitive battlefield.
Once we call that battlefield a national-security front, we must have the courage to treat breaches of it accordingly.
And the next person who decides that personal conviction entitles him to risk Israel’s strategic interests may inflict damage that no amount of hasbara money can undo.

“That the name of the author should be inscribed on the book is now customary and almost a duty; yet it is one of the main reasons books produce so little effect. For if they are good, then, as the quintessence of the personality of their authors, they are worth more than these; but as soon as the author announces himself on the title page, the reader at once dilutes the quintessence again with the personality, indeed with what is most personal, and thus thwarts the object of the book. It is the intellect’s ambition to seem no longer to belong to an individual.”

Belgians invest €345 million so far in government bond (though website is a source of ridicule)

Belgium’s new government bond, offering more interest than savings accounts, is popular with the public – if the website isn’t
Belgians invest €345 million so far in government bond (though website is a source of ridicule)
The Belgian state opened up investments in its new government bond on Wednesday, and so far some €345 million has been invested. Any individual can invest in the bond, which offers 1.93% net interest for a year-long commitment. A 10-year investment yields net 2.59% interest.
The one-year option is by far the most popular, netting €310 million. Investors have until 3 September to sign up for the bond, via a bank or the dedicated website.
Debtagency.be
About that website … Anyone who has invested via the official website before will remember that the site is far from user friendly, and this year the criticism is particularly loud. “It already starts with the URL,” user experience expert Christophe Leuckx told VRT. “The website of Belgium’s Debt Management Office is debtagency.be. That is just not done. You get the feeling you’re visiting a fake website.”
The website is also not in the style of any other of the federal government sites. “This looks like it was built in about 1995, with old images and an odd structure,” says Leuckx. “The information about the new government bond, for instance, requires a lot of scrolling.”
It’s a textbook example of how not to make a website
Crucial information is delivered rather flippantly, he continues. “The interest rate information is included on a photo, and it’s difficult to read on a mobile device. Also, for people with a visual impairment, this information is simply unavailable because they are using screen readers. Every government website, including the VRT, is required to meet strict accessibility standards, and this one does not.”
Leuckx goes on to point out spelling errors, aged visuals and a PowerPoint presentation that comes from another era. “It’s a textbook example of how not to make a website.”
To be clear, the website is safe to use. It’s not security that’s the problem, it’s the sense of a lack of security. Like most people, journalists at VRT noticed these problems years ago and reported them to the Debt Management Office. They were told improvements to the site would be planned. This year they were told that there is no budget for a redeveloped website.

Analysis: Kevin Warsh sharpens inflation warning at Jackson Hole, signaling possible rate hike
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
17:44:02 UTC
02:44:02 KST

Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh used his Jackson Hole speech Friday to answer critics of his muddled July news conference, delivering a clearer warning that stubborn inflation could push the Fed toward a rate hike.
Warsh's first pair of news conferences as Fed chairman left many in the markets uncertain about where he stood on the path of interest rates, prompting bond traders to sell off long-term debt to account for the uncertainty. At a closely watched speech in Jackson Hole, Wyoming, on Friday, Warsh showed he had heard those critics. He came as close as he is ever likely to do to indicating he is on the precipice of raising interest rates if inflation doesn't improve, based on his own idiosyncratic reading of price data.
Warsh at Jackson Hole gave a more hawkish reading of the economy than he had in July. He said elevated prices needed to be the Fed's main focus and described financial conditions as not being broadly restrictive, a change from his July news conference, when he said they were uneven. He did that while swiping back at his critics and insisting his policy of deliberate ambiguity about Fed policy is here to stay.
"We can be held accountable for delivering on our remit — the only true test of our credibility," Warsh said, dismissing widely echoed critiques that he had come across as not credible at his July news conference.
The Fed won't meet to set rates until mid-September, and Warsh didn't explicitly say how the central bank would handle interest rates. But he dived into several of the critiques recently leveled at him.
One of the harshest focused on Warsh's description of how he sees the Fed's core mission of assessing and responding to inflation. The Fed is formally committed to trying to keep inflation to 2% over the long term as measured by the personal consumption expenditures price index. Some economists interpreted Warsh's muddled answers to reporters' questions last month as saying he might want to change that target — even as inflation remains elevated.
PCE inflation was 3.7% for July, according to government data released this week.
At Jackson Hole, Warsh recommitted to maintaining the 2% PCE goal, calling it a "firm, fixed target."
And he went further. Warsh gave examples of how he uses multiple measures of inflation to reach the conclusion that elevated prices are a concern. He referred to the underlying components of PCE inflation, saying 54% of components of PCE had been above 3% annualized inflation in the past 12 months, while 49% were above 3% in the past six months.
Warsh described those figures as being lower than the recent pandemic inflation but still above the long-term trend — an indication he believes the Fed may need to raise rates.
Warsh also referred to another gauge of inflation, the consumer price index, which is running at 3.4%.
"None of these measures are perfect, but they all tell a similar story: Inflation is running above our 2 percent target," he said.
That statement by Warsh is a sharper view of his understanding of inflation metrics than he has given previously. He sees the various prominent inflation measures as individually flawed, but believes the Fed can draw from them collectively to come to a view of how prices are behaving. And right now, he is worried about price increases.
That had concerned him in July, too, he said at Jackson Hole on Friday.
"A good majority of my colleagues and I thought the wiser course was to await new information in the intermeeting period."
Warsh also addressed another critique of his performance in July — that he wouldn't turn quickly to interest rates to fight inflation. President Donald Trump — who has made clear his desire for lower rates — picked Warsh. At Jackson Hole, Warsh was unambiguous: "short-term interest rates are the predominant tool to achieve the dual mandate."
Warsh also reiterated that the Fed is watching developments in artificial intelligence closely, but wasn't ready to act on them. A Fed task force examining AI use and economic impact was "encouraging" but so far had "no bearing on decisions we make in the current policy conjuncture."
Warsh's treatment of AI is part of a broader reset he is attempting to deliver to the views he effectively campaigned on when seeking the job as Fed chairman in 2025.
In the past, he had said advances in AI might be a reason to reduce interest rates. That lined up with Trump's demands for lower rates. He had also said cutting the Fed's balance sheet would be a reason to lower interest rates.
Warsh is now indicating that considerations of AI don't have much to do with current policymaking. And there was no signal at Jackson Hole that balance sheet cuts were coming.
Trump has continued to demand lower rates, leading some to infer Warsh is holding off raising rates until after the November midterm election to unleash his hawkish impulses. The two men have spoken directly since Warsh became chairman, breaking with a tradition that sees contact between the Fed and the administration channeled through the Treasury secretary.
Warsh didn't address Trump at Jackson Hole. But his reading of the economy as showing signs of elevated price concerns puts him clearly at odds with the president. Trump continues to want interest rate decreases and often touts market performance and what he says are strong economic indicators, but Warsh's message Friday was that the Fed is considering the opposite — a near-term raise in interest rates.
The Jackson Hole speech won't eliminate worries about Warsh's time at the Fed helm. Trump has continued to meddle with the Fed, including reinstating an effort on weak evidence to fire Governor Lisa Cook. And Warsh hasn't yet delivered concrete action against inflation.
But Warsh's performance at Jackson Hole will give his colleagues at the Fed a reason to back him if he decides in September to take that action. His speech at the influential forum should help dispel the idea that he is simply flying blind.

Chile, Argentina, Bolivia, Peru sign pact to boost cooperation on strategic minerals
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
17:40:26 UTC
02:40:26 KST

Maryam Ashalem de Andres
28 August 2026•Update: 28 August 2026
Chile, Argentina, Bolivia and Peru signed a joint declaration Thursday to strengthen regional cooperation on strategic minerals, particularly copper and lithium, local media reported.
The declaration aims to promote responsible investment, strengthen regional supply chains and deepen cooperation on geological information, regulation and technological development.
The four countries are seeking to capitalize on their mineral wealth and strengthen their position as global suppliers of resources considered critical for the energy transition and other strategic industries, according to the reports.
Chilean Economy and Mining Minister Daniel Mas said growing demand linked to the energy transition and the expansion of artificial intelligence could increase global demand for critical minerals by between 400% and 600% over the next decade, according to local media.
Argentine Mining Secretary Luis Lucero highlighted the region’s geological potential and said the four countries could strengthen their role in global copper production through long-term mining projects.
Bolivia’s Deputy Minister of Mining Policy, Regulation and Oversight Walter Landivar said the regional challenge was to “transform mineral resources into opportunities for greater value-added production, economic development and technical integration.”
The declaration establishes cooperation mechanisms covering geological information, mining policies, regulatory standards and oversight criteria, while seeking greater coordination among the four countries.
The governments also agreed to establish working groups to develop joint initiatives in areas including geological research, specialized training and human capital development for the mining sector.
The agreement also calls for cooperation with multilateral institutions to seek technical and financial support for projects related to strategic minerals.
Chile, the world’s largest copper producer, and Argentina hold significant copper resources, while Bolivia has some of the world’s largest lithium resources. Peru is also among the world’s leading copper producers.
The declaration comes as countries seek to secure supplies of critical minerals needed for renewable energy technologies, electric vehicles, batteries and advanced industries.
The agreement reflects growing efforts among South American countries to coordinate mining policies and attract investment as global demand for copper, lithium and other strategic minerals continues to rise.

Mexico’s disappearances crisis could affect 165,000 children: Report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
17:37:36 UTC
02:37:36 KST

Maryam Ashalem de Andres
28 August 2026•Update: 28 August 2026
Around 165,000 children and adolescents in Mexico could have a missing parent, according to an exploratory estimate by human rights organization Tejiendo Redes Infancia, local media reported Friday.
The organization published a report titled “Daughters and Sons of Missing Persons in Mexico,” highlighting the impact of disappearances on children who remain largely invisible in official records.
Juan Martin Perez Garcia, regional coordinator of Tejiendo Redes Infancia, said the estimate was not an exact count but was intended to highlight gaps in official data on the family ties of missing people and how those gaps affect public policies for indirect victims.
The estimate is based on 103,176 people aged 15 to 49 who were registered as missing or not located in Mexico as of August 2026, according to the report.
Tejiendo Redes Infancia applied a national average of 1.60 children per person, based on Mexico’s 2023 National Survey of Population Dynamics, to estimate that 165,081 children could potentially be affected by the disappearances, local media reported.
Mexico’s National Registry of Missing and Not Located Persons (RNPDNO) records missing people but does not identify their children, their ages, who cares for them or what support they receive.
The organization said the lack of such information prevents authorities from identifying these children as indirect victims and from designing policies and allocating resources to protect and assist them.
The report said the disappearance of a parent can disrupt childcare, reduce household income, affect children’s education and increase insecurity, stigma and the risk of revictimization.
Tejiendo Redes Infancia called on Mexican authorities to create a specific mechanism to identify, protect and assist children whose parents have disappeared.
Perez Garcia also called for dedicated public funding, saying there is currently no specific budget to address the needs of these children.
The organization said the absence of family information also places a greater burden of care on mothers, grandmothers, siblings, partners and other relatives.
The report comes as Mexico continues to face a major crisis of missing and disappeared people, with more than 100,000 cases involving people aged 15 to 49 alone, according to the organization’s analysis.
