Gaza forced to use unreliable online payments amid ‘cash famine’
Israeli restrictions and war damage have created a liquidity crisis, crippling Gaza’s banking system and daily commerce.
Gaza City, Gaza Strip – In a clothing shop in Gaza City’s Sheikh Radwan neighbourhood, Firas Zaqloul stands helplessly as he tries to pay for his purchases.
The problem is that he can’t get the seller to accept his money.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Israeli protesters block aid trucks from reaching Gaza
- list 2 of 3Fatah meets Palestinian breakaway faction in effort to head off rivals
- list 3 of 3Most US Democrats in early 2028 primary states oppose aid to Israel: Poll
Zaqloul’s home was destroyed during Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza, burying his Palestinian identity card beneath the rubble. Without it, he says, he has been unable to open a bank account or electronic wallet, leaving him dependent on increasingly scarce and badly-worn banknotes that many merchants refuse to take.
“I suffer every day when I want to buy something,” Zaqloul said. “The seller refuses worn-out banknotes, so I have to … find some way to pay him.”
“I just hope merchants in Gaza will take the money from us,” he added. “In the end, it’s all money.”
Zaqloul’s experience has become increasingly common in Gaza, where an acute shortage of usable cash has become known locally as a “cash famine”.
Since the war began on October 7, 2023, Israel has severely restricted the entry of cash into Gaza, while its military campaign has devastated much of the territory’s banking infrastructure. The result is an economy in which people may technically have money but struggle to access it, or find someone willing to accept the notes in their possession.
According to the Palestine Monetary Authority, which oversees banking, Israeli attacks have destroyed more than 50 bank branches across Gaza, as well as dozens of cash machines. Large quantities of cash were also trapped inside the vaults of damaged or destroyed banks.
Even after the October 2025 ceasefire allowed banks to reopen some branches, services remained limited largely to administrative transactions, without providing badly needed new liquidity. Palestinians in Gaza say they find it difficult to open new accounts for anyone using replacement identification documents issued after 2023, depriving thousands of people unable to access the electronic banking system at a time when digital payments have become increasingly essential.
Waiting for a transfer
In the same clothing store, 23-year-old student Israa Najm waits for a notification to appear on the shopkeeper’s phone.
“As you can see, I have been standing here for two hours, waiting for my mother to transfer the money to the shop owner from home,” she said. “He won’t let me leave with the abaya I want to buy unless he sees the confirmation that the transfer has arrived.”
Najm said that the identity document she obtained during the war is not accepted by banks, meaning that she can’t operate her Bank of Palestine account or electronic wallet.
“Every time I want to go to the market, I have to call my mother and ask her to transfer the money,” she said. “Sometimes she doesn’t have internet, so we both struggle just to make the payment. There is a crisis of trust between the seller and the buyer. I want to deal in cash. The last time I received cash was a year ago, but no one wanted to take it from me because the notes were worn out.”
Due to the lack of cash, everyday transactions are now increasingly complicated.
Inside Abu Jabara Food Mall, modern technology stands in the way of 45-year-old Najwa Kahil’s attempts to buy food for a reasonable price. She explained that using electronic payments made it more difficult to haggle with shopkeepers, and struggles with using the payment apps.
“I don’t know how to transfer to the seller,” Kahil said, explaining that her phone was old and can’t run banking apps. “I take my young son with me so he can call one of his brothers to make a transfer to the supermarket owner. Sometimes I feel I’m begging when I go out to buy; I feel like I’m 100 years old, not 45. Everything is suffering, from buying food, cooking over a fire, and filling water. I spend all day just suffering.”
Complicated purchases
For Mohammed Awida, a 22-year-old nut seller, shopping now requires planning that would have been unimaginable before the war.
“Buying something has become an operation that requires complete preparation,” Awida said.
“If I’m going to buy food for my mother on Friday, I charge my phone the day before,” Awida added. “I also have to make sure I have access to every electronic payment method, because each seller may demand a particular method, and as the buyer you have to accept their terms.”
Internet outages create another complication.
Some merchants prefer transfers made through mobile phone services that generate an SMS confirmation because banking applications require an internet connection that may disappear at any moment.
“Without that message, the seller isn’t convinced that you’ve paid,” Awida said. “They start looking at you as though you’re trying to steal from them. I hope buying things stops requiring all of this complexity. We are tired.”
The collapse of Gaza’s communications infrastructure, combined with the shift towards electronic payments, has even begun to reshape where people conduct business.
Shops and other businesses offering free internet connections have become informal commercial hubs, drawing sellers and customers who need a reliable connection simply to complete a transaction.
At Bahloul Junction in western Gaza City, 14-year-old Abdul Hadi Abu Shaaban, sells bread outside al-Qadi sweets shoppe, where customers can connect to a free Wi-Fi network. He is one of several street vendors who gather there for the same reason.
“I don’t have a mobile phone, but I ask the buyer to transfer to my father’s bank account, and then I ask him to show me the transfer notice,” Abu Shaaban said. “I don’t receive cash, because all of the cash is old and worn out, and even if I had change, I couldn’t give it to the buyer.”

Hundreds of foreign nationals remain missing
Nearly 3,000 people are missing and at least 626 people have been killed in the deadly flash floods that struck villages in the border region between Nepal and Tibet.
Nepal's disaster agency on Friday said 517 foreigners, which could include tourists as well as foreign workers, were still missing, while Chinese officials put the number of foreigners missing on China's side of the border at 260.
Here are the latest numbers of foreign nationals missing:
- AUSTRALIA: The number of Australians missing has risen to 41.
- INDIA: The Nepal Tourism Board on Friday said 98 people from India were missing, but 85 others were rescued.
- BRITAIN: Thirty-three people from the United Kingdom were missing, the Nepal Tourism Board figures showed.
- CANADA: The Nepal Tourism Board said 25 Canadians were among the missing on Friday. Canada's foreign ministry put the figure at 30 in both Nepal and Tibet.
- CHINA: China's foreign ministry said on Thursday that nearly 100 Chinese nationals were among the missing in Nepal. That was in addition to the 554 still missing on the Chinese side of the border, state news agency Xinhua reported on Saturday.
- MALAYSIA: The Nepal Tourism Board put the number of Malaysians missing at 51.
- NEW ZEALAND: Five New Zealanders remain missing, according to the Nepal Tourism Board.
- SOUTH KOREA: The Nepal Tourism Board said on Friday that nine South Korean tourists were missing, while South Korea's foreign ministry has said they had had no news of nine hydropower workers.
- UKRAINE: The number of Ukrainians still missing on Friday was 61, the Nepal Tourism Board said.
- UNITED STATES: The Nepal Tourism Board put the figure at 65 missing on Friday, and two rescued.
The Nepal Tourism Board also said citizens of Latvia, France, Germany, Spain, Belgium, Hungary, Portugal, Netherlands, Italy, Ireland, Kazakhstan, Belarus, Finland, Israel, Japan, Lithuania, Philippines, Russia, Serbia, Singapore, South Africa, Sweden, Switzerland, and Vietnam were unaccounted-for.
The missing figure released on Thursday by China from its side of the border did not include a breakdown of nationalities.

Vigil for flood victims underway in Adelaide
Hundreds of members of South Australia’s Nepali community have come together in Adelaide’s south-east for a candlelight vigil to remember the victims of the flooding tragedy.
Gathered in Oaklands Park, they lit candles spelling out the words "Pray for Nepal" and held a moment of silence.
Vigil organiser Thir Gurung said some members of the community still haven’t heard from family members in Nepal and hope is quickly fading.
“We couldn’t sleep, we can’t work, we are in stress,” Mr Gurung told crowds.
“At this moment, the Nepalese community wants to come together and pay our respects.”
Risk of lake bursting wanes near China-Nepal border disaster site
The threat of a lake bursting near the China-Nepal border has decreased, Chinese authorities say.
The authorities said on Saturday the lake's size appeared to have shrunk.
The lake formed after a glacier collapsed in the location where the devastating flood occurred earlier this week.
Satellite images from Thursday to Saturday morning suggest that water in the lake — straddling the China-Nepal border at the confluence of two rivers — has been slowly flowing through, decreasing the reservoir gradually, state broadcaster CCTV reported citing the water resources ministry.
The ministry said satellite imagery of the surface area of the lake at Purepu Tsangpo river showed it was 99,000 square metres in size on early Saturday morning — about the size of 14 football fields combined — having shrunk by 21,000sqm compared with images from Thursday.
Experts and authorities have warned of the extremely high risk of secondary disasters in the valley, especially from the lake that was formed by glacier debris, potentially endangering rescue operations downstream.
Reporting with Reuters
'Enormous' trauma from disaster, Red Cross warns
Nepal's government has called for aid as it continues to assess the scale of destruction from catastrophic floods, and as the threat of more flooding remains.
Humanitarian organisations have described some of the challenges ahead.
The trauma of Wednesday's flash flood had been "enormous", with as many as 93,000 people potentially affected in the country of about 30 million, the Red Cross said.
Entire communities have been swept away, leaving families homeless or sheltering in temporary facilities.
"Multiple bridges have been washed away and major roads disrupted, leaving some of the worst-affected communities extremely difficult to reach," the Red Cross said.
At least 18 schools have been destroyed and another 20 damaged, leaving about 10,000 school-age children affected, according to the United Nations Children's Fund.
The floods destroyed three health posts and partially damaged a hospital, with access to two other hospitals affected, according to the UN's World Health Organization (WHO).
"Displacement, overcrowding, damaged water and sanitation systems, and disrupted health services may increase the risk of communicable diseases," the WHO said.

Nepal's flood damage may cost up to a tenth of its economy to rebuild
Nepal may need up to $US5 billion ($6.9 billion) to rebuild after this week's devastating floods, Nepal's Finance Minister, Swarnim Wagle, has told Reuters.
That would be a bill equal to nearly a tenth of Nepal's economy.
"The initial estimate is between $4-$5 billion ... we will require much less than what we needed for the 2015 earthquake. Loss and damage is being assessed," he said.
Mr Wagle did not elaborate on why the reconstruction bill was expected to be less than the $US9 billion spent after the 2015 magnitude-7.8 quake.
That disaster, Nepal's worst on record, killed nearly 9,000 people, destroyed more than half a million homes and caused losses estimated to have been about a third of Nepal's economy.
The recent floods will nevertheless be a major blow to an economy reliant on remittances, tourism and hydropower, damaging power projects that account for more than 12 per cent of national generating capacity.

Police and volunteers are set up at desks taking the names and numbers of those who have missing relatives.
Some people come here multiple times a day in the desperate hope they will receive good news.
More than 400 injured people, airlifted from the disaster area, have been brought here.
Chief of the emergency medicine department Ramesh Kumar Maharjan said most of those patients had been buried in mud.

Ukraine reinforces Donetsk as it seeks to disrupt Russia’s weapons flow
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

Ukraine reinforces Donetsk as it seeks to disrupt Russia’s weapons flow
After repeated disappointments over US Patriots, Ukraine switches to attacking Russian ballistic production using European weapons.
Ukraine has reinforced the defence of its eastern Donetsk region as Russia mounted renewed efforts to seize Sloviansk, a key part of Ukraine’s “fortress belt” of cities that include Kramatorsk, Druzhkivka and Kostiantynivka.
At the same time, Britain and France made a crucial decision to transfer Storm Shadow cruise missile technology to Kyiv, as Ukraine shifts its air defence strategy to destroying Russia’s means of ballistic missile production and launch, rather than intercepting the missiles individually.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items
- list 1 of 4‘Not going to sacrifice my life’: Russia mobilisation fears grow
- list 2 of 4Ukrainian strikes kill 12 in Russia and Donbas, target Wildberries
- list 3 of 4Russia warns it could target UK in response to Kyiv firing British missiles
- list 4 of 4Russian military serviceman killed in car bomb in St Petersburg
Ukrainian commander-in-chief Mykhailo Drapatyi made the first major decision of his new command on August 26 to reinforce two units defending Sloviansk.
Russia has also been infiltrating the fortress city of Kostiantynivka to the south of Sloviansk, but does not control it.
Ukrainian military observer Kostyantyn Mashovets said Kyiv still maintains positions in central and northern Kostiantynivka.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said 70-80 percent of Russian casualties were taking place on the Kostiantynivka front. He estimated Russian losses this year at 267,000, including at least 155,000 killed.
Russian commander-in-chief Valery Gerasimov said on Thursday that his troops were within four kilometres (2.5 miles) of Sloviansk.
But maps published by Deep State and the Institute for the Study of War, which observe territorial changes through geo-located, open-source information, suggest Russian troops are between 12km (7.4 miles) and 16km (10 miles) of Sloviansk.
Ukraine hobbles Russian front line
Ukraine is pressing a campaign to hobble the supply of Russian men, munitions and fuel to the front line by targeting storages, airfields and transport routes.
It has been largely successful in bringing Russia to a standstill.
The ISW estimated Russia has lost 27 square kilometres (10.4 square miles) in August, and at least 233sq km (90sq miles) this year.
On August 20, Ukraine destroyed 18 buildings storing aerial drones at the Primorsko-Akhtarsk airfield in Krasnodar Krai, just across the Sea of Azov from Crimea, and a Sukhoi-24 fighter at the Saky airfield in Crimea itself.
Two days later, Ukraine’s unmanned systems destroyed a Sukhoi-33 fighter and a MiG-29 fighter at the Vityazevo airfield in Krasnodar, along with a strike and reconnaissance Orion drone. On the same day, they struck an oil trans-shipment terminal at Yeisk, in Krasnodar.
On August 24, Ukraine destroyed another MiG-29 at Millerovo airfield in Rostov.
Ukraine also targeted and destroyed ballistic missile launchers and radar complexes.
It has hit a dozen Russian military supply vessels, bringing the total number of ships disabled during the campaign to 242.
Separately, Ukraine has struck 267 Crimean power stations and substations in six weeks. The result has been a near-blackout across the Crimean Peninsula.
Russia-installed head of Crimea Sergey Aksyonov acknowledged “objective difficulties that cannot be resolved in the short term for technical reasons”.
Ukraine’s Commander of Unmanned Systems Forces Robert Brovdi recently suggested Crimean households and businesses had electricity for an average of about an hour a day.
Russian refineries smoulder
Ukraine’s long-range strikes have hit Russian refineries 31 times since the beginning of June.
Since August 20, it has struck the Akhtubinsk refinery and the Astrakhan gas processing plant in the Caucasus, Lukoil refineries in Perm and Nizhny Novgorod – 1,300km (808 miles) and 800km (497 miles) from Ukraine respectively – the Novokuybyshevsk refinery in Samara, and the Afipsky refinery in Krasnodar.
Several were hit repeatedly to ensure they remain out of action.
Russian Union of Industrialists and Entrepreneurs President Alexander Shokhin reportedly said that Ukrainian drone strikes had removed 25-30 percent of Russian oil refining capacity – a conclusion also reached by the Financial Times.
This economic warfare has also incinerated 15 of the largest distribution centres of Russia’s largest online retailer, Wildberries, causing an estimated three trillion roubles ($35bn) worth of damage.
On August 24, Ukraine also struck Russia’s second-largest online retailer, Ozon, for the first time.
Russian strikes and Ukraine’s response
Russia has been hitting Ukraine’s cities in what it claims are reciprocal strikes.
“[We] have begun to respond to the enemy’s actions against our civilian industrial and logistics facilities. The Kyiv regime has set out to damage our economy. What has it done? It’s opened Pandora’s box itself,” Russian President Vladimir Putin told journalist Pavel Zarubin.
Russia, too, has launched economic warfare against Ukraine, recently striking its main grain exporting ports of Odesa and Chernomorsk.
Zelenskyy said four to five ships were still making it in and out every day, but added that was three to four times fewer than before Russia’s blockade this summer.
Russia has also been striking border crossings between Ukraine and Moldova, an alternative export route for grain.
However, many Russian strikes have also hit residential and civilian sites, causing heavy casualties far from the front line.
On August 21, Russian drones killed 16 people and injured 130 who were shopping in Kryvyi Rih, in central Ukraine, far from the front line. On August 27, they injured several people after residential buildings in the Poltava, Sumy and Kherson regions were hit.
On the latter occasion, Russia also used Iskander-M/KN-23 ballistic missiles, and Ukraine stopped seven of them – its first interception since the end of July, when it ran out of Patriot missiles, the only weapon in its arsenal that reliably stops ballistics. Two days before the strike, Zelenskyy said: “A few more Patriot missiles have also arrived.”
Zelenskyy told journalists on August 23 that he had been hoping to amass some 360 Patriot missiles ahead of winter, as requested by the Ukrainian air force, but admitted that “when they produce 600 per year, 360 is not easy to obtain”.
The United States has refused to give Ukraine 5-10 percent of its stockpile, and as missile expert Fabian Hoffmann has detailed, investment in higher Patriot production has come too late to help Ukraine this winter, and the Patriot is not a cost-effective solution even in the long run.
At the NATO Summit in July, US President Donald Trump had granted Ukraine licences to build Patriot interceptors at the scale it needs, but soon rescinded the offer without explanation.
“Russia could potentially produce up to 1,300 ballistic missiles per year,” said Zelenskyy. “We are working to prevent [that].”
Ukraine’s long-range strikes have increasingly targeted Russian aerospace industries.
On August 24, for example, they struck the Kamensk-Shakhtinsk factory manufacturing solid rocket fuel for missiles in Rostov. They have also been striking missile launchers and radar stations wherever possible.
On August 6, former Defence Minister Mykhailo Fedorov promoted a strategy of “counter-ballistic warfare”.
Ukraine is working on putting its own ballistic missiles into scaled production by next year, and Zelenskyy said he would have a firm timetable by early September.
In the meantime, Zelenskyy hopes to strike launchers by building its own version of the Anglo-French Storm Shadow missiles, also known as SCALP.
British Prime Minister Andy Burnham handed Zelenskyy the blueprints to do just that when he visited Kyiv on its Independence Day, August 24 – a move that infuriated Russia.

Netanyahu pleads with far-right allies to 'save right-wing bloc'
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu is pleading with his far-right allies to group together to "save the right-wing bloc" as the right-wing camp in Israel balkanises following the introduction of smaller right-wing parties in the upcoming elections.
Netanyahu made the plea on X on Friday, inviting his far-right National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir and finance minister Bezalel Smotrich to a meeting this Sunday.
"No vote can go to waste; the parties must unite in order to save the right-wing bloc!" he was quoted as saying by the Times of Israel.
It's Netanyahu's second plea in 24 hours, having previously issued a statement on Thursday, calling on the two to join together and overcome their "personal grievances".
He also warned that, if the two parties don't come together, Israel could see a repeat of the 1992 election that saw the entrance of Labor and Yitzhak Rabin, which led to the signing of the Oslo Accords.
"In 1992, the right, like today, had more votes than the left, but because there were three parties, we didn't cross the electoral threshold, we lost to the left, we got the Oslo disaster, Arafat here, Hamas here, and everything that followed was disaster after disaster," he said.
Ben-Gvir says 'no'
Netanyahu's pleas come amid a balkanization of the right-wing, pro-Netanyahu camp in Israel's election, with several small parties running that are set to draw away votes from the coalition parties, without getting past the 3.25% electoral threshold for Knesset seats.
In particular, the launch of the new People of Israel party led by former army commander Ofer Winter has made a significant impact in the polls, several of which show the party drawing voters away from both Netanyahu's Likud party and Smotrich's Religious Zionist Party, to the extent that the later loses all its seats in the Knesset.
This is despite Winter pledging to support Netanyahu, saying: "We are part of the right-wing camp. Netanyahu is the leader of the right-wing camp, and he is the only person we will recommend [for prime minister]."

"Accordingly, there will be no talks or meetings, or discussions on the topic, not directly, and not indirectly."
Like Netanyahu's pleas, Ben-Gvir's rebuttal was also his second, accusing Netanyahu on Thursday of attempting to weaken his party to get into coalition with opposition front-runner Gadi Eiseknot.
He also recommended Smotrich work with Winter: "Only with a strong Otzma Yehudit, and with Smotrich and Winter running together - only that way can a fully right-wing government be formed."
Polling conducted by Otzma Yehudit shows that if it joined with Smotrich's party, 80 percent of Religious Zionist party voters would switch to Winter, according to Haaretz, potentially offering a reason for why Ben-Gvir is reluctant to join Smotrich.
The two had run on a joint list in 2022, though negotiations were frayed and required support from Netanyahu to enter together in the election. They have since split.
In response to Otzma Yehudit's latest statements, Likud told Ben-Gvir to "get over your personal ego".
"In his decision to burn tens of thousands of right-wing votes and not unite with Smotrich, Ben-Gvir decided today to coronate a left-wing government of Gadi Eisenkot, Avigdor Leiberman, Yair Golan, and the Arab parties," Netanyahu said.
They too warned of a repeat of 1992's election.
Most polling across Israel shows that Eisenkot's Yashar is set to gain the most seats in the Knesset, with the opposition also predicted to gain more seats than Netanyahu's coalition bloc.
Polling from the Times of Israel puts the opposition bloc at 58 seats, against Netanyahu's bloc at 51 seats. The Palestinian parties, made up of a joint list of Hadash-Ta'al-Balad and Ra'am, are at 6 and 5 seats.
While the opposition is ahead, a majority of 61 seats is needed to form a government.
It is widely believed that the inclusion of a Palestinian party is needed to get over the electoral threshold, a place that Ra'am is positioning itself for.

Photo: Bloomberg
The impressive earnings emerged a month after CXMT pulled off China’s second-biggest initial public offering (IPO) in Shanghai, raising 66.6 billion yuan with an overallotment option.

The Gospel of the Great Leader
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
16:37:28 UTC
01:37:28 KST

US President Donald Trump’s latest effort to re-engage with North Korean dictator Kim Jong-un has strained relations with South Korea and deepened the growing conviction in Asia that Washington is an unpredictable ally. By curtailing joint military exercises with South Korea, Trump has risked creating greater instability in a volatile region. Not even Chinese President Xi Jinping (習近平) will be pleased, because Kim seems almost certain to interpret Trump’s move as empowering his efforts to secure greater independence from China.
As with the current war with Iran, the Trump administration appears to have acted without fully considering the potential consequences of its actions. Even more than the Soviet Union, North Korea embodies Winston Churchill’s “riddle wrapped in a mystery inside an enigma.” This means that dealing with it can rarely, if ever, succeed with a policy based on impressionistic judgement.
Instead, the Trump administration should avail itself of efforts to shed new light on what is widely considered the world’s most closed society. By tracing how a perverse interpretation of Christianity helped shape North Korea’s communist dynasty, Jonathan Cheng’s recent book, Korean Messiah: Kim Il Sung and the Christian Roots of North Korea’s Personality Cult, is an invaluable addition to the canon.
Illustration: Louise Ting
At the heart of Cheng’s narrative is the remarkable story of how North Korea’s founder, Kim Il-sung, drew on his Christian upbringing to develop and consolidate a personality cult that has endured for eight decades. By appropriating religious structures, doctrines and imagery, he also laid the foundation for the hereditary communist regime now ruled by his grandson, Kim Jong-un.
Academics have long observed that North Korea’s official ideology, Kimilsungism and Juche (self-reliance), functions, in some respects, like a faith. Cheng’s contribution is to place the regime’s religious dimension within a much broader historical and geopolitical context, tracing the forces that have shaped the Korean Peninsula through the centuries, from the imperial rivalries of the late 19th century and Japanese colonial rule to liberation in 1945, the division between North and South, the Cold War and the famine of the 1990s. Running through this larger story is the book’s central theme: the complex interplay between political power and Christianity that gave rise to Kim Il-sung’s personality cult.
Cheng’s reliance on archival documents, letters, photographs, diaries and biographies — many of them previously unknown or unavailable — allows him to reconstruct the roles of the many figures who shaped Korea’s turbulent modern history. By comparing official accounts with a wide range of independent sources, he manages to produce a historical narrative that is both rigorous and vividly drawn.
His striking account of Pyongyang’s transformation, in particular, captures the paradox of a regime that brutally suppressed organized religion while demanding near-religious devotion to its ruling family. Once dubbed the “Jerusalem of the East,” the North Korean capital became the epicenter of the Kims’ deification — the very kind of idolatry Christianity expressly forbids.
CHRISTIAN ROOTS
Cheng traces the roots of Christianity’s revival in Korea to Samuel Moffett, a US missionary from Madison, Indiana, who arrived in Pyongyang in 1893 and helped spread the faith throughout the peninsula despite numerous obstacles.
Christianity gained converts after Korea was caught up in the Sino-Japanese and Russo-Japanese Wars and, in 1905, lost control of its foreign affairs to Japan. Amid the devastating reality of a crumbling country, many Koreans placed their hopes in what was, to them, an unfamiliar Western religion. In January 1907, Pyongyang became the center of an extraordinary Christian revival, one of Asia’s largest ever. The movement soon spread throughout the peninsula and beyond, reaching expatriate communities in Manchuria.
Korean Messiah then turns to Kim Il-sung himself. His father, Kim Hyong-jik, attended a missionary school and was deeply religious. Influenced by missionaries like Moffett and William Baird, he initially hoped to become a pastor. Kim’s mother, Kang Pan-sok, was even more devout, while her father, Kang Ton-uk, was a church leader who had founded a missionary school.
However, under Japanese rule, Christian missionaries generally adhered to the Japanese Government-General’s policy that churches stay out of politics and confine themselves to religious affairs. This increasingly alienated Korean nationalists who yearned for independence.
The cause of Korean self-determination appeared to receive a major boost on Jan. 8, 1918, when then-US president Woodrow Wilson presented Congress with his “14 Points” for ending World War I. His fifth point declared that, in resolving colonial disputes, “the interests of the populations concerned must have equal weight” with those of imperial powers.
However, nationalists’ hopes were eventually dashed, prompting some to turn to socialism, much as radicals in China and Vietnam had done. The brutal suppression of the non-violent March First Movement in 1919 further weakened the appeal of the moderate Christian strain of Korean nationalism.
Kim Il-sung came of age amid this radical ferment. According to his memoirs, he formed the Down-with-Imperialism Union at the age of 14 while attending Huacheng Academy. North Korean historiography would later portray the organization as a precursor to the Workers’ Party of Korea.
A major turning point came with the death of the Reverend Son Chong-do — a Christian gradualist and a friend of Kim’s father who had been a major influence on the young Kim — in February 1931. Shortly thereafter, Kim began to gravitate toward socialism, with its emphasis on the power of the masses, rather than the gradualist enlightenment movement associated with activist An Chang-ho — and the reliance on US support championed by future South Korean President Rhee Syngman.
By late 1940, Kim had crossed the Amur River into the Soviet Union, where he later became a captain in the Soviet military’s 88th Brigade, placing him firmly within the Soviet political and military orbit. These were desperate years for Korea. Japan’s invasion of China had turned the peninsula into a military supply base, while colonial authorities sought to suppress Christianity by requiring Koreans to attend ceremonies at Shinto shrines.
BIRTH OF THE KIM CULT
Much of Korean Messiah’s second half focuses on the Soviet occupation of North Korea, when the seeds of Kim Il-sung’s personality cult were sown. The historical irony is that Kim and his followers systematically persecuted Christianity, only to fill the spiritual vacuum by repurposing Christian language and symbolism to create a political religion centered on Kim himself.
Cheng contrasts Soviet leader Joseph Stalin’s swift and shrewd maneuvering during the final stages of World War II with the US’ relative indifference to Korea’s postwar fate. On Aug. 8, 1945 — two days after the atomic bomb was dropped on Hiroshima—the Soviet Union declared war on Japan and quickly sent forces into the Korean Peninsula. Alarmed by the speed of the Soviet advance, the Truman administration hastily proposed the 38th parallel as a temporary dividing line, which Stalin accepted.
The Allied powers soon went further, agreeing to place the country under an international trusteeship for up to five years rather than grant it immediate independence. The idea itself was not new. At the 1943 Tehran Conference, then-president Franklin Roosevelt proposed to Stalin that Korea be placed under trusteeship for 40 years, arguing that Koreans were not yet capable of self-government. That period was subsequently shortened at the Moscow Conference of Foreign Ministers, with the US, the Soviet Union and the UK announcing the agreement on Dec. 27, 1945.
Koreans saw the agreement as a profound betrayal. Coming after the 1905 Taft-Katsura Agreement and Wilson’s reneging on his promise of national self-determination in 1919, the trusteeship reinforced the sense that Korea’s fate remained at the mercy of foreign powers. The Korean War would ultimately vindicate those fears, as the 1953 armistice replaced the 38th parallel with the Military Demarcation Line that separates North and South Korea to this day.
In Korea, news of the agreement triggered a fierce struggle between supporters and opponents of trusteeship. The vast majority of Korea’s political factions initially opposed the plan, but after Stalin directed the communists in the North to support it, Kim Il-sung and his allies quickly fell in line.
Notably, the Soviet authorities occupying North Korea did not initially intend to install Kim Il-sung as its leader. Their first choice was Cho Man-sik, a Christian nationalist and gradualist who enjoyed overwhelming popular support. But when Cho steadfastly resisted pressure from both the Soviets and Kim Il-sung’s supporters to endorse the trusteeship plan, the Soviets abandoned him and threw their support behind Kim Il-sung.
To consolidate communist rule, Kim Il-sung and his Soviet patrons needed to win over the North’s highly influential Christian population. A crucial ally in this endeavor was Kang Yang-uk, a distant relative on his mother’s side who had also been his Sunday school teacher.
Kang established the Choson Christian Federation to bring Christian leaders sympathetic to Kim Il-sung under the regime’s control, penalizing those who refused to join. The 1946 land reform dealt another severe blow to the church and other centers of opposition by undermining their economic foundations. Meanwhile, missionaries increasingly found themselves denounced as agents or spies of US imperialism. As persecution intensified, more than 1 million Christians fled southward between 1945 and 1950, contributing to Christianity’s emergence as a powerful force in the South.
FROM CULT TO DYNASTY
Because Kim Il-sung lacked a strong political base, the Soviet authorities embellished his wartime record. His idolization took on a life of its own in February 1956, when Nikita Khrushchev denounced Stalin’s own cult of personality and launched the de-Stalinization process, deeply unsettling Kim Il-sung. That August, Kim Il-sung’s domestic rivals tried and failed to remove him from power. North Korea responded by further distancing itself from the Soviet Union and China while doubling down on Kim Il-sung’s deification. By the early 1960s, in Cheng’s account, his personality cult surpassed even Stalin’s.
Faith in Kim Il-sung, the Great Leader, soon came to dominate everyday life in North Korea. Citizens underwent three to four hours of ideological education each day, alongside regular sessions of “self-criticism.” Just as Catholics confess their sins before God, North Koreans were required once a week to acknowledge before their peers their failures to live according to Kim Il-sung’s teachings. Art and literature were similarly remolded to place Kim Il-sung at the center of people’s hopes, dreams and imaginations, systematically weaving his cult into the country’s cultural fabric.
At the same time, the regime sought to seal off the country from ideas, ideologies and cultural influences that challenged Kim Il-sung’s supremacy. Under Kang’s leadership, Christianity — regarded as an ideological rival to Kim Il-sung’s personality cult — was uprooted and outside influences were increasingly shut out. After visiting Pyongyang in October 1964, the British economist Joan Robinson observed that Kim Il-sung appeared “not as a dictator, but as a savior Messiah.”
After thwarting another coup plot in 1967, Kim Il-sung further expanded his personality cult by enshrining his absolute authority. The regime subsequently codified its demand for total loyalty in the “Ten Principles for the Establishment of a Monolithic Ideological System,” which took precedence over the constitution and ordinary law, and which Cheng compares to the biblical Ten Commandments. As Kang Myung-do, a defector and great-nephew of Kang Yang-uk, wrote in his 2017 book Now I Can Speak!, Kim Il-sung “used the deep-rooted Christian background of his family to idolize himself.”
Deification soon extended beyond Kim Il-sung to his family, laying the ideological groundwork for hereditary succession. Kim Il-sung’s parents became “saints of the revolution,” while his mother was elevated to “Mother of Korea,” a status mirroring that of the Virgin Mary. In the process, North Korea rejected the conventional wisdom within the socialist bloc — shared by Stalin and Mao Zedong — that leadership should not be passed down through bloodlines.
The interplay between Christianity and the Kim cult continued to shape North Korea over the following decades. In the wake of then-US president Richard Nixon’s 1972 visit to China and the subsequent July 4 South-North Joint Communique, Kim Il-sung began openly acknowledging the Christian influences on his early life. In the 1980s, the regime softened its hostility toward Christianity and allowed exchanges with international Christian organizations. The publication of Kim Il-sung’s memoirs in 1992 marked another shift, followed by visits from prominent Christian figures, including the American evangelist Billy Graham.
Kim Jong-il, who assumed leadership following his father’s death in 1994, further developed the religious dimensions of Kim Il-sung’s personality cult. Faced with the Great Famine and the Arduous March, he transformed Kimilsungism and Juche into a system of faith designed to endure across generations, preserving Kim Il-sung as an immortal presence at the center of North Korean life.
Cheng credits the regime’s survival under Kim Jong-il to a potent combination of tactical savvy and the continued deification of his father. North Korea’s current ruler, Kim Jong-un, receives comparatively little attention, with only about eight of the book’s 768 pages devoted to his rule. Yet Cheng emphasizes the cult’s continuity across generations. Like his father and grandfather before him, regime propaganda depicts Kim Jong-un as a genius, descended from the sacred Mount Paektu bloodline, who has mastered virtually every field. He is described as being “one and the same with President Kim Il-sung in all aspects,” linking the grandson to the dynasty’s founder through blood and character.
CAN THE CULT SURVIVE?
Korean Messiah’s focus on the origins and extraordinary reach of Kim Il-sung’s personality cult can leave readers with the impression that its grip on North Korea is permanent. However, the forces that sustain autocratic regimes are never static. Geopolitical conditions change, economies and societies evolve, and public attitudes shift with them.
In this respect, the book pays too little attention to the deeper structural forces that might be eroding the foundations of the Kim dynasty. Readers interested in North Korea’s future will be left wondering whether a system built around the deification of Kim Il-sung can prove as durable under Kim Jong-un and whoever might succeed him.
Kim Jong-un’s governing style offers little reason to believe that it can. Since 2023, he has abandoned the goal of national unification, a cornerstone of Kim Il-sung’s vision and the ultimate objective of Juche, in favor of treating North and South Korea as two hostile states. In doing so, he has undermined a core pillar of the ideological patrimony that sustains the Kim regime.
Moreover, exclusion of competing ideas and outside influences has become increasingly difficult. After the Great Famine and the Arduous March of the 1990s, the partial introduction of market mechanisms revitalized trade and contact with the outside world, creating new channels for foreign information to seep through. The spread of South Korean pop culture among the jangmadang (market) generation has been particularly significant. As one defector recently told me, almost every North Korean citizen has likely encountered South Korean dramas or music at least once, exposing them to a reality vastly different from the one portrayed by the regime.
The consequences are potentially profound: losing its monopoly over information makes it much harder to conceal North Korea’s poverty or maintain its carefully constructed image of the outside world. Kim Jong-un’s own rhetoric suggests that he is keenly aware of these risks. At a military parade marking the 75th anniversary of the Workers’ Party of Korea in October 2020, he shed tears and apologized for having “failed to always live up” to the enormous trust placed in him by the North Korean people. A year later, while praising the Party’s revolutionary achievements, he acknowledged that “great changes are taking place in the state of people’s consciousness and the social environment.”
Against this backdrop, Kim’s abandonment of unification and embrace of the “two hostile states” doctrine can be seen as an attempt to contain the South’s growing appeal. As access to outside information exposes the gulf between the two countries, the prospect of unification carries the dangerous implication that North Koreans might begin to imagine a better life as part of a unified, democratic Korea.
All this suggests that the Kim family’s personality cult might no longer be enough to withstand the pressures created by economic hardship, changing public attitudes and the growing influence of South Korean culture. While the regime’s political religion proved enormously effective in consolidating Kim Il-sung’s power and legitimizing hereditary succession, its hold appears to have weakened. Kim Jong-un has responded by tightening information controls and reinforcing the barriers between North Koreans and the outside world, relying on the politics of fear to keep the population in check.
Meanwhile, Kim Jong-un has begun appearing publicly with his daughter Kim Ju-ae — believed to be 13 years old — prompting speculation that he is grooming her as his eventual successor. But even if she assumes power, it remains to be seen whether the personality cult built by her great-grandfather can carry the Kim dynasty through a fourth generation.
The final irony is that however effectively North Korea’s rulers appropriated Christian doctrines and rhetoric to elevate Kim Il-sung to near-divine status, the entire system rests on the deification of a mortal man. For all their efforts to fashion the Kim dynasty into an eternal kingdom, the most fitting biblical parallel may be the Tower of Babel.
Cheng’s nuanced, compassionate account of North Korean Christianity also resonates with me personally. I became a Christian through my wife and her mother, a Christian who fled Pyongyang during the Korean War. As both a believer and a political scientist, I am therefore left with the hope that North Koreans will one day find relief from their suffering and freedom from the regime that has perpetuated it.
Yoon Young-kwan, a former South Korean minister of foreign affairs and trade, is chairman of the Asan Institute for Policy Studies.

Taiwan is not only drawing lessons from those conflicts, but also translating them into practice. Far from seeking to match China ship for ship, missile for missile or aircraft for aircraft, Taiwan needs to make Chinese aggression so costly, problematic and uncertain that Beijing is deterred from launching an attack. Student safety a shared responsibility: unions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
16:37:28 UTC
01:37:28 KST

A coalition of nine education unions yesterday called for a clearer delineation of responsibilities for student traffic safety, saying that teachers should focus on safety guidance and education on school grounds, while police and other trained personnel should assist at public roads and dangerous intersections outside school gates.
The call came as elementary and junior-high schools prepare for the start of a new school year on Monday.
Teachers are not opposed to helping ensure student safety on their way to and from school, but they neither have the authority to enforce traffic laws nor have they received comprehensive training in traffic enforcement, Formosa Education Union president Kuo Yen-cheng (郭彥成) said.
Photo: Taipei Times
The unions called for a clearer division of professional responsibilities, with teachers primarily responsible for student guidance and safety education within schools and inside school gates, while traffic management and safety at public roads and hazardous intersections should be handled with the assistance of police, volunteer traffic controllers and other appropriate personnel.
The Ministry of Education said it has been assessing schools’ actual needs.
In a survey on dangerous road sections and intersections surrounding school campuses that require assistance from police or volunteer traffic controllers, the ministry asked schools to identify specific hazardous locations, describe local traffic conditions and specify the assistance required.
Schools were also asked to report on coordination with local police precincts, it said.
Examples listed in the survey include illegal parking, vehicles making U-turns in front of school gates, heavy traffic, speeding and running red lights.
The ministry is also surveying how schools deploy personnel for traffic safety duties to gain a clearer picture of staffing arrangements at individual schools. The list of personnel includes teachers, military training instructors, student affairs personnel, students, parents, volunteers, volunteer traffic controllers and police officers.
The ministry is also reviewing the condition of pedestrian routes used by students and improvements to roads and other facilities surrounding school campuses.
Yilan County Teachers’ Union president Hsiao Chia-yi (蕭家怡) said that although the central government has begun identifying dangerous intersections, local authorities could still face shortages of funding and personnel.
The government’s efforts should not end with completing surveys, but should be followed by the provision of resources based on the needs of individual schools, she said.
The union also called for recurring funding for dangerous road sections, as well as additional resources for professional traffic safety personnel, police and volunteer traffic controllers.
It further proposed establishing a tracking mechanism covering individual schools and intersections to monitor and improve traffic safety measures.
The nine unions said that ensuring students’ safety on their way to and from school is a shared goal.
They called for teachers’ traffic safety duties to focus primarily on guidance within school grounds, while education authorities, police agencies and local governments work together to gradually establish a safer and more sustainable system for students commuting to and from school.

SK Hynix starts construction at site in US’ Indiana
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
16:37:24 UTC
01:37:24 KST

SK Hynix Inc on Thursday held a groundbreaking ceremony for its advanced memory packaging facility in Indiana, marking a milestone in Washington’s expansive campaign to rebuild domestic supply chains and manufacturing for strategically important sectors.
The West Lafayette plant, costing more than US$4 billion and occupying a 54-hectare site, is to be SK Hynix’s first high-bandwidth memory (HBM) packaging base in the US. Its cleanroom is expected to open by October 2028, with mass production of next-generation HBM scheduled to begin in the second half of 2029, chief executive officer Kwak Noh-jung said at the event.
When fully operational, it would be a major HBM hub employing about 1,000 people, Kwak said.
Photo: Reuters
HBM is an indispensable part of the global artificial intelligence (AI) hardware boom, as it is prerequisite for assembling Nvidia Corp’s most advanced AI acceleration systems.
That has helped SK Hynix grow to become South Korea’s second-most valuable company, behind Samsung Electronics Co, which has also been lifted by runaway demand for HBM and other memory products.
The Indiana project is backed by the US CHIPS and Science Act, a signature law signed by then-US president Joe Biden in 2022 that allowed for the South Korean chipmaker to receive as much as US$458 million in direct funding and up to US$500 million in loans.
The program was designed to reduce US dependence on overseas semiconductor production and bring critical chip manufacturing, packaging and research capabilities to US soil.
At the event, Kwak said the plant would help strengthen a domestic AI chip supply chain in the US that Washington views as essential to economic and national security.
“We will expand our investments and collaboration in the US, grow together and become the most trusted partner in shaping the future of AI in America,” he said.
The Indiana investment is particularly significant because it targets a weak link in the US semiconductor supply chain: advanced packaging.
The technology combines multiple chips into a single package, often stacking them vertically to boost performance, as conventional tech miniaturization approaches become increasingly difficult.
Wafers produced by SK Hynix in South Korea would be shipped to Indiana for packaging and testing before being supplied to US customers, the company said.
The project is expected to create about 7,000 direct and indirect jobs through construction, operations and related industries.
SK Hynix is considering more than 100 companies to supply materials, components and equipment, potentially creating a broader semiconductor cluster.
SK Hynix also signed an agreement with nearby Purdue University to cooperate on HBM, system integration and advanced packaging research.
An advanced packaging research and development test bed would be built alongside the production lines.
Reflecting Indiana’s historic ties with South Korea — the state sent about 140,000 troops to the Korean War — parent SK Group also said it would provide new employment and career opportunities for former US Forces Korea service members.

====================================================================================================

‘Power of the purse’ not a weapon
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
16:37:21 UTC
01:37:21 KST

Chinese Nationalist Party (KMT) Legislator Weng Hsiao-ling (翁曉玲) has discovered an extraordinarily simple theory of constitutional government: If you have enough votes in the legislature, apparently you can attach almost any demand to a budget and call it oversight.
Her latest proposal freezes Premier Cho Jung-tai’s (卓榮泰) salary from next month through December. He can have it back after fulfilling what Weng considers his constitutional and legal obligations — including budgeting for legislation and countersigning laws — and submitting a written report to the Legislative Yuan for approval.
There is a perfectly respectable instrument for what Weng wants to do: a non-binding resolution. Legislatures around the democratic world use them to express condemnation, demand action or declare political positions without pretending that a majority vote creates powers the legislature does not possess.
Weng wants something different. She wants the resolution to bite.
If the KMT believes Cho has violated the Constitution or is unfit to govern, Taiwan’s constitutional system provides political and legal mechanisms for confronting him. Most obviously, legislators can pursue a vote of no confidence. What they should not assume is that a legislative majority allows them to invent new punishments: obey us, report back to us, obtain our approval — or lose your salary.
A majority gives legislators the votes to exercise the powers they possess. It does not give them the power to invent new ones, a distinction that seems increasingly lost on Weng.
Her assault on the Presidential Office’s budget offers another example of the same mentality. After cuts and freezes to the Presidential Office’s state affairs expenditure reportedly affected orders for Mid-Autumn Festival gift boxes from shelter workshops, Weng defended her approach by calling budgetary action the legislature’s “only remaining, very humble means of checks and balances.”
There is nothing humble about wielding budgetary power without sufficient regard for what lies downstream.
This does not mean that all government expenditure must be protected because someone benefits from it. Legislators have the right and the responsibility to scrutinize public spending. Waste should be cut. Dubious programs should be challenged. Officials should be made to explain how taxpayers’ money is spent.
However, scrutiny requires discrimination. A scalpel is an instrument of oversight. A hammer swung at everything in sight is not.
The shelter workshops controversy exposed precisely this problem. The political target was the Presidential Office; the consequences reached workers who had nothing to do with the constitutional battle Weng wanted to fight.
If a minister refuses a legislative demand, would legislators freeze his salary too? If another constitutional official makes a decision Weng dislikes, should his office lose electricity? At what point does “budget oversight” cease to mean deciding how public money should be spent and begin to mean using money to force other branches of government to obey the legislative majority?
Democratic government is not simply majority rule. Every constitutional democracy deliberately places boundaries around majorities. Parliament legislates and scrutinizes. The executive administers. Courts adjudicate. Each possesses powers the others cannot simply appropriate because they have the votes.
Perhaps most revealing is the reported reaction inside the KMT itself. Some KMT legislators are apparently so frustrated by Weng’s actions that they have privately asked caucus leader Fu Kun-chi (傅?萁) to “control her.” Others reportedly worry that her behavior could damage the party’s electoral prospects.
If KMT legislators believe Weng has gone too far, their constitutional remedy is wonderfully uncomplicated: stop voting for proposals they consider excessive.
A political party cannot repeatedly provide the votes and then distance itself from the consequences when public opinion turns sour.
Weng might be less an aberration than a useful revelation. She exposes what can happen when a legislative majority begins to confuse winning votes with possessing unlimited authority.
Taiwan needs a strong legislature. It needs legislators willing to challenge the executive, expose waste and resist abuses of power, but checks and balances work in both directions. The legislature exists to check executive power; constitutional limits exist to check legislative power as well.
The power of the purse is one of parliament’s greatest constitutional weapons, and that is precisely why it should not be treated as a toy.
John Cheng is a retired businessman from Hong Kong living in Taiwan.
The Iran and Ukraine wars are rewriting modern military strategy. These conflicts are demonstrating that a less conventionally powerful state, by leveraging asymmetric capabilities, can impose major costs on an aggressor and fundamentally reshape the outcome of conflict. Taiwan is not only drawing lessons from those conflicts, but also translating them into practice. Far from seeking to match China ship for ship, missile for missile or aircraft for aircraft, Taiwan needs to make Chinese aggression so costly, problematic and uncertain that Beijing is deterred from launching an attack. Taiwan cannot become a bigger wolf than China, but it can ensure that

Ministry decries new drone legislation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
16:37:21 UTC
01:37:21 KST

The Ministry of Economic Affairs on Thursday expressed regret over the passage of an opposition-backed uncrewed vehicle industry bill in the legislature, warning that the new regulations could hamper the sector’s development.
The legislature on Thursday passed the Act on Strengthening Defense Autonomy and Developing the Unmanned Vehicles Industry, which calls for the central government to allocate NT$240 billion (US$7.59 billion) over six consecutive years through annual budgets.
The ministry would oversee the act, while the Ministry of National Defense would be responsible for military procurement.
Photo: CNA
The Cabinet in June approved the defense ministry’s draft special act on the procurement of domestically developed uncrewed vehicles — which proposed allocating up to NT$210 billion over multiple years — and urged the legislature to pass its version.
The economic ministry said it was concerned that the version would create extra hurdles for development of the drone industry, preventing it from developing new technologies if local drone developers did not get government funding.
The legislature’s version says that the Executive Yuan is required to establish a special committee to coordinate industry policies and review development plans, including funding needs and financing, with more than half of its members to be experts and academics nominated by legislative caucuses, the economics ministry said.
The arrangement could create political gridlock if legislative caucuses delay nominating members or their nominees obstruct proceedings, potentially preventing the committee from operating, it said.
It could also delay government agencies drawing up budgets, as well as defense procurement and industrial development, it said.
The Executive Yuan already holds quarterly interagency meetings with experts to coordinate uncrewed vehicle development, including defense autonomy, industrial development and democratic supply chains, it said.
The mechanism already serves the functions of the proposed committee, while the legislation would only add administrative procedures, it added.
Regarding military uncrewed vehicle procurement, relying on annual government budgets could expose procurement to budget constraints, review delays and cuts, making orders less stable and predictable for the industry, the economics ministry said.
The industry has high research and development (R&D) costs, and technological barriers, making stable government procurement essential for investments, it said.
Taiwan’s drone supply chain comprises more than 274 companies spanning chips, communications, flight controls, navigation, optoelectronics, batteries, motors, materials, systems integration and application services, it said.
Many companies have already invested heavily in funding, personnel and equipment in line with government policy, it added.
Government procurement is intended to share R&D risks with the private sector and spur investment, but unstable orders could increase the financial pressure on companies and undermine business confidence, it said.
Government programs already provide a framework for developing the industry, while the defense ministry can fund military procurement through its regular budget without the legislation, it said.
The act carries more symbolic than practical significance, it added.

The Ministry of Labor last week vowed to launch an investigation after Indonesian technicians working on renewable energy projects in Taiwan accused their employer of forced labor and wage theft.
Democratic Progressive Party Legislator Lin Yueh-chin (林月琴) joined advocacy groups in accusing Singapore-based Sheffield Green Co of changing employees’ contracts and cutting their pay after their arrival in Taiwan.
Workers also said that Sheffield Green, among other companies, failed to give employees time to recover from work-related injuries and pay for their health and labor insurance.
It would be expected that such practices are illegal, yet this case highlights a regulatory gap that leaves foreign workers vulnerable to exploitation. Some companies are taking advantage of Article 51 of the Employment Service Act (就業服務法) — which allows Taiwanese companies to hire skilled foreign workers through expedited work permits — to cut costs and induce foreign employees to accept wages lower than they were promised, while attempting to justify the practice by arguing that these short-term foreign workers are not covered by the Labor Standards Act (勞動基準法).
Migrant workers across multiple industries regularly face a long list of abuses — from delayed, reduced or withheld wages, deceptive recruitment and debt bondage to excessively long working hours, lack of rest days and, in extreme cases, physical abuse.
Domestic caregivers, who make up about 30 percent of Taiwan’s migrant workforce, are unprotected by the Labor Standards Act and lack many of the basic protections afforded to other workers, including statutory guarantees on wages, working hours and days off.
Taiwan’s distant-water fishing industry, which relies heavily on migrant labor, has likewise developed an international reputation for worker abuse following reports of hunger, unhygienic living conditions and physical violence aboard fishing vessels. Like live-in caregivers, distant-water fishing workers are also excluded from the Labor Standards Act because they are classified as “overseas employees.”
Migrant workers in the manufacturing sector have also reported exploitative conditions, including excessive working hours, inadequate rest, crowded dormitories, restrictive curfews and deductions from their wages for recruitment fees, accommodation and other expenses.
Victims of abusive employers are left with few options: endure the abuse, leave their jobs and risk losing their legal protections, or speak out. Increasingly, many are choosing the latter.
Earlier this week, Indonesian migrant fishers launched the “Freedom for Fishers Campaign” in Pingtung County, calling for fair wages and employment contracts, safe working conditions, transparent grievance mechanisms and the right to organize without intimidation or retaliation. The campaign is the latest in a series of demonstrations and initiatives by migrant workers and advocacy groups demanding better working conditions and stronger legal protections.
Although demands vary across industries, they share common ground — migrant workers are seeking the same basic legal protections and guarantees that domestic workers have.
Hardly an outrageous request, yet the government has instead prioritized expanding the supply of migrant labor to meet demand and address labor shortages. Meanwhile, the rights and protections afforded to those workers have not kept pace.
On Monday, the Chinese National Federation of Industries urged the government to further ease restrictions on the hiring of migrant workers and double the quota for migrant workers in the general construction sector, highlighting growing labor shortages facing traditional industries.
It is undeniable that Taiwan’s aging population and declining birthrate would only widen labor shortages. However, as the nation comes to terms with the reality that it needs migrant workers, it must likewise recognize that these workers must be afforded fundamental rights. Expanding the former without guaranteeing the latter would only worsen existing systemic problems and deepen tensions between migrant workers, employers and society as a whole.
If Taiwan continues to increase its reliance on migrant labor without addressing the many regulatory loopholes, tightening enforcement and ensuring workers have meaningful avenues to seek help, employers would continue to have opportunities to exploit those vulnerabilities — and there is little reason to believe they would not.
Taiwan cannot expect migrant workers to sustain its economy and care for its aging population while leaving them to bear the cost of the system’s failures. If the nation is going to depend on migrant workers, it must be prepared to protect them — and not simply when their mistreatment makes headlines.
The Iran and Ukraine wars are rewriting modern military strategy. These conflicts are demonstrating that a less conventionally powerful state, by leveraging asymmetric capabilities, can impose major costs on an aggressor and fundamentally reshape the outcome of conflict. Taiwan is not only drawing lessons from those conflicts, but also translating them into practice. Far from seeking to match China ship for ship, missile for missile or aircraft for aircraft, Taiwan needs to make Chinese aggression so costly, problematic and uncertain that Beijing is deterred from launching an attack. CEC approves nuclear referendum, rejects other two
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
16:37:18 UTC
01:37:18 KST

The Central Election Commission (CEC) yesterday announced it has approved holding a referendum on nuclear power, but rejected proposals on caning and traffic fines.
The Legislative Yuan on Aug. 14 approved three referendums: introducing caning as a criminal punishment, abolishing the government’s nuclear-free homeland policy and using traffic fines to improve road safety.
The commission met for more than two and a half hours, and ruled that the referendum on caning did not meet the requirements of the Referendum Act (公民投票法), CEC Chairman Michael You (游盈隆) said.
Photo: Chen Yi-kuan, Taipei Times
The caning proposal, put forward by the Chinese Nationalist Party (KMT), seeks to introduce caning as a punishment for sexual assault, crimes against children, large-scale fraud and aggravated fraud.
However, caning or similar forms of corporal punishment are not recognized under Taiwan’s criminal justice system, You said.
The CEC therefore determined that the proposal amounted to creating new legislative principles, and was not a referendum on the initiation or repeal of a major policy, as defined by the act, he added.
The proposal involves using state power to inflict physical pain on prisoners and is considered by many countries to be cruel, inhuman and a violation of human dignity, he said.
That would contravene the Act Governing Execution of the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights and the International Covenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights (公民與政治權利國際公約及經濟社會文化權利國際公約施行法), which states that no one shall be subjected to torture or to cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment, he added.
Of the eight CEC members, seven voted that the caning proposal did not qualify as a referendum, said You, who chaired the meeting, adding that he did not cast a vote.
Regarding the Taiwan People’s Party’s (TPP) proposed referendum on earmarking traffic fines exclusively for road-related purposes, four commission members found that it did not meet the requirements of the Referendum Act, he said.
The commission held three rounds of voting, with the same 4-3 split each time, he added.
As for the proposal to repeal Taiwan’s nuclear-free homeland policy, six CEC members supported the referendum, with one abstention, You said.
The CEC ruled that the proposal meets the requirements of the Referendum Act, he said, adding that the referendum vote would be held on Nov. 28, alongside the local elections.
The KMT caucus condemned the CEC’s decision to reject the two proposals, saying that referendums exist to give people a direct say when a country faces major disputes over public policy.
“Yet what has happened now is that whether people want to vote no longer matters, and neither does whether the Legislative Yuan approves the proposal,” it said. “Instead the CEC has decided on behalf of 23 million people: ‘You are not entitled to answer this question.’”
“Is this direct democracy, or the direct confiscation of democracy?” it asked.
The TPP slammed You, saying he had claimed that “referendums submitted by the Legislative Yuan should be approved in principle and rejected only as an exception.”
“Yet he has now turned that exception into a pretext for arbitrarily expanding his powers, abandoning his principles as an academic, enabling the ruling party to flout the law and obstructing the public’s right to initiate referendums,” it said. “Such actions have brought shame on Taiwan’s democratic constitutional system.”
Additional reporting by Lin Hsin-han

DPP China Affairs warns of election interference
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
16:37:15 UTC
01:37:15 KST

With Taiwan’s year-end local elections approaching, the Democratic Progressive Party’s (DPP) China Affairs Department has warned that cooperating with Chinese election interference could carry a sentence of up to 15 years in prison, while those who report foreign interference could receive rewards of up to NT$20 million (US$632,351).
The department outlined seven types of illegal conduct involving Chinese election interference.
One form of interference is recruiting tour groups at China’s direction. That means accepting Chinese instructions, commissions or funding to recruit borough chiefs, local figures or voters to participate in a tour including transportation, accommodation or meals and asking them to support specific political parties or candidates, the department said.
Photo: Chen Cheng-yu, Taipei Times
Another form of election interference is recruiting people for free or significantly underpriced tours in exchange for votes, which could constitute bribery even without directly receiving instructions from China, it said.
Accepting any travel, accommodation or other benefits in exchange for political support could also be illegal if the person knowingly agrees to vote for a specific political party or candidate, the office said.
Producing or publishing fake opinion polls using foreign funding or at China’s direction to manipulate elections, influence voters or shape cooperation between political parties could constitute election interference, it said.
Assisting China with propaganda by accepting its instructions, commissions or funding to campaign for specific candidates, speak at rallies, hold press conferences, produce promotional materials or conduct media campaigns is also election interference, it said.
Serving as an intermediary to relay instructions related to election interference, such as helping China find, direct or fund people in Taiwan to mobilize supporters, promote candidates or conduct online operations, could also result in penalties, it added.
Lastly, developing organizations or gathering intelligence for China, as well as spying on, collecting or handing over official secrets, could constitute more serious national security offenses, it said.
These seven types of conduct could contravene the Anti-Infiltration Act (反滲透法), the National Security Act (國家安全法), the Election and Recall Act (公職人員選舉罷免法), the Presidential and Vice Presidential Election and Recall Act (總統副總統選罷法) or the Criminal Code, with penalties of up to 15 years in prison, the department said.
Criminal liability could extend beyond those who accept money to people who recruit others, relay instructions, mobilize supporters, spread propaganda or accept benefits to vote for a particular candidate, it said.
People who encounter suspected election interference should hold onto evidence such as messages, itineraries, payment records, photos and videos, and call 0800-024-099 and press 4 to report them to prosecutors or investigators, it said.
It urged people not to accept benefits, travel to China, follow Chinese instructions nor assist with propaganda to protect democracy, freedom and Taiwan’s right to determine its own future.

Murder case puts spotlight on postpartum psychosis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
16:37:12 UTC
01:37:12 KST

The murder trial of Lindsay Clancy, a woman who said she experienced postpartum psychosis before strangling her three children, has sparked a debate in the US over maternal mental health.
The 36-year-old nurse does not deny strangling Cora, 5, Dawson, 3, and Callan, eight months, with fitness bands in their home in Duxbury, Massachusetts, in January 2023. She then jumped out of a second-story window, leaving her paralyzed from the waist down and using a wheelchair.
However, Clancy has pleaded not guilty by reason of insanity, saying she heard a voice ordering her to kill her children.
Photo: The Patriot Ledger via AP
Her lawyers said this was caused by postpartum psychosis.
Prosecutors have rejected her argument, saying she had planned to murder her children and was able to understand the consequences of her actions.
For the past several weeks, dozens of women dressed in pink have come to the court in Plymouth to show their support for Clancy — and to make a statement about women’s health more generally.
Lawyer Kelly Woods said she was attending the trial as a “big advocate” for people who experience postpartum psychosis.
“That is a very under-considered element of this case,” Woods said. “I certainly hope that the medical community can learn from this.”
“I ultimately hope that there is more advocacy for postpartum depression and psychosis,” she added.
Psychiatrists and people close to Clancy, as well as her estranged husband, described her distress during the five-week trial.
The nurse faces life in prison without the possibility of parole if found guilty.
Postpartum psychosis is a medical emergency that affects about one to two women in every 1,000 births, Action on Postpartum Psychosis national training coordinator Sally Wilson said.
Clancy’s case is “an incredibly distressing and rare outcome of postpartum psychosis,” Wilson said.
During closing arguments, Clancy’s lawyer, Kevin Reddington, said the mother had made several pleas for help before the killings and received “lousy medical care” from the doctors she consulted.
“She was doing everything that she could to get help, and for whatever reason, she still slipped through the cracks,” Maternal Mental Health Leadership Alliance executive director Adrienne Griffen said. “That is the question that everybody is asking, is how do we prevent something like this from happening in the future.”
Prosecutors acknowledged that Clancy was “suffering from mental illness” and tried to kill herself, but said the killings were planned and particularly cruel.
Right-wing political voices have condemned the level of violence in the killings and the supporters who have gathered outside the courthouse.
“Lindsay Clancy deserves to die for murdering her three children,” podcaster Katie Miller wrote on social media.

HK hears arguments over vigil organizers’ sentences
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

16:37:12 UTC
01:37:12 KST

Three former organizers of Hong Kong’s annual vigils in remembrance of the 1989 Tiananmen Square crackdown yesterday returned to court to argue over their sentences after being convicted of inciting subversion under a National Security Law imposed by China.
Lee Cheuk-yan (李卓人), Chow Hang-tung (鄒幸彤) and Albert Ho (何俊仁), former leaders of the Hong Kong Alliance in Support of Patriotic Democratic Movements of China, were charged in 2021 under the law that has effectively stifled the territory’s previously thriving pro-democracy movement.
Lee and Chow, who pleaded not guilty, were convicted on Friday last week.
Photo: AP
Ho earlier entered a guilty plea, which could result in a reduced sentence.
They face a maximum prison term of 10 years and are expected to be sentenced at a later date.
The disbanded alliance also was found guilty on the same charge. It was best known for organizing the only large-scale public commemoration in China that drew tens of thousands of people annually for three decades to remember the crackdown’s victims.
The verdict has drawn concerns from foreign governments.
Critics said the case illustrates a decline in freedoms Beijing promised to maintain when the former British colony returned to Chinese rule in 1997, but the Hong Kong government insisted the court only considered the laws and evidence and that many rights and freedoms are not absolute.
Three government-approved judges ruled the trio of former vigil organizers had intentionally encouraged supporters of the alliance to wait for the right time to carry out “end one-party dictatorship,” one of the group’s core demands, through unlawful means.
The call carried the notion of overthrowing or undermining the Chinese Communist Party’s (CCP) leadership status, the judges said, adding that the defendants have long held enmity against the party, and they did not genuinely believe their words and deeds would not contravene the security law.
Lawyer Erik Shum (沈士文), who represents Lee and Ho, told the judges that China’s fundamental system did not change because of the alliance members’ promotional work and the CCP was still stable and carrying out its duties, while the defendants’ advocacy work did not involve violence.
Chow insisted she did not do anything wrong and did not deserve even one day in prison.
The verdict was saying that pursuing democracy is a crime, she added.
“If the law truly has no room for our beliefs, then I would rather be a criminal than be a fake person,” she said.
Regardless of whether she is in or outside prison, she would persistently strive to vindicate the 1989 pro-democracy movement, end one-party dictatorship and build a democratic Hong Kong and China, among other goals, she wrote on social media.
The security law calls for sentences of between five and 10 years for convictions of inciting subversion, if the offense is deemed serious. If the circumstances are considered minor, sentences should not be more than five years, short-term detention or other restrictions.

UEFA preparing complaint
UEFA is preparing a criminal complaint against FIFA president Gianni Infantino in Swiss courts for possible financial mismanagement over his failed plan to sell future FIFA World Cup profits to private investors. The governing body of European soccer announced its intentions in court documents filed on Thursday in the US seeking access to material related to the sell-off plan, which was withdrawn after a backlash by UEFA and other global soccer leaders. UEFA filed documents in a Manhattan court requesting discovery of potential evidence from the New York investment fund Thrive Capital Management. UEFA also filed a request in a Florida district for authorization of discovery “in a foreign proceeding” against FIFA itself, which has offices in the Miami suburb of Coral Gables. “UEFA and its counsel are contemplating a Swiss criminal proceeding against Infantino and possibly other FIFA officials for criminal mismanagement under Article 158 of the Swiss Criminal Code,” UEFA’s lawyers state in a 56-page document.
