Sudan authorities lift Khartoum curfew after two years
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
16:32:02 UTC
01:32:02 KST

Breadcrumb
Sudan authorities lift Khartoum curfew, state of emergency after two years
Sudanese authorities have lifted a curfew and state of emergency in Khartoum after two years, allowing residents of the capital to move freely as the government seeks to project an improving security picture, despite warnings from international agencies that serious risks remain.
The measure was announced on Thursday by the government’s Security Affairs Coordination Committee, which said people would be able to travel and work across the city without time restrictions. Previously, movement by people and vehicles had been restricted between 11pm and 5am.
Following a meeting chaired by Khartoum Governor Ahmed Othman Hamza, the committee said security checkpoints and army patrols would remain in place. It advised residents travelling late at night to carry identification.
The committee also barred foreign nationals from entering Khartoum State without valid entry visas or permits.
Authorities introduced the curfew introduced in May 2024, citing deteriorating security conditions in Khartoum amid fighting between the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF).
Following the outbreak of the war in April 2023, the RSF seized the presidential palace, Khartoum International Airport and much of the capital and its wider tri-city metropolitan area. The SAF retained a foothold in Omdurman, west of the Nile.
In late September 2024, the army launched a major offensive across Khartoum State. It eventually recaptured Khartoum city at the end of March 2025, pushing out remaining RSF positions from much of the state.
Since then, the government has returned to Khartoum from its temporary administrative base in Port Sudan, seeking to re-establish the capital as the centre of state administration.
Risks remain for returnees
International agencies and analysts have cautioned against treating the army’s recapture of the city, or the lifting of the curfew, as proof that Khartoum is safe or ready for a large-scale return of displaced residents.
In a report released on Friday, the UN refugee agency, UNHCR, described major challenges facing people returning to Khartoum State, as the effects of the war continue to endanger civilian life. The agency highlighted security concerns in some areas of the state, particularly at night, when reports of shootings, theft and drone activity are most frequent.
Drone attacks remain a threat in parts of Khartoum State. On 13 August, RSF drones targeted the capital, prompting anti-aircraft fire from Omdurman as residents reported explosions.
UNHCR also warned of the threat from unexploded ordnance, saying that "safety risks from unexploded ordnance remain present in some areas". It said returnees were confronting "interlinked challenges that constrain their ability to reintegrate sustainably", including unreliable electricity, limited access to basic services and a shortage of adequate housing.

Trump vows legal order to break up ‘nasty monopoly’ in food processing
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

Trump vows legal order to break up ‘nasty monopoly’ in US food processing
WASHINGTON - US President Donald Trump on Aug 28 said he was preparing a legal order to allow farmers and ranchers to be given the right to process their own food aimed at breaking what he called “a nasty monopoly” among the nation’s top processors.
Trump did not name a particular food or industry in his post on Truth Social but said he was “authorising legal documents to be drawn” quickly.
Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins posted on X that there would be “big announcements” related to beef processing beginning on Aug 31, including expanding ranchers’ ability to sell across state lines, added support for smaller meat processors and rescinding “outdated guidance.”
Earlier this week, Trump said on the Glenn Beck programme that he would look into whether there are too many beef processing plant regulations.
Beck, who owns a ranch, suggested to Trump that Department of Agriculture regulations were impeding ranchers from processing their own animals, leaving them to rely on the nation’s highly consolidated meat processing industry.
Four companies control about 85 per cent of US meat processing: Cargill; Tyson Foods, JBS USA and National Beef Packing Co.
The companies did not immediately respond to requests for comment. White House spokeswoman Anna Kelly said, “The administration is drafting several policy actions to further support those who feed the world.”
Trump’s move comes as consumers continue to face rising grocery prices ahead of November’s midterm election.
Consolidation fight
Meat is inspected by the USDA’s Food Safety and Inspection Service, which posts inspectors at meat processing plants to ensure products meet federal standards. Ranchers are generally prohibited by federal food safety laws from selling meat from animals they have slaughtered and processed themselves, with some exceptions.
Farm and ranch groups have argued for years that consolidation in the meat processing sector has made it difficult for small producers to stay afloat because there are not many companies competing to buy their cattle and they must transport their animals to USDA-inspected meat processing plants, sometimes at a high cost.
The Meat Institute, which represents meatpacking companies, said food safety could be at risk if more ranchers process their own meat.
“Allowing uninspected meat to be sold to unwitting consumers is the wrong approach, and risks undermining this country’s reputation for producing the safest meat products in the world,” the group said.
“If the goal is to lower beef prices for American families, lowering food safety standards is the wrong response.”T
he National Cattlemen’s Beef Association, which represents ranchers, said it supports creating more opportunities for small beef processors and eliminating unnecessary regulations but warned Trump against weakening meat inspection standards.
David Anderson, agricultural economist at Texas A&M University, said that he did not think that Trump’s plan would have a significant impact on competition in the beef industry.
“The numbers on that would be so small,” he said of on-farm slaughter. “That really doesn’t change the bigger broader market at all.”
The administration of former president Joe Biden attempted to tackle consolidation in meatpacking in part through rules to promote competition and fairer pay for chicken farmers, which the Trump administration has indicated it will rescind.
Both the Biden and Trump administrations have steered funds towards supporting smaller meat processors, in an attempt to offer more options to ranchers.
Trump’s move comes as the nation’s meat processing sector grapples with a 75-year trough in supply as rising cattle costs outpace gains from soaring prices.
Trump also announced last week that more ground beef could be imported into the United States without tariffs. The Justice Department has also said it is investigating whether meatpacking companies were illegally driving up consumer beef prices. REUTERS

What it’s like to live through Kyiv’s constant air raids
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
16:29:12 UTC
01:29:12 KST

KYIV — Before I go to sleep, I make a second bed — my air alert bed.
When the chorus of sirens announcing a Russian attack howls behind my windows and jolts me out of my slumber, I’m trained to jump up and run to my hallway, where this other bed is waiting. There, I usually try to sleep and wait until the attack ends in the morning.
Over the past two days, however, the alerts did not end at sunrise; they droned on into the day and the following night. It’s a nerve-wracking wailing, on top of explosions and the knowledge that your life is constantly under threat.
Advertisement
Kyiv has survived more than 20 air raid alerts since Thursday night. Some were an hour long, while others lasted for up to 10 minutes.
Indeed, every alert, as Russia continues its persistent destruction of millions of books, food warehouses and liquor factories, also means everything has to stop until we hear the words: “Air raid alert is over.” Dozens of trains are delayed, and businesses shut down and wait, losing customers and money.
But “survivors must still go to work,” as we like to joke bitterly. People are still expected to commute, even though Kyiv’s subway has stopped running between the left and right banks of the River Dnipro. Sleep-deprived civilians need to walk for hours, squeeze themselves into buses, or get stuck in traffic on bridges, just to get to work and back home. Transport chaos overground means even more danger for people stuck in large groups all around the city.
But our wartime economy, on which we need to rely more and more due to the slowing of foreign aid, cannot afford to stop.
“The country’s defense spending is constantly growing, and this requires maximum mobilization of domestic resources,” said Hlib Vyshlinsky, the executive director of the Center for Economic Strategy think tank based in Kyiv. “The policy of zero tolerance for the risk to the life and health of civilians under constant missile and drone strikes becomes irrelevant, because the state is still not able to protect them at 100 percent.”
As a Kyivan, I can tell you that this terror sends your mental stability into a spiral.
Advertisement
And that is exactly why Russia keeps it going.
“You think we are calling for some kinds of atrocities, while we are aiming to demoralize the public to such an extent that they come out with their little paws raised to meet our troops,” Deputy Speaker of the Russian Duma Pyotr Tolstoy said this week.
That cuts no ice in Kyiv.
A smoke rises above one of Kyiv’s residential districts after a Russian strike on August 27, 2026. | Veronika Melkozerova/POLITICO
“Such statements by a Russian official calling for war crimes and demanding unbearable living conditions for civilians should lead to an ICC arrest warrant. As for ‘raised hands’ — the only reason to raise them is to give Tolstoy and his fellow war criminals the middle finger,” Ukrainian Foreign Ministry Spokesperson Heorhii Tykhyi responded.
Of course, it’s not as if Ukraine isn’t giving Russia a taste of its own medicine.
While peace negotiations have stalled, both sides have turned to total war tactics to the extent their capacity allows. While Ukraine has now also extended its targets from oil depots and military factories to bombing retail warehouses and energy facilities, Russia has embarked on a maximum escalation, attacking civilian housing, postal services, businesses, book and food warehouses — and that list covers only the past couple of days.
Advertisement
In July, the U.N. recorded the highest mortality rates among civilians in Ukraine since March 2022. Russia also reports more civilian deaths caused by Ukrainian attacks, even though, unlike Moscow, Kyiv does not deliberately target civilians but aims to bring the war “where it came from.“
Ukraine’s Deputy Prime Minister Denys Shmyhal best described the situation when talking to me about the attacks on the energy system last month: “It’s like the 12th round and each boxer hopes their rival will fall first.”
While troops on the frontline are largely stuck, with neither side making much progress on the ground, it’s us, civilians, who are being targeted more and more frequently.
Ukrainian military analyst Mykola Bielieskov called it “a mutual driving of each other into the Stone Age, with the hope to do it before the other side does.”
While our soldiers hold the Russian army at the front line, it’s ordinary Ukrainians — with our mental fortitude, our ability to outlive yet another missile, our capacity to adapt and go to work to keep the economy running no matter what — who will eventually decide the outcome of this war, Vyshlinsky said.
“As Mr. Tolstoy said, this is a tactic of deliberate exhaustion of civilians, pushing the rear to accept a war outcome unfavorable to the state,” Vyshlinsky added.
So we must endure until the other fighter falls.
And first, we need to wait for the best words that can boom from our loudspeakers: Air raid alert is over!

Sovereignty on the ballot in Iceland’s EU referendum
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
16:27:28 UTC
01:27:28 KST

Sovereignty on the ballot in Iceland’s EU referendum
After decades outside the bloc’s periphery, Iceland is about to hold a referendum on reopening membership talks with the EU. Is the Viking nation preparing to trade sovereignty for stability? Or is it climbing aboard a sinking ship?
Icelanders go to the polls on Saturday, August 29 to answer a straightforward, yes or no question: “Should Iceland resume accession negotiations with the European Union?”
The referendum is not legally binding, but liberal Prime Minister Kristrun Frostadottir has pledged to honor its result.
What stage are talks between Iceland and Brussels at?
Iceland applied for EU membership in 2009, in the chaotic aftermath of the 2008 financial crisis. The country’s three biggest banks, Kaupthing, Landsbanki, and Glitnir, collapsed in the same week, and rather than force taxpayers to cover their balance sheets, Reykjavik washed its hands of the problem and let them fail.
The Icelandic krona plummeted, inflation soared, and center-right Prime Minister Geir Haarde resigned. Amid the meltdown, the newly empowered Social Democrats argued that by joining the EU and adopting the euro, Iceland could shield itself from future shocks – even as Iceland recovered far more quickly than EU members such as Greece, Ireland, and Portugal, which were subjected to crippling austerity measures by Brussels, the World Bank, and the IMF in the wake of the crisis.
The Social Democrats won the argument, convincing their left-wing, Euroskeptic coalition partners to vote for application. The left agreed, with the caveat that the final membership deal would be put to the people in a referendum.
Following a change of government, accession talks were shelved in 2013. Iceland, it was reasoned, had emerged from the financial crisis in good shape, and joining the EU would erode the island nation’s sovereignty, potentially diluting its control of rich fishing grounds, with no tangible benefits in return.
How do the polls stand before the vote?
With less than a day to go, the latest polls suggest that the vote will come down to the wire. A poll by market research firm Maskina published on August 25 shows the referendum passing by 51.3% to 48.7%. Two days later, a Gallup poll showed a near mirror inversion of these results, with the ‘no’ side leading by 51.6% to 48.4%. The result in both surveys was inside the margin of error, making the outcome impossible to predict. However, the ‘no’ side has been steadily closing the gap since July, and if the trend holds, could succeed in putting membership talks on ice for the foreseeable future.
The Yes vote: Safety in numbers
The two major parties in Frostadottir’s coalition – her Social Democrats and Foreign Minister Thorgerdur Katrin Gunnarsdottir’s Reform Party – support EU membership. Their arguments are the same as they were in 2009, with one key addition: Membership would add a layer of defense against any potential attempts by US President Donald Trump to gain control over Iceland, as he is currently threatening Greenland. Although this is an unlikely scenario, the current US ambassador in Reykjavik caused widespread anger in January when he joked “that Iceland will be the 52nd state and he’ll be governor."
To Foreign Minister Gunnarsdottir, membership provides safety in numbers. “That is so important for us to see a group of like-minded nations stand together on principles and values,” she told AP. “That is also what I’m looking at when I see the European Union in this volatile world.”
Iceland’s six other major parties – from conservatives to centrists to leftists – all oppose membership. In an effort to persuade their voters, Frostadottir has sold the referendum as a zero-risk proposition. A ‘yes’ vote would merely restart talks, she has argued, pointing out that any deal offered by Brussels would still have to pass another referendum. It would also give Icelanders “the option of seeing what an agreement looks like,” she said last month.
Why does the EU want Iceland?
Home to fewer than 400,000 people, Iceland would be the EU’s smallest member state in terms of population. It sits just south of the Arctic Circle between Greenland and the UK, occupying a chokepoint known as the GIUK gap. Russian submarines and naval vessels entering the North Atlantic must pass through the GIUK gap, and with the EU’s foreign policy now bent on confrontation with Moscow, establishing an outpost here is high on Brussels’ list of priorities.
Frostadottir has reportedly warned the European Commission not to interfere in the vote. “The commission never intervenes in national elections or in referenda in any way,” a spokesperson told Euractiv, an outlet that the commission funds.
RT readers will recall that the European Commission has intervened in every national election in the bloc since 2024. This year alone, Brussels imposed online censorship measures ahead of elections in Bulgaria and Hungary. A US House Judiciary Committee report released in early 2026 alleged that the European Commission pressured social media platforms to censor populist and conservative speech during elections in Romania, France, the Netherlands, and Ireland.
While neither Commission President Ursula von der Leyen nor her chief diplomat Kaja Kallas have made the case for joining the bloc publicly, EU-funded media have filled in the blanks. According to Euronews, a ‘no’ vote would “close off a strategic opportunity to expand [the EU’s] positioning in the North Atlantic and Arctic region for generations.”
Is Iceland already embedded in the Western military nexus?
Despite presenting a “strategic opportunity” for the EU, Iceland is not some neutral territory waiting to be claimed. Iceland is a founding member of NATO, hosts the bloc’s air forces at Naval Air Station Keflavik, in return for which the military bloc financed the country’s major ring road, and has a network of radar stations described by the bloc’s officials as “the eyes and the ears of NATO in the north.”
At exercise Northern Viking in Iceland, I saw firsthand how U.S. and Icelandic forces train alongside fellow @NATO Allies to protect vital sea lanes and secure the Arctic, and how Icelandic technology is giving Allied forces an operational edge. Building our readiness and… pic.twitter.com/ZToq3GiBvH
— U.S. Ambassador to NATO (@USAmbNATO) August 21, 2026
Iceland has no standing army, but is a protectorate of the US under a 1951 defense agreement. The annual US-led ‘Northern Viking’ military exercise is currently underway in Iceland, and concludes on September 4.
On top of being fully integrated into the Western military camp, Iceland is already a member of the European Economic Area and visa-free Schengen zone, and has incorporated most EU legislation into its domestic laws.
No: A choice between war and peace
The EU’s militarization has directly harmed the bloc itself, Gunnar Palsson, Iceland’s former ambassador to Brussels, said in August, pointing to the EU’s flatlining economy as a result of its self-imposed embargo on Russian energy.
“The EU is now, for the first time in its history, a direct party to a military conflict in Europe,” Palsson wrote in an op-ed for Iceland’s Morgunbladid newspaper. “The Union’s escalating involvement in the Ukraine war, which is unlikely to lead to an optimal outcome for European countries, has already had a far-reaching impact on their economic situation, their relations with each other and with the outside world.”
The EU Iceland considered joining in 2009 is not the same as the hyper-aggressive, militarized bloc of 2026, he concluded.
‘Left Against the EU’, a social movement founded this year to oppose the referendum, has argued that joining the EU would subjugate Iceland’s foreign policy to the whims of the European Commission, which is “rapidly moving towards militarization.”
“The European Union and NATO have given in to the demands of the arms industry for vastly increased military spending, and it has never been more urgent than now for peace-loving people to withdraw from the warring forces,” reads a policy statement from the group.
“A European army is just around the corner, and Icelanders must seriously ask themselves whether they want to prepare their children and society for the future of serving under the arms of a European military power.”
Should the referendum pass, “Icelanders will become citizens of a union that has a strong political will for militarization and is increasingly involved in conflicts and escalating tensions in Europe,” Haraldur Olafsson, who leads the anti-EU ‘Heimssyn’ movement, warned in May. 
Sovereignty over stocks: Why fish are at the center of the argument
For most Icelandic Euroskeptics, however, the referendum comes down to a simpler issue: fish. Fishing accounts for around 4% of Iceland’s GDP, and a third of the country’s exports. Signing up to the EU’s Common Fisheries Policy risks surrendering control over this vital economic and culturally symbolic sector.
Ireland, another island on the EU’s seaboard, was subjected to these rules when it joined the bloc, and more than five decades later, it is likely that Irish fishermen will demand Icelandic fishermen be treated as they were.
French trawlers are allowed to catch five times more of certain fish in Irish waters than Irish trawlers. “The other countries are making fun of us for the lack of quota we have in our own waters,” Irish opposition leader Peadar Toibin claimed during a parliamentary debate last year.
Any Icelandic politician who trades away sovereignty over the country’s waters would “be expelled from the country,” Eirikur Bergmann, a professor at Iceland’s Bifrost University, told the BBC.
The ‘yes’ side has claimed that Iceland could negotiate exemptions to the Common Fisheries Policy, but no member state has done so to date, and Euroskeptics are unconvinced. Brussels would not even welcome such a debate, never mind find a workable solution.
“Contrary to the government’s claims, membership of the European Union is not a tailor-made agreement where each country chooses the parts that suit it and rejects the others,” Independence Party leader Gudrun Hafsteinsdottir argued earlier this year. It is unacceptable, Olafsson declared in May, “for a foreign union to legislate on Icelandic resources for its own benefit.”
The EU’s treaties – Rome, Lisbon, Maastricht – “are non-negotiable,” ‘no’ campaigner Sigridur Maria Egilsdottir warned at a rally on August 27. “We wouldn’t show up to the negotiations alone. Brussels would send its most capable team, loaded with conditions, demands and inescapable assumptions that all EU nations have had to abide by.”

Top year for the coast, less for Limburg, and Americans love Ghent

Not surprisingly, the weather sent more people to the coast this year, but made them hesitate to book a stay in Limburg. And Americans have taken to Ghent, spending more there than any other group of foreign tourists
Tourism figures show that Flanders’ coastline was bustling this summer, while fewer people turned to recreation-laden Limburg province. We’ll give you one guess why … the weather.
More than six million daytrippers descended on the coast in July and August, and more than 11 million people stayed overnight. July’s 5.6 million overnight stays is an all-time record.
This summer saw a 10% increase in overnight stays compared to last summer, resulting in the highest figures the coast has seen since the Covid crisis. More than 80% of overnight tourists were Belgians.
There are always peak periods, but this summer it was constantly busy.
Ice cream seller Francis De Buck
Because of the consistently warm weather, tourism was also consistent over the two months rather than concentrated in certain weeks or weekends. Restaurants and other catering services were as satisfied as the hotels.
“Normally the first 10 days of July are a bit calmer, but this year the start of the vacation period was immediately busy,” said Francis De Buck, who owns an ice cream and waffle parlour in Blankenberge. “That was because of the nice weather, of course. There are always peak periods, but this summer it was constantly busy. People were here the minute we opened our doors. I estimate that we earned up to 18% more than usual.”
In Flanders’ other popular summer holiday destination – Limburg – there were in fact fewer overnight stays. The province – typically the warmest in Flanders – saw 1.7 million nights booked, a 3.5% decline on last summer. Daytrippers actually increase in the province, however, particularly to hike and to cycle.
“Nearly one million cyclists in two months’ time confirms that cycling is synonymous with Limburg,” said Laura Olaerts of Visit Limburg. “With the heat that we are facing, it’s increasingly important to promote water recreation and forests.”
Ka-ching!
Finally, the biggest share of money spent in Ghent this summer by foreign tourists came from Americans. Whether this means there were more American tourists than other nationalities or that they simply spent more is unclear, but in any case, some 40% of expenditures recorded in Ghent were linked to American bank accounts. A distant second were Dutch tourists at 19%, followed by British tourists at 11%.
Looking at all of East Flanders, Americans also spent more than anyone else in Oudenaarde and in Aalst, though the Dutch outspent them in Sint-Niklaas. The figures come from Worldline and so do not include transactions that were not linked to Worldline payment terminals.

VW eyes defense deal with Israel’s Rafael for Osnabrueck plant: Report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
16:15:48 UTC
01:15:48 KST

German automaker Volkswagen is considering entering the defense industry through a potential agreement with Israeli company Rafael Advanced Defense Systems, according to media reports Friday.
An agreement involving VW’s plant in the northwestern city of Osnabrueck could be imminent, daily BILD reported.
The plan would involve manufacturing components for the Iron Dome air defense system at the Lower Saxony facility, including trucks, launchers and power generators, Bloomberg reported.
The Osnabrueck plant has been a key concern for VW management as the automaker restructures operations under a cost-cutting program. The T-Roc Cabrio is still produced at the site, but Europe’s largest automaker decided at the end of 2024 to phase out production there next year.
The future of the plant, which employs around 2,300 people, remains uncertain after production ends. The possibility of manufacturing defense components for Rafael at the site has reportedly been under discussion for months.
Major shareholder Qatar reportedly objects to plans
According to Bloomberg, however, VW major shareholder Qatar has raised objections to a partnership with an Israeli company.
The report said a potential solution could involve the state of Lower Saxony taking over parts of the Osnabrueck plant and subsequently establishing a joint venture with Rafael.
No decision has yet been made.
“We are currently examining whether—and in what form—a stake in a potential future industrial solution for the Osnabrück site could be considered,” Lower Saxony Prime Minister Olaf Lies said.
VW’s next supervisory board meeting is scheduled for Sept. 4, when a decision could potentially be made.
Daily Hannoversche Allgemeine Zeitung reported that the state could invest at least €200 million ($232 million) in the project.
“The specific structures of such a stake are currently still the subject of ongoing reviews and discussions,” a spokesperson for the prime minister said.
“As such, we cannot speculate at this time on either a specific stake amount or a particular investment model.”
Public broadcaster NDR reported as early as March that VW had also held talks with other companies, including German-French defense contractor KNDS.
Volkswagen undergoes restructuring program amid widespread criticism
Volkswagen has been grappling in recent years with sluggish demand, persistently high production costs in Germany, the negative impact of trade tensions with the US, and fierce competition from Chinese electric-vehicle makers.
Volkswagen CEO Oliver Blume had said in March that the company will stop manufacturing Volkswagen Group vehicles at Osnabruck starting in 2027 and confirmed talks with several defense firms about shifting the plant for military vehicles production. 
The proposal, since then, has sparked significant controversy within Germany. Volkswagen employees, peace activists and opposition politicians have criticized the plan, arguing the automaker should focus exclusively on civilian production.
The Osnabruck Peace Initiative (OFRI) has also organized multiple protests urging Volkswagen to abandon any defense contracts.
Germany’s opposition Left Party called Volkswagen’s planned cooperation with Israel’s state-owned Rafael Advanced Defense Systems “unacceptable,” citing the Netanyahu government’s ongoing military campaigns across the Middle East, accusing it of war crimes and genocide against Palestinians in Gaza.
Rafael, meanwhile, has been expanding its European footprint as governments across the continent boost defense spending and procurement following the war in Ukraine.
Although a US-brokered truce went into effect in the Gaza Strip last October, repeated Israeli truce violations have killed more than 1,300 Palestinians across the enclave.
More than 4,300 others were injured ever since. 
Hundreds of bodies of slain Palestinians, meanwhile, have been pulled from under the rubble of destroyed infrastructure.
According to Gaza’s Health Ministry, more than 73,000 Palestinians have been killed since Israel began its genocidal war on the coastal strip in October 2023.

Mongolia Hosts COP17, Urging Global Partners to Action on Climate Issues
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
16:15:00 UTC
01:15:00 KST

The 17th Conference of the Parties to the U.N Convention to Combat Desertification (UNCCD COP17) was convened in Ulaanbaatar from August 17-28, bringing together 196 country representatives plus the European Union to negotiate action-based measures on several climate challenges facing the world today. This year’s COP17 included segments on finance, water, land and people, and food systems. Parties agreed on a new initiative that includes $1.3 billion in financing, but failed to approve a new financial mechanism to combat drought.
On August 17, the opening ceremony was attended by Mongolian President Khurelsukh Ukhnaa, U.N. Deputy Secretary-General Amina J. Mohammed, Executive Secretary of the UNCCD Dr. Yasmin Fouad, Saudi Arabia’s Deputy Minister of Environment, Water and Agriculture (and president of UNCCD COP16) Dr. Osama Ibrahim Fakiha, and Mongolia’s Minister of Foreign Affairs Batmunkh Battsetseg. The global climate gathering also included a visit by South Korea’s former president, Moon Jae-in, and business leaders from Rio Tinto, Trade Development, Oyu Tolgoi, Asian Development Bank, Global Green Growth Institute, and more.
Welcoming the guests and opening the COP17 gathering, Mongolian Prime Minister Uchral Nyam-Osor stated: “The greatest change we want to see from COP17 is a shift from talk to action, from targets to implementation, and from commitments to measurable results.”
As Fouad, the UNCCD executive secretary, put it in an interview with The Diplomat before the gathering: “COP17 comes at a pivotal moment for global action on land… I believe countries will come to Mongolia with a shared understanding that the challenge is no longer understanding the problem – we know what is at stake. The priority now is implementation.”
In the last two weeks, the Mongolian government, civil society, and environmental organizations cooperated with global financial institutions, policymakers, businesses, and environmental scientists to advance solutions to emerging issues facing not just Mongolia but the globe, including desertification, drought, and land degradation. Building on the progress made at COP16 in Riyadh, governments at COP17 aimed to negotiate practical tools, partnerships, and financing mechanisms needed to help countries turn existing plans into action.
According to the UNCCD, more than 70 countries have now developed national drought plans, compared with only three in 2013 – reflecting growing recognition that drought must be managed proactively rather than only once it becomes a humanitarian and economic crisis.
Desertification, land degradation, and climate change are all interconnected and demand integrated solutions. In Mongolia, the challenge includes extreme climate fluctuations, such as dzud and drought, as well as loss of water, water pollution due to mining activities, as well as mismanagement of rangelands and pastoralism. The combination of these issues in turn becomes additional hindrance to the country’s development.
The last two days of COP17 were designated for all 197 parties to come to some sort of an agreement on a mechanism to combat drought. The Asian Development Bank Partnership estimated $355 billion is needed every year to combat land degradation and drought, yet current investment stands at only around $77 billion, leaving an annual financing gap of $278 billion.
Unfortunately, on August 28, last day of the COP17, parties failed to come to an agreement and passed the issue to the next COP gathering.
One of the main disagreements was whether to establish a new drought protocol initiated by the African Group. The bloc of developed countries – including the European Union, Australia, and the United Kingdom – opposed the establishment of a new drought protocol, preferring to utilize previously agreed multilateral frameworks such as Global Environment Facility and to avoid overlapping agreements.
While drought – and a financial mechanism to combat drought – posed a challenge for the 197 parties to negotiate, rangeland, pastoralism, and water deserve equal attention.
One of the most important segments of COP17 was the High-Level Ministerial Meeting and Finance Day, where delegates, multilateral banks, and participating organizations announce strategic commitments and financial mechanisms focusing on specific issues such as land restoration, rangeland preservation, and invigorating environmentally friendly, green growth.
At the High-Level Ministerial Meeting, Mongolia officially launched the global “Rangelands Flagship Initiative,” which focus on sustainable management and restoration of global pasture lands. The initiative was viewed as one of the most important outcomes of the climate gathering. It will bring together 45 projects across 23 countries, amounting to $1.3 billion in funding, making it the largest investment in the rangelands sector in the history of the UNCCD Convention.
The financial commitments will be assessed by the implementation of individual projects. Participating governments are expected to consider a new policy framework on rangelands and pastoralists designed to increase long-term investment in sustainable rangeland management and strengthen pastoral livelihoods. The initiative also mentioned the establishment of an Eurasian Center for Climate-Resilient Rangelands in Mongolia.
On August 24, Business for Land Forum and Finance Day brought together government, businesses, and investors looking to invest in regenerative landscapes. The Business Council of Mongolia and the UNCCD signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) to establish a Business4Land (B4L) platform and Mongolia Hub. The MoU “aims to link consumption, production, and finance through environmental and social standards, as well as financial products focused on preserving natural capital.”
Moreover, Mongolia also signed a Host Country Agreement (HCA) with Global Green Growth Institute to strengthen the legal and institutional framework for climate financing and augmenting investment environments for green projects.
The director of the Protected Areas Policy Department at Mongolia’s Ministry of Environment and Climate Change, Uranchimeg Tserendorj, stated that for the last 32 years, Mongolia’s Law on Protected Areas has protected land all around the country. The legal framework has allowed the country to protect “20.8 percent of land,” Uranchimeg said.
Mongolia is also seeking a deeper action-based cooperation with both UNCCD and the Ramsar Convention on Wetlands. Mongolia’s Environment and Climate Change Minister Sandag-Ochir Tsend met Ramsar Convention Secretary General Dr. Musonda Mumba, “proposing closer cooperation between the Ramsar Convention and U.N. Convention to Combat Desertification (UNCCD) during Mongolia’s COP17 presidency.”
At COP17, mining giants such as Rio Tinto announced their strategy to contribute to Mongolia’s fight against desertification, water pollution, and restoration of forestry by planting 5,000 hectares of forest, investing in renewable energy for company usage, as well as introducing new technology to replenish groundwater. According to the environmental manager of Oyu Tolgoi, one of Mongolia’s largest mining companies, the firm began paying water pollution fees in 2026, a regular quarterly payment of 150-200 million Mongolian tugrik (roughly $42,000 to $55,000). These practices meant to set an example for other mining giants operating in the country.
In the last two weeks, global partners gathered in Ulaanbaatar, Mongolia to discuss and negotiate an issue that has long been a focus for climate advocates. Mongolia’s hosting of the UNCCD COP17 is viewed as a step up in its global engagement and contribution and commitment to climate change. Considering the country’s own struggle with wetland loss, drought, rangeland and pastoral management, the platform urged global businesses, government, and civil society to take actions to help contribute solve these challenges.
Although the convention did not reach an agreement on solving drought, it has made progress in promoting and implementing global partnership in climate issues.

US judge questions but won't yet block Trump's new birthright citizenship order
GREENBELT, Maryland, Aug 28 - A federal judge on Friday declined to immediately block U.S. President Donald Trump's newest executive order limiting the number of people eligible for birthright citizenship, even as she sharply questioned its viability after the U.S. Supreme Court rejected his previous effort to do so.
U.S. District Judge Deborah Boardman in Greenbelt, Maryland, rejected a request for a temporary restraining order sought by immigrant rights advocates who had last year secured a ruling from her blocking the Trump administration from enforcing his initial 2025 executive order curtailing birthright citizenship.
Boardman, an appointee of Democratic President Joe Biden, said because the plaintiffs' lawsuit did not even mention Trump's 2026 order, she was unable to block it from being implemented at this time.
But she said she would allow the groups to supplement their complaint and set a swift briefing schedule for the plaintiffs to once again challenge the order, which "tries to strike out exceptions to birthright citizenship with the stroke of a pen."
"As far as I can tell, this is unprecedented," Boardman said.
The U.S. Supreme Court on June 30 rejected Trump's initial effort to end birthright citizenship for children whose parents were not American citizens or legal permanent residents, known as green card holders, finding it violated the citizenship clause of the U.S. Constitution's 14th Amendment.
Following that decision, Trump signed a new order on August 6 that took particular aim at "birth tourism," in which women travel to the United States to give birth so their children can obtain automatic citizenship.
Citizenship would also be denied to children whose parents work for foreign governments in the United States, engage in fraud to obtain citizenship, or are classified as "alien enemies."
After he signed that order, lawyers pursuing a class-action lawsuit on behalf of babies who would be deprived of citizenship under Trump's 2025 order asked Boardman to block enforcement of the Republican president's newest order and ensure their clients' citizenship continued to be honored.
U.S. Department of Justice attorneys opposed, noting federal agencies had yet to issue the necessary public guidance detailing how the president's directive would be implemented, which they are expected to do by September 5.
But Boardman at Friday's hearing expressed skepticism about waiting until then to consider the matter, as she questioned where in the Supreme Court's ruling "is there any reference to an exception for birthright citizenship for birth tourism?" REUTERS

Kenyan police fire tear gas at Nairobi protest against import duty hike
Traders frustrated by more than $5,000 duty hike they say will hurt small businesses.
Police in Kenya have fired tear gas at small-scale traders who are protesting against a hike in import duties, as hundreds of businesses closed in central Nairobi.
The demonstrations on Friday brought parts of the capital city to a standstill, with tear gas hurled at protesters frustrated with the rising cost of living and business expenses.

- list 3 of 4Seven people, mostly foreign tourists, killed in helicopter crash in Kenya

Kenya’s revenue authority says the higher import duty – which took effect last week – is designed to tackle the under-declaration and undervaluation of imported goods, which it said disadvantages compliant businesses and local manufacturers.
The duty change raises the minimum customs benchmark for a consolidated 40-foot (12-metre) container to 3.2 million Kenyan shillings ($24,700) from 2.5 million ($19,320) shillings.
The traders said the extra charges will drive up the cost of bringing goods into the country and hurt small businesses that rely on consolidated shipments to reduce import costs.
“We are standing for our citizenship and our right to do business and our right to build our future,” Muturi Kariuki, who joined the demonstrations, told the Reuters news agency.
Kariuki was among the traders who closed their businesses in order to protest, while others did so for safety reasons, according to traders.
Reporting for Al Jazeera from Nairobi, where traders were marching to parliament to get their message across, Malcolm Webb said the protests “come at a time where many Kenyans are frustrated with the rising cost of living, a feeling that they are being asked to give more, getting less in return”.
“There is deep mistrust in the government and a widespread perception that corruption is worse than ever,” he said.
Kenya’s revenue authority said the 3.2 million shilling figure was a minimum reference point, not a fixed value for every container. Importers whose goods exceed that value have to declare their actual worth and pay the applicable duties.

It would have come even without you asking, but before that must come accountability," he added.The letter comes at a time when reports suggest that the Srinagar MP is likely to resign from the Lok Sabha on November 3, coinciding with the death anniversary of his father Aga Syed Mehdi, who was assassinated by terrorists in an IED blast on November 3, 2000.

Fed Chairman Warsh expresses concern about inflation, advocates for 'quieter' central bank
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
16:11:51 UTC
01:11:51 KST

Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh expressed concern Friday about elevated inflation while hinting that interest rates could need to move higher if more progress isn't made on easing price pressures.
Warsh's closely watched remarks at the Fed's annual symposium in Jackson Hole, Wyoming, avoided committing either to forward guidance — or verbal cues about the Fed's intentions — or reaction function, the economic signals that would warrant an adjustment in rates.
However, he did acknowledge that inflation is running hot, saying, "while this summer's [inflation] readings were better than expected, they do not tell me that underlying trends have meaningfully improved."
"We must be confident that underlying inflation is moving to our objective, clearly and at sufficient speed. Otherwise, we have work to do. That's our job, our mandate and our charge to keep," he added.
Stock market indexes climbed after digesting the speech, delivered at 10 a.m. ET, while Treasury yields moved substantially higher. The policy-sensitive 2-year note soared nearly 8 basis points, or 0.08 percentage point, to 4.31%, its highest since late July.
Read Kevin Warsh's full speech at Jackson Hole
Traders also raised the probability for a rate hike at the September policy meeting to 55.7%, or about 20 percentage points higher than a day ago, according to the CME Group's FedWatch tool.
Warsh "opened the door to a Fed rate hike. A hike probably won't come in September, but it will by October or December," said Heather Long, chief economist at Navy Federal Credit Union. "Warsh explicitly said this summer's encouraging inflation readings don't indicate 'meaningful' improvement on inflation. Bond markets reacted swiftly by pricing in a hike."
Warsh noted that "market prices show confidence that we will deliver price stability. And I can assure you they're right."
Aside from the inflation concerns, which he said should be the Fed's primary focus, Warsh largely expressed confidence in the economy which he said "appears to have strengthened."
As he has done previously, the chairman cited benefits from artificial intelligence and said business and consumer spending has held up well. While acknowledging a slowdown in hiring, he attributed that to a flattening labor supply.
Warsh also used the speech to outline his philosophy on policymaking while carefully sidestepping any signals on what he thinks should be done to achieve the Fed's dual mandate of low inflation and full employment.
"I stand here today committed to a discipline, not to a decision," Warsh said in prepared remarks for a group that includes his fellow policymakers on the Federal Open Market Committee as well as economists and media members.
Responding to critics
The chairman has been criticized for being cagey about his approach to policy at a time when inflation continues to run well above the Fed's 2% goal. He has opposed the prior use of forward guidance as hand-holding for markets that should be interpreting data, not Fed rhetoric.
Early in the speech, titled "In Our Time," he quipped that, "You can call it an outline, you can call it a trail map, just don't call it forward guidance," a practice that he said "has overstayed its welcome."
However, the broader message was in seeking a change in approach to how the Fed sees its role with the market and the public.
Since taking office in May — Warsh noted that this is his 100th day in office — he has initiated five task forces to look at a variety of Fed functions. One overriding theme has been getting markets away from hinging on every word that comes from policymakers. He called for a "quieter Fed, more purposeful in its communications."
"The Fed plays an essential role in the economy and the markets. And our tools are powerful. We determine the path of short-term interest rates. And market participants will always try to anticipate what we will do next," he said. "But we should not indulge a regime in which market participants are looking primarily to the Fed for their next trade."
Warsh's speech differed from his predecessors, who often utilized Jackson Hole either as a cue on the direction of rates, broad changes to the Fed's framework, or to delineate new ways of approaching monetary policy. At last year's event, then-Chair Jerome Powell hinted at rate cuts ahead, setting off an aggressive rally on Wall Street.
No reaction function
In his brief time at the helm, Warsh has sought to chart a new course that harkens back to the pre-financial crisis Fed where markets were given less certain signals and the Fed had a smaller hand.
While market participants have adjusted to the lack of forward guidance, they have looked to Warsh at least to provide a reaction function on what would trigger a policy response. Even on that note, he was reluctant to commit.
"So, if forward guidance is ill-suited to normal times, then how about the new Fed chief commits—at the very least—to an explicit reaction function? Surely, he should tell us his interest rate path—if, say, the data were to come in hot or cold." he said, in seeming acknowledgement of the criticism. He specifically asked whether the Fed should provide a specific rule that it would follow.
Warsh, though, asserted that "our knowledge just doesn't extend that far—at least not yet—and the factors most relevant to the proper conduct of monetary policy change over time."
"In my term as Chairman, my colleagues and I will endeavor to construct more reliable models and more robust rules to guide policy decisions. We'll do this knowing that accuracy in economic forecasting is still just an aspiration. With so much changing so fast in geopolitics, global supply chains, and technology, it's wise to be modest about what we can and cannot know," he said.
Warsh did not mention in the speech the recent announcement from Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent of accelerated buybacks of government debt, a move that seems contrary to the Fed chair's desire for less government involvement in markets.

EXPLAINER – What will change for teens after Meta’s landmark settlement?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
16:10:03 UTC
01:10:03 KST

Meta agreed Wednesday to pay up to $18 billion and introduce new restrictions for teenage Facebook and Instagram users to settle lawsuits alleging that it deliberately designed the platforms to addict children and contributed to mental health problems.
The agreement with nearly all US states and several territories ends a major federal trial and resolves other state cases, while potentially establishing a model for future settlements involving TikTok, YouTube and Snapchat.
What was case about?
The states accused Meta of using features such as infinite scrolling, constant notifications, visible “like” counts and personalized recommendations to keep children online longer and increase advertising revenue.
They alleged that Meta knew its products could harm young users’ mental health but misled parents and the public about their safety.
The claims went beyond harmful posts uploaded by users. They also targeted how Facebook and Instagram were designed and how Meta’s systems selected, presented and promoted content to children.
The states alleged that these systems could expose young people to material promoting eating disorders, self-harm and suicide.
Meta rejected the allegations and maintained that it had invested heavily in protections for young users. It also argued that social media addiction was not a formally recognized psychiatric condition.
The settlement ended the trial without a verdict. Meta did not admit wrongdoing, meaning the agreement does not amount to a court finding that the company violated the law.
Four states involved in the federal trial — California, Colorado, Kentucky and New Jersey — had been expected to seek nearly $200 billion in penalties.
Under the broader settlement, Meta will make guaranteed payments of about $12.7 billion over 10 years, with another $5.3 billion contingent on whether other major platforms adopt similar protections and meet related payment conditions.
What will change for teens?
Users under 18 in participating US states and territories will face a combined two-hour daily limit across Facebook and Instagram. Parents will be able to authorize additional time, while direct messages will not count toward the limit.
Most parts of the platforms, including feeds, Stories, Explore and Reels, will be blocked by default between midnight and 6 am, although messaging will remain available.
Most push notifications will be silenced from 10 pm to 7 am and during school hours, from 8 am to 3 pm on weekdays during the school year.
Meta will introduce “productive pauses” after 15 minutes of continuous use, along with additional reminders when combined daily use reaches 60 and 90 minutes.
Visible “like” and reaction counts will be hidden for teens by default. Meta will also maintain its ban on cosmetic surgery filters and extend the restriction to what it calls “extreme makeup” filters.
The company will continue to strengthen restrictions on content related to bullying, eating disorders, suicide and self-harm.
Parental controls will also be expanded, with parents receiving information about secondary accounts and attempts to change protective settings.
Meta will introduce stronger age-verification measures to identify young users who falsely register as adults.
Yet the agreement leaves a central question unresolved: whether reducing time online is enough when the systems determining what young people see remain largely intact.
Will Meta change its algorithms?
The settlement does not require Meta to abandon personalized recommendations, targeted advertising or the algorithms underlying its main feeds.
Teenagers will, however, be able to choose a non-personalized chronological feed showing posts from accounts they follow. Parents using Meta’s supervision tools will also be able to make that feed the default for their children.
Teens can disable autoplay, while parents can require it to remain turned off.
Critics argue that leaving personalized recommendation systems largely intact means a central driver of engagement and exposure to potentially harmful content remains unaddressed.
The agreement therefore gives families greater control over recommendations without fundamentally changing Meta’s algorithm-driven business model.
Why is settlement considered landmark?
The case challenges the long-standing argument that social media companies merely provide platforms and that users alone are responsible for how they use them.
By imposing restrictions on engagement features, the settlement establishes that platform design can be subject to legal safeguards when children are involved, even though Meta has not admitted causing harm.
The agreement addresses both how long teenagers spend on social media and some of the content and design features they encounter online.
Its financial scale is also significant, with Meta agreeing to pay at least $12.7 billion and potentially up to $18 billion over 10 years.
Most terms will remain in effect for 10 years, while an independent auditor will review Meta’s compliance annually for five years and report to participating states.
What could it mean for TikTok, YouTube and Snapchat?
The settlement is structured to encourage other major platforms to adopt similar restrictions.
About $5.3 billion of Meta’s potential $18 billion payment is contingent on industry-wide adoption of comparable safeguards and related payments by TikTok and YouTube.
If Snap, TikTok and YouTube adopt comparable protections, Meta’s two-hour combined daily limit would be replaced by a 60-minute limit on each of its platforms, while nighttime restrictions would expand from midnight-6 am to 10 pm-7 am.
The agreement does not automatically bind the other companies, which continue to face lawsuits and regulatory pressure over their treatment of young users.
However, it gives states a framework they could seek to apply in future settlements and increases pressure on social media companies to accept greater responsibility for the design of products used by children.
The settlement is therefore unlikely to end the debate over teen safety online. Its broader significance will depend on whether the restrictions prove effective and whether competing platforms adopt similar protections.

Marine engineering centre planned for Clyde dry dock site

Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
17:09:30 BST
01:09:30 KST

Plans for a marine engineering centre of excellence at Inchgreen in Inverclyde have taken a step forward with a partnership agreement between the local council, the National Manufacturing Institute Scotland and West College Scotland, Inverclyde Council stated.
A memorandum of understanding signed by the three parties commits them to developing a full business case for the centre, which would then be submitted to the UK Government. The proposed hub could draw on £20 million of UK Government funding announced in December 2025, subject to that case being developed and approved.
The intention is to build an innovation and training centre providing research capacity for businesses on the site while feeding trained people directly into skilled jobs there. Potential areas of focus include marine robotics, naval architecture, plating and welding, and the proposals will explore how the centre could support defence as well as net zero work.
Councillor Stephen McCabe, leader of Inverclyde Council, said: “This is an important step in the ongoing evolution of Inchgreen and the development of a new marine engineering centre of excellence. Inchgreen has huge potential and we’re delighted to be collaborating with NMIS and West College Scotland to help us to unlock that potential by creating an environment where people can be trained and then move into quality jobs all at the same location.”
Chris Courtney, chief executive of NMIS, said: “Working in partnership with Inverclyde Council, West College Scotland and industry, we have a brilliant opportunity to create a distinctive centre of excellence that builds on Inverclyde’s strengths and supports growth and high-quality jobs.
“Together, we can connect manufacturing and engineering innovation with education and skills, helping businesses strengthen and scale while creating opportunities for people to build rewarding careers and contribute to a bright industrial future for the region.”
Anne Campbell, principal of West College Scotland, said: “As an anchor institution within the region, West College Scotland is committed to responding to the needs of our communities, employers and key industries. Through this partnership, we will combine skills, innovation and industry expertise to create new opportunities for learners, support economic growth and help build the highly skilled workforce needed for the future of Scotland’s marine and engineering sectors.”
The involvement of the two institutions is intended to open routes for young people in the area from apprenticeships through to PhD level.
The Inchgreen site consists of a marine park and a dry dock, the latter among the largest in the United Kingdom and a facility that has drawn periodic interest as a location for ship repair and offshore renewables work. An £11 million upgrade of the marine park was completed in March 2025, funded by an £8.4 million Glasgow City Region City Deal grant alongside £1.36 million each from Inverclyde Council and the Scottish Government, the latter drawn from the Clyde Mission Fund for refurbishment of the Platers Shed. A second phase using £3 million of City Region funding was approved earlier this year, covering berthing and quay wall improvements and the purchase of the adjacent former St Mungo’s Church site.
NMIS is headquartered in Renfrewshire within the Advanced Manufacturing Innovation District Scotland, is operated by the University of Strathclyde and forms part of the High Value Manufacturing Catapult.
First Minister John Swinney also toured Inchgreen dock on 24 August during a series of engagements across Inverclyde, alongside visits to Ferguson Marine, CalMac and CMAL, saying the area has a proud heritage as an industrial powerhouse and strong foundations for growth, and that the Scottish Government is working with the council and local partners to attract investment and create jobs.
Martin McCluskey, the Labour MP for Inverclyde and Renfrewshire West, attended the partnership announcement alongside Councillor McCabe and the two institution heads.

Belgium is one of the major gateways for drugs being smuggled into Europe, with the mammoth port of Antwerp serving as a key entry point for criminal gangs.
In recent years, there has been an increase in armed violence related to conflicts between gangs.
Belgian authorities have been active in trying to go after the revenues of the gangs.
Moinil said that some 350 bars and restaurants in Brussels had been closed over ties to the drug trade since 2025, and that 3,500 luxury vehicles had been seized. AFP

America's midterm fight intensifies as Democrats, Republicans lock in November contenders
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
16:03:46 UTC
01:03:46 KST

Washington, DC — Sixty-six days remain before Americans vote in the crucial 2026 midterms, and Republicans hold narrow majorities in both chambers, leaving control of Congress closely contested.
In the House of Representatives, the GOP holds 219 seats to Democrats' 213, with three vacancies still unfilled. In the Senate, it's 53-45, though two independents who caucus with Democrats narrow that gap to 47.
Democrats need just three more House seats and four more Senate seats to flip both chambers.
The numbers tell a nervous story for Republicans.
Democrats lead by 6.4 points on the generic congressional ballot, according to the RealClearPolitics average, a gap wide enough historically to sweep dozens of seats.
The Senate map still favours Republicans on paper: most of the competitive seats sit in territory Trump won comfortably. Several races, however, have become more competitive.
The nonpartisan Cook Political Report moved both Texas and Iowa from "lean Republican" into the toss-up column, pointing to Republican candidate Ken Paxton's approval numbers in Texas and rising fertiliser prices squeezing Iowa's farmers.
The House looks no calmer. Mid-decade redistricting has shrunk the number of genuinely competitive districts, but what's left is bracing for a fight.
Money is pouring in to match the stakes. Corporate donors have funnelled a record $646M into US political campaigns over the 18 months through June, a 40 percent jump on the entire 2024 presidential cycle, according to watchdog group Public Citizen.
In a Michigan swing district just north of Detroit, Democratic congressional candidate Christina Hines said voters are far more worried about affording fuel, groceries and healthcare than about left-wing politicians gaining ground in her party.
“It costs me $73 to fill up our minivan right now," she said. "This is just not acceptable for working families.”
Some 600 miles away, radical politics is exactly what Republican Representative Mike Lawler wants to talk about in his New York battleground district.
He said the Democratic Socialists of America “is going to be a big issue, in part because that’s the platform that Democrats are running on.”
A transition is underway over these final days of summer as Democrats and Republicans push past internal fights.
Specifically, Democrats are working to refocus on the economy, which voters say is their top concern as the cost of everyday goods remains high, even though inflation has fallen from the peak of Democratic President Joe Biden's term.
Republicans, meanwhile, are seeking to keep the focus on Democrats' lurch to the left, warning about socialism.
GOP talking points
Republican strategist David Urban, a Trump ally, acknowledged that the message “has limits.”
“Right now I think people see the war as a drag on the economy and therefore they don’t like it,” Urban said, warning that the road ahead for the Republican Party may be painful.
The word “gasoline” is mentioned only one time across more than a dozen separate talking points released by the Republican National Committee this month, according to documents reviewed by The Associated Press.
Pertinently, the average price of gasoline in the US was $4.18 last week, the fifth consecutive week that national gas prices exceeded $4.
The talking points place the blame for high costs on Biden administration.
“President Trump is fixing what Biden broke,” they say.
Meanwhile, the word “Democrat” is cited 73 times in this month’s RNC talking points.
US Vice President JD Vance briefly addressed affordability during a visit to Ohio last week, pointing to homeownership as a key concern for young Americans.
“We got a lot of work to do, but we’re finally seeing that American dream of homeownership become accessible again to our young people,” he said.
Vance targeted the rise of Democratic socialists.
“If these radicals take control of Congress, they’re going to pass the craziest agenda America has ever seen,” the vice president said.
Ideological fractures among Democrats 
Some Democratic officials worry that the rise of democratic socialists within the party presents a political problem for candidates in swing districts.
At least eight DSA members or DSA-backed candidates secured Democratic nominations for Congress this primary season.
That includes seven for the House, as well as Democratic Senate nominee Angie Nixon in Florida.
While such candidates represent only a fraction of the 257 seats Democrats currently hold in Washington, Democrats know they cannot ignore the issue altogether.
The Democratic Socialists of America are still far from a household name for most voters.
Only about 2 in 10 US adults had a favourable view of the DSA, according to a CNN/SSRS poll conducted in July, while about one-third had an unfavourable opinion and the rest have not heard of the organisation or do not have an opinion.
About 7 in 10 Democrats or people who lean toward the Democratic Party said they would feel “enthusiastic” or “okay” about their party nominating a candidate who describes themselves as a democratic socialist.
The countdown starts
The clock now shifts from message testing to ballot casting.
Mail voting opens in 17 states and Washington, DC, in the second half of September, with the rest of the country following in October.
In-person early voting starts even sooner, with Minnesota and South Dakota opening polling stations on September 18, 46 days before Election Day.
Congress will barely be in Washington to watch it happen. Both chambers are scheduled to be out of session for nearly all of October and into the first week of November, a deliberate blackout that sends lawmakers home to campaign as the count begins.
What voters will be thinking about as they fill out those ballots looks settled for now: the economy, prices, and Trump's approval rating, layered over legal fights about voting rules that neither party shows signs of dropping.
The House remains close because there simply aren't many competitive districts left to fight over, a legacy of redistricting.
The Senate comes down to a handful of toss-up races.
In the end, these crucial midterms will be decided by two groups that pollsters can barely measure: people who have not made up their minds yet, and people who might not bother showing up at all.

China Focus: China adopts new law to strengthen healthcare security
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-29
00:02:34 CST
01:02:34 KST

BEIJING, Aug. 28 (Xinhua) -- Chinese lawmakers on Friday voted to adopt a new law on healthcare security to improve healthcare services and strengthen the country's healthcare security system.
The law, passed at a session of the Standing Committee of the National People's Congress, will take effect on Jan. 1, 2027.
Consisting of 56 articles in seven chapters, the law covers the healthcare security system, healthcare security funds and services, supervision and administration, and legal liability.
The legislation is part of efforts to implement the country's health-first strategy and advance the Healthy China initiative, according to the new law, which also states that the level of healthcare security should be commensurate with the level of economic and social development.
The draft healthcare security law has undergone three rounds of review by the NPC Standing Committee, with the first in June last year and the second in April this year.
IMPROVED SYSTEM
The 2010 Social Insurance Law and the 2014 interim measures for social assistance contain provisions on basic medical insurance, maternity insurance and medical assistance, with further reforms following amid economic and social development.
Experts noted that a healthcare security law is needed to keep up with the healthcare security system reform and address problems such as fragmented regulations and a lack of integration.
"A multi-tiered healthcare security system for all shall be established and improved, with basic medical insurance as its mainstay," the new law reads, adding that the basic medical insurance consists of schemes both for urban workers and for rural and non-working urban residents.
The law stipulates that basic medical insurance shall provide fair and appropriate benefit coverage for insured people, while encouraging the development of commercial health insurance, healthcare-related charitable donations and medical mutual-aid programs to meet diverse healthcare security needs.
The law also has a dedicated chapter on healthcare security services, specifying provisions for a sound public service system and a standardized list of public services.
China has built the world's largest basic healthcare security network, with more than 1.33 billion people covered by basic medical insurance as of the end of 2025, according to official data.
SUPPORT FOR AGING, BALANCED POPULATION DEVELOPMENT
To address population aging and shore up weaknesses in the social security system, the law specifies that a long-term care insurance system should be established and improved.
Long-term care insurance is a social insurance program that provides services or financial support for basic daily care and related medical nursing for people who have lost some or all of their ability to care for themselves. By the end of 2025, this insurance had covered 308.55 million people, with 1.93 million benefiting from it.
The scheme is a priority in the country's five-year plan to improve medical security. At the end of 2025, the country had 323.38 million people aged 60 or above, accounting for 23 percent of its population. The figure is projected to exceed 400 million around 2035.
Lou Yu, a professor at China University of Political Science and Law, said the growing number of elderly people with disabilities has led to increasing demand for long-term care, while existing medical insurance mainly covers expenses related to medical treatment.
"Writing long-term care insurance into law will turn years of local pilot experience into a statutory system and help meet the care needs of people with disabilities, extending the coverage of the healthcare security system," Lou said.
To promote balanced population development over the long term, the law stipulates that the country shall improve the maternity insurance system and steadily expand its coverage.
The law, for the first time, specifies that the maternity insurance fund and the basic medical insurance fund for employees should be merged into a single accounting system.
Experts noted that the two types of insurance have similar arrangements in terms of enrollment, financing, administration and benefits, and that unified accounting will help address fragmentation in the social insurance system, making enrollment more convenient without reducing benefits. ■

====================================================================================================

The gender gap in politics is not widening as much as you think
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
16:00:32 UTC
01:00:32 KST

Despite popular narratives about a widening political divide between men and women, the gender gap on most social and cultural issues has remained relatively stable over the past two decades. A recent analysis of public opinion data reveals that while men and women often hold different views, their attitudes shift in parallel in response to current events. The research was published in Social Science Quarterly.
Researchers have tracked differences in political attitudes between men and women for over half a century. Women typically show higher support for social welfare and environmental protection, a trend often linked to socialization around caregiving and economic vulnerability. On the other hand, differences between the sexes are often smaller or less predictable on morality issues like abortion or immigration.
Some scholars suggest that younger, more egalitarian generations are driving a wedge between the sexes as they replace older generations. This type of generational change is known as a cohort effect. It happens when a specific age group develops distinct attitudes during their formative years and carries those views throughout their lives. As older generations pass away and younger ones enter the electorate, the overall public opinion shifts.
Alternatively, changes in public opinion might stem from period effects. These are widespread shifts in attitudes caused by historical events, such as a major economic recession or a global pandemic, which influence people of all ages at the same time. Political scientists April K. Clark of Northern Illinois University, Izabelle P. Chick and Juliet E. Carlisle of the University of Utah, and Eric R. A. N. Smith of the University of California, Santa Barbara, designed a study to see which of these two forces actually shapes the gender gap.
The research team analyzed data from the Gallup Poll Social Series. They looked at national surveys conducted annually between 2000 and 2024. The researchers organized responses to ten specific social and cultural issues into three distinct categories.
The first category focused on care and social protection, which included issues like hunger and homelessness, crime and violence, drug use, and healthcare access. The second category covered social stability and societal change, encompassing race relations, illegal immigration, and the quality of the environment. For these first two categories, respondents were asked to rate how much they personally worried about each problem.
The final category centered on morality and rights conflicts, specifically abortion policies, gun laws, and LGBTQ+ acceptance. For this category, respondents rated their level of satisfaction with the nation’s policies or social climate.
Using a statistical technique known as cross-classified random effects modeling, the researchers evaluated how opinions changed over time. This approach allowed them to separate the influence of a person’s birth year from the specific year they took the survey. In doing so, they could isolate whether generational replacement or time-specific events were responsible for shifts in public opinion. They also accounted for individual demographic factors like educational attainment, income, race, marital status, and political ideology.
Across nearly all the issues studied, the researchers found that period effects accounted for a large share of the variation in attitudes. When major national events occurred, the opinions of both men and women shifted in the same direction. Generational differences, or cohort effects, played a much smaller and less consistent role in changing public opinion.
Women consistently expressed higher levels of worry than men regarding care and social protection issues, such as hunger, homelessness, and healthcare. Yet, when concern spiked, as it did during the 2008 economic recession and the COVID-19 pandemic, it spiked for both sexes equally. Following these peaks, worry generally decreased for both groups. Because men and women responded to these external shocks similarly, the overall distance between their opinions barely changed.
The researchers observed similar parallel movements on issues of crime and drug use. Concern about both topics has generally declined since the early 2000s among all respondents. This downward trend aligns with documented drops in actual crime rates over the same period.
Similar patterns emerged in the other categories. Men and women showed comparable levels of concern regarding race relations and illegal immigration. Their views on these topics rose and fell together over the last two decades. The fluctuations regarding race relations likely reflect heightened public awareness in response to specific cultural moments, such as the Black Lives Matter movement. While the researchers noted a slight gap regarding the environment, with women expressing more worry, the two groups experienced parallel increases in concern in recent years.
On matters of morality and rights, satisfaction levels fluctuated in tandem for both sexes. Satisfaction with the nation’s abortion policies and gun laws has generally declined since the early 2000s for all respondents. Decreased satisfaction with gun policies in the early 2010s, for instance, aligns with the public outcry following the 2012 Sandy Hook school shooting. On the other hand, satisfaction with LGBTQ+ acceptance grew steadily among both men and women throughout the study period.
The findings indicate that the idea of a growing culture war strictly divided by gender might be inaccurate. Instead of drifting apart into separate ideological camps, men and women appear to process and react to national events in similar ways. Broad social, economic, and political developments shape public opinion much more than any gender-specific divergence.
The study has certain boundaries. The data analysis begins in 2000, meaning it does not capture earlier decades when foundational shifts in gender roles and partisan alignments first occurred. Because the observed opinion shifts are primarily driven by current events rather than permanent generational changes, today’s trends might not predict future public opinion. An economic downturn, a major court decision, or a large policy shift could alter the current trajectory of these attitudes.
Future studies might expand the timeline to include earlier decades and incorporate more specific data on how factors like race, class, and geography interact with gender. Examining differences among women or among men, such as comparing married and unmarried individuals, could provide a more detailed picture of how political attitudes form in the United States.
The study, “Generational Shifts and Gendered Divides: Exploring Attitudes on Social, Cultural, and Political Issues in the United States,” was authored by April K. Clark, Izabelle P. Chick, Juliet E. Carlisle, and Eric R. A. N. Smith.
