UNCCD conference in Mongolia set the stage for enhanced global drought resilience with innovative initiatives.
NEW DELHI: The seventeenth session of the United Nations Convention to Combat Desertification (UNCCD) conference concluded in Ulaanbaatar, Mongolia, on Friday by presenting a new global architecture for drought resilience that will help countries bridge the gap between plans and implementation.Multiple new initiatives were announced during the 12-day conference (COP17). They include $1.3 billion in new and pipeline finance for land restoration and strengthening drought resilience in vulnerable countries.These initiatives — the world’s first Drought Resilience Index (DRI) and the Drought Resilience Investment Facility (DRIF) — will help countries in assessing their capacity to anticipate, prepare for and adapt to drought, and unlock much larger flows of institutional and private finance for projects that strengthen water security, sustainable agriculture, nature-based solutions and land restoration.DRI’s technical monitoring metrics will enable countries to identify vulnerabilities and inform more effective policies and investments. Its new AI-powered features can help policymakers, technical experts and the public interpret complex data and turn it into practical insights.
DRIF, on the other hand, aims to mobilise up to $400 million in public and private capital for drought resilience. The facility, launched by UNCCD and Luxembourg, will use public capital to reduce investment risks.
“We came to Ulaanbaatar saying that COP17 must be a COP of implementation. We leave with more of the architecture needed to make that possible: political decisions, stronger science, innovative financing mechanisms, investment pipelines and partnerships that can move solutions to scale,” said UNCCD executive secretary Yasmine Fouad.The conference took place against a stark global backdrop as up to 40 percent of the world’s land is degraded, while countries have committed to restoring more than one billion hectares, including 26 million hectares by India, by 2030. India was represented by a team led by Union environment minister Bhupender Yadav at COP17.
Vishwa Mohan is Senior Editor at The Times of India. He writes on environment, climate change, agriculture, water resources and clean energy, tracking policy issues and climate diplomacy. He has been covering Parliament since 2003 to see how politics shaped up domestic policy and India’s position at global platform. Before switching over to explore sustainable development issues, Vishwa had covered internal security and investigative agencies for more than a decade.

helen & hard revives viking boatbuilding with whole-tree cabin on norway’s atlantic coast
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
15:45:05 UTC
00:45:05 KST

On a rocky headland in Randaberg, Norway, 18 whole spruce trees rise through Helen & Hard’s Cabin Sande, their root systems branching across the ceiling where columns meet beams. Studio founders Reinhard Kropf and Siv Helene Stangeland built the 112-square-meter retreat as their own cabin after twelve years of sketching and refinement. It replaces a 1970s cabin on the same site, where local planning restrictions required the replacement to stay within the earlier footprint and height. From outside, the low form sits close to the rock. Inside, the trees give the home its structure and much of its character.
Helen & Hard looked to Norwegian boatbuilding traditions dating back to the Viking Age for those junctions. Shipbuilders used naturally curved sections where trunk meets root to strengthen the ribs of wooden vessels. For Cabin Sande, each spruce was excavated with its roots intact, cleaned and air-dried for eight months before being scanned. Digital models mapped the irregular forms, then robots milled fitted joints directly from the roots so each tree could work within the column-and-beam system.
Four rows of columns spread across Helen & Hard’s Cabin Sande in a fan-shaped formation, which opens the main room toward the western horizon. Cantilevered roof beams meet in pairs above the space and span a horizontal opening more than nine meters wide toward the Atlantic, leaving the sea view uninterrupted. At the opposite end, the plan narrows toward an entrance facing the garden and morning sun. A long sightline runs straight through the cabin, with vegetation at one end and open water at the other.
The roof projects beyond the glazing to shelter the interior from the Atlantic weather, while concealed tension cables and springs help support the cantilever. Continuous glass wraps much of the perimeter, so changing light and coastal conditions stay visible from across the room. Below, a stone plinth uses rock found on the site, while the planted roof follows the surrounding topography and keeps the building low against the headland.
Cabin Sande sits on a rocky headland overlooking Norway’s Atlantic coast
the timber frame becomes the interior
The main living area occupies the broad center of the plan, with the kitchen along one side and two workspaces along the other. One workspace rises half a level above the bathroom, giving the compact interior a shift in section without breaking up the larger room. The spruce structure continues into bookshelves and benches, then into room dividers and window frames. Columns and built-ins share the same timber language, so the cabin reads as one continuous piece of construction instead of a frame filled later with separate furniture.
Closer to the sea, the broad glass opening pulls the horizon deep into the room. Along the side zones, branching timber creates smaller places for sitting and working while the central space stays open toward the water. The root forms remain visibly irregular after robotic milling, keeping each tree legible in the finished cabin. Digital fabrication works here by accepting those irregularities: the scans make each joint precise while the structure still reads as eighteen individual trees.

Algeria battles scores of wildfires that have killed 12, injured dozens

Yakoota Al Ahmad and Lina Altawell
28 August 2026•Update: 28 August 2026
Sixty-four wildfires were still burning across 10 Algerian provinces on Friday, most of them in the eastern Jijel province, after authorities extinguished 110 out of 174 fires that erupted nationwide over the past 24 hours.
According to a statement by the General Directorate of Civil Protection, Jijel topped the list of provinces for ongoing fires with 20, followed by Skikda with 14, El Tarf near the Tunisian border with 10, Guelma with six, Annaba with five, and Bejaia with four.
Bouira, meanwhile, is still contending with two fires, while Tebessa, Constantine and Mila are still battling one each.
Emergency teams have continued efforts to extinguish the blazes with aerial support from BE-200 military aircraft, AT-802 firefighting aircraft and Mi-26 helicopters.
Areas where firefighting efforts remain underway include Taxenna, Ziama Mansouriah, El Milia, Ouled Yahia Khedrouche and Chekfa in Jijel, along with areas in Skikda, El Tarf and Annaba.
12 killed, 54 injured
The spate of fires that erupted Wednesday has killed 12 people to date -- five in Jijel, four in Bejaia and three in Tizi Ouzou, according to Interior Minister Said Sayoud.
Another 54 people have sustained injuries, including six in critical condition, the minister said.
On Thursday, Algerian President Abdelmadjid Tebboune declared three days of national mourning, ordering flags to be flown at half-staff in honor of the victims.
On the same day, Prime Minister Sifi Ghrieb traveled to Jijel to oversee firefighting efforts and visit the injured and local residents in affected areas.
The fires come amid a severe heat wave affecting North Africa, where authorities say they have mobilized land and air resources with a view to protecting lives and property.
On Tuesday, Algeria’s meteorological service warned of an anticipated heat wave in several provinces this week, with temperatures forecast to reach 49C in some areas.
According to Civil Protection data, around 4,000 fires were recorded in the period from May 1 to July 20, compared with 1,501 during the same period last year, representing an increase of nearly 167 percent.

Alleged Narco-Terrorist Moves to Toss U.S. Indictment on Jurisdictional Grounds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
15:42:00 UTC
00:42:00 KST

Reported by
Attorneys for the accused South American drug kingpin Sebastián Marset have filed motions to dismiss all drug trafficking, money laundering, and narco-terrorism charges against him, challenging the U.S. government’s authority to prosecute the case.
Marset is seeking a complete dismissal of the indictment, alleging that agents of the Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA) interrogated him without advising him of his Miranda rights, denied him access to counsel, and brought vindictive charges after he rejected a plea deal. His defense team has also filed motions accusing DEA agents of attempting to extort cryptocurrency from him.
However, Marset’s primary defense rests on a novel jurisdictional argument. His lawyers contend that the United States lacks the authority to prosecute him because the alleged offenses took place outside the country. Prosecutors accuse Marset of leading a massive cartel that shipped cocaine from South America to Europe, with illicit proceeds allegedly wired back to South America through banks in Hong Kong and China.
According to court filings, federal jurisdiction hinges on a single financial transaction. Prosecutors allege that one wire transfer - sent from a Chinese bank to a Portuguese account by Marset's alleged co-conspirator, Federico Ezequiel Santoro Vassallo - routed through a U.S. correspondent bank server located in Richmond, Virginia. Santoro has since pleaded guilty and is cooperating with prosecutors.
Marset’s lead attorney, Robert Feitel, argues that a single automated server transfer is insufficient to establish U.S. jurisdiction, noting that Marset was never physically in Virginia, did not initiate the wire, and could not have known the money would pass through a local server.
“This is the most egregious effort I’ve seen from the United States to assert jurisdiction over things that have nothing to do with them at all,” Feitel, a former federal prosecutor, told OCCRP, adding that he would never have brought charges in Virginia on such grounds. “One transaction, according to the government, came through a Virginia server. We’re talking about one transaction out of 203.”
Marset faces a steep legal battle given the expansive reach U.S. courts typically exercise over international cases with even minimal domestic touchpoints. The U.S. government previously offered a $2 million reward for his capture, and the presiding judge recently denied his request for private visits with his Uruguayan attorney. Still, his defense team remains steadfast.
“To the extent that this case appears to be the first of its kind, it’s because no one else had the temerity” to charge someone based on these facts, Feitel told OCCRP.

The Bigger Bet Behind Nvidia’s $12.9 Billion Hugging Face Deal
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
15:41:00 UTC
00:41:00 KST

Nvidia has reportedly agreed to buy popular AI library Hugging Face for $12.9 billion. The deal is partly a hedge against an emerging threat: AI companies which consume enormous quantities of Nvidia hardware are increasingly developing chips of their own. In a future where AI becomes centralized in a small group of players with their own chips, those companies could demand lower prices from Nvidia or bypass it altogether.
Hugging Face, an online hub where developers share open AI models and datasets, gives Nvidia a stake in an alternative future, where downloadable AI models allow startups and governments to build systems of their own. Few would have the scale to develop custom chips. (Nvidia and Hugging Face did not respond for comment.)
With roughly 85% of the AI chip market, Nvidia’s share has only one way to go. But a smaller slice of a much larger market could still mean more sales, says Umesh Padval, a Managing Partner at Seligman Ventures. “If the deal goes through, I think it’s a brilliant chess move.”
Nvidia has thrown its weight behind open-source AI in recent months. It successfully lobbied Washington to loosen restrictions on selling its chips to China, which leads in open AI development. More recently, it struck a $6 billion deal with Poolside, to develop an American open alternative. In July, Nvidia helped lead an open letter defending open-source AI and urging Washington not to restrict it. “Open models strengthen safety and cybersecurity, accelerate innovation and diffusion, and enable sovereignty,” Nvidia boss Jensen Huang wrote in his first post on X.
Meanwhile, Google now exclusively uses its custom TPU chips to train its Gemini AI models. In August, Anthropic hired, Amir Salek, a former TPU team-lead at Google to spearhead a new in-house chip division. The same month, OpenAI shared the first results from its custom chip, Jalapeño. SemiAnalysis, the firm which conducted tests on OpenAI’s chip, said it beat “every Nvidia, AMD, and Google chip we have been able to test.”
“There’s kind of this two-way strategic battle,” says Richard Clode, a technology portfolio manager at Janus Henderson. “On the one hand, Nvidia doesn’t want to be reliant on just three customers, so [it] is deliberately trying, with financing and allocation of chips, [to] encourage other players and neo-clouds. And then vice versa, those hyperscalers don’t want to be completely reliant on just one compute provider.”
Nvidia’s 75% margin means that other firms’ in-house chips do not need to match its performance to save large customers money. Custom silicon has other benefits, too. Nvidia has previously given smaller cloud providers early access to its newest chips, ensuring that the largest players do not dominate supply. Developing chips in-house reduces exposure to those allocations, Clode says, while allowing AI companies to tailor hardware to their specific workloads.
AI companies are not developing these chips completely alone. Google, OpenAI, and Meta have partnered with Broadcom to help turn their specifications into custom silicon.
Those efforts are yet to make a dent in Nvidia’s bottom line. In August, Nvidia reported a blockbuster earnings report with record revenue of $96.2 billion, more than doubling year-over-year and beating Wall Street expectations. Companies like Google and OpenAI continue to buy large quantities even as they develop alternatives. They’ve “poured a lot of infrastructure capex into the existing infrastructure,” says Sriram Viswanathan, a founding managing partner at Celesta Capital and a former Intel executive. Moving to a different architecture, he said, is “a huge lift-and-pour-concrete situation. So I think it’s going to happen over a period of time, but not in one fell swoop.”
He points to Apple as a warning. Apple first developed chips for the iPad and iPhone while continuing to buy Intel processors for Macs. As its expertise matured, its silicon moved into Mac computers and Intel was cut out.
“Nvidia is executing like crazy, so in some ways it’s theirs to lose,” says Sean Lie, co-founder and chief technology officer at AI chip company Cerebras. “But I think we’re seeing a lot of cracks in that armor.”

Tim Cook’s Dark Legacy in China
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
15:41:00 UTC
00:41:00 KST

On September 1, 2026, Tim Cook will hand over control of Apple to John Ternus. He leaves behind one of the most efficient manufacturing systems in consumer electronics, one he helped build as operations chief from 1998.
In China, Cook leaves a second, but related, legacy: workers on Apple lines toiling 60 hours a week or more, often without a rest day and depending on overtime to cover the basic cost of living.
Ternus will have to decide how to handle both of these realities.
At China Labor Watch, we just completed a new investigation into Apple’s supply chains in China. Our conclusion is not simply that Apple’s compliance system fails to prevent violations. Many of the labor conditions that the report identified are baked into the production model itself.
I once asked a worker on an Apple line at a Foxconn factory what he made of the human rights standards Western countries talk about. He called them Western propaganda. What taught him about America, he said, was not standards on paper but the machine-like pace of Apple’s line and pay he was never sure would arrive.
Since 2006 we have investigated Apple’s suppliers in China, publishing 19 reports. I have come to believe blaming Apple alone would be unfair. Apple’s supply chain in China was built on a trade. China needed foreign capital, technology, and jobs. In return, Western firms got cheap labor and speed built on long overtime and extreme scheduling flexibility.
The Chinese government, Apple, and the supplier factories all bear responsibility for the conditions workers face. But Apple has treated allegations of wrongdoing as a compliance problem, rather than the output of its own production model.
Apple’s product cycles are fast, and launches send order volumes sharply higher. Suppliers work on thin margins and must deliver enormous volumes quickly. The component prices are set; equipment costs are sunk. There is only one place left to ensure profits: labor costs. Workers’ hours and income become the buffer, absorbing the volatility Apple itself generates.
Apple’s answer has been to police this through a Supplier Code of Conduct, audits, public reporting and worker training. While these steps do have an impact, the overall pattern is clear: individual violations may be corrected, but the same problems return.
In 2019 we found withheld wages at Foxconn’s Zhengzhou plant. At the same plant, more than half the workforce was on dispatch contracts, far above the legal cap of 10 percent. Apple disputed most of our findings but acknowledged excessive use of dispatch workers. In 2022 thousands at the same plant clashed with police over pay promised at recruitment; Foxconn apologized, blaming a computer input error. In 2025 we found dispatch workers still being used above the legal cap.
This August we found a full-time assembly worker at Foxconn’s Zhengzhou plant on a base wage of 2,450 yuan a month, about $363, a little above the city’s legal minimum of 2,350 yuan. To reach 4,200 yuan he has to work 60-hour weeks, totaling roughly 87 hours of overtime a month, against a statutory ceiling of 36.
Raising his base wage by 1,750 yuan, about $260 a month, would let him earn the income he needs on a legal schedule. Even if all 200,000 workers employed at peak operating times received that increase for a full year, the cost would be roughly $620 million – about half of one percent of Apple’s $112 billion in net income in the year to September.
Clearly, Apple can afford to pay more. The discrepancy, then, points to a deeper issue: labor conditions are not given the same priority as output, speed, and profit margin.
Look at how Apple manages suppliers. Yield rates and delivery deadlines are tracked precisely. Missing them can cost a supplier its orders. A labor violation, by contrast, will just produce another audit. Foxconn went through the 2010 suicides and has gone through one labor dispute after another since. To this day it remains one of Apple’s most important partners.
Suppliers know exactly which metrics are most important to Apple.
Apple could have set an enforceable wage floor and made labor conditions matter as much as quality and delivery. It has not.
China has changed, economically and politically. If Apple wants to keep relying on China as its main production base, maintaining the old model now comes at a higher price in both Beijing and Washington. Apple has been willing to pay that price. It has never paid a comparable price to the people who build its phones.
As if the suffering of thousands of workers wasn’t enough, there are other costs as well. When the United States preaches labor rights while its most emblematic company leaves Chinese workers dependent on illegal overtime to live, the contradiction erodes the very labor and human rights standards it promotes.
Cook proved Apple can control how an iPhone is made. He never showed that Apple is willing to take responsibility for the welfare of the people who make those phones. For 20 years Apple’s priorities have been consistent: production first, responsibility second.
On September 1, Ternus inherits the manufacturing system Cook helped create – and the unpaid debt to the workers who power that system. Whether the debt is paid will not be recorded in the next Supplier Responsibility Report, but it will show up in how the worker on the line describes America to everyone he knows.

Libya energy crisis leaves parts of oil-rich country struggling
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
15:39:03 UTC
00:39:03 KST

Breadcrumb
Libya energy crisis leaves parts of oil-rich country struggling
Long power cuts and severe fuel shortages have disrupted daily life in Libya, a country already plagued by an enduring political deadlock, conflict, and corruption, and home to Africa's largest oil reserves.
As the summer heat peaks, the worst crisis in years has tightened its grip on many Libyans who struggle to stay cool and keep their houses, cars and businesses running.
Experts and United Nations officials say the root of the problem lies in corruption, weak governance and years of inadequate maintenance at power plants.
Libya holds about 48 billion barrels of proven oil reserves and produces roughly 1.5 million barrels a day. It is seeking to raise output to 2 million barrels a day.
But the country only produces a third of the fuel it needs for domestic consumption. Last year, it imported $7.8 billion worth of fuel, according to figures from the National Oil Corporation.
For ordinary Libyans, the crisis has meant spoilt food and stalled businesses amid unbearable heat.
'Poor governance'
Libya has been politically divided for more than a decade, after being plunged into war during the 2011 overthrow of former leader Muammar Gaddafi.
Two administrations are currently vying for power: a UN-recognised government in Tripoli and its rival in Benghazi, backed by military leader Khalifa Haftar.
"Libya produces less than its energy needs during peak periods, and the electricity crisis and fuel shortage are complex, since the country is an oil producer but relies on importing fuel," international relations researcher Bechir Jouini told AFP.
But the issue is also compounded by "the problem of smuggling oil out of the country as well as the failure to implement maintenance programmes for power plants", Jouini said.
He also blamed mismanagement and corruption in the budgets allocated to the energy sector.
"Libya has resources and funds, but it suffers from poor governance and corruption is rampant... despite the allocation of huge budgets to the electricity company," he said.
Hanna Tetteh, the UN envoy to Libya, has also linked the energy crisis to broader failures in the country's institutions.
"The recent widespread electricity outages and public discontent, exacerbated by a prolonged heatwave, have exposed the consequences of institutional fragmentation, large-scale diversion of public resources, underinvestment and uncoordinated decision-making, all of which are essentially failures of governance," the envoy recently told the UN Security Council.
"The contradiction is that this is occurring in a country that does not lack energy resources and has the largest petroleum deposits on the African continent," Tetteh said.
Earlier this month, a key reservoir containing about 4.5 million litres of petrol was targeted by several drone attacks in Zawiya, some 45 kilometres (27 miles) west of Tripoli.
Zawiya has for years been the scene of armed conflict between rival groups who fight over the territory, which is a hotspot for fuel, drugs and migrants trafficking.

The session highlighted the process of documenting Israeli violations of international humanitarian law during the recent war on Lebanon, as well as the methodology and mechanisms adopted by the National Committee for International Humanitarian Law in Lebanon to collect information, document violations and verify them.
Mitri recalled statements by "enemy leaders and their threats to make Lebanon another Gaza".
He also discussed the civilisational and environmental genocide to which Lebanon is being subjected, as well as Israel's crimes against humanity, reviewing the issue of documenting Israeli crimes and violations to work toward prosecuting Israel for its crimes.
Mitri called on civil society groups, and everyone who has worked to document Israeli crimes, to share their research with the Lebanese government to enrich the reports that the government is preparing.
He stressed the need to unify efforts and endeavours on this issue, praising in this regard "the volunteers who are working without pay so far in the National Committee for International Humanitarian Law to document Israeli crimes".
He said the Lebanese government is working to establish a permanent centre to carry out this task.
Regarding the possibility of pursuing Israel before the International Criminal Court (ICC), Mitri said Lebanon is not a party to the Rome Statute, which established the ICC, preventing the Lebanese state from taking up a case against Israel there.
At the same time, Mitri said the ICC can, under specific circumstances and through defined mechanisms, accept jurisdiction to consider crimes committed during a certain period, even if the state concerned has not fully joined the Rome Statute.
However, he stressed that the inability of the Lebanese state at present to approach the ICC does not remove the right of Lebanese individuals to pursue Israel before many European courts, such as those in Spain, Belgium and France.
Some European judicial systems allow, under specific conditions, the filing of cases related to international crimes or serious violations.
For his part, Nasser Yassin, director of the Arab Centre for Research and Policy Studies in Beirut, said the centre in Beirut has worked since the beginning of the recent war on Lebanon to highlight Israeli violations and the cost of the war, particularly the direct and indirect damage to various vital sectors in Lebanon.
It has done so by holding discussion sessions and workshops, as well as preparing and publishing situation assessment reports, position papers and research papers covering the education, health and agriculture sectors.
Yassin stressed the urgent need at this stage to "activate respect for international humanitarian law by respecting civilians and their lives and not targeting health workers or humanitarian service workers".

Syrian President Ahmed al-Sharaa appointed former SDF ringleader Ferhat Abdi Şahin, also known as Mazloum Abdi, as a presidential adviser Friday, cementing a dramatic political shift just days after the group announced its dissolution and integration into state institutions.
The appointment was announced in a decree signed by al-Sharaa and carried by state news agency SANA.
“Mustafa Khalil Abdi is appointed as adviser to the presidency of the republic,” the decree said, using one of the names by which Abdi has been known.
His appointment comes after he announced Tuesday that the SDF would dissolve under an agreement reached with Damascus in January to integrate its armed units and civilian administration into Syrian state institutions.
Abdi said the move followed “the completion of the process of integrating our forces into the brigades of the Syrian army.”
Syria’s new authorities, which took power after the ouster of longtime dictator Bashar Assad in 2024, have sought to restore central government control across the country after years of fragmentation during the civil war.
U.S. special envoy for Syria Tom Barrack welcomed the agreement Tuesday, describing it as an example of former rivals reaching a diplomatic settlement aimed at strengthening Syrian sovereignty.
Barrack also said securing meaningful government roles for Kurdish figures, including Abdi, would recognize their leadership and contributions to regional stability.
Abdi agreed to integration with Damascus after government forces captured significant territory from terrorist PKK/YPG-led forces during clashes and as Washington strengthened relations with the new Syrian leadership.
In another major step, Syria’s Education Ministry authorized Kurdish-language instruction in public and private schools Thursday in areas where Kurdish citizens constitute a significant share of the population.
The decision allows Kurdish to be taught alongside Arabic and English.
It follows an earlier decree by al-Sharaa recognizing Kurdish as a national language and affirming the national rights of Syria’s Kurdish population, a major policy shift in a country where Kurds have long complained of discrimination.
Abdi said last week that the integration of the Kurdish administration into the Syrian state had been completed but pledged to continue efforts to secure Kurdish rights in the country’s new constitution.
Syria’s Kurdish population is estimated at around 2 million out of roughly 20 million people, with communities concentrated mainly in the northeast as well as in Damascus and Aleppo.

ICE deports Venezuelan father from Texas to West Africa
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
15:37:44 UTC

ICE deports Venezuelan father from Texas to West Africa: A situation "I don't wish on anybody"
A 35-year-old Venezuelan man who lived in Texas for years is now nearly 6,000 miles from his wife and 5-month-old American son after U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement deported him to West Africa.
Carlos Tellez Sanchez said he had never heard of Liberia until last week, when he found out he was being deported to the country that sits between Sierra Leone and Côte d'Ivoire just hours before his flight took off. He said he spent the 15-hour flight across the Atlantic in handcuffs, and is now stranded in a remote area of the West African nation.
"I do not understand how a country that considers itself a global hero can act this way towards a human being," he told CBS News in Spanish over a video call.
Tellez Sanchez said he now spends much of his time inside a hotel more than an hour away from Monrovia, Liberia's capital, where he was placed alongside deportees from Brazil, Colombia, Honduras and other countries.
President Trump's crackdown on illegal immigration has intensified this summer, with ICE making a record number of arrests. Increasingly, some detainees are being sent to countries that are not their own and banished to far-flung places. Tellez Sanchez, who entered the U.S. illegally five years ago, is one of them.
The Venezuela native had been in the U.S. since 2021 after fleeing his home country. He worked at a car dealership in Dallas during the day and drove for Uber Eats at night to support his family. CBS News could not find any criminal charges or convictions for Tellez Sanchez, beyond civil immigration violations.
In December 2025, Tellez Sanchez was detained by ICE during what he expected would be a routine immigration appointment. He spent eight months in ICE detention centers before his deportation to Africa.
An immigration judge in 2021 granted Tellez Sanchez protection from being sent back to Venezuela, finding that he could be persecuted there. Legally, however, that order did not prevent ICE from deporting him to any other country.
Over the past year and a half, the Trump administration has brokered so-called "third country" deportation agreements with dozens of nations around the world, including some notoriously dangerous places like South Sudan and the Central African Republic.
Tellez Sanchez' brother in Dallas, Juan Tellez, said he has no idea why Tellez Sanchez was sent to Liberia and that no one has given him an explanation. He described his brother as a good person and a hard worker who "doesn't deserve what happened to him."
The Department of Homeland Security did not respond to CBS News' questions about Tellez Sanchez' case, including why Liberia was chosen as his country of deportation.
In Liberia, Tellez Sanchez says he has no clear plan.
"It's a very difficult situation," he said, "one that I don't wish on anybody."

Six months of US-Israeli war with Iran: Rattansi, Sweeney, Dubenskij, Helali, Maloof on conflict takeaways (VIDEOS)
Iran has become stronger while the US has exposed its weakness during the conflict in the Middle East, which is still far from over, experts have told RT on the day marking six months since Washington and Israel attacked the Islamic Republic.
‘US and Israel underestimated resilience of Iranians and Lebanese’
RT’s correspondent in Lebanon, Steve Sweeney, said the Iran war is widely seen in the Middle East as “a strategic defeat for the US and its regional proxy, Israel.”
Israel used Iran as a pretext to launch an invasion of Lebanon, which “wreaked devastation across southern towns and villages, many of them have been destroyed completely,” Sweeney said.
“What Washington has done, what Israel has done is underestimated the resilience of the people on the ground here in Lebanon and also the resilience and the resistance being waged by the Iranians,” he added.
Trump looks like ‘Iranian agent’: Going Underground host Afshin Rattansi
“An alien from outer space might think that Trump has been… sent here as an Iranian agent to confirm the end of the US empire and the end of US power in this region,” Going Underground host Afshin Rattansi suggested.
The 180 days that have passed since February 28 “is not the end of the war,” but “a confirmation that Iran may have to respond... when it comes to retaliation and consequences for the NATO powers bent on their destruction, let alone the destruction of the entire Global South.”
‘If the goal of the operation was to make Israeli territory more secure, then it has been a complete failure’
RT correspondent Charlotte Dubenskij, reporting from the West Bank, said that since Israel launched its war with the US against Iran, it has opened up additional fronts, including operations in Lebanon and Syria, while the conflict in Gaza continues.
The West Bank, Dubenskij said, has become a “tinderbox,” with nationalist attacks by Israeli settlers taking place on a daily basis. She warned that the rising violence could trigger a backlash from Palestinians.
‘Iran has become a superpower’: DD Geopolitics reporter Christopher Helali
Tehran has become a “super power” over the 180 days that have passed since the attack by Washington and West Jerusalem, according to DD Geopolitics reporter Christopher Helali.
“What we can say unequivocally is that... Iran is not going back to the status quo of February 27 and before that. What has happened since has turned Iran into a major world power that doesn’t possess nuclear weapons, but possesses the Strait of Hormuz, which can bring the global economy to its knees and, of course, force the US and other regional powers to make enormous concessions,” he said.
‘A long, drawn-out conflict only beginning’
Former Pentagon analyst Michael Maloof called the US-Israeli operation “irresponsible,” saying it has resulted in “nothing but chaos, confusion, and greater turmoil and economic and political uncertainty in the world today.”
Half a year has passed since the initial attack on Iran, but “we’re only seeing the beginning of what’s going to be a long, drawn-out conflict,” he argued.

Slovak Police Foil Possible Napalm Attack on Factory Producing Drones for Ukraine
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
15:29:00 UTC
00:29:00 KST

Reported by
Officers from ÚBOK—Slovakia’s Office for the Fight Against Organized Crime—thwarted a potential arson attack on the Skyeton factory near Prešov, which manufactures unmanned systems for the Ukrainian military, police announced earlier this week.
The Ukrainian company's Raybird-3 drones can stay airborne for up to 28 hours and travel up to 2,500 kilometers, operating deep behind enemy lines.
Had the attack succeeded, police said, it would have risked a large-scale fire, endangered the roughly 70 employees who could have been on site, and caused damage worth tens of millions of dollars.
The Slovak Information Service and Military Intelligence played a key role in uncovering the plot, providing information that prompted ÚBOK to launch an intensive investigation. Police identified the perpetrators before the attack could take place and seized a large quantity of incendiary mixture—identified by the Police Force's Institute of Forensic Science as a blend of gasoline and polystyrene commonly known as napalm—along with tools, a mobile phone, an action camera and a hand-drawn plan of the attack.
Three foreign nationals were charged with preparing an especially serious crime of general endangerment, committed as accomplices for hire. Two were detained in Slovakia. German authorities arrested the third under a European arrest warrant issued in an exceptionally short time. Their identities and nationalities have not been made public yet.
When asked for comment, Román Hájek, a spokesperson for the Police Force Presidium, said investigators moved quickly once the tip came in, launching an immediate operational search effort that allowed them to identify those involved before any damage was done. He said officers from the regional police directorate in Prešov also provided significant support during the operation.
"Thanks to the timely intervention of police, no one was injured, and no property damage occurred," Hájek said. He added that the investigation is ongoing and that a change in the case's legal classification has not been ruled out.
In comments to Ukrainian media Skyeton accused Russia of orchestrating the sabotage, noting that Moscow regularly targets the company's domestic facilities as well as its reputation.
"The recent attempted attack on our facility in Slovakia is further proof that Ukrainian defense manufacturers have become a real thorn in their side, and that we are on the right path," the company said.
The case lands amid heightened concern across Europe over sabotage targeting firms tied to Ukraine's defense supply chain, with security officials increasingly describing such plots—often involving foreign nationals recruited for hire—as part of a broader pattern of hybrid attacks reaching well beyond the war's front lines.

‘Latin Poison’: Kazakhstan’s Latinization in Russian Media Discourse
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
15:25:00 UTC
00:25:00 KST

In July 2025, my feature titled “Scripts and Power: How Russian Media Frame the Latinization of the Kazakh Language” was published in The Diplomat. There, I argued, based on my analysis of over 200 articles, that Russian media views Latinization through a politicized lens and relies on conspiratorial, colonial, and nostalgic narratives in commenting on Kazakhstan’s script reform.
Shortly after, Russian outlet Ritm Evrazii published a piece, “Latin Poison for Kazakhstan,” as a direct response to my feature. Its author, Vladislav Makarov, discussed “the bewilderment among Russians caused by Kazakh officials’ stubborn desire to ban the Cyrillic alphabet.” Makarov further argued that Moldovan or Azerbaijani cultures have not become known worldwide because of their switch to Latin and that the new alphabet serves to “tie [post-Soviet republics] to their new overlords.”
This piece does not mean that my feature caused a significant stir in Moscow. Nevertheless, it is interesting evidence of how, in responding to an English-language feature about Kazakhstan’s script reform, Makarov reproduced the same Russia-centric narratives described in the original feature. In his words, Kazakhstan has been “connected to the Russian World for centuries,” thus justifying Russia’s commentary on Latinization.
The script reform in Kazakhstan, aimed at transitioning the Kazakh language from Cyrillic to the Latin alphabet, has been ongoing since 2017. Among the official reasons for the script change are the intentions to strengthen Kazakh identity and language and to rectify the true Kazakh pronunciation, which was affected by the Soviet-imposed Cyrillic script. Conceived under Kazakhstan’s first president, Nursultan Nazarbayev, Latinization is to be fully implemented by 2031.
Current President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev called for a cautious approach to Latinization. The latest version of the alphabet was presented in 2021, which shares similarities with the common Turkic alphabet adopted by the Organization of Turkic States in 2024. With less than five years left, the alphabet is yet to be finalized. A recent statement by the Ministry of Science and Higher Education assured that the work to improve the latest alphabet version was underway.
Latinization is intended for the Kazakh language only. So why does Kazakhstan’s script reform, which does not touch Russian at all, provoke such a strong reaction among Russian media? Makarov’s take on the reform sheds light on how Russia perceives Kazakhstan as part of the Russian world, and following this logic, any change within the Russian world affects Moscow.
The Russian world can be conceptualized as a socially constructed ideological and geopolitical order, which Russia uses to foster belonging, political loyalty, and hierarchy. It rests on the understanding that what unifies the Russian world are the Russian language, the Cyrillic alphabet, and shared history. Its proponents argue that the Russian world is a diverse community representing a multitude of cultures, with Russia holding a legitimately central position.
The Russian world is not a fixed construct and can be adjusted to align with Moscow’s political motivations. It is often juxtaposed with the Western world, portrayed as a civilization in decline. In practice, Moscow uses the Russian world at a variety of levels. One such use is the Russian World Foundation, a state-run institution primarily aimed at promoting and expanding the Russian language, literature, and culture abroad, particularly in Central Asia. Conceptually, Russian media employ the Russian world notion to perpetuate the ideas of Russia’s symbolic and civilizational power.
My analysis of 77 articles covering Latinization published between 2001 and 2025 by both mainstream (such as Gazeta.Ru, Lenta.Ru, Kommersant) and fringe nationalist outlets (Regnum, Ritm Evrazii) shows how Russian media instrumentalizes the Russian world to engage discursively with the Kazakh alphabet reform.
Latinization as a Tool to Exit the Russian World
Kazakhstan’s portrayal as a legitimate and natural part of the Russian world is foundational in Russian media coverage of Latinization. Kazakhstan’s presupposed membership in the Russian world enables Russian outlets to present Latinization as a tool Astana is using to exit this transnational civilizational community. Headings such as “Non-Russian World: Kazakhstan is replacing its ‘big brother’” or “Passive defense against the ‘Russian World’” illustrate how Russian media interprets Latinization as a threat to the Russian world’s integrity. The alphabet reform is argued to have the potential to erode the “common cultural space,” which is one of the “invisible links tying together the CIS countries.” The CIS refers to the Commonwealth of Independent States, an intergovernmental organization formed following the dissolution of the Soviet Union that counts among its members most, though not all, of the former Soviet republics.
At the same time, the idea of the Russian world is fused with both the imperial and Soviet past, demonstrating the concept’s flexible nature, and this fusion has a variety of effects. First, as discussed in a 2021 article published by Lenta.Ru, Kazakhstan’s very existence is portrayed as an outcome of Soviet politics, since it was the Bolsheviks “who turned Kazakhs into a nation and gifted them a state.” According to the article, Kazakh “statehood, culture, and script were all created in Moscow.” This framing of Latinization not only links Kazakhstan’s nationhood to the Soviet regime but also presents the alphabet reform as a sign of ingratitude to Moscow, which perceives itself as a successor of the Soviet Union.
In another Lenta.Ru article, from 2017, the authors expressed frustration with how Kazakh history books critically approach the Soviet past, one of the outcomes of which was the devastating famine of the 1930s, claiming the lives of over 1.5 million people (one-third of the ethnic Kazakh population of that period). They labeled Latinization as a “symbolic distancing from Russia’s legacy in Kazakhstan,” signs of which they also see in changing the Soviet geographical names to Kazakh. Hierarchical narratives can be observed in a 2017 Vedomosti article, which calls Russia “a metropole,” from which post-Soviet countries are trying to separate out of fear of being “swallowed by the ‘Russian world.’”
Within the Russian world framework, the Russian language holds a central position and serves as a link that ties Kazakhstan to this transnational community. The Russian language is inseparable from Cyrillic, which Russian media treat not as a mere script but as a symbolic and visual representation of the Russian world. In presenting Latinization as a threat to both the Russian language and its alphabet, Russian media follow the mechanism that scholar Lara Ryazanova-Clarke defined as an “inverse transnational pride.” This mechanism explains that Moscow treats the Russian language as a shared transnational commodity benefiting a majority of communities across the Russian world. These narratives change once a foreign government starts implementing policies that Russia perceives as hostile, which shifts the perception of Russian from a shared commodity to an object requiring Moscow’s protection.
The idea that Latinization is threatening the Russian language and Cyrillic is present across the pieces analyzed. Kazakhstan’s alphabet reform is called “an offensive against the Russian language and Cyrillic” in several articles, and the choice of this specific militaristic term aims at equating Latinization with a military operation against the Russian world’s most valuable commodity. Such an offensive is reported to cause an outmigration of ethnic Russians from Kazakhstan, thus drastically altering the country’s demography. Moreover, Latinization is expected to split “the Kazakh nation into two parts” since there will be people refusing to consume information in Latinized Kazakh who will turn to Russian.
Media call Latinization “a problem for Russia” and view the reform as a broader trend toward the worldwide decline of the Russian language. At the same time, Russian media frames Latinization’s negative impact on Russian as affecting the Kazakh language as well. To support this assumption, Russian media introduce a linguistic hierarchy, whereas they present Russian as superior and more resourceful compared to Kazakh, which is portrayed as subordinate. Kazakh and languages of other post-Soviet countries are called “colloquial in nature,” with Russian media claiming that it would be impossible for scholarship in these countries to develop without a proper proficiency and use of Russian, which provides access to global knowledge. Interestingly, this assumption seems to be internalized by Kazakhs as well, as a Regnum article in 2017 quoted famous Kazakh publicist and writer Seydakhmet Kuttykadam stating that “the Kazakh language and literature will fade away without its donor-language,” which is Russian.
Equally, Russian media securitize Latinization’s impact on Cyrillic. Latinization is called “terrible news for Russia” because it will no longer be able to “formulate cultural codes” through the alphabet, meaning that Kazakhstan will drift further toward the West. Such narratives help us understand how Russian media view Latinization not as a linguistic reform but as a geopolitical reconfiguration impacting Russia’s standing as a regional superpower. In discussing alleged effects of Latinization on Russian and Cyrillic, authors rarely discuss the practical implications of the new alphabet but rather defend the hierarchical and symbolic order created by Russia and perpetuated through the Russian world notion.
Latinization as Externally Driven
Another salient theme present in the Russian media is Latinization’s framing as administered externally by the Western powers or Turkiye. Through such narratives, it becomes more evident how Russian media contrasts the Russian world with competing civilizational entities.
This theme relies heavily on conspiratorial language. For instance, coverage by KM.Ru in 2010 claimed that the planned alphabet change means “preparations for a transformation of public consciousness to adapt it to European civilizational standards.” Similarly, Nezavisimaya Gazeta in 2021 referred to “Anglo-Saxons” who, through imposing the Latin alphabet, want to gain “total control over defeated and enslaved peoples.”
Turkiye, on the other hand, is seen as a greater civilizational competitor, since it offers Kazakhstan kinship based on Turkic identity, culture, and religion. Media portray Latinization as an outcome of Turkiye’s interference in the internal affairs of Russia, communicated through such headings as “Turkiye is displacing Russia in the post-Soviet space” and “A yatagan in the back. Turkiye is edging ever closer to Russia’s borders.” There seems to be awareness in Russian media that between Turkic and post-Soviet identities, Kazakh people might prefer the former.
Makarov, in his 2025 Ritm Evrazii piece, asked, “Will the Latin alphabet bring the Kazakhs closer to the Turkic world they consider their own? But would a Turk from Istanbul really feel closer to a Kazakh than a Russian from Chelyabinsk?” In asking these questions, he assumed that Latinization was developed in Astana to draw Turkiye and Kazakhstan closer. Such questions are intended to emphasize proximity between Kazakhstan and the Russian world, which is natural and historical, unlike Kazakhstan-Turkiye relations, which are, in this view, politically manufactured rather than based on genuinely shared culture.
Externalization of Latinization indicates that Russian media view Kazakhstan as subjugated either to the West or Turkiye. Such subjugation is branded as inappropriate and malicious, as these powers seek to meddle in Kazakhstan’s affairs through Latinization. At the same time, the hierarchical positioning of Kazakhstan in relation to Russia is also subjugated in nature, even though never explicitly named as such or criticized. Instead, it is portrayed as beneficial and legitimate.
The outcome of such rhetoric is that Russian media strips Kazakhstan of any agency in carrying out its domestic linguistic reform. By presenting Latinization as a plot by Western or Turkish powers, Russian media negate Kazakhstan’s sovereign decision to reform the alphabet for the Kazakh language on account of its own interests and aims.
Conclusions
Makarov’s article was never about Cyrillic or Latin. It was about the anxiety across the Russian media over Kazakhstan’s distancing from the hierarchy Makarov and other authors assume to be natural. Readers familiar with Russian foreign policy will not be surprised by the imperial narratives Russian media produce in relation to the Russian world, the Russian language, and Cyrillic. What might be surprising is that such narratives are activated by the script reform intended for the Kazakh language.
At the same time, among the fear-mongering articles about the destructive consequences of Latinization, there are rarely concrete examples of why the reform would impact Russian and Cyrillic. Instead, Russian media primarily focus on the superiority of the Russian language and its alphabet and on delegitimizing Latinization as an externally driven project by foreign actors. In the end, Russian media is not defending the Russian language or the Cyrillic alphabet, but the symbolic, ideological, and geopolitical hierarchy of the Russian world.
This feature is based on the author’s ongoing doctoral research on Kazakhstan’s script reform. All data and analysis are from the author’s original corpus and critical discourse analysis. Quotes are translated from Russian to English.

D&B for Ukrainian SMEs — Increasing Visibility to Foreign Partners
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
18:22:53 EEST
00:22:53 KST

Ukrainian small and medium-sized businesses are increasingly seeking customers, investors, and partners abroad. However, for many small companies, the main problem is not the quality of their product but their low international visibility: a foreign partner simply does not have enough data to quickly identify and assess the company.
In international trade, a corporate presence consists of more than just a website and social media pages. Large companies and banks use professional business databases to verify legal information, addresses, management, industries, the scale of operations, corporate connections, and other information.
“For small businesses, the problem often sounds like this: ‘We are a real company, but no one abroad knows anything about us.’ That is why international business identification is important not only for large corporations. It helps a small Ukrainian company become understandable to a procurement professional, bank, or potential partner in another country,” Maksym Urakin noted.
SMEs should monitor the consistency of their legal and commercial information, maintain a consistent English-language spelling of their name, provide up-to-date contact details, and have a clear description of their activities. It is also important for a company planning to export to understand how it is classified in international systems and whether it can be easily found using industry-specific parameters.
D&B’s international data can be used not only to verify other companies but also to create and update a company’s own business profile. This is particularly relevant for companies seeking to connect to global procurement platforms or work with corporate clients.
Greater visibility does not guarantee a contract, but it reduces the information barrier between Ukrainian SMEs and foreign markets. In many cases, the speed at which a company can be verified determines whether a potential partner will proceed to the next stage of negotiations.
D&B — Interfax-Ukraine helps Ukrainian companies work with international business data and business identification tools.
Dun & Bradstreet is an international provider of business data and analytical solutions whose history began in 1841. D&B works with data on companies worldwide and provides tools for business identification, counterparty verification, credit and commercial risk assessment, compliance, and supply chain management.
The Interfax-Ukraine News Agency is the official representative of Dun & Bradstreet in Ukraine. Israel ruling party blasts Ben-Gvir for ruling out electoral alliance

2026-08-28

Abdelraouf Arnaout and Mohammad Sio
28 August 2026•Update: 28 August 2026
Likud, Israel’s governing party led by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, slammed National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir on Friday for rejecting Netanyahu’s appeal to join Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich’s Religious Zionism party ahead of upcoming polls.
“By deciding to burn tens of thousands of right-wing votes and not unite with Smotrich, Ben-Gvir has decided today to enthrone a left-wing government of [Yashar party leader] Gadi Eisenkot, [Yisrael Beiteinu party leader Avigdor] Lieberman, [Democratic Party leader] Yair Golan, and the Arab parties,” Likud said in a statement.
The party questioned whether Ben-Gvir wanted a “broad national government led by Prime Minister Netanyahu that will continue the historic momentum we achieved in settlement in Judea and Samaria [i.e., the West Bank] over the past four years,” or whether the national security minister “for personal considerations, will burn right-wing votes to enthrone a left-wing government?”
Addressing Ben-Gvir, the party warned that an “Eisenkot-Lieberman-Yair Golan and Arab parties government will evict you from your home, Itamar. It will establish a Palestinian state. It will capitulate to every international dictate. It will destroy everything we've built.”
“Overcome the personal ego,” Netanyahu’s party urged Ben-Gvir. “Show maturity and responsibility.”
Opinion polls in Israel currently project Ben-Gvir’s Jewish Power party to win nine of the Knesset’s 120 seats, while a poll published Friday by Israeli daily Maariv projected that Smotrich’s Religious Zionism party would fail to win any seats.
Such a result would weaken the bloc supporting Netanyahu’s return to government and strengthen the opposition’s chances of forming the next governing coalition.
Slated for Oct. 27, the election is seen as crucial to the political future of Netanyahu, who faces a range of criminal charges, including bribery, fraud and breach of trust.
Netanyahu’s current government is widely described as the most right-wing in Israel’s history.
The 76-year-old prime minister has led the government since December 2022.
Netanyahu is also wanted by the International Criminal Court over war crimes committed against Palestinians in the embattled Gaza Strip.

France seeks to cash in on weapons for Ukraine (VIDEO)
France hopes to line its own arms manufacturers’ pockets with a €90 billion European Union loan to Ukraine by limiting Kiev's ability to procure weapons from outside the bloc, according to Euronews.
After overcoming Hungary’s opposition, the EU member states in April approved the €90 billion Ukraine Support Loan, aimed at propping up Kiev’s war effort in 2026 and 2027; €60 billion of the total sum has been earmarked for arms procurement.
The scheme, which is backed by joint EU borrowing on the capital markets, is premised on the assumption that it would be repaid when Ukraine secures reparations from Russia – a prospect Moscow has dismissed as “unrealistic.”
In an article on Tuesday, Euronews claimed that France is seeking to place a time limit on wavers allowing Ukraine to purchase weapons from outside the EU using EU-backed funds.
At present, Kiev can request an exemption if there is no EU-made system on offer that meets its immediate needs. According to the publication, Ukraine has so far made use of this mechanism on at least two occasions: when sourcing Chinese-made drone components and US-made Patriot interceptor missiles.
In early May, then-UK Prime Minister Keir Starmer announced London’s intention to also gain access to military contracts funded through the EU loan, despite the UK not being part of the bloc.
Following the escalation of the Ukraine conflict and amid the subsequent EU-wide rearmament drive, a number of European arms manufacturers have seen their profit margins surge.
Shares in Rheinmetall, Europe’s largest defense contractor, for instance, have risen more than tenfold over the past six years. Earlier this month, the company reported a nearly 70% increase in second-quarter revenue at €3.29 billion, having more than doubled its operating profit to €562 million.
RT’s Chay Bowes believes that behind a veneer of self-righteous talk lies ulterior motives, and that France is ultimately looking to funnel billions into its own military industrial complex.

Rwandan genocide suspect jailed for life in Netherlands for 1994 war crimes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
15:18:09 UTC
00:18:09 KST

A Dutch court on Friday sentenced a 67-year-old man to life in prison for war crimes and genocide committed in Rwanda in 1994, where it said he had been involved in the killing of around 3,000 Tutsis who had sought refuge from Hutu attacks at a stadium.
The defendant, identified only as Eugene N., had fled to the Netherlands in 1998 and later obtained Dutch nationality. Dutch prosecutors opened an investigation into him in 2020, which led to his arrest in the Netherlands in 2024.
The court said the man had been at the stadium in Byiza in April 1994 and gave the Hutus present "instructions to let no Tutsi escape the stadium."
"In the afternoon, shots were fired at the Tutsis, they were pelted with stones, and hand grenades were thrown onto the field. One grenade was thrown by the defendant. Survivors of the afternoon attack were killed with clubs and machetes," it said.
The defendant's lawyers have denied that he had a role in the massacres. Instead, they said he tried to avoid the genocide.
Over 800,000 killed in 1994 Rwanda genocide
More than 800,000 Tutsis and moderate Hutus were killed in 100 days in the 1994 genocide, orchestrated by the Hutu ruling majority and meticulously executed by local officials and ordinary citizens.
The court said the man also took part in raids on two communities predominantly inhabited by the Tutsi population in Mbazi, the municipality where he was "a person of authority."
During these attacks, houses were looted and set afire, after which people fled to the stadium, where they thought they would be safe - but instead were ultimately killed.
The Netherlands has tried and convicted other Rwandan genocide suspects before under universal jurisdiction, which allows courts to try certain grave international crimes regardless of where they were committed, and has in the past also extradited genocide suspects to Rwanda.

India’s BrahMos at Sea: Implications for South Asian Stability
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
15:14:00 UTC
00:14:00 KST

In May 2025, the confrontation between India and Pakistan was limited to the land and air domains. In the naval domain the two sides took to signaling and positioning but did not engage in active combat. At the start of the conflict, India deployed its naval aircraft carrier INS Vikrant for four days in the Arabian Sea but later moved it back to its base in Karnataka. The Pakistan Navy undertook counter-deployments with an operational offensive-defensive posture. It dispersed its surface combatants, intensified maritime ISR, and moved its coastal missile units into a state of heightened readiness. However, there was no confrontation between the two navies during the crisis.
However, a few weeks after the announcement of the ceasefire between India and Pakistan, Indian Defense Minister Rajnath Singh visited INS Vikrant and issued a stern warning for Pakistan. He said, “If Pakistan tries anything nefarious again, the opening move might come from our Navy.”
Since the May 2025 clashes, both states have actively invested in further strengthening the capabilities of their naval forces. Recently, the Indian Navy announced its plan to equip more frontline warships with BrahMos supersonic cruise missiles. The plan is to work toward a fleet-wide integration of the BrahMos weapon system by 2030.
This development may also increase pressure on Pakistan to take both defensive and offensive measures to maintain naval parity in the region.
Currently, the Indian Navy operates a diverse range of missiles for anti-ship and land-attack roles. This includes the BrahMos missile deployed across 20 major frontline combatant platforms, the Klub series deployed on Talwar-class frigates, Kh-35E Uran deployed on older systems, and French-made Exocet missiles and American Harpoon missiles on its diesel-electric submarines. However, the BrahMos system has proven its operational relevance for the Indian military after its combat use during the May 2025 crisis. Further integration of the BrahMos would provide India with an indigenous option that can help reduce its reliance on a diverse array of imported missile systems.
In 2024, the Indian Cabinet Committee on Security approved the purchase of 220 Extended Range (ER) BrahMos missiles for naval ships. The ER-BrahMos has a range of 800 kilometers that can increase the operational space for Indian naval platforms against the Pakistan Navy and also engage coastal targets without getting very close to Pakistan. Moreover, the BrahMos is a supersonic missile with a speed of around Mach 3, reducing the time available for an adversary to detect, identify, and respond to the incoming missile. Also, the precision-strike capability of BrahMos provides a major advantage while targeting moving naval platforms. Because of its indigenous production, range, precision, and speed, the BrahMos has emerged as a major weapon for India and an ideal candidate for deployment across all its naval platforms.
To achieve its target, the Indian Navy is equipping its older and smaller naval vessels with BrahMos launchers, as evidenced by its replacement of the P-15 Termit with four twin-tube BrahMos launchers on Veer-class corvettes, starting with INS Vidyut. The latest Indian warships including the Nigri-class stealth frigates – INS Udaygiri, INS Himgiri, and INS Mahendragiri –are equipped with eight vertically launched BrahMos missiles. All four Visakhapatnam-class destroyers carry 16 BrahMos missile each. The Indian Navy is also planning to retrofit its older warships with BrahMos systems to achieve system-wide integration. India has also successfully tested the BrahMos missile from an underwater platform, paving way for its integration with diesel-electric submarines. Further, India is developing six highly agile compact missile vessels that can carry eight BrahMos missiles each. These are called next-generation missile vessels.
These developments have significant implications for Pakistan’s naval strategy and also regional strategic stability. Pakistan is undertaking its own efforts to further strengthen its sea-denial strategy. Pakistan has developed an indigenous anti-ship ballistic missile – P282 SMASH – and integrated them with surface combatants like Zulfiqar-class frigates and Babur-class corvettes. The missile has a range of 350 km. Moreover, it has developed the Harbah subsonic cruise missile and acquired Chinese-imported YJ-83 anti-ship cruise missiles. Pakistan Navy has also tested anti-ship air-launched cruise missiles (ALCM) Taimoor to strengthen its maritime capabilities.
Pakistan is working on its defense systems by deploying CAMM-ER missiles on Babur-class corvettes and LY-80 missiles on Tughril-class frigates. Both offensive and defensive capabilities developed by Pakistan are designed to maintain operational parity with the Indian Navy. However, there would be certain challenges for Pakistan if India successfully integrates all its naval warships with BrahMos missile systems. This would increase pressure on Pakistan to strengthen its maritime surveillance as India would have a quantitative edge in its missile carrying naval platforms.
As the naval domain is a possible battlefield for a future crisis between India and Pakistan, these developments can have serious repercussions for regional stability. Any attacks on naval systems and coastal areas carry serious escalation risks in a nuclearized environment. India’s accidental launch of a BrahMos missile in May 2022 showcased a serious problem with command and control of this platform in an environment in which two nuclear weapon states operate. Another major problem with the deployment with BrahMos is that the missile is dual-capable in nature and can carry nuclear weapons. This conventional-nuclear entanglement further increases the risks of miscalculation and inadvertent escalation.
In conclusion, the Indian deployment of the BrahMos missile on all of its naval warships has negative implications for deterrence stability, crisis stability, and arms race stability between India and Pakistan. Increasing the number of mobile platforms capable of conducting long-range precision strikes could create greater pressure for Pakistan to adopt countermeasures, while simultaneously increasing the incentives for pre-emption during a crisis. The combination of BrahMos’s long range, high speed, and dual-capable nature further complicates escalation management between two nuclear-armed states, particularly when the origin and intent of a naval strike may be difficult to determine in real time. The developments risks transforming the Arabian Sea from a domain of signaling and maneuver into a potential trigger for rapid escalation, with consequences extending beyond South Asia to the wider Indian Ocean Region.

Warsh says US Fed has ‘work to do’ if above-target inflation lingers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
15:13:26 UTC
00:13:26 KST

Warsh signals US Fed may need to raise rates if above-target inflation lingers
This was the closest he has come to acknowledging interest rate hikes may be needed to ease price pressures
The US central bank will “have work to do” if policymakers are not confident that underlying inflation is returning to its 2 per cent target, Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh said on Friday in remarks that acknowledged financial conditions do not appear restrictive and marked the closest he has come to acknowledging interest rate hikes may be needed to ease price pressures.
“Here is my standard: We must be confident that underlying inflation is moving to our objective, clearly and at sufficient speed. Otherwise, we have work to do. That’s our job … our mandate … and our charge to keep,” Warsh said in remarks prepared for delivery to the Fed’s Jackson Hole economic symposium in Wyoming.
The remarks drew applause from an audience of global central bankers hungry for more than the vague promises to deliver price stability that have been a feature of Warsh’s previous remarks. Markets also heard the message, raising bets on a rate hike next month that had previously been priced in as more of a long shot.
While much of the 16-page address focused on large issues, like the influence of artificial intelligence, that Warsh feels will be critical in the long run, it also included some key acknowledgements – including that “short-term interest rates are the predominant tool to achieve the dual mandate”.
Notably, Warsh said the recommendations of five task forces he has commissioned to study longer-term issues “will come later and have no bearing on decisions we make in the current policy conjuncture. But I believe that for future policy challenges, this intellectual investment today will leave us far better prepared”.
He did not directly address recent market interventions by US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent but did say that the Fed “needs clear market signals, as unfiltered as possible”, to set proper monetary policy. But it was his comments on inflation that arguably went the furthest to meet what some had seen as a gap in Warsh’s remarks at his first two press conferences.

Trump declares himself ‘greatest’ US president
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
15:09:30 UTC
00:09:30 KST

Trump declares himself ‘greatest’ US president
Donald Trump has declared himself the “greatest” president in US history while branding Joe Biden and Barack Obama “failures” in a ranking posted on Truth Social.
Abraham Lincoln, who led the US through the Civil War and abolished slavery, and George Washington, the first US president and a founding father, were placed one tier below Trump.
The US president shared the ranking on Thursday alongside a CNN clip highlighting polling showing his dominance among Republican voters. The graphic divides US presidents into six tiers – ‘The Greatest’, ‘Great’, ‘Near Great’, ‘Average’, ‘Below Average’, and ‘Failures’ – with Trump alone at the top.
Lincoln, Washington, Franklin D. Roosevelt, Woodrow Wilson, Thomas Jefferson, and Andrew Jackson were placed in the ‘Great’ category. Theodore Roosevelt, Grover Cleveland, John Adams, and James K. Polk were rated ‘Near Great’, while Bill Clinton was among those deemed ‘Average’.
Biden and Obama were placed at the opposite end of Trump’s chart alongside fellow Democrat Jimmy Carter and former presidents Ulysses S. Grant and Warren G. Harding. The list contains 34 presidents and leaves out 11 others, including Ronald Reagan, Dwight D. Eisenhower, John F. Kennedy, Richard Nixon, and both George Bushes.
The graphic appears to be an altered version of a ranking published by LIFE magazine in 1948, when Harvard historian Arthur Schlesinger Sr. asked 55 experts in American history to classify presidents as ‘great’, ‘near great’, ‘average’, ‘below average’, or ‘failure’. Trump’s version largely retains the original categories but adds himself at the top and several more recent Democratic presidents.
Trump posted the image after CNN highlighted an Elon University poll showing 53% of Republicans named him the Republican president they admired most, far ahead of Reagan at 18% and Lincoln at 8%. CNN analyst Harry Enten called it a “historic comparison,” saying Trump “nearly triples up” on Reagan.
Expert surveys, however, have placed Trump at the opposite end of the scale. The Presidential Greatness Project ranked him last in 2018 with 12.34 points out of 100, versus 95.03 for Lincoln, and put him last again in its 2024 survey of 154 presidential scholars and experts. Lincoln topped both rankings.
Trump’s broader approval has also slumped during his second term. A Reuters/Ipsos poll conducted August 21-24 put his approval at a record-low 33%, with 65% disapproving. A Marquette survey showed even weaker numbers on the economy, with 30% approving of his handling of it and just 22% backing his record on inflation and the cost of living.

DUSHANBE, Aug. 28 (Xinhua) -- China is helping transform the Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) from a security-focused regional body into a comprehensive platform -- one spanning economy, technology, transport and finance, a Tajik economist said.
In an interview with Xinhua, Rahmon Ulmasov, a professor at the Russian-Tajik (Slavonic) University, described China's 2024-2025 rotating presidency as one of the most productive periods in the SCO history.
During its presidency, China hosted over 200 events, issued 92 outcome documents, and put forward 36 major cooperation initiatives, Ulmasov noted. "The SCO has gone beyond being solely a regional platform and is gaining global significance."
China has become one of SCO's primary economic engines, said Ulmasov, highlighting SCO leaders' approval of a development strategy for the organization in the 2026-2035 period and the member states' decision to establish an SCO development bank at the SCO summit held last year in China's port city of Tianjin.
These measures are particularly important for Central Asia, where there is significant demand for financing in transport, energy, water management and digital infrastructure, he said, noting that once the bank becomes fully operational, it could provide countries in the region with new sources of long-term financing.
On the logistics front, Ulmasov said that Belt and Road cooperation on infrastructure is fostering closer transport, trade and logistics links among SCO member states, particularly in Central Asia.
New cross-border routes are transforming Central Asia from a landlocked area in the Eurasian transport grid into a dynamic hub connecting East and West, as well as North and South, he said.
The China-Kyrgyzstan-Uzbekistan railway could also become a new driver of regional economic development, said the Tajik expert. The project is designed to create a new land route connecting China and Central Asia and shorten the existing China-Europe route by about 900 km, providing an alternative to traditional transport routes.
Looking ahead, Ulmasov said the SCO is embarking on a new development stage with cooperation expanding beyond traditional trade, transport and conventional energy to technological modernization in green energy, artificial intelligence, the digital economy and emerging industries.
China is aligning its own modernization drive with the development needs of fellow SCO member states, creating a new model of cooperation that combines Chinese technology, local resources, joint production and access to regional markets, he said.
China, he said, is offering SCO members more than a share in its economic momentum; it is offering a way into the high-tech supply chains of the future.
As these initiatives take root, he added, the SCO could become a premier hub for the region's green and digital economic transformation. ■
