Run, Don't Walk, to See Coyote vs. Acme
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
12:00:04 UTC
21:00:04 KST

If you’re still not convinced that creativity and originality are under siege, particularly in the movie business, look no further than the tangled tale of how the wholly joyous Coyote vs. Acme very nearly didn’t make it to a theater near you. As of summer 2018, the picture—a blend of animation and live action, adapted from a 1990 New Yorker article by Ian Frazier inspired by the forever-enduring Looney Tunes shorts—was already in development. In the spring of 2022, live-action filming took place in New Mexico. In November 2023, seeking a tax write-off, Warner Bros. Discovery decided to shelve the film; the company eventually agreed to allow the filmmakers to look for another distributor. After numerous false starts, Ketchup Entertainment acquired the rights to Coyote vs. Acme, which is why you’re now able to see the film in theaters, and eventually via streaming. In a world where entertainment conglomerates are clearly focused only on profits, this seems like a small miracle, which is why you should run—Beep beep!—not walk to see this late-summer delight on the big screen.
The premise is simple yet ingenious: After years of being zonked out by iron wrecking balls, of having slingshots overshoot the mark not by feet but by miles, of having dynamite blow his face off, Wile E. Coyote, a longtime consumer of ACME products, has decided to sue the company that has caused him so much misery. He has used all that ACME stuff for one purpose only: to ensnare the object of his eternal salivation, the tufted blue-and-yellow speed demon known as the Road Runner, both uncatchable and unknowable. But now, it seems, enough is enough, and maybe ACME is the problem. Wile E. enlists the help of a law firm specializing in personal injury cases (it’s called Avery, Jones & Maltese, a nod to three of the Looney Tunes’ chief architects, Tex Avery, Chuck Jones, and Michael Maltese), and it's headed by Kevin Avery (Will Forte), whose specialty is getting settlements of a hundred bucks here or there from cartoon characters who have had limbs and such blown off—temporarily, thank god—by faulty products.
Coyote vs. Acme is set in a world where cartoons and humans coexist without batting an eye, so it’s business as usual when Wile E. shows up at Avery’s Albuquerque headquarters. Avery is pretty sure he can get his client a few hundred smackers for the defective rocket-powered roller skates our coyote friend has hauled in as Exhibit A. But then Wile E. unfurls, magically, a bundle including every single ACME product that has ever clocked his noggin or blasted him to oblivion: these million and one instruments of pain and suffering spring high into the sky, like magic rocks gone wild. Avery is still reluctant to sue the pants off ACME. But his niece and intern Paige (Lana Condor) persuades him this is one case that could really make a difference for thousands of disadvantaged cartoon characters, many of whom, including Porky Pig, Daffy, and Tweety Bird, show up in sprightly cameos. That’s how Avery finds himself up against ACME’s bulldog lawyer Buddy Crane (John Cena, who, with his square, precise jaw and squinty smirk, looks like a work of vintage hand-drawn animation himself). He also learns that Wile E.’s case isn’t isolated: ACME has long been involved in a nefarious plot to make millions by taking advantage of hapless cartoon characters.
Coyote vs. Acme was directed by Dave Green, whose highest-profile movie to date may have been 2016’s Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles: Out of the Shadows. But his confidence sings here: to say Coyote vs. Acme benefits from a light touch may seem odd—this is, after all, a movie where heads are clonked with mallets and facial features are rearranged by malfunctioning explosives. But the spirit of Coyote vs. Acme is everything. The script was written by Samy Burch, James Gunn, and Jeremy Slater; the voices of most of the characters—including Bugs Bunny, as a trenchcoat-wearing informant, and Elmer Fudd, as an earnest senator in charge of questioning “Mr. Runner” during a hearing—are provided by voice actor Eric Bauza, who clearly aced his studies at the University of Mel Blanc. Forte makes a fabulous foil for his cartoon costars: he never tries to outdo them, preferring to bow to their lunatic majesty. He knows they’re what we’ve come here for.
Because the Road Runner cartoons—which, along with the other works of genius in the Looney Tunes galaxy, made many of us the warped individuals we are today—were never really about the Road Runner. He’s moving too fast for us to ever get a handle on him; his job is to outsmart the coyote who hopes to catch him and turn him into stew, and he’s simply too good at that job. We know he’s always going to win, which makes him less interesting than his nemesis. Wile E. Coyote, with his conniving yellow eyes, a voiceless beast who communicates by holding up a series of signs scrawled with simple lines of dialogue, is the character we love in spite of ourselves. His untrustworthiness is his greatest quality; when he pretends to be nice, his canine lips turning up in a facsimile of a canine smile, we know it’s an act, and we can wear the joy of not being taken in by his deceptions as a badge of honor. It’s both funny and a little horrible when he goes splat into a slab of rocky desert clay, cutting a Wile E.-shaped hole into nature’s landscape. In Coyote vs. Acme, we almost feel something for him—almost. But in the end, he lets us off the hook; he will not let us fall victim to sentimentality. We're in on his con, and it's a pleasurable place to be.
Coyote vs. Acme is all about the little guys fighting, and winning against, a corporate behemoth. Could it be that Chuck Jones and his cohorts, by inventing a do-it-all, know-it-all company that could fulfill our every material desire, dropping off packages almost before we’d even placed an order, had in some cracked way foreseen the rise of Amazon? They probably couldn’t have imagined it, and it’s just as well, because the world they dreamed up—one of slapstick escape, of kerpow explosions that never did any actual harm, of faces and voices that we can summon in our memories as easily as those of our loved ones—is better than anything money can buy. In Coyote vs. Acme, the little guy wins, and we do too. Instead of being handed, in movie form, an exploding cigar that someone else thinks we want, we get the thing we didn’t know we wanted: a movie about a coyote, a bird, and a lawsuit, one that both speaks to our time and allows us, for the space of an hour or two, to escape it.

Risks of child recruitment by armed groups rise in post-quake Colombia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
12:00:00 UTC
21:00:00 KST

Risks of child recruitment by armed groups rise in post-quake Colombia
The recent earthquake in Colombia could increase the risk of child recruitment by armed groups in Chocó and Valle del Cauca, where thousands of children remain out of school in areas already affected by conflict, the UN warned on Friday.
The quake damaged more than 3,800 educational facilities and has affected the education of more than one million students. Nearly 178,000 attend schools that suffered serious structural damage.
UN Resident Coordinator in Colombia María José Torres Macho said recruitment was already a concern in those areas before the disaster, where illegal armed groups are active.
“We are concerned that the situation of children out of school can exacerbate this problem,” she told reporters at UN Headquarters.
In Chocó, some rural schools were completely destroyed, others partially collapsed and several remain at imminent risk of collapse. Assessments are also continuing in Risaralda and Caldas to determine which schools can reopen safely.
For the UN, restoring access to education is a priority not only to ensure learning can continue, but also to return children to protective environments.
Emergency in conflict-affected areas
The 7.4-magnitude earthquake on 10 August left 331 people dead, 4,449 injured and 219 missing. More than 406,000 people have been affected across 15 departments and 496 municipalities.
Many of the hardest-hit areas were already facing high levels of poverty, isolation and armed violence.
“Those areas most affected are those areas most vulnerable,” she said, adding that the pre-existing conflict is creating challenges for both the emergency response and recovery.
Assessing needs
In Chocó, the UN still does not have complete information on the needs of some rural communities, particularly Afro-Colombian and Indigenous communities. Damage to roads, difficulties travelling along some rivers and electricity and connectivity problems are hampering both assessments and the delivery of aid.
Conflict-related displacement is also continuing alongside the earthquake response. In Sipí, Chocó, around 95 Afro-Colombian people were displaced from the community of Charco Hondo, with concern that displacement could spread to two neighbouring communities.
Ms. Torres Macho also highlighted the role of local authorities and Indigenous and Afro-Colombian organisations, which have been among the first responders in some of the most isolated areas. At the same time, she warned that some municipalities have limited capacity and are overwhelmed by the scale of the emergency.
Since 10 August, the UN system and humanitarian partners have reached around 72,000 people in 36 municipalities across Chocó, Valle del Cauca, Risaralda and Caldas with food, water, medical care, medicines, shelter, psychosocial support, protection and education services.
Watch the full press confererence here:
Response amid funding shortfall
Following the earthquake, the United Nations updated its humanitarian response plan and estimates that 1.2 million people need assistance. Within that group, around 127,000 have been identified as among the most severely affected and in need of priority support, Ms. Torres Macho said.
The response requires $148.1 million, she said, but only 40 per cent of that has been received.
Among the most urgent needs are shelter, medical care, medicines, safe water, education and support to restore livelihoods.
Supply shortages emerge
In some places, available supplies are already beginning to run out. In Caldas, for example, food and hygiene distributions have relied in part on donations, but those stocks are being depleted, and there is not enough capacity to sustain the next rounds of assistance.
Problems also persist in temporary shelters. Among those assessed in Chocó, Risaralda, Valle del Cauca and Caldas, 33 per cent have sanitation and hygiene needs, 31 per cent face problems accessing water and 22 per cent need food.
Ms. Torres Macho said the response will also need to move quickly towards recovery and reconstruction, particularly in communities that were already vulnerable before the earthquake.
“It is very important to also provide support to the municipalities, so there is some urban planning and we don’t reproduce vulnerability and end up creating another disaster.”

Security Council LIVE: Deadly gang attacks spike in Haiti
        
      Peace and Security      
    Following a deadly spate of gang attacks on civilians in Haiti and amid reports of illicit weapons slipping into the Caribbean country, the Security Council has called an emergency meeting at 3pm (local time) to hear and discuss the latest developments. UN News app users can follow our coverage here.
What you need to know:
- On 23 August, gangs killed at least 47 people, injured 22 others and kidnapped more than 52 people in Kenscoff, near the capital, Port-au-Prince
- 1,408 people have been killed and 656 injured in the context of gang-related violence and 326 people had been subjected to sexual violence between 1 April and 30 June, according to the latest report of the UN Integrated Office in Haiti (BINUH)

As the Himalayas melt, deadly floods become the new normal
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
12:00:00 UTC
21:00:00 KST

As the Himalayas melt, deadly floods become the new normal
A day before a wall of ice, rock and muddy water tore through Himalayan valleys along the Nepal-China border, Dipesh Chapagain was discussing with a colleague just how devastating such a disaster could be.
For the 40-year-old climate researcher, who grew up in the hills of eastern Nepal and now studies mountain hazards at the United Nations University in Bonn, Germany, the subject was both professional and deeply personal.
He has watched the risks facing the region change within his own lifetime.
“When I was kid, it was not like that,” he told me. “Or when my parents were kids or my grandparents, that was not the major challenge [they faced].”
A glacier fails, a mountain collapses
Then, on Wednesday morning at 8:37, a mountainside high in the Himalayas gave way.
The collapse was so vast that seismic instruments registered it as a magnitude-5.2 event, initially mistaking it for an earthquake. Bedrock beneath a glacier failed, carrying a huge mass of ice and rock roughly 1,200 meters toward the valley floor.
Water, sediment and boulders surged into the rivers below, sweeping through towns and villages along one of Nepal’s most important trade routes with China. At one monitoring station, the water rose as much as nine meters in half an hour.
By Friday, more than 500 people had been reported dead across Nepal and Tibet and more than 1,500 remained missing, including hundreds of foreign nationals.
Dr. Chapagain’s immediate family was spared. Still, the news took a toll on him.
“It’s always hard to get these devastating messages from back home,” he said. “It’s getting more frequent and more intense.”
The catastrophe is a brutal illustration of a problem climate scientists have been warning about for years. The frozen architecture of the Himalayas is changing, exposing millions of people to hazards that are becoming harder to predict and, in some cases, more destructive.
How a mountain collapse became a deadly flood
Experts are still piecing together the sequence of events that led to Wednesday’s disaster. Analysis of satellite imagery suggests that bedrock beneath a glacier gave way, sending a huge mass of ice and rock into the Lhende Khola, a tributary of the Bhotekoshi River, and triggering the destructive cascade that followed.
The mechanics differ from those of the glacial lake outburst floods that Dr. Chapagain and his colleagues at the Global Mountain Safeguard Research programme, known as GLOMOS, study across the Hindu Kush Himalaya. GLOMOS is part of UNU’s Institute for Environment and Human Security.
Their recent research analyzed 493 such floods from the earliest available records through 2024. It found that these events have become roughly five times more frequent since 1950, rising from an average of about seven per decade to 34.
Such floods typically occur when meltwater collects in lakes around retreating glaciers, often held back by unstable ice or loose rock and sediment. When those natural dams fail, enormous volumes of water can be released almost instantaneously.
Wednesday’s disaster appears to have followed a different chain of events.
“This time, the intermediate step was skipped,” Dr. Chapagain said.
Rather than a glacial lake bursting, rock and ice collapsed from the mountainside, generating a torrent below. Researchers are investigating whether the debris temporarily dammed the river before the obstruction gave way, a sequence Dr. Chapagain cautioned had not yet been confirmed.
For scientists, the distinction matters. Downstream, the result can look frighteningly similar: a vast volume of water, ice and debris released with little warning into narrow, inhabited valleys.
It is unclear whether climate change caused Wednesday’s collapse. But global warming is rapidly transforming the high-altitude environment in which such disasters occur. As glaciers melt and permafrost thaws, rock once supported or bound by ice can become unstable, while increased meltwater can further weaken mountain slopes.
The consequences extend far beyond mountain villages. The Hindu Kush Himalaya feeds 10 major river basins on which some 2.1 billion people depend for water, food, energy and livelihoods.
As people move into harm’s way
But the mountains are not the only thing changing. So is the geography of human life below them.
When Dr. Chapagain was a child, he said, families in many of Nepal’s hilly areas traditionally built their homes higher on the slopes while cultivating rice and other crops on flatter land closer to rivers. His own family’s home garden was on a mountaintop. Its rice paddies lay below, near the river.
Over time, roads, businesses, hotels and hydropower projects have increasingly concentrated in river valleys, where construction is easier and economic opportunities are greater. Water sources in some higher settlements have also been drying up, Dr. Chapagain said, encouraging people to move downhill.
That has created a dangerous convergence: as warming alters the mountains above, more people and infrastructure are gathering in the corridors through which water and debris descend.
The valley devastated by Wednesday’s flood embodies that collision. The Bhote Koshi-Trishuli corridor carries a major trade route toward Kathmandu and is lined with hydropower plants, bridges, roads, hotels and settlements. The floods damaged power facilities and severed transport and communications links across the region.
The danger was already apparent. A glacial lake outburst struck the same river system last year, killing nine people and leaving 24 missing.
When minutes matter
For Dr. Chapagain, Wednesday’s catastrophe also exposed a critical weakness. How little warning communities may receive before a disaster born high in the mountains reaches them.
Nepalese authorities, he said, learned of the flood only as it was approaching the border. Alerts then went downstream through text messages, social media, telephone calls and alarms.
Reducing the danger, he argues, begins higher up: continuous monitoring of glaciers and unstable slopes, satellite observation, weather and river gauges, and early-warning systems capable of buying communities enough time to evacuate. Because rivers and glaciers cross national frontiers, China, Nepal and countries farther downstream must also exchange data quickly.
There is a deeper problem. Even if greenhouse gas emissions fell sharply, Dr. Chapagain said, glaciers would continue losing mass for decades because of warming already locked into the climate system. How much is eventually lost remains within humanity’s control. What happens in the near term, however, is far less so.
That makes adaptation, in his view, no longer preparation for a distant future.
For communities beneath the Himalayas, that future arrived Wednesday.

‘Immense impact’ of Nepal flood disaster highlighted as casualties mount
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
12:00:00 UTC
21:00:00 KST

‘Immense impact’ of Nepal flood disaster highlighted as casualties mount
The impact of the deadly flood in Nepal has been described as “immense” as the authorities there confirm that 538 bodies have been recovered from the disaster-stricken area.
The catastrophic flooding occurred at the border between Nepal and the Tibet autonomous region of China.
It is thought to have been caused by the collapse of a glacier and the resulting landslide, leading to the destruction of entire communities as well as key infrastructure including bridges and roads.
On Friday, quoting Government of Nepal figures the UN’s aid coordination office OCHA said that 538 people had died, while almost 3,750 had been rescued. Around 1000 people are still missing, many of whom are thought to be tourists.
The Tibet autonomous region of China was also affected and some 560 people remain missing there, according to the authorities.
Lila Pieters Yahia, the UN Resident Coordinator in Nepal who visited the disaster zone said the search and rescue effort was ongoing.
“We witnessed people had just been rescued as we were walking and visiting the site, one of the sites which has been severely damaged,” she said. “We saw a whole truck full of people, an entire family had just been rescued and I can tell you it was very, very emotional.”
Her visit was cut short after a renewed flood alert was issued.
Relief effort
Aid teams have been working around the clock to reach communities cut off by the disaster in the Nepalese districts of Rasuwa, Nuwakot and Dhading.
The UN is supporting the relief effort with emergency food rations, medical kits for about 10,000 people for three months, as well as tents and logistics support. It is also providing satellite imagery and analysis of the area affected by the flood.
Meanwhile, the World Health Organization (WHO) has warned of the risk of disease. “As always, when we have disaster of this scale and we have displacement, overcrowding, and we may have disruption of water, sanitation and health services, and that can increase the risk of infectious diseases,” said spokesperson Tarik Jašarević in Geneva.
UN Children’s Fund (UNICEF) spokesperson Ricardo Pires told reporters that while 18 schools have been completely destroyed and another 20 have been damaged, “dozens more are located close to the riverbanks and remain at high risk,” meaning an estimated 10,000 school-aged children in the area need support to continue their education.
Disaster-affected region
The area was hit by a 7.8 magnitude earthquake in April 2015, which killed more than 8,800 people.
Last October, torrential rains caused fast-moving floods and landslides across eastern and central Nepal, affecting more than 30,000 people.
Kamal Kishore, the Head of the UN Office for Disaster Risk Reduction (UNDRR) highlighted the seriousness of the disaster. “In living memory, we haven't seen a mountain hazard event like this for a very, very long time,” he said, adding that “the impact on lives, livelihoods, buildings, infrastructure, bridges, hydroelectric projects, power generation, it's really immense. And I think we are still coming to grips with the extent of the damage.”
He added that the current situation is marked by “extremely high risk as well as a lot of uncertainty.”
“It's a unique challenge for the emergency response itself, because in a sense, the disaster is not yet completely over,” he stressed.
The floods have “again highlighted how fragile mountain ecosystems are and how challenging it is to set up early warning systems in mountain environments,” focusing on a range of cascading hazards.
The International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies (IFRC) which is working alongside the UN in Nepal said it was “very, very concerned about the secondary flood.”
The IFRC believes that at least 93,000 people have been affected and are “in great need.”

APA Member Interview: Graham Curtiss-Rowlands
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
12:00:00 UTC
21:00:00 KST

Graham Curtiss-Rowlands is a philosophy PhD student at Washington University in St. Louis, who works primarily on social, political, and moral epistemology. His first published philosophy paper, “A Permissivism You Can Rely On,” is forthcoming in Synthese.
What excites you about philosophy?
I’m excited by the notion that philosophy is a sort of conceptual plumbing, as Mary Midgley described it. Philosophy offers the opportunity to question conceptual presuppositions that often go unquestioned. I like the thought of being a sort of philosophical Mario.
What are you working on right now?
My dissertation is on deference. I’m exploring things like the transformative potential of deference, whether deference can actually make us more autonomous, and the rationality of deferring to those with different fundamental commitments from oneself. I’m especially interested in these topics as they relate to deliberation about political and moral questions.
What do you like to do outside work?
I love music, both listening to and playing it (I mainly play guitar). There’s a soft spot in my heart for 70’s British prog rock (King Crimson, Genesis, Yes, etc.) and contemporary bands of a similar vein (Black Country, New Road, and Black Midi), though I like all sorts of music. Recently, I’ve been on a big Beatles kick, but before that I was really into this South African artist, Brenda Fassie.
I also enjoy consuming other sorts of media, especially video games. I’m a firm believer that video games are an exciting new medium for creating art. I think Celeste is an excellent example of this. You play as a woman who’s determined to climb a mountain, but is hounded by self-doubt that eventually becomes personified. The difficulty of the game mirrors this struggle. It is brutally hard, but not punishing; it gives you just enough encouragement to persevere and succeed at things that initially seemed impossible
I also love hiking and going for long walks with my wife.
What is your favorite book of all time? (Or top 3). Why? To whom would you recommend them?
One of my favorite books is Jonathan Strange and Mr. Norrell by Susanna Clarke. It’s an alternative historical fantasy, set during the Napoleonic Wars, in which magic used to be practiced in Britain long ago, but is now mainly studied by stuffy scholars. However, one stuffy scholar, Mr. Norrell, turns out to be a practical magician who can actually do magic. He’s recruited to the British war effort against Napoleon, and takes on an apprentice, Jonathan Strange, who has very different ideas about the future of British magic. It reads a bit like a 19th-century novel in the best sort of way, and is a fun exploration of academic squabbles. It also has a delightfully amoral fae character who is totally unaware of what a jerk he is.
Where is your favorite place you have ever traveled and why?
I really liked Prague. Everything there has many layers of history, like an old church I saw that was used by the communist government in the 1960s-80s to spy on neighboring Western embassies. It houses all sorts of Cold War spy equipment, like purses with hidden cameras. I also enjoy that the communism museum is above a McDonald’s and across from a casino.
What advice do you wish someone had given you?
Don’t waste time worrying about whether you’re smart enough. Also, it’s probably good to not wrap up your self-identity entirely in your work.
What is your least favorite type of fruit and why?
Honeydew. It tastes the way Monty Python’s Australian Bruces described American beer—“like making love in a canoe; f***ing close to water.”
This section of the APA Blog is designed to get to know our fellow philosophers a little better. We’re including profiles of APA members that spotlight what captures their interest, not only inside the office, but also outside of it. We’d love for you to be a part of it, so please contact us via the interview nomination form.
The post APA Member Interview: Graham Curtiss-Rowlands first appeared on Blog of the APA.

Risks of child recruitment by armed groups rise in post-quake Colombia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
12:00:00 UTC
21:00:00 KST

Risks of child recruitment by armed groups rise in post-quake Colombia
The recent earthquake in Colombia could increase the risk of child recruitment by armed groups in Chocó and Valle del Cauca, where thousands of children remain out of school in areas already affected by conflict, the UN warned on Friday.
The quake damaged more than 3,800 educational facilities and has affected the education of more than one million students. Nearly 178,000 attend schools that suffered serious structural damage.
UN Resident Coordinator in Colombia María José Torres Macho said recruitment was already a concern in those areas before the disaster, where illegal armed groups are active.
“We are concerned that the situation of children out of school can exacerbate this problem,” she told reporters at UN Headquarters.
In Chocó, some rural schools were completely destroyed, others partially collapsed and several remain at imminent risk of collapse. Assessments are also continuing in Risaralda and Caldas to determine which schools can reopen safely.
For the UN, restoring access to education is a priority not only to ensure learning can continue, but also to return children to protective environments.
Emergency in conflict-affected areas
The 7.4-magnitude earthquake on 10 August left 331 people dead, 4,449 injured and 219 missing. More than 406,000 people have been affected across 15 departments and 496 municipalities.
Many of the hardest-hit areas were already facing high levels of poverty, isolation and armed violence.
“Those areas most affected are those areas most vulnerable,” she said, adding that the pre-existing conflict is creating challenges for both the emergency response and recovery.
Assessing needs
In Chocó, the UN still does not have complete information on the needs of some rural communities, particularly Afro-Colombian and Indigenous communities. Damage to roads, difficulties travelling along some rivers and electricity and connectivity problems are hampering both assessments and the delivery of aid.
Conflict-related displacement is also continuing alongside the earthquake response. In Sipí, Chocó, around 95 Afro-Colombian people were displaced from the community of Charco Hondo, with concern that displacement could spread to two neighbouring communities.
Ms. Torres Macho also highlighted the role of local authorities and Indigenous and Afro-Colombian organisations, which have been among the first responders in some of the most isolated areas. At the same time, she warned that some municipalities have limited capacity and are overwhelmed by the scale of the emergency.
Since 10 August, the UN system and humanitarian partners have reached around 72,000 people in 36 municipalities across Chocó, Valle del Cauca, Risaralda and Caldas with food, water, medical care, medicines, shelter, psychosocial support, protection and education services.
Watch the full press confererence here:
Response amid funding shortfall
Following the earthquake, the United Nations updated its humanitarian response plan and estimates that 1.2 million people need assistance. Within that group, around 127,000 have been identified as among the most severely affected and in need of priority support, Ms. Torres Macho said.
The response requires $148.1 million, she said, but only 40 per cent of that has been received.
Among the most urgent needs are shelter, medical care, medicines, safe water, education and support to restore livelihoods.
Supply shortages emerge
In some places, available supplies are already beginning to run out. In Caldas, for example, food and hygiene distributions have relied in part on donations, but those stocks are being depleted, and there is not enough capacity to sustain the next rounds of assistance.
Problems also persist in temporary shelters. Among those assessed in Chocó, Risaralda, Valle del Cauca and Caldas, 33 per cent have sanitation and hygiene needs, 31 per cent face problems accessing water and 22 per cent need food.
Ms. Torres Macho said the response will also need to move quickly towards recovery and reconstruction, particularly in communities that were already vulnerable before the earthquake.
“It is very important to also provide support to the municipalities, so there is some urban planning and we don’t reproduce vulnerability and end up creating another disaster.”

WHO reports more than 3,200 attacks on Ukraine’s healthcare system since full-scale invasion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
12:00:00 UTC
21:00:00 KST

WHO reports more than 3,200 attacks on Ukraine’s healthcare system since full-scale invasion
Since the beginning of Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, 3,205 attacks on healthcare facilities have been carried out, World Health Organization (WHO) Representative for Ukraine Jarno Habicht reported on Friday following fresh overnight strikes.
Key points
- Attacks on humanitarian warehouses in Ukraine have destroyed medical supplies meant for hundreds of thousands of people
- Despite the dangers, WHO and UN partners continue delivering aid to hard-to-reach areas while supporting Ukrainian healthcare workers facing severe psychological strain
- Fresh overnight attacks killed at least 12 civilians and damaged more aid warehouses, prompting renewed UN calls for a ceasefire
Such attacks undermine the ability of humanitarian organizations to provide support to people in need.
“In 2026, 20 attacks on warehouses containing humanitarian aid have already been recorded, including 13 warehouses where medical supplies were stored,” Dr, Habicht said.
“WHO faced similar attacks in Kyiv in July and Dnipro in August, resulting in the loss of significant amounts of medicine and equipment intended to help 225,000 people,” he added.
Despite the difficult and dangerous conditions, WHO and its partners continued to deliver humanitarian aid, provide consultations and support the Ukrainian healthcare system.
Delivering in hard-to-reach areas
So far this year, nine WHO humanitarian convoys and 22 UN inter-agency convoys, including two that departed for the Donetsk region on Friday, delivered medicines, equipment and other medical supplies to more than 50 settlements in hard-to-reach areas.
With WHO support, primary health care teams have provided 13,130 consultations in seven regions of Ukraine over the past eight months.
In areas where pharmacies are not operating, 28,400 people received over-the-counter drug kits this year.
“As part of WHO’s comprehensive humanitarian response, we supported the health system by providing equipment and supplies to more than 300 health facilities – including primary health care centres, hospitals, laboratories and transit points – enabling them to help three million people,” Dr. Habicht said.
Medical staff face enormous stress
The WHO representative also said that the war is placing a heavy burden on Ukrainian medical workers.
A recent WHO study found that more than one quarter of doctors and nurses reported symptoms consistent with depressive disorder, and one in five health workers exhibited signs of anxiety disorder.
“Our task is to implement additional measures and support tools for those who help people and save lives,” said Dr. Habicht.
To support the psychological wellbeing of healthcare workers, WHO has incorporated elements of psychological first aid and self-care skills into ambulance crew training programs. More than 40 specialists from 11 regions have completed the training.
The organization also runs a programme for primary healthcare and rehabilitation professionals, with more than 700 healthcare workers taking part.
Participants demonstrated significant improvements in psychological wellbeing and performance as well as a reduction in symptoms of stress, depression, anxiety and post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD).
Preparing for winter
Dr. Habicht warned that Ukraine faces another difficult winter, and WHO is doing everything possible to help Ukrainians prepare for the cold season.
To ensure the smooth operation of medical services, the UN health agency has already installed 30 heating systems in medical facilities.
Another 22 are planned for installation before winter, WHO said.
Part of wider pattern
Authorities say attacks across Ukraine between yesterday and the early hours of this morning have killed at least 12 civilians and injured more than 65 others, with frontline regions were especially hard hit, UN Spokesperson Stéphane Dujarric said on Friday.
Other UN agencies are reporting fresh attacks on its aid storage sites, including the UN Children’s Fund (UNICEF), which said strikes in the Kyiv region hit one its warehouses, destroying humanitarian supplies that will hamper the delivery of vital assistance ahead of winter.
“This is part of a wider pattern, with at least six warehouses belonging to humanitarian operations impacted by attacks in Ukraine in this month,” Mr. Dujarric said.
“We reiterate, once again, the Secretary-General’s condemnations of large-scale missile and drone attacks by the armed forces of the Russian Federation in urban centres in Ukraine,” the UN Spokesperson said, reiterating the UN chief’s call for an urgent de-escalation, leading to a full, immediate and unconditional ceasefire.

Four children killed as separate attacks in Gaza destroy aid supplies
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
12:00:00 UTC
21:00:00 KST

Four children killed as separate attacks in Gaza destroy aid supplies
Israeli attacks killed four children and destroyed humanitarian aid supplies in what turned out to be a deadly week in war-ravaged Gaza, the UN emergency relief agency, OCHA, said on Friday.
Key points
- UN agencies concerned about deadly attacks in civilian areas
- Israeli strikes destroyed over $770,000 in nutrition supplies and damaged critical water infrastructure serving thousands, the UN Children’s Fund (UNICEF) reported
- The World Health Organization (WHO) evacuated 106 patients and 132 companions from Gaza in the past week, but thousands more await medical evacuation
According to UNICEF, the four children – aged two to 16 – were reportedly killed in separate strikes, including one who died of wounds sustained last week.
On Tuesday, five children – aged eight to 17 – were reported hit by live fire or shrapnel following strikes and suffered life-changing injuries.
OCHA raised concerns about the impact of ongoing air strikes and other attacks across the Gaza Strip amid reports of civilian casualties and damage, despite the October 2025 ceasefire that ended the two-year-long Hamas-Israel war.
Aid supplies destroyed
The recent attacks also destroyed humanitarian supplies and damaging critical water infrastructure, the UN Children’s Fund (UNICEF) said on Friday.
A UN partner’s warehouse was heavily damaged by a nearby strike last week. UNICEF says the incident destroyed more than $770,000 worth of its nutrition supplies, which were intended to support more than 45,000 children, pregnant women and breastfeeding mothers.
In addition, a UNICEF-supported water well and desalination facility serving more than 4,000 people in Deir al Balah was severely damaged by a nearby strike on Monday. Partners are now providing water from other sources by truck.
UN convoy
An explosive munition detonated about 30 metres from a UN convoy returning with fuel from the Kerem Shalom crossing as it crossed the so-called “Yellow Line” in Rafah on Thursday, OCHA reported.
Fortunately, there were no casualties, with the explosion causing a minor mechanical issue involving one of the vehicles in the convoy, the agency said.
Civilians and civilian objects, including humanitarian facilities and infrastructure, must always be protected, OCHA said.
Tackling unexploded ordnance
The UN and its partners are working across Gaza to address the risks posed by explosive ordnance.
They are assessing and marking hazards, educating people on safety measures and referring those affected for support, OCHA said.
However, the authorisation needed to bring in equipment and remove explosive ordnance still has not been granted.
Medical evacuations
The UN World Health Organization (WHO) supported the evacuation of 106 patients, including 19 children, along with 132 companions from the Gaza Strip through the Rafah and Kerem Shalom crossings over the last week, the agency chief said on Friday.
WHO chief Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus said that since October 2023, over 13,000 patients and more than 16,000 companions have been evacuated.
Still, thousands are awaiting medical evacuations, he said, adding that to ensure timely treatment for patients, medical evacuations require sustained access through multiple crossing routes.

“Operation Economic Outcast” amounts to state terrorism

20:59:52 KST

The Iranian Foreign Ministry condemned a new wave of US sanctions unveiled on Monday under the title “Operation Economic Outcast,” which came after Washington failed to reach its war objectives against Iran, a report of the foreign ministry's statement by the Press TV said.
The ministry said Washington was abusing the dollar as a tool to intimidate other countries into following its interventionist policies toward Iran. It said such pressure violated the national sovereignty and right to self-determination of all UN member states.
The ministry also said US sanctions against Iran, because of both their nature and consequences, constituted a serious violation of the UN Charter.
It cited the principle of non-intervention in the internal affairs of states and the prohibition of obstructing cooperation between countries. It referred in this regard to UN General Assembly resolutions adopted in 1981 and 1970 on non-intervention, friendly relations and cooperation among states.
The Foreign Ministry further described the declaration of economic war against Iran as a continuation of an aggressive war waged by the United States and Israel against Iran over the past year and a half, using “unfounded pretexts”.
The ministry denounced the indifference and accommodation of the UN system and its member states toward serious violations of international law by the United States and Israel.
“Unfortunately, the indifference and complacency of the United Nations system and its member states toward the flagrant violations of international law by the United States and the Zionist regime have led to the formation of a highly dangerous pattern of lawlessness and the commission of the most severe international crimes by them—the consequences of which have exposed the entirety of human civilization to an unprecedented threat,” added the ministry.
The ministry said “Operation Economic Outcast” itself demonstrated “the criminal intent of those who designed and implemented it to inflict suffering on the Iranian people and deprive Iranian citizens of their fundamental human rights; therefore, it is tantamount to an international crime and a crime against humanity.”
Iran further noted that US sanctions continued to violate the October 3, 2018 order of the International Court of Justice, which required the United States to remove obstacles and restrictions affecting the free flow of trade in food and agricultural products, medicines and medical equipment, and essential civil aviation safety equipment and services, as well as related funds.
“The new US sanctions had created a new situation that requires the international community, including UN bodies, to take necessary measures to safeguard the rule of law and the principles of the UN Charter,” added the statement.
Iran calls on states to reject implementation
The Foreign Ministry said US economic sanctions against Iran were “completely illegal and unjustified,” regardless of the name or title given to them.
“Accordingly, all countries are obliged to refrain from implementing such sanctions,” the ministry said.
It added that all governments were also obliged to avoid recognizing or endorsing situations or effects resulting from the illegal measures.

Armed raid on cattle camp kills at least 49 in South Sudan
Thirty-three people were also wounded as gunmen raided village and seasonal cattle camp in northwest of the country.
An armed raid on a seasonal cattle camp and village in the northwest of South Sudan has killed least 49 people, according to local officials.
The raid, which also wounded 33 people, took place early on Thursday, as gunmen attacked the Machar-Pakuek cattle camp and Mading Juer Boma in Majak Payam, Tonj North County, Warrap State, according to an official statement.
The young African nation is plagued by violent cattle raids, with herders competing for scarce grazing lands and water for their livestock.
“The attack was perpetuated by an armed cross-border, criminal network,” said Warrap spokesperson William Wol Mayom Bol.
“We extend heartfelt condolences to the families that lost loved ones in the attack and appeal for restraint,” he added.
The local government condemned the attack and called on humanitarian organisations to help respond to the “humanitarian catastrophe resulting from conflict-induced displacement”.
The attack comes barely three weeks after another raid in the same area left 60 people dead and 50 wounded.
Last year, President Salva Kiir declared a six-month state of emergency across South Sudan amid a surge of violent inter-communal cattle raids.
Earlier this month, the head of the United Nations Mission in South Sudan (UNMISS), Anita Kiki Gbeho, expressed concerns over the cycle of communal violence in places such as Warrap.

Syrian president names former commander of Kurdish-led force as adviser
Aug 28 - Syrian President Ahmed al-Sharaa appointed the former commander of a now-dissolved Kurdish-led fighting force as a presidential adviser on Friday, reflecting a rapprochement between the two long-time civil war adversaries.
For over a decade, Mazloum Abdi led the Kurdish-led Syrian Democratic Forces, which aligned with the U.S. to fight Islamic State and seize swathes of northern and eastern Syria during the country's war to create a semi-autonomous zone.
After former President Bashar al-Assad's ouster in late 2024 by a rebel coalition led by Sharaa, Syria's new Islamist-led authorities insisted that SDF-run territory and institutions must be integrated into the state.
The integration process stalled for more than a year, until a lightning January offensive by Syrian government forces against Abdi's fighters produced a roadmap to merge the SDF into the Damascus-based authorities.
Abdi announced on Tuesday that the SDF would formally dissolve, hailing the start of a new phase of "peace and participation in the construction of the new Syria".
His appointment as a presidential adviser was announced in a decree issued by Sharaa. It was not clear whether the role would be purely ceremonial.
APPOINTMENT FOLLOWS YEARS OF DISTRUST
Under Abdi, the SDF and its affiliated institutions introduced governing structures that were co-chaired by a man and a woman in a bid to foster equality.
It fought ultraconservative groups, including Islamic State and al Qaeda's local branch, which was once headed by Sharaa, before he broke off ties with the organisation.
Under the integration, SDF fighters are being incorporated into Syria's Defence Ministry, including senior figures who had been critical of the ruling Syrian administration.
During the fighting in January, leading Kurdish commander Sipan Hamo suggested Israel should carry out airstrikes on Syrian troops. After the integration deal was announced a few weeks later, he was appointed deputy defence minister.
The question of how the SDF's female fighters will be integrated into the nation's armed forces, which otherwise have no female troops, has yet to be resolved.
Turkey, a close ally of Sharaa, welcomed the dissolution of the SDF, which it long accused of links to its own outlawed Kurdistan Workers' Party (PKK) militant group. REUTERS

Explainer: What to know about Iceland's vote on reopening EU accession talks
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
19:53:45 CST
20:53:45 KST

REYKJAVIK, Aug. 28 (Xinhua) -- Icelanders will head to the polls on Saturday to decide whether the Nordic island nation should reopen accession negotiations with the European Union (EU), more than a decade after the talks were put on hold.
The referendum comes as Iceland reconsiders its relationship with Europe amid domestic concerns over the economy and growing geopolitical uncertainty in the North Atlantic.
But the outcome remains too close to call.
So what exactly are Icelanders voting on? Why has the EU question returned now? And what would a "Yes" or "No" vote mean?
WHAT EXACTLY IS ICELAND VOTING ON?
The nationwide referendum will be held on Aug. 29. Voters will be asked whether Iceland should reopen accession negotiations with the EU, with a simple choice of "Yes" or "No." Iceland's parliament, the Althingi, approved the referendum in late May by 34 votes to eight, with 14 abstentions.
It will be the first time Icelanders have been asked directly at the ballot box whether their country should pursue accession negotiations with the EU.
A "Yes" vote would not mean Iceland is joining the bloc. Instead, it would give the government a mandate to reopen negotiations and see what terms Iceland could secure.
If the talks eventually produced an accession treaty, the deal would be put to Icelanders in a second referendum. Prime Minister Kristrun Frostadottir has stressed that Iceland would not join the EU unless voters had said "yes" twice.
Iceland is already closely integrated with the EU. It has been part of the European Economic Area (EEA) since 1994 and is also a member of the Schengen Area and the European Free Trade Association. Through the EEA, it participates in the EU's single market and applies a significant share of EU legislation, but has no vote on many of the rules it later implements.
WHY IS THE EU QUESTION BACK NOW?
Iceland applied for EU membership in July 2009 after the global financial crisis devastated its banking system and sharply weakened the Icelandic krona. Formal accession negotiations began in 2010.
The process stalled after the 2013 election brought the EU-skeptic Independence and Progressive parties to power. The government at the time suspended the talks, with some of the most sensitive issues, particularly fisheries and agriculture, still unresolved. In 2015, it informed the EU that Iceland should no longer be considered a candidate country.
The issue returned after another political shift. The coalition formed in December 2024 by the Social Democratic Alliance, the Reform Party and the People's Party pledged to hold a referendum on continuing EU accession negotiations no later than 2027, and parliament later set the vote for Aug. 29.
Economic concerns remain a major factor behind the renewed push. The 2024 coalition agreement paired the referendum pledge with a review of Iceland's currency options, while the inflation, high interest rates and the vulnerabilities of a small, open economy have long featured prominently in the country's European debate.
Finnish Arctic geopolitics scholar Lassi Heininen told Xinhua that the referendum is "mainly driven by Iceland's domestic politics," including financial and political considerations, much as economic difficulties had helped drive the country's first membership bid.
But the external environment has also changed significantly. Tobias Etzold, a senior adviser at the Brussels-based European Policy Centre, said growing great-power competition in the strategically important North Atlantic has increased uncertainty for smaller states and given fresh momentum to Iceland's EU debate.
Etzold pointed to "growing doubts over an unreliable U.S.," Washington's stated interest in "buying" or "taking" Greenland, and concerns over a weakened NATO.
For Iceland, a NATO member with no standing army, uncertainty over U.S. President Donald Trump's commitment to the country's security has strengthened the case for looking more closely to Europe, Etzold said.
Icelandic Foreign Minister Thorgerdur Katrin Gunnarsdottir has also pointed to a more protectionist international environment, sudden U.S. tariffs and the growing use of trade as a foreign policy tool.
CAN THE REFERENDUM PASS? AND WHAT HAPPENS NEXT?
The vote remains too close to call. A Gallup poll released on Thursday put "No" at 51.6 percent and "Yes" at 48.4 percent among decided voters, with the difference not statistically significant. A survey released on Tuesday by the Maskina polling agency showed the opposite, giving "Yes" 51.3 percent and "No" 48.7 percent.
Fisheries and agriculture remain among the most sensitive issues in the referendum debate. Marine products accounted for 38.9 percent of Iceland's goods exports in 2025, while concerns center on control over natural resources, food security and how EU common policies could affect Iceland's fisheries and highly protected farm sector.
Brussels has nevertheless signaled some room for negotiation. EU Commissioner for Fisheries and Oceans Costas Kadis said in April there was "definitely room for flexibility" on fisheries, while Kos has suggested that "creative solutions" could be explored for Icelandic agriculture and fisheries.
If "Yes" wins, the government has said it will notify the EU, establish a negotiating team and seek to reopen the talks.
Icelandic authorities estimate negotiations could take around one and a half to two years, while EU Commissioner for Enlargement Marta Kos said they could potentially be completed within one to two years because Iceland already applies much of the EU rulebook through the EEA.
The process, however, would not simply resume where it stopped in 2013. An Icelandic parliamentary committee said in May that negotiating positions across all chapters would need to be reviewed after more than a decade of changes, including those previously provisionally closed.
The result could also have implications beyond Iceland. Steven Blockmans, deputy director of the International Centre for Defence and Security, said a positive result could sustain momentum behind EU enlargement and strengthen the bloc's geopolitical credibility, while a rejection could reinforce skepticism toward enlargement.
Heininen told Xinhua that a "Yes" vote could have "direct influences" on domestic politics in Norway and possibly Greenland. If the process eventually led to Iceland joining the EU, he said, Nordic politics and some regional security affairs would become more "Europeanized," while the EU would gain greater weight in Arctic affairs and cooperation.
If "No" wins, the current Icelandic government has said accession negotiations will not resume, while Iceland's relationship with the EU would continue largely through the EEA and Schengen frameworks. ■

China moves to improve commercial housing sales system
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
19:53:27 CST
20:53:27 KST

BEIJING, Aug. 28 (Xinhua) -- China will steadily advance reforms to its commercial housing sales system and accelerate efforts to foster a new development model for the real estate sector, according to a recent circular jointly issued by three government departments.
The circular calls on local authorities to regulate presale conditions for commercial housing and strengthen supervision of presale funds to ensure the safety of such funds, effectively guard against housing delivery risks, and protect the legitimate rights and interests of homebuyers.
For commercial housing projects offered for presale, the main structure of each building should be topped out, according to the circular.
For commercial housing projects that had obtained construction project planning permits before the circular took effect and are offered for presale, existing policies and regulations will continue to apply to presale conditions and the supervision of presale funds.
The circular also calls on local authorities to advance the sale of completed new homes in an effective and orderly manner, so as to realize the goal of "what you see is what you get" and reduce disputes over housing delivery.
Meanwhile, local authorities should improve supporting policies concerning land supply and financial support for commercial housing projects, optimize the management of project development and construction, sales and real estate registration, and promote the issuance of real property ownership certificates upon housing delivery, the circular notes.
The circular was released by the Ministry of Housing and Urban-Rural Development, the Ministry of Natural Resources and the National Financial Regulatory Administration. ■

BEIJING, Aug. 28 (Xinhua) -- China's healthcare system recorded 10.65 billion patient visits in 2025, up 510 million from the previous year, reflecting improved access to medical services across the country.
By the end of 2025, China had more than 1.1 million healthcare institutions and a medical workforce of 16.12 million, both exceeding the previous year's figures, according to a report released by the National Health Commission on Friday.
As China's healthcare system, already the world's largest, continues to expand, access to primary healthcare is improving. The government is promoting a tiered healthcare system, and the number and share of visits to primary healthcare facilities continued to rise in 2025. More than 90 percent of residents can now reach a nearby healthcare facility within 15 minutes.
Healthcare costs fell in real terms in 2025, the report shows. The average cost of a hospital stay declined by 1 percent to 9,768.9 yuan (about 1,454 U.S. dollars), while the average cost of an outpatient visit dropped by 0.9 percent to 357.7 yuan. Healthcare spending stood at 6.7 percent of GDP last year.
These improvements have contributed to better health outcomes nationwide. In 2025, average life expectancy in China rose to 79.25 years. The maternal mortality rate fell to 13.4 deaths per 100,000 live births, and the infant mortality rate dropped to 3.8 deaths per 1,000 live births. ■

The level of trust in Chairman of the Russian Communist Party (CPRF) Gennady Zyuganov stands at 32.3%, leader of A Just Russia party Sergey Mironov - 28%, head of the Liberal Democratic Party of Russia (LDPR) Leonid Slutsky - 22.4%, leader of the New People party Alexey Nechayev - 12.1%.
The level of support for the United Russia party was 39.2%, the CPRF - 11.7%, the LDPR - 9.7%, A Just Russia party - 4.1%, the New People party - 10.8%.

Can international stocks continue to beat S&P 500? A weak U.S. dollar will help
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
11:51:45 UTC
20:51:45 KST

For years, U.S.-based investors ignored international markets and the argument for geographic diversification in stocks, and they paid no penalty for their provincial approach. Booming large-cap U.S. stocks trounced their overseas counterparts. But many investors woke up to the opportunity in foreign stocks in 2024 and 2025 as concerns about the valuation of the U.S. market relative to the world and its concentration in a narrow technology theme intensified. The trade was timed well, and it is still working, with large-cap international stocks continuing to beat the S&P 500 in 2026. Can the overseas bull market continue?
David Botset, head of strategy, innovation and stewardship at Schwab Asset Management, says there are no signs yet that investors are rushing to take gains from international winners, with the 2025 trend continuing in 2026. "We are seeing far more flows into international index across the industry," he said on this week's "ETF Edge."
"$90 billion in foreign large-cap blend," he said.
And it is not just performance chasing, according to Botset. "It starts with the returns," he said, but he added that investors are starting to think more about the benefits of diversification from multiple angles, whether it is business cycle or sector diversification offered by geography, especially as the concerns around the narrowness of U.S. stock leadership remain in focus.
And then there is the U.S. dollar, which can juice the returns of international holdings for U.S.-based investors.
Josh Jones, portfolio manager at Boston Partners, said on "ETF Edge" that since the pandemic, the setup for international stocks has been "incredibly attractive" for fundamental value investors like his firm, with much lower valuations in large-caps overseas than in the U.S. Healthy earnings growth and healthy return on capital profiles support the P/E analysis. But the weakness in the U.S. dollar is a trend that overlapped with the move by investors into foreign stocks throughout 2025, and it is a factor that should not be overlooked by investors, Jones said.
"When I look back at history, the best periods for international — for U.S. investors — have been when it is generating good returns in local markets and you are getting a weak dollar environment translated back for U.S. investors, and that's what kicked things off in 2025," he said. "We've done really well for the last 18 months," he added.
Jones cautioned that neither he nor his firm are in the business of forecasting currencies, but he said when you look at recent headlines, including U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent's desire to lower interest rates by aggressively buying back bonds, "it is reasonable to assume we could see some dollar weakness, and that could continue to kind of help support returns in international equities from a dollar-[based] investor standpoint."
To date, the bond market has expressed skepticism that Bessent's plan will work as intended, and the idea has attracted many high-profile doubters, including hedge fund manager Stanley Druckenmiller, who wrote in a recent Wall Street Journal op-ed that "the only thing that durably lowers long-term yields: address the primary deficit."
As a portfolio manager, Jones said he always starts by looking at fundamental value metrics, and company-specific business momentum and earnings growth. Even if returns are not aided by a weak dollar, investors need to be able to have confidence the stocks will generate alpha over time. The John Hancock Disciplined Value International Select ETF (JDVI), which Boston Partners serves as subadvisor on for the insurer, is a concentrated portfolio that has a high active share compared to the core international index, holding between 30-50 stocks and which at any time could be "zero Japan or all Europe," Jones said. But the investment goal is to identify companies that it thinks can outperform on a three- to five-year basis.
But in those periods of time when the dollar is weak, currency is an added benefit, he said, with one important caveat. Investors need to make sure that the foreign stocks they are holding are not overly reliant on U.S.-based revenue, which can dilute the currency benefit.
Currently, Jones said the sectors of the overseas large-cap market that investors may benefit from the most are materials, industrials, and metals and mining. In past periods when there is a weak dollar, such as the 1970s and 2000s, international did very well and these periods were associated with real assets and commodities super-cycles, Jones said. Today, central banks around the world continue to add gold to reserves and the electrification trend globally should continue to be a driver for metals such as copper, he added.
It is true, Jones said, that metals and mining companies have historically been difficult businesses to trust over the long-term for investors — capital intensive companies that have tended to have too much leverage while making questionable capital allocation decisions. But metals and mining companies have bucked that reputation in the past few years, Jones said, and that is a trend "could potentially stick around for a few years."
"For U.S. investors, it fits the profile of historical cycles," he said, and with "companies with exposure to sectors you don't see as much of in the S&P 500," he added.
The overseas stock story does remain very much a large-cap one, with Schwab seeing much more interest, according to Botset, in its large-cap Schwab International Equity ETF (SCHF), which is approaching $70 billion in assets and has added $12 billion since early 2024. SCHF is up close to 17% this year, versus 13% for the S&P 500. Its developed markets Schwab International Small Cap Equity ETF (SCHC), has not generated similarly strong interest because the stronger fundamentals overseas are "largely playing out in the large-cap space," he said.
International dividend stocks, such as those held by the Schwab International Dividend Equity ETF (SCHY) are finding some favor with investors due to all of the uncertainly in the markets, from inflation to geopolitics and commodities supply shocks, concerns that interest more investors in the sustainability of strong dividend payers, Botset said, but it is still a small fund compared to SCHF, approaching $2.6 billion in assets.
The recent performance by international stocks has narrowed the valuation gap with the U.S. market, but it has not closed it. In the decade from 2010-2020, so many investors ignored value-based companies — from banks to the materials and industrials plays — that their cost of capital went up and their P/Es were depressed even more as a result, Jones said. That shunning of international stocks took P/Es down to as low as 10 times forward earnings, and even if JDVI is now trading at a P/E of 12 — up from a range of 9 to 10 at the start of 2025 — the S&P 500 remains at a valuation of 16 to 17 times earnings, and that is when you remove the Mag 7 component from the valuation analysis. "So there is still a valuation argument there," Jones said.
Botset said the first step for many investors is to check their current allocations and see if either intentionally or unintentionally they have "over-pivoted" to the U.S. market. If investors intended to have a 10% to 20% allocation to international as part of their strategic long-term planning, that could have eroded to as little as 2% to 5% given the extent of the bull market in the S&P 500 in recent years. Investors in this situation would benefit by coming back to strategic long-term weights, he said.
To hear more from these managers on how they are positioned in the current market, watch this week's full "ETF Edge" show above or listen to the podcast.

Eight communities in Lviv and Ivano-Frankivsk regions join forces to support the development of the Carpathian region
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
14:48:34 EEST
20:48:34 KST

The new partnership is intended to provide a framework for closer coordination between communities connected by shared infrastructure, tourism routes and the wider Carpathian economy.
On 25 August in Slavske, the heads of eight communities from the Lviv and Ivano-Frankivsk regions signed a Memorandum of Cooperation to support the joint development of the wider Carpathian region. The partnership brings together the communities of Drohobych, Truskavets, Slavske, Skhidnytsia, Skole, Boryslav, Vyhoda and Bolekhiv.
The eight communities are closely connected geographically and economically. They share the Carpathian landscape, river systems, tourism routes and a hospitality-based economy. At the same time, they face many of the same challenges, including transport infrastructure, waste management, workforce shortages, tourism seasonality, climate change and the need for reliable data to support effective decision-making.
Each community also brings its own distinct strengths to the partnership, creating the potential for a broader and more diverse regional offer. Slavske is becoming a major focus for new investment with the development of GORO Mountain Resort. Skole combines the natural attractions of Skole Beskids National Nature Park with Tustan, one of the region’s most important historical and cultural destinations, while Skhidnytsia and Truskavets are well-established centres for wellness and resort tourism.
Boryslav has a unique industrial and oil heritage with significant potential for tourism and cultural development. Drohobych can strengthen the region’s role as a centre for education, culture and services, while integrating one of Europe’s oldest continuously operating saltworks into wider regional tourism routes. Vyhoda is home to the Carpathian Tram and its historic narrow-gauge railway, while the Bolekhiv community offers major natural attractions, including the Dovbush Rocks.
By connecting these different strengths, the communities aim to move beyond a collection of individual destinations and develop a more integrated regional experience — one that encourages visitors to travel between communities, stay in the Carpathians for longer, support local businesses and experience a wider range of nature, culture, history, wellness and outdoor activities within a single trip.
The Small Carpathian Circle, a state-funded infrastructure project connecting tourism centres across the Ukrainian Carpathians, runs through the region. However, the communities involved in the partnership believe that transport links alone are not enough to drive long-term regional development. A shared vision is also needed for how the wider area around this infrastructure should grow.
“For us, it is particularly important that Slavske was the place where this step towards broader cooperation was taken. We can already see in practice that the development of one community cannot be separated from the development of the wider region. Major investments, including the construction of GORO Mountain Resort, create opportunities that extend far beyond Slavske itself. Visitors will travel on shared roads, move between neighbouring communities, discover new routes and use local businesses and services. That is why it is important to agree now on how we develop the region in a coordinated way, so that these opportunities deliver long-term benefits for every community,” said Oleh Danyliak, Acting Head of the Slavske community.
The Memorandum focuses on areas where coordinated action can deliver greater impact than individual initiatives by each community. At the same time, every participating community will retain its own development strategy, identity and priorities.
The next step will be to establish a working group, agree on shared priorities and launch the first joint projects. Key areas of cooperation will include tourism and regional promotion, infrastructure, education and workforce development, environmental issues, data, investment attraction and access to grant funding. The partnership will develop in cooperation with the NGO Agency for Territorial Initiatives, with expert involvement from Mariana Oleskiv and Ihor Chava. The initiative remains open to expansion, and other communities that see themselves as part of the wider Carpathian region will be able to join in the future.

US-Israel war on Iran, six months down the line: In numbers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
11:45:39 UTC
20:45:39 KST

US-Israel war on Iran, six months down the line: In numbers
Al Jazeera tracks six months of the Iran war, from the dead and displaced to the shock delivered to the global economy.
Six months ago today, the United States and Israel launched their first strikes of on Iran, assassinating Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei in Tehran and hitting nuclear and military sites around the country.
Those attacks prompted Iran to begin strikes on US military assets and infrastructure in Gulf countries – and for the Lebanese armed group, Hezbollah, to fire rockets into northern Israel, prompting near-daily Israeli responses since then and, at one point, control over one-fifth of Lebanon.
Neither side has gained the upper hand since. Iran has used its control of the Strait of Hormuz to squeeze Washington and global energy markets, and the conflict has settled into a stalemate, which months of negotiation have not broken.
Al Jazeera tracks the first six months of the war, from the numbers killed and displaced to the shock suffered by the global economy.
Here are some of the key numbers:
At least 7,900 people killed
According to the latest official figures, at least 4,350 people are confirmed killed in Lebanon, 3,527 in Iran and 28 in Gulf states since the war began on February 28.
A further 60 Israelis and 18 US service members have been killed in Iranian attacks. The Pentagon says 757 US personnel have been wounded.
Figures are compiled from national health ministries and official bodies, and may change as the situation evolves and more information becomes available.
More than 5,500 attacks
According to the Armed Conflict Location and Event Data project (ACLED), a US-based conflict monitoring group, the US and Israel have carried out at least 3,580 attacks on Iran since February 28. Over the same period, Iran carried out at least 2,053 attacks across the Gulf and the wider Middle East.
Hormuz: From 100 ships daily to seven
Before the war, at least 100 ships passed through the Strait of Hormuz each day, more than half of them tankers, carrying tens of millions of barrels of oil, as well as liquefied petroleum gas (LPG) and other petrochemicals.
That collapsed within days of the war beginning. After the IRGC announced the strait’s closure on March 2, traffic fell to an average of five vessels a day and stayed there through the April ceasefire and the US blockade of Iranian ports.
The June 17 interim agreement increased the daily average to 20, but still only one-fifth of normal traffic, before the US resumed its blockade on July 14 and traffic sank back to five per day.
In the six months since fighting began, an average of seven vessels a day have passed through the strait.
70 confirmed attacks on ships
Attacks on dozens of vessels have also been responsible for the decrease in shipping.
According to the International Maritime Organization (IMO), there have been 70 confirmed incidents involving ships in the Strait of Hormuz, resulting in 19 seafarer fatalities as of August 26.
War has cost the US $37.5bn … and counting
Last month, US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth told a Senate hearing that the war had cost $37.5bn so far, up from about $25bn in late April and roughly $30bn in July. He said the total included payroll, operations, maintenance and anticipated costs through to the end of the budget year on September 30.
The true figure is likely higher. US media have reported the Pentagon’s internal estimate at $80bn to $100bn, including repairs to damaged US bases, replacing destroyed aircraft and replenishing weapons stocks.
The administration has not published an itemised breakdown.
Oil price is 22 percent higher than pre-war
Since the start of the war, Brent crude has risen roughly 22 percent, from $72.48 a barrel to $88.58 on August 28. It peaked at $120.88 on April 30, 67 percent higher than its pre-war level, after six months of volatile trading.
US oil reserve at lowest level since 1982
The US Strategic Petroleum Reserve, the government’s emergency stockpile of crude oil, has fallen to 290 million barrels, about 41 percent of its 714-million-barrel capacity and its lowest level since November 1982.
Other countries have released stocks too. The US pledge was the largest national share of a coordinated release of 400 million barrels agreed on March 11 by the 32 member countries of the International Energy Agency – the largest emergency stock release in its history.
Israel still occupies parts of Lebanon
Despite a ceasefire agreement between Lebanon and Israel that took effect on April 17 and was renewed on June 26, Israeli forces continue to occupy parts of Lebanon and carry out attacks.
Before the ceasefire, Israeli forces occupied nearly one-fifth of Lebanon – about 2,000sq km (770sq miles). A buffer zone covering roughly six percent of the country remains in place.
Fighting resumed on March 2, after Iran-backed Hezbollah fired at Israel in support of Tehran, three days into the US-Israeli war on Iran. Israel responded with a major offensive in Lebanon, killing at least 4,350 people over the months since and leaving 12,510 injured, according to Lebanon’s Ministry of Public Health.
Trump approval falls to 33 percent
Trump’s approval rating has fallen to the lowest of his presidency.
A Reuters/Ipsos poll, which closed on August 24, found that 33 percent of Americans approved of his performance in the White House and 65 percent disapproved, matching the December 2017 low of his first term.
The poll found that 80 percent of Americans, including 87 percent of Democrats and 71 percent of Republicans, think US involvement in Iran “will go on for an extended period of time”. Just 16 percent expect it to end within weeks.

Baltic Sea countries plan joint drone defence task force amid growing hybrid threat
Countries bordering the Baltic Sea are planning to set up a joint drone defence task force that will allow them to respond quickly to the growing threat of hybrid attacks.
Source: German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt, as cited by Reuters and European Pravda
Details: The aim is to establish a working group that will enable the rapid exchange of information, Dobrindt said ahead of a meeting with his counterparts from the Baltic region in the city of Flensburg.
"Foreign states are trying every day to attack and undermine democracy, security and economic strength within the EU," he said.
The interior minister warned that such attacks could "take on a new dimension in the coming months" and that the hybrid threat is "omnipresent".
Since Moscow launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, the Baltic Sea, which borders eight NATO countries (Germany, Sweden, Finland, Estonia, Latvia, Lithuania, Poland and Denmark) as well as Russia, has seen numerous suspected acts of sabotage involving underwater cables and critical gas pipelines.
Germany has been particularly vigilant about drone-related threats after a drone carrying explosives was discovered earlier this month near a Ukrainian Antonov cargo aircraft used to transport military equipment at Leipzig/Halle airport, a key military logistics hub.
Background:
- German investigators also suspect that a second drone may have collided with a DHL cargo aircraft that night, shortly after the airport was temporarily closed.
- On 25 August, it emerged that law enforcement officers had found another drone carrying explosives, which was reportedly involved in the incident at Leipzig/Halle airport.
- German authorities suspect possible Russian involvement in the incident, although the origin of the drones has not yet been established.

Russian CEO to lead $1 billion Indian neurotech fund
A new fund launched in India plans to invest $1 billion in the country’s neurotechnology sector over the next five years.
ADI Neuroscience is backed by SPEC Finance India, with Aleksandr Panov, a serial investor and CEO of Russian neurotechnology firm Neiry, serving as the fund’s lead adviser.
The sector includes technologies and devices that enable communication with the human brain. Billionaire investor Elon Musk’s Neuralink is the most famous BCI company.
India ranks third in the BCI sector, with 12 startups – behind China’s 23, and 101 in the US – according to market intelligence company Tracxn. However, Indian BCI startups have pulled in only about $8.5 million in the last ten years, compared to $3.03 billion by US startups and $117 million by Chinese firms.
The global BCI market is expected to grow to $15.14 billion by 2035, from $2.87 billion in 2024, according to a report by Spherical Insights & Consulting.
Launched last week, ADI sees India as a platform where research teams, engineering expertise, and capital can come together to make the country a hub for the development of neurotechnologies.
”India has the rare opportunity to participate in shaping the standards and regulatory frameworks for the sector rather than adapting to frameworks developed elsewhere,” ADI Neuroscience said in a statement.
”The fund’s resources will be directed toward advancing neurotechnology R&D in India, creating competitive products, and developing the industry domestically,” SPEC Finance Group CEO Karan Dinesh Singh Rawat added.
The fund has deep links to Russian technology leadership. Panov, an ambassador for deep-tech entrepreneurship, is its scientific adviser, while Mikhail Lebedev, a professor at the Moscow State University who specializes in brain-to-brain interfaces, is a member of its scientific board.

With Kuwait deal, Pakistan expands defence umbrella across Middle East
